indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.1.1: Demonstrate understanding of variety of songs
indicator.objective: Identify and discuss values in songs

skills.description: Identify the value(s) taught in a song (e.g. honesty, patriotism, respect, diligence)
Explain what a given value means in the context of the song
Discuss how the value in a song applies to real life
Identify the central message of a song and distinguish it from the value

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: The value and the message are the same thing
If a song mentions a good thing, that is its value

questions.stem: The song 'God Bless Our Homeland Ghana' teaches us to love our country. What value does this song teach?
hints: The song is about love for Ghana.
Patriotism means love for one's country.
questions.explanation: The song teaches patriotism — love and devotion to one's country, Ghana.
misconceptions: Honesty is about telling the truth.
Kindness is about being good to others.

questions.stem: A song says, 'Work hard every day, do not be lazy.' What value does this song teach?
hints: The song tells us to work hard.
Diligence means hard work.
questions.explanation: The song teaches diligence — the value of working hard and not being lazy.
misconceptions: Dishonesty is about not telling the truth.
Laziness is the opposite of what the song teaches.

questions.stem: A song says, 'Tell the truth, my child, even when it is hard.' What does this song teach about honesty?
options: You should only be honest when it is easy
Honesty is important even when it is difficult
hints: The song says 'even when it is hard'.
Honesty should not depend on how easy it is.
questions.explanation: The song teaches that honesty is important even when it is difficult to tell the truth.
misconceptions: The song is for everyone, not just adults.
The song says honesty is important.
The song says to be honest even when it is hard, not only when it is easy.

questions.stem: Your friend finds a purse with money and returns it to the owner. Which value from a song about honesty is your friend showing?
hints: Returning something that is not yours is honest.
Honesty means doing the right thing.
questions.explanation: Your friend is showing honesty by returning the purse to its owner instead of keeping it.
misconceptions: Dishonesty would be keeping the purse.
Greed is wanting more than you need.
Laziness is not wanting to work.

questions.stem: What is the main message of a song that says, 'Love your neighbour as yourself'?
options: You should love and care for others
You should fight with your neighbours
hints: The song says to love your neighbour.
It also says 'as yourself'.
questions.explanation: The main message is that you should love and care for others just as you love and care for yourself.
misconceptions: The song says to love your neighbour, not just yourself.
The song says to love, not ignore.
The song says to love, not fight.

questions.stem: A song says, 'Respect your elders, for they have wisdom.' Why does the song teach respect for elders?
options: Because elders are older than you
Because elders have wisdom and experience
hints: The song mentions 'wisdom'.
Elders have lived longer and learned more.
questions.explanation: The song teaches respect for elders because they have wisdom and experience that young people can learn from.
misconceptions: Age alone is not the reason given in the song.
The song does not mention riches.
The song does not say elders are strict.

questions.stem: The song 'Arise Ghana Youth' calls on young people to serve their nation. How can a Basic 4 pupil show patriotism?
options: By refusing to go to school
By keeping the classroom clean and helping others
By throwing rubbish on the street
hints: Patriotism means caring for your country.
Small good deeds at school show love for the nation.
questions.explanation: A Basic 4 pupil can show patriotism by keeping the classroom clean, helping others and being a good citizen.
misconceptions: Throwing rubbish is bad for the nation.

questions.stem: A song says, 'A lazy farmer has an empty barn.' What is the message of this song?
hints: A lazy farmer has nothing in the barn.
What happens when you work hard?
questions.explanation: The message is that hard work brings good results, while laziness leads to nothing.
misconceptions: The song is about farming as an example, not saying farming is unimportant.
An empty barn is the result of laziness, not the goal.
The song warns against laziness, not encourages it.

questions.stem: What does 'kindness' mean in a song about helping others?
options: Being generous and caring to people
hints: Kindness is about being good to others.
It means caring and generous.
questions.explanation: Kindness means being generous and caring towards other people.
misconceptions: Being mean is the opposite of kindness.

questions.stem: A song says, 'Clean your environment, keep Ghana beautiful.' How can pupils practice this value at school?
options: By sweeping the classroom and keeping the compound clean
hints: The song is about keeping the environment clean.
What can you do at school to keep it clean?
questions.explanation: Pupils can practice this value by sweeping the classroom and keeping the school compound clean.
misconceptions: Writing on walls makes the school untidy.

questions.stem: What is the message of a song that says, 'We are one people, one nation, one Ghana'?
hints: The song says 'one people, one nation'.
Unity means togetherness.
questions.explanation: The message is that Ghanaians should be united as one people and one nation.
misconceptions: Fighting is the opposite of unity.
Living alone is not the message.
Ignoring others is not the message.

questions.stem: A song says, 'The tall tree does not block the sun from the small tree.' What value does this song teach?
hints: The tall tree allows the small tree to get sun.
This shows fairness.
questions.explanation: The song teaches fairness and equality — the tall tree does not use its height to deny the small tree sunlight.
misconceptions: Jealousy is wanting what others have.
Anger is not the value being taught.

questions.stem: A song says, 'Share your bread with a friend in need.' What does this teach about sharing?
options: You should share what you have with others
hints: The song says to share.
Sharing means giving to others.
questions.explanation: The song teaches that you should share what you have with others, especially those in need.
misconceptions: Eating alone is the opposite of sharing.
Fighting over food is not sharing.

questions.stem: A song says, 'A patient person achieves more than a strong person.' Which of these real-life situations shows this value?
options: Ama waited patiently for her turn and won the game
Kojo rushed his homework and made many mistakes
Esi gave up when the work was difficult
Yaw broke his pencil in anger
hints: The song values patience.
Which person waited calmly?
questions.explanation: Ama showed patience by waiting for her turn, and she was rewarded by winning the game.
misconceptions: Kojo rushed and made mistakes — the opposite of patience.
Esi gave up — the opposite of patience.
Yaw broke his pencil in anger — the opposite of patience.

questions.stem: A song says, 'Never tell a lie, never cheat.' What value is this?
hints: The song says 'never tell a lie'.
This is about being truthful.
questions.explanation: The song teaches honesty — never telling lies and never cheating.
misconceptions: Dishonesty is the opposite of what the song teaches.
Laziness is not about telling lies.

questions.stem: Your class wants to sing a song for a school event. Which value would you want the song to teach?
hints: Think about positive values.
Which option has good values?
questions.explanation: A song for a school event should teach positive values like hard work and honesty.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.3.1: Appreciate poems and other pieces of literary materials
indicator.objective: Recite poems with stress, rhythm and actions and interpret them in own their words

skills.description: Identify stressed words and the rhythm pattern in a poem line
Explain the meaning of a poem or a line in the learner's own words
Match appropriate actions to poem lines
Recite a poem with appropriate stress, rhythm and actions

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Every word in a poem gets equal stress
Poems must rhyme to be good

questions.stem: What does 'stress' mean when we recite a poem?
options: Putting more emphasis on certain words
hints: Stress is about emphasis.
Some words are said with more force.
questions.explanation: Stress in poetry means putting more emphasis or force on certain words to give them importance.
misconceptions: Reading fast is about speed, not stress.
Reading quietly is about volume, not stress.
Reading without stopping is about fluency, not stress.

questions.stem: What does the line 'The sun is bright' mean?
options: The sun gives a lot of light
hints: Bright means giving a lot of light.
The sun shines.
questions.explanation: The line means that the sun gives a lot of light and shines brightly.
misconceptions: Dark is the opposite of bright.
Cold is about temperature, not light.
Small is about size, not brightness.

questions.stem: What action would you do for the line 'The bird sings in the tree'?
options: Open your mouth like singing and flap your arms like wings
hints: The line is about a bird.
Birds sing and have wings.
questions.explanation: For 'The bird sings in the tree', you can open your mouth like singing and flap your arms like wings.

questions.stem: What is rhythm in a poem?
options: The pattern of beats when we read
hints: Rhythm is about beats.
We clap or tap to the beat.
questions.explanation: Rhythm is the pattern of beats or sounds when we read a poem.
misconceptions: Paper colour has nothing to do with rhythm.
The poet's name is not rhythm.

questions.stem: A poem says, 'The wind is cold today.' What does this mean?
hints: Cold means chilly.
The wind is not warm or hot.
questions.explanation: The line means the wind feels chilly or cold today.
misconceptions: Hot is the opposite of cold.
Warm is the opposite of cold.
Strong is about force, not temperature.

questions.stem: Which action best matches the line 'The fish swims in the river'?
options: Move your hands like a swimming fish
Stomp your feet like an elephant
hints: Fish swim.
Move your hands like a fish swimming.
questions.explanation: For 'The fish swims in the river', you can move your hands together like a fish swimming through water.

questions.stem: In the line 'I love my school', which word is usually stressed?
hints: The most important word in the line is the place you love.
School is the key word.
questions.explanation: In 'I love my school', the word 'school' is usually stressed because it is the most important word in the line.
misconceptions: 'I' is not the most important word.
'love' is important but 'school' is the focus.

questions.stem: A poem says, 'The moon is a silver ball.' What does this mean?
options: The moon is made of silver
The moon is round and shines like silver
The moon is a ball you can play with
hints: Silver describes the colour and shine.
A ball is round.
questions.explanation: The line means the moon is round like a ball and shines with a silvery light.
misconceptions: The moon is not actually made of silver.
The moon is not a toy ball.
The line does not say the moon is small.

questions.stem: Which action best matches 'The wind blows the leaves'?
options: Wave your hands like blowing wind
hints: The wind moves.
Wave your hands like the wind.
questions.explanation: For 'The wind blows the leaves', you can wave your hands gently like the wind blowing.
misconceptions: Sitting still does not show wind.

questions.stem: A poem says, 'The stars twinkle like diamonds.' What does this mean?
options: The stars are made of diamond
The stars shine brightly and sparkle
hints: Twinkle means to shine with a sparkle.
Diamonds sparkle.
questions.explanation: The line means the stars shine and sparkle like diamonds in the sky.
misconceptions: Stars are not made of diamond.
The line does not say stars are cold.

questions.stem: In the line 'Happy children play outside', which word is usually stressed to show how the children feel?
hints: The word that describes how the children feel is stressed.
Happy describes their feeling.
questions.explanation: The word 'Happy' is stressed because it shows how the children feel.
misconceptions: 'children' is the subject but not the feeling word.
'play' is the action but not the feeling.
'outside' is the place but not the feeling.

questions.stem: Which set of actions best matches these three lines: 'The rain falls down. The wind blows soft. The sun shines bright.'?
options: Wave hands for rain, clap for wind, jump for sun
Wiggle fingers downward for rain, wave hands for wind, open arms wide for sun
Stomp for rain, sit for wind, sleep for sun
Run for rain, jump for wind, clap for sun
hints: Rain falls downward.
Wind moves gently.
The sun shines broadly.
questions.explanation: Wiggle fingers downward shows rain falling, waving hands shows wind, and opening arms wide shows the sun shining.
misconceptions: Clapping for wind and jumping for sun do not match the images.
Stomping and sitting do not match rain and wind.
Running and jumping do not match the images well.

questions.stem: A poem says: 'The little seed sleeps in the ground. / It wakes when the rain comes down. / It stretches up to touch the sun. / A new plant has begun.' What is this poem about?
options: A seed growing into a plant
A bird flying in the sky
A fish swimming in the sea
hints: The seed sleeps, wakes, stretches and becomes a plant.
The poem is about growth.
questions.explanation: The poem is about a seed that grows into a new plant when it receives rain and sunlight.
misconceptions: The poem mentions a seed, not a bird.
There is no fish in the poem.
There is no child in the poem.

questions.stem: Two pupils explain the line 'The wind whispers secrets to the trees.' Pupil A says: 'The wind is soft and quiet like a whisper.' Pupil B says: 'The wind is shouting at the trees.' Which pupil gives a better interpretation?
options: Pupil A, because whispers are quiet and gentle
Pupil B, because wind is loud
hints: Whisper means to speak softly.
The line uses 'whispers', not 'shouts'.
questions.explanation: Pupil A gives a better interpretation because the word 'whispers' suggests a soft, gentle wind, not shouting.
misconceptions: Wind can be loud, but the poem says 'whispers'.

questions.stem: A pupil recites the line 'I will never give up' but stresses the word 'I'. Another pupil stresses 'never'. Which stress better shows determination?
hints: Determination means refusing to quit.
'Never' means not at any time.
questions.explanation: Stressing 'never' better shows determination because it emphasises that the speaker will not quit at any time.
misconceptions: Stressing 'I' is less powerful than stressing 'never'.
The two stresses give different meanings.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.3.1: Appreciate poems and other pieces of literary materials
indicator.objective: Identify and discuss values in poems

skills.description: Identify the value(s) taught in a poem
Explain what a value means in the context of the poem
Relate the value in a poem to real-life situations

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: The value is always stated directly
A poem about a tree has no value

questions.stem: A poem says: 'Always tell the truth, my child, / Even when it hurts.' What value does this poem teach?
hints: The poem says 'tell the truth'.
Telling the truth is honesty.
questions.explanation: The poem teaches honesty — always telling the truth even when it is difficult.
misconceptions: Laziness is not about telling the truth.
Anger is not the value being taught.

questions.stem: A poem says: 'Help the old, help the weak, / A kind heart is what we seek.' What value does this poem teach?
hints: The poem says 'help' and 'kind heart'.
Helping others is kindness.
questions.explanation: The poem teaches kindness — helping the old and the weak.
misconceptions: Fighting is the opposite of helping.
Jealousy is not the value taught.

questions.stem: A poem says: 'Be patient, little one, / Good things come to those who wait.' What does 'patience' mean here?
hints: Patience is about waiting.
The poem says 'those who wait'.
questions.explanation: Patience means waiting calmly without complaining, knowing that good things will come.
misconceptions: Getting angry is the opposite of patience.

questions.stem: A poem titled 'My Dear Country Ghana' teaches love for Ghana. What value is this?
hints: Love for one's country is called patriotism.
The poem is about Ghana.
questions.explanation: The poem teaches patriotism — love and devotion to one's country, Ghana.
misconceptions: Laziness is not about love for country.
Fear is not the value being taught.

questions.stem: A poem says: 'Share your bread with a friend in need.' What does 'sharing' mean in this poem?
options: Giving part of what you have to others
hints: The poem says 'share your bread'.
Sharing means giving to others.
questions.explanation: Sharing means giving part of what you have to others who need it.
misconceptions: Keeping everything is the opposite of sharing.

questions.stem: A poem says: 'Work hard from dawn to dusk, / A lazy hand brings nothing but dust.' What value does this poem teach?
hints: The poem says 'work hard'.
Diligence means hard work.
questions.explanation: The poem teaches diligence — working hard and not being lazy.
misconceptions: Laziness is what the poem warns against.
Sleeping is not the value taught.
Playing is not the focus of the poem.

questions.stem: A poem says: 'Respect your elders, young and old, / Their wisdom is more precious than gold.' What value does this poem teach?
hints: The poem says 'respect your elders'.
Respect is the value.
questions.explanation: The poem teaches respect — honouring elders for their wisdom.
misconceptions: Disrespect is the opposite of what the poem teaches.

questions.stem: A poem says: 'A honest word is like a lamp, / It lights the way for all.' How does the poem show that honesty is important?
options: It says honesty is like a lamp that lights the way
It says honesty is for children only
hints: The poem compares honesty to a lamp.
A lamp gives light and helps people see.
questions.explanation: The poem shows honesty is important by comparing it to a lamp that lights the way for everyone.
misconceptions: The poem says honesty is like light, not darkness.
The poem praises honesty, not dismisses it.
The poem is for everyone, not just children.

questions.stem: A poem says: 'A kind word costs nothing, / But it warms a heart for days.' What does the poem teach about kindness?
options: Kindness is free and has great value
Kindness is only for the rich
hints: The poem says kindness 'costs nothing'.
It 'warms a heart' — it helps people.
questions.explanation: The poem teaches that kindness is free but has great value because it makes people feel good.
misconceptions: The poem says kindness costs nothing, not that it is expensive.
The poem says kindness warms hearts, so it is valuable.
The poem does not say kindness is only for the rich.

questions.stem: A poem teaches the value of honesty. How can you show honesty at school?
options: By telling the teacher the truth when you make a mistake
By blaming your friend for your mistake
hints: Honesty means telling the truth.
Admitting a mistake is honest.
questions.explanation: You show honesty by telling the teacher the truth when you make a mistake, instead of blaming others or hiding it.
misconceptions: Hiding your test paper is dishonest.

questions.stem: Which line from a poem teaches the value of perseverance?
options: 'Try again and again until you succeed'
'Let others do the work for you'
hints: Perseverance means not giving up.
Which line encourages trying again?
questions.explanation: 'Try again and again until you succeed' teaches perseverance — continuing to try even when it is difficult.
misconceptions: Giving up is the opposite of perseverance.
Stopping after one failure is not perseverance.
Letting others work for you is not perseverance.

questions.stem: A poem teaches the value of cleanliness. How can you practice this at home?
options: By throwing rubbish in the bin and sweeping your room
By throwing rubbish on the floor
By leaving dirty dishes in the sink
hints: Cleanliness means keeping things clean.
Which action keeps the home clean?
questions.explanation: You practice cleanliness by throwing rubbish in the bin and sweeping your room.
misconceptions: Throwing rubbish on the floor makes the home dirty.
Leaving dirty dishes makes the kitchen dirty.
Making the bed messy is not clean.

questions.stem: A poem says: 'A lazy farmer sleeps at noon, / His crops are few, his barn is bare. / A busy farmer works till dusk, / His crops are many, his barn is full.' What value does this poem teach?
hints: Compare the lazy farmer and the busy farmer.
The busy farmer has a full barn.
questions.explanation: The poem teaches that hard work brings rewards, while laziness leads to nothing.
misconceptions: The poem warns against sleeping too much, not encourages it.
The poem criticises laziness, not praises it.
An empty barn is the result of laziness, not the goal.

questions.stem: A poem says: 'A patient farmer waits for rain, / He does not curse the sky in vain. / He trusts that seasons come and go, / And in due time, his crops will grow.' What does the poem teach about patience?
options: Patience means giving up when things are hard
Patience means waiting calmly and trusting the process
Patience means getting angry at the weather
Patience means doing nothing at all
hints: The farmer waits for rain without cursing.
He trusts that his crops will grow in time.
questions.explanation: The poem teaches that patience means waiting calmly and trusting that good things will come in due time.
misconceptions: The farmer does not give up; he waits.
The farmer does not get angry; he trusts.
Patience is active waiting, not doing nothing.

questions.stem: A poem teaches the value of respect for elders. Which real-life situation shows this value?
options: Offering your seat to an elderly person on a trotro
Ignoring an elderly person who needs help
hints: Respect means showing honour and care.
Offering a seat is a sign of respect.
questions.explanation: Offering your seat to an elderly person on a trotro shows respect for elders.
misconceptions: Pushing an elderly person is disrespectful.
Shouting at an elderly person is disrespectful.
Ignoring someone who needs help is disrespectful.

questions.stem: A poem says: 'Do not laugh at those who fall, / Lend a hand and stand up tall. / Do not mock the weak and small, / Kindness is the greatest call.' What is the main value taught in this poem?
hints: The poem says 'lend a hand' and 'kindness'.
It warns against laughing at others.
questions.explanation: The main value is kindness and compassion — helping others instead of mocking them.
misconceptions: The poem warns against mocking, not encourages it.
Laughing at people is what the poem says not to do.
Pride is not the value being taught.

questions.stem: A poem says: 'The bamboo bends but does not break, / It bows to the storm for its own sake. / The mighty oak stands stiff and proud, / And crashes down beneath the cloud.' What value does this poem teach?
hints: The bamboo bends and survives.
The oak stands stiff and breaks.
questions.explanation: The poem teaches flexibility and humility — being willing to bend and adapt helps us survive difficult times.
misconceptions: Stubbornness is like the oak, which breaks.
Pride is what brings down the oak.
Anger is not the value being taught.

questions.stem: A poem teaches the value of patience. Which real-life situation best shows this value?
options: Ama waited calmly for her turn and was rewarded
Esi gave up when the work was hard
Yaw got angry and broke his pencil
hints: Patience means waiting calmly.
Which person showed patience?
questions.explanation: Ama shows patience by waiting calmly for her turn, and she was rewarded for it.
misconceptions: Rushing is the opposite of patience.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.3.1: Appreciate poems and other pieces of literary materials
indicator.objective: Compose four-line poems

skills.description: Recognise that a four-line poem has four lines and may have a rhyme pattern
Identify rhyming words and choose words that rhyme to complete a couplet or quatrain
Arrange given lines into a logical four-line poem
Compose a four-line poem on a given topic

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Any four sentences are a poem
Rhyming words must be spelled the same
A poem must have a title

questions.stem: How many lines does a four-line poem have?
hints: The name 'four-line poem' tells you the answer.
Count the lines in a four-line poem.
questions.explanation: A four-line poem has exactly four lines.

questions.stem: Which word rhymes with 'cat'?
hints: Rhyming words have the same ending sound.
Cat ends with '-at'. Which word also ends with '-at'?
questions.explanation: 'Hat' rhymes with 'cat' because both end with the '-at' sound.

questions.stem: Which of these is a four-line poem?
options: Roses are red, / Violets are blue.
Roses are red, / Violets are blue, / Sugar is sweet, / And so are you.
Violets are blue, / Sugar is sweet, / And so are you.
hints: Count the lines.
A four-line poem has exactly four lines.
questions.explanation: The option with four lines ('Roses are red, / Violets are blue, / Sugar is sweet, / And so are you.') is a four-line poem.

questions.stem: Which word rhymes with 'tree'?
hints: Rhyming words end with the same sound.
Tree ends with '-ee'. Which word also ends with '-ee'?
questions.explanation: 'Bee' rhymes with 'tree' because both end with the '-ee' sound.

questions.stem: Which line should come first in a poem about a cat?
options: The cat sat on the mat
And then it went to sleep
hints: The first line usually introduces the subject.
Which line tells us what the poem is about?
questions.explanation: 'A very busy cat' introduces the subject of the poem — the cat.
misconceptions: The other lines add details after the subject is introduced.

questions.stem: Complete the poem: 'The sky is blue, / The grass is ___.'
hints: The poem is about the sky and grass.
What colour is grass?
questions.explanation: The grass is green. This completes the poem with a factual statement.

questions.stem: Complete the rhyme: 'I have a little dog, / He likes to play with a ___.'
hints: Dog ends with '-og'. Which word also ends with '-og'?
Find the rhyming word.
questions.explanation: 'Frog' rhymes with 'dog' because both end with the '-og' sound.
misconceptions: 'Log' rhymes with 'dog', but 'play with a log' is less natural.

questions.stem: A four-line poem usually has how many pairs of rhyming lines?
hints: Four lines can be split into two pairs.
Lines 1 and 2 rhyme, and lines 3 and 4 rhyme.
questions.explanation: A four-line poem often has two pairs of rhyming lines: lines 1 and 2 rhyme, and lines 3 and 4 rhyme (AABB pattern).
misconceptions: One pair would mean only two lines rhyme.
Four pairs would need eight lines.

questions.stem: Arrange these lines into a logical poem: (1) And then it flew away. (2) A little bird sat on a tree. (3) It sang a happy song. (4) The bird was singing all day long.
hints: Start with the line that introduces the bird.
End with the line that tells what happened last.
questions.explanation: The logical order is: (2) A little bird sat on a tree. (3) It sang a happy song. (4) The bird was singing all day long. (1) And then it flew away.
misconceptions: Starting with the ending does not make sense.
Reversing the order confuses the story.
Starting with line 3 skips the introduction.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a feature of a four-line poem?
options: It must be at least ten lines
hints: A four-line poem has exactly four lines.
Ten lines is more than four.
questions.explanation: A four-line poem has exactly four lines, not ten. It may rhyme and has rhythm.
misconceptions: Four lines is the defining feature.
Rhythm is a feature of poems.

questions.stem: Complete the poem: 'The sun is bright, / It gives us ___.'
hints: The sun gives us something related to brightness.
'Bright' rhymes with 'light'.
questions.explanation: The sun gives us light. 'Light' also rhymes with 'bright'.
misconceptions: The sun does not give night.
The sun gives light, not dark.
The sun gives heat, not cold.

questions.stem: Arrange these lines into a four-line poem about rain: (1) The rain comes down. (2) The flowers bloom. (3) The sky is grey. (4) The children play.
hints: Start with the sky, then the rain, then what happens after.
The flowers bloom after the rain.
questions.explanation: The logical order is: (3) The sky is grey. (1) The rain comes down. (2) The flowers bloom. (4) The children play.
misconceptions: Starting with the rain skips the sky setting.
Reversing the order confuses the sequence.
Starting with flowers skips the cause (rain).

questions.stem: Which pair of lines rhymes correctly?
options: The cat is fat, / The dog is big.
The cat is fat, / It wears a hat.
The cat is fat, / It likes to run.
The cat is fat, / The sun is hot.
hints: Rhyming words end with the same sound.
Cat and hat rhyme.
questions.explanation: 'The cat is fat' and 'It wears a hat' rhyme because 'fat' and 'hat' end with the same sound.

questions.stem: Which line is the best ending for this poem? 'The little seed sleeps in the ground. / The rain falls softly all around. / The sun shines warm and bright above. / ___'
options: The seed begins to grow with love.
hints: The poem is about a seed growing.
The ending should complete the idea of growth.
questions.explanation: 'The seed begins to grow with love' is the best ending because it completes the poem's message about the seed growing.
misconceptions: The seed is not dead; it is growing.
The seed already slept in line 1.
The poem is about growth, not doing nothing.

questions.stem: Which set of rhyming words can complete this poem? 'The moon is bright, / It shines at ___.' / 'The stars are high, / They light the ___.'
hints: Night rhymes with bright.
Sky rhymes with high.
questions.explanation: 'Night' rhymes with 'bright', and 'sky' rhymes with 'high'. Together they complete the poem's rhyme pattern.
misconceptions: Day does not rhyme with bright.
Morning does not rhyme with bright.
Noon does not rhyme with bright.

questions.stem: A pupil wrote these four lines but they are mixed up: (1) And then it flew up high. (2) The butterfly is so pretty. (3) It landed on a flower. (4) It has colours bright and witty. Which arrangement makes the best poem?
hints: Start with the line that introduces the butterfly.
End with the line that tells what happened last.
questions.explanation: The best order is: (2) The butterfly is so pretty. (4) It has colours bright and witty. (3) It landed on a flower. (1) And then it flew up high.
misconceptions: The reversed order does not flow.
Starting with colours skips the introduction.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.4.1: Respond to stories
indicator.objective: Retell stories sequentially, including key details

skills.description: Identify the beginning, middle and ending parts of a story
Arrange story events in the correct order
Recall key details (characters, setting, main events) from a story heard or read
Retell a story sequentially in the learner's own words, including key details

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: The middle is the same as the ending
Any detail is a key detail
Retelling means copying the story word for word
The beginning always introduces every character

questions.stem: Which part of a story introduces the characters and the setting?
hints: The beginning comes first.
It tells us who the story is about and where it happens.
questions.explanation: The beginning of a story introduces the characters and the setting.
misconceptions: The middle contains the problem or events.
The title is just the name of the story.

questions.stem: Which part of a story usually contains the problem or the main events?
hints: The problem usually happens after the characters are introduced.
It comes before the ending.
questions.explanation: The middle of a story usually contains the problem or the main events.
misconceptions: The title is just the name.

questions.stem: In the story of 'The Hawk and the Hen', what happened first?
options: Hen agreed to give one chick every day
hints: The story starts with Hen.
What did Hen have?
questions.explanation: The story begins with Hen having beautiful chicks.
misconceptions: Hawk seeing the chicks happens after Hen has them.
Hawk taking a chick is at the end.

questions.stem: Who are the main characters in the story of 'The Hawk and the Hen'?
hints: The title tells you the main characters.
The story is about a hawk and a hen.
questions.explanation: The main characters are Hawk and Hen.
misconceptions: The chicks are important but the main characters are Hawk and Hen.
The chicks are not the main characters.
The farmer is not in the story.

questions.stem: Where did the story of 'The Hawk and the Hen' take place?
options: On a farm or near Hen's home
hints: Hen and her chicks live on a farm.
Hawk flies down to see them.
questions.explanation: The story takes place on a farm or near Hen's home where she keeps her chicks.
misconceptions: There is no market in the story.
There is no school in the story.
There is no beach in the story.

questions.stem: In 'The Hawk and the Hen', which event belongs to the middle of the story?
options: Hawk made a deal with Hen
Hawk takes a chick every day
hints: The middle contains the problem or main events.
The deal is the main event.
questions.explanation: Hawk making a deal with Hen is the main event in the middle of the story.
misconceptions: Hen having chicks is the beginning.
Hawk taking chicks every day is the result/ending.
Hen living on a farm is the setting (beginning).

questions.stem: Which part of a story tells us how the problem was solved?
hints: The problem is solved at the end.
The ending comes last.
questions.explanation: The ending of a story tells us how the problem was solved.
misconceptions: The title is just the name.

questions.stem: What happened after Hawk saw the chicks?
options: Hen gave Hawk all the chicks
hints: Hawk is a bird of prey.
Hawk saw the chicks and wanted them.
questions.explanation: After Hawk saw the chicks, he wanted to eat them.
misconceptions: Hen did not chase Hawk away.
The chicks could not fly away.
Hen did not give all the chicks.

questions.stem: Put these events in order: (1) Hen agreed to the deal. (2) Hawk made a deal. (3) Hen had chicks.
hints: Start with what happened first.
The deal comes after the chicks are seen.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: (3) Hen had chicks, (2) Hawk made a deal, (1) Hen agreed to the deal.
misconceptions: Starting with the agreement skips the cause.
The deal comes after the chicks.
Hen cannot agree before the deal is made.

questions.stem: Which of these is a key detail in the story of 'The Hawk and the Hen'?
options: Hawk wanted to eat the chicks
Hen had a friend called Duck
The farm had a big gate
hints: A key detail is important to the story.
What was Hawk's plan?
questions.explanation: Hawk wanting to eat the chicks is a key detail because it drives the story forward.
misconceptions: The colour of the chicks is a minor detail.
Duck is not in the story.

questions.stem: What did Hawk agree to do in the story?
options: To spare the chicks if Hen gave him one every day
To build a new nest for Hen
To teach the chicks to fly
hints: Hawk made a deal with Hen.
Hawk wanted something in return.
questions.explanation: Hawk agreed to spare the chicks if Hen gave him one chick every day.
misconceptions: Hawk did not help Hen find food.
Hawk did not build a nest.
Hawk did not teach the chicks to fly.

questions.stem: A pupil retells 'The Hawk and the Hen' but only says: 'Hen had chicks and Hawk took them.' Which part of the story is missing?
options: The middle (the deal between Hen and Hawk)
hints: The retelling skips how Hawk came to take the chicks.
The deal is the middle part.
questions.explanation: The retelling is missing the middle — the deal between Hen and Hawk that explains why Hawk takes the chicks.
misconceptions: The beginning is present (Hen had chicks).
The ending is present (Hawk took them).
The title is not a story part.

questions.stem: Arrange these four events in the correct order: (1) Hawk takes a chick every day. (2) Hen begs Hawk. (3) Hawk sees the chicks. (4) Hawk makes a deal.
hints: Start with Hawk seeing the chicks.
Hen begs before the deal is made.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: (3) Hawk sees the chicks, (2) Hen begs Hawk, (4) Hawk makes a deal, (1) Hawk takes a chick every day.
misconceptions: Hawk cannot take a chick before the deal.
Hen cannot beg before Hawk sees the chicks.
The deal comes before Hawk takes chicks.

questions.stem: A pupil retells the story: 'Hawk took Hen's chicks.' What key detail is missing from this retelling?
options: The deal that Hen agreed to
hints: The retelling jumps straight to the ending.
What made Hawk take the chicks?
questions.explanation: The retelling is missing the deal — Hen agreed to give Hawk one chick every day, which is why Hawk takes them.
misconceptions: The farmer is not in the story.
The colour of the chicks is a minor detail.
The size of the farm is not important.

questions.stem: A pupil retells a story but forgets the ending. What is missing from the retelling?
hints: The ending resolves the problem.
Without the ending, the problem is not solved.
questions.explanation: The ending contains the resolution of the problem, so forgetting the ending means the resolution is missing.
misconceptions: Characters are usually in the beginning.
The title is not a story part.

questions.stem: Arrange these events from a different story: (1) The tortoise tricked the birds and took all the food. (2) The birds invited the tortoise to a feast in the sky. (3) The tortoise fell from the sky. (4) The birds learned a lesson about trust.
hints: Start with the invitation.
The trick happens at the feast.
The fall comes after the trick.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: (2) The birds invited the tortoise to a feast, (1) The tortoise tricked them, (3) The tortoise fell, (4) The birds learned a lesson.
misconceptions: The trick cannot happen before the invitation.
The fall comes after the trick.
The lesson comes at the end.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.4.1: Respond to stories
indicator.objective: Tell own stories

skills.description: Identify the elements of a story (characters, setting, events, ending)
Recognise that an own story must have a beginning, middle and ending
Tell an original story to the class with clear voice and sequence

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: An own story has no structure
A story must be very long
Only made-up stories count as own stories
The ending can be left out

questions.stem: Which of these is a story element?
hints: Story elements are the parts that make up a story.
A character is a person or animal in a story.
questions.explanation: A character is a story element — a person or animal in the story.
misconceptions: Page numbers are not story elements.
Book covers are not story elements.

questions.stem: What is the 'setting' of a story?
options: Where and when the story happens
hints: Setting tells us where and when.
It is the place and time.
questions.explanation: The setting is where and when the story happens.

questions.stem: How many main parts does a story have?
hints: Beginning, middle, ending.
Count the parts.
questions.explanation: A story has three main parts: the beginning, the middle and the ending.

questions.stem: Which part of a story comes last?
hints: Last means at the end.
It comes after the middle.
questions.explanation: The ending comes last in a story.
misconceptions: The title comes before the story.

questions.stem: In a story about a girl who lost her book, who is the main character?
hints: The main character is the person the story is about.
The story is about the girl.
questions.explanation: The girl is the main character because the story is about her losing her book.
misconceptions: The book is the object, not the character.
The teacher may be in the story but is not the main character.

questions.stem: Which of these is the best opening for your own story about a visit to the market?
options: One sunny Saturday, my mother and I went to the market.
hints: An opening introduces the characters and setting.
It tells us who, where and when.
questions.explanation: 'One sunny Saturday, my mother and I went to the market' is the best opening because it introduces the characters, setting and time.
misconceptions: 'And then I went home' is an ending, not an opening.
'I bought some oranges' is a detail that comes later.

questions.stem: Which of these is the best ending for your own story?
options: Finally, we all went home happy.
hints: An ending tells how things turned out.
'Finally' signals the end.
questions.explanation: 'Finally, we all went home happy' is the best ending because it tells how the story concluded.
misconceptions: 'Once upon a time' is a beginning.

questions.stem: In your own story, the events that happen are called the ___.
hints: Events are what happens in the story.
It is also called the plot.
questions.explanation: The events that happen in a story are called the plot or the events.
misconceptions: The title is the name of the story.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a story element?
hints: Story elements are the building blocks of a story.
Spelling mistakes are errors, not elements.
questions.explanation: Spelling mistakes are not story elements. Characters, setting and events are story elements.

questions.stem: Which line belongs in the middle of your own story about a lost dog?
options: I have a dog named Rex.
I searched everywhere but could not find him.
Finally, I found Rex under the bed.
hints: The middle contains the problem or main events.
Searching for the dog is the main event.
questions.explanation: 'I searched everywhere but could not find him' belongs in the middle because it describes the problem/searching.
misconceptions: 'I have a dog named Rex' is the beginning.
'Finally, I found Rex' is the ending.
'Rex is a brown dog' is a description (beginning).

questions.stem: Your own story is about a day you went to the beach. What is the setting?
hints: The setting is where the story happens.
The story is about going to the beach.
questions.explanation: The setting is the beach because that is where your story takes place.
misconceptions: School is not where the story happens.
The market is not where the story happens.
The forest is not where the story happens.

questions.stem: A pupil tells a story but forgets to say where it happened. Which story element is missing?
hints: 'Where' refers to the setting.
The setting is where the story happens.
questions.explanation: The setting is missing because the pupil forgot to say where the story happened.
misconceptions: Character is who is in the story.

questions.stem: Arrange these lines into a logical own story: (1) I looked under the bed and found my shoe. (2) I could not find my shoe. (3) I woke up late for school. (4) I put on my shoe and ran to school.
hints: Start with waking up late.
Finding the shoe comes before running to school.
questions.explanation: The logical order is: (3) I woke up late, (2) I could not find my shoe, (1) I found it under the bed, (4) I ran to school.
misconceptions: Finding the shoe first skips the problem.
Starting with looking under the bed skips the cause.
Running to school comes after finding the shoe.

questions.stem: A pupil's story is: 'I woke up. I ate. I went to school.' What is missing from this story?
hints: The story has no interesting event.
A good story usually has a problem or main event.
questions.explanation: The story is missing a problem or interesting event. It just lists routine activities without a story line.
misconceptions: A title is not essential to the telling.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.5.1: Perform stories
indicator.objective: Role-play a story/play

skills.description: Identify characters and their roles in a story or play
Identify key events and scenes in a story/play suitable for role-play
Role-play a character in a scene from a story/play using appropriate voice, actions and dialogue

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Role-play means reading the story aloud
Any character can say any line
Actions are not important in role-play

questions.stem: In the story 'Ananse and the Black Pot', who is the main character?
hints: The title of the story tells you the main character.
Ananse is the spider in the story.
questions.explanation: Ananse is the main character in 'Ananse and the Black Pot'.
misconceptions: The black pot is an object, not a character.
The village chief is not the main character.
The farmer is not in this story.

questions.stem: Which character is known for being clever and tricky in many Ghanaian stories?
hints: Ananse is the spider known for trickery.
Ananse stories are popular in Ghana.
questions.explanation: Ananse the spider is known for being clever and tricky in many Ghanaian stories.
misconceptions: The lion is strong but not known for trickery.
The tortoise is slow and wise but not the main trickster in Ghanaian stories.
The hen is not known for trickery.

questions.stem: Which of these is a key event in a role-play about 'Ananse and the Black Pot'?
hints: The black pot is central to the story.
Finding the pot starts the main events.
questions.explanation: Ananse finding the black pot is a key event that starts the main action of the story.
misconceptions: Going to the market is not the main event.
Eating rice is a detail, not a key event.
Sleeping is not a key event.

questions.stem: Which of these is a scene from a story that you could role-play?
hints: A scene has characters doing something.
A scene has dialogue and action.
questions.explanation: A scene like 'Ananse talking to the chief' can be role-played because it has characters and action.
misconceptions: A list of names is not a scene.
A page of a book is not a scene.
A picture is not a scene you can act out.

questions.stem: What does it mean to role-play a character?
options: To act as the character with voice and actions
To draw a picture of the character
hints: Role-play means acting.
You speak and move like the character.
questions.explanation: Role-playing a character means acting as that character, using your voice and actions.

questions.stem: In a play about 'Ananse and the Black Pot', which character would say: 'This pot is mine and I will not share'?
hints: Ananse is known for being selfish with the pot.
The pot belongs to Ananse in the story.
questions.explanation: Ananse would say 'This pot is mine and I will not share' because he is selfish with the black pot.
misconceptions: The chief would not say this.
A child would not say this.
The farmer is not in the story.

questions.stem: When role-playing a greedy character like Ananse, how should you speak?
hints: Greedy characters often sound selfish.
Ananse is proud of his pot.
questions.explanation: A greedy character like Ananse should speak in a selfish, proud tone to show his character.
misconceptions: Sad and soft is not greedy.
A scared whisper does not show greed.
A kind voice is not greedy.

questions.stem: Which scene from 'Ananse and the Black Pot' would be best for role-play?
options: Ananse finding the pot and deciding not to share it
hints: The best scene has conflict and dialogue.
Finding the pot and making a decision has action and emotion.
questions.explanation: Ananse finding the pot and deciding not to share it is the best scene for role-play because it has conflict and emotion.
misconceptions: Sleeping has no dialogue or action.

questions.stem: In a role-play, what should happen first?
options: The characters introduce themselves and the scene
hints: The beginning of a play sets the scene.
The audience needs to know who and where.
questions.explanation: The characters should introduce themselves and the scene first so the audience understands the play.
misconceptions: Fighting comes after the scene is set.

questions.stem: What voice would you use for a character who is angry?
hints: Angry people often speak loudly.
The voice should match the feeling.
questions.explanation: An angry character should use a loud, sharp voice to show their anger.
misconceptions: A soft voice does not show anger.
A sleepy voice does not show anger.
A happy voice does not show anger.

questions.stem: What actions would you use to show a character who is tired?
hints: Tired people yawn.
Tired people move slowly.
questions.explanation: Yawning and rubbing your eyes shows a character who is tired.

questions.stem: What is a 'scene' in a play?
options: A part of the play where something happens in one place and time
hints: A scene is a section of a play.
It happens in one place and time.
questions.explanation: A scene is a part of a play where something happens in one place and at one time.
misconceptions: The title is not a scene.
The list of characters is not a scene.
The end is part of a scene, not a scene itself.

questions.stem: When role-playing, why should you speak loudly and clearly?
options: So the audience can hear and understand you
So you can scare the audience
So you don't have to act
hints: The audience needs to hear the dialogue.
Clear speech helps understanding.
questions.explanation: You should speak loudly and clearly so the audience can hear and understand the play.
misconceptions: Speaking loudly is not about finishing quickly.
Scaring the audience is not the goal.
Speaking loudly does not replace acting.

questions.stem: Arrange these events from a role-play in the correct order: (1) Ananse refuses to share the food. (2) Ananse finds the black pot. (3) The villagers ask Ananse for food. (4) The pot is taken away from Ananse.
hints: Start with finding the pot.
The villagers ask after Ananse has the pot.
The pot is taken after Ananse refuses to share.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: (2) Ananse finds the pot, (1) he refuses to share, (3) the villagers ask for food, (4) the pot is taken away.
misconceptions: Refusing to share comes after finding the pot.
The villagers ask after Ananse has the pot.
The pot is taken at the end.

questions.stem: Two pupils role-play Ananse. Pupil A speaks in a selfish, proud voice and refuses to share. Pupil B speaks in a kind, sharing voice. Which pupil is correctly playing Ananse?
options: Pupil A, because Ananse is selfish in the story
Pupil B, because Ananse is kind
hints: Ananse is known for being selfish with the pot.
The character's voice should match their personality.
questions.explanation: Pupil A is correctly playing Ananse because Ananse is selfish in the story and refuses to share.
misconceptions: Ananse is not kind with the pot.
Only one pupil matches Ananse's character.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to role-play a scene from 'Ananse and the Black Pot' but chooses the scene where Ananse is sleeping. Why is this NOT a good scene for role-play?
options: Because sleeping is boring and has no dialogue or action
Because sleeping is too difficult to act
Because the scene is too long
hints: A good role-play scene has dialogue and action.
Sleeping has no dialogue or action.
questions.explanation: Sleeping is not a good scene for role-play because it has no dialogue or action to perform.
misconceptions: Ananse does sleep sometimes, but it's not a good scene.
Sleeping is not difficult to act, just boring.
The scene is not too long, just uneventful.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.5.2: Perform stories
indicator.objective: Identify moral values in sketches and relate them to real life situations

skills.description: Identify the moral value(s) shown in a sketch or play
Explain how the characters or events in a sketch show a particular value
Relate the moral value from a sketch to real-life situations

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Every sketch has only one value
The value is always stated directly
Moral values are only for school
If a character does something bad, the sketch has no value

questions.stem: In a sketch, a pupil finds a purse and returns it to the owner. What value does this show?
hints: Returning something that is not yours is honest.
Honesty means doing the right thing.
questions.explanation: Returning the purse to its owner shows honesty.
misconceptions: Dishonesty would be keeping the purse.
Laziness is not about returning things.
Anger is not the value shown.

questions.stem: In a sketch, two pupils share their books with a friend who has none. What value does this show?
hints: Sharing is a kind act.
Kindness means caring for others.
questions.explanation: Sharing books with a friend shows kindness.
misconceptions: Selfishness is the opposite of sharing.
Pride is not the value shown.

questions.stem: A sketch shows a pupil helping an old woman carry her load. How does this show kindness?
options: The pupil is being helpful and caring
hints: Helping someone is a kind act.
Kindness means caring for others.
questions.explanation: The pupil shows kindness by being helpful and caring towards the old woman.

questions.stem: A sketch teaches honesty. Which real-life action shows honesty?
options: Telling the truth when you make a mistake
hints: Honesty means telling the truth.
Admitting a mistake is honest.
questions.explanation: Telling the truth when you make a mistake shows honesty.

questions.stem: A sketch shows a pupil who always tells lies. The sketch ends with the pupil losing all his friends. What value does this sketch teach?
hints: The pupil loses friends because of lying.
The sketch warns against lying.
questions.explanation: The sketch teaches that honesty is important because lying leads to losing friends.
misconceptions: The sketch warns against lying, not encourages it.
The sketch shows friends are important.
Telling lies is shown as bad.

questions.stem: In a sketch, a pupil works hard on a school project and gets a good grade. Another pupil copies and gets caught. What value does this sketch teach?
options: Hard work and honesty are rewarded
hints: The hardworking pupil gets a good grade.
The copying pupil gets caught.
questions.explanation: The sketch teaches that hard work and honesty are rewarded, while cheating is punished.
misconceptions: Cheating is shown as wrong, not good.
Working hard is shown as good.

questions.stem: A sketch shows a pupil who is always patient, even when others are angry. How does this show patience?
options: The pupil stays calm and does not get angry
hints: Patience means staying calm.
The pupil does not get angry.
questions.explanation: The pupil shows patience by staying calm and not getting angry when others are angry.

questions.stem: A sketch shows a pupil who refuses to join others in mocking a new pupil. What value is shown?
hints: The pupil refuses to mock someone.
This shows respect for others.
questions.explanation: The pupil shows respect for others by refusing to mock the new pupil.
misconceptions: Bullying is what the pupil refuses to do.

questions.stem: A sketch teaches the value of respect. Which real-life action shows respect?
hints: Respect means valuing others.
Listening is a sign of respect.
questions.explanation: Listening when someone is speaking shows respect for them.
misconceptions: Making fun of people is disrespectful.

questions.stem: A sketch teaches the value of teamwork. Which real-life action shows teamwork?
options: Working alone on a group project
Helping your classmates clean the classroom
hints: Teamwork means working together.
Helping classmates is working together.
questions.explanation: Helping your classmates clean the classroom shows teamwork.
misconceptions: Refusing to help is not teamwork.

questions.stem: A sketch shows a pupil who never gives up even when a task is difficult. What value does this show?
hints: Not giving up is perseverance.
Perseverance means continuing to try.
questions.explanation: Never giving up shows perseverance.
misconceptions: Fear might make someone give up.
Anger is not the value shown.

questions.stem: In a sketch, a pupil obeys her parents and teachers and is praised. What value is shown?
hints: Obeying parents and teachers is obedience.
The pupil is praised for doing what is right.
questions.explanation: The sketch shows obedience — doing what parents and teachers say.
misconceptions: Pride is not the value shown.

questions.stem: A sketch teaches that honesty is important. In your own life, what should you do if you find money on the ground at school?
options: Give it to the teacher or headteacher
hints: Honesty means doing the right thing.
The money is not yours.
questions.explanation: If you find money that is not yours, honesty means giving it to the teacher or headteacher so the owner can be found.
misconceptions: Using it to buy sweets is dishonest.

questions.stem: A sketch shows a pupil who is patient and eventually succeeds, while an impatient pupil fails. How does the sketch show the importance of patience?
options: The patient pupil succeeds, the impatient pupil fails
hints: Compare the patient and impatient pupils.
The patient pupil succeeds.
questions.explanation: The sketch shows the importance of patience by contrasting the patient pupil (who succeeds) with the impatient pupil (who fails).
misconceptions: The patient pupil does not give up.
The impatient pupil does not succeed.

questions.stem: A sketch shows a pupil who always says 'please' and 'thank you' and waits his turn. What value does this sketch teach?
hints: 'Please' and 'thank you' are polite words.
Waiting your turn shows good manners.
questions.explanation: Using polite words and waiting your turn shows good manners and politeness.

questions.stem: A sketch shows the importance of being honest. How can you apply this value in your community?
options: By returning lost items to their owners
hints: Honesty means doing the right thing.
Returning lost items is honest.
questions.explanation: You can apply honesty in your community by returning lost items to their owners.

questions.stem: A sketch shows a pupil who refuses to cheat in an exam even when his friends are cheating. What value does the sketch teach, and how can you apply it in real life?
options: Honesty — by refusing to cheat even when others do
hints: The pupil chooses not to cheat.
This is honesty.
questions.explanation: The sketch teaches honesty. You can apply it by refusing to cheat even when others around you are cheating.
misconceptions: Following the crowd is not the lesson.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.6.1: Use culturally acceptable language for communication
indicator.objective: Describe/talk about objects, events, dates and time

skills.description: Describe familiar objects (classroom items, home items) using size, colour, shape, use
Talk about familiar events (festivals, birthdays, school events) — when, why, how celebrated
State and write dates and times correctly (e.g. 'half past 8', '10th March')
Identify and talk about important places in Ghana (regions, landmarks)

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: A description is just naming the object
Dates are written the same way everywhere
All festivals are celebrated the same way

questions.stem: Ama has an object. It is small, round and red. You can eat it. What is it?
hints: The object is small, round and red.
It is something you can eat.
questions.explanation: The object is an orange — it is small, round, red and you can eat it.
misconceptions: A football is round but you cannot eat it.
A pencil is not round or red.
A ruler is not round or red.

questions.stem: Which of these is a festival celebrated by the Ga people of Ghana?
hints: The Ga people live in the Greater Accra Region.
Homowo means 'hooting at hunger'.
questions.explanation: Homowo is the festival celebrated by the Ga people of Ghana.
misconceptions: Christmas is a Christian festival, not a Ga festival.
Independence Day is a national holiday.

questions.stem: If the clock shows 8:00, how do we say the time?
hints: When the minute hand is on 12, it is o'clock.
It is exactly 8:00.
questions.explanation: When the clock shows 8:00, we say '8 o'clock'.

questions.stem: What is the capital city of Ghana?
hints: It is in the Greater Accra Region.
It is where the government sits.
questions.explanation: Accra is the capital city of Ghana.
misconceptions: Kumasi is the capital of the Ashanti Region.
Tamale is the capital of the Northern Region.
Cape Coast is the capital of the Central Region.

questions.stem: What is a table used for?
options: To write on or put things on
hints: Tables are found in classrooms and homes.
You put books or food on it.
questions.explanation: A table is used to write on or put things on.
misconceptions: You sleep on a bed, not a table.
You wear clothes, not a table.
You eat from a plate, not a table.

questions.stem: Which word best describes a school bag that is very heavy?
hints: The bag is heavy.
Find the word that means 'heavy'.
questions.explanation: 'Weighty' is another word for heavy, so it best describes a very heavy school bag.

questions.stem: When is Christmas celebrated?
hints: It is in December.
It celebrates the birth of Jesus.
questions.explanation: Christmas is celebrated on 25th December every year.

questions.stem: If the clock shows 8:30, how do we say the time?
hints: The minute hand is on 6.
It is thirty minutes after 8.
questions.explanation: When the clock shows 8:30, we say 'half past 8'.

questions.stem: Which region is Kumasi the capital of?
hints: Kumasi is known for the Ashanti Kingdom.
It is in the middle belt of Ghana.
questions.explanation: Kumasi is the capital of the Ashanti Region.

questions.stem: Which festival is celebrated by the people of Winneba?
hints: It involves deer hunting.
It is celebrated in the Central Region.
questions.explanation: Aboakyere is the festival celebrated by the people of Winneba in the Central Region.
misconceptions: Homowo is celebrated by the Ga people.
Damba is celebrated by the people of the Northern Region.
Odwira is celebrated by the Akuapem people.

questions.stem: How do you write 'the tenth of March, 2024' using numbers?
hints: The day comes first, then the month, then the year.
10 is the day, 3 is the month (March).
questions.explanation: The tenth of March, 2024 is written as 10/3/24 (day/month/year).
misconceptions: 3/10/24 would be the third of October.
3/24/10 is not a correct date format.

questions.stem: Which is the best description of a classroom clock?
options: It is round, white and on the wall
hints: A good description includes shape, colour and position.
It is round, white and on the wall.
questions.explanation: 'It is round, white and on the wall' is the best description because it includes shape, colour and position.
misconceptions: 'It is a clock' just names the object.
'It tells time' is its use, not a description.

questions.stem: Why do the Ga people celebrate Homowo?
options: To remember a victory over hunger
hints: Homowo means 'hooting at hunger'.
It is about overcoming hunger.
questions.explanation: The Ga people celebrate Homowo to remember a victory over hunger in their history.
misconceptions: New Year is a separate celebration.
Homowo is about hunger, not honouring the chief.

questions.stem: If the clock shows 7:45, how do we say the time?
hints: It is 15 minutes before 8 o'clock.
When the minute hand is on 9, it is quarter to the next hour.
questions.explanation: 7:45 is 'quarter to 8' because it is 15 minutes before 8 o'clock.

questions.stem: Which important place in Ghana is known for its castle where enslaved people were once held?
hints: It is in the Central Region.
It is a historical site.
questions.explanation: Cape Coast Castle is an important historical place in Ghana where enslaved people were once held.
misconceptions: Kakum National Park is a rainforest with a canopy walkway.
Mole National Park is a wildlife park.
Lake Volta is the largest man-made lake.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'My school bag is blue, rectangular and has two pockets. It is used for carrying books.' What is missing from this description?
hints: The description mentions colour, shape and use.
What about how big or small it is?
questions.explanation: The description is missing the size of the bag. It mentions colour (blue), shape (rectangular) and use (carrying books), but not size.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'During Homowo, we eat kpoikpoi and sing songs.' What else is likely to happen during Homowo?
options: People dress in colourful clothes and there is a procession
People go to the market to buy books
hints: Festivals usually involve dressing up and processions.
Homowo is a joyful celebration.
questions.explanation: During Homowo, people dress in colourful clothes and there is a procession, along with eating kpoikpoi and singing.
misconceptions: Festivals are not about buying books.
People do not stay indoors all day during a festival.
Fireworks are not a traditional part of Homowo.

questions.stem: Which region is Lake Volta located in?
hints: The lake is named after the region.
It is in the eastern part of Ghana.
questions.explanation: Lake Volta is located in the Volta Region (and extends into other regions).
misconceptions: Greater Accra is not where Lake Volta is located.
Ashanti Region is not where Lake Volta is located.
Northern Region is not where Lake Volta is located.

questions.stem: Two pupils describe a chair. Pupil A: 'It is brown and made of wood.' Pupil B: 'It is brown, has four legs and a backrest, and is made of wood. We sit on it.' Which description is better and why?
options: Pupil A's, because it is shorter
Pupil B's, because it includes more details (shape, parts, use)
hints: A good description includes size, colour, shape and use.
Pupil B includes more details.
questions.explanation: Pupil B's description is better because it includes colour, shape (four legs and backrest), material (wood) and use (we sit on it).
misconceptions: Pupil B's description is clearly better.

questions.stem: Compare Homowo and Aboakyere. What do both festivals have in common?
options: Both are celebrated by the Ga people
Both are traditional Ghanaian festivals celebrated with processions and community gatherings
hints: Both are traditional festivals.
Both involve community celebrations.
questions.explanation: Both Homowo and Aboakyere are traditional Ghanaian festivals celebrated with processions and community gatherings. Homowo is for the Ga people; Aboakyere is for the people of Winneba.
misconceptions: Aboakyere is not celebrated by the Ga people (it's for Winneba).
Kpoikpoi is associated with Homowo, not necessarily Aboakyere.
Neither is specifically a December festival.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.6.2: Demonstrate positive listening and viewing attitudes and behaviour by showing attentiveness and understanding
indicator.objective: Listen and view attentively and for a sustained period (e.g., look at the person speaking) and maintain eye contact

skills.description: Recognise what attentive listening looks like (eyes on speaker, quiet body, nodding)
Understand why eye contact matters and when it is appropriate
Identify good and poor listening behaviours in given scenarios
Demonstrate sustained listening during a conversation or presentation

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Listening is the same as hearing
You can listen while doing something else
Only the speaker needs to be attentive

questions.stem: Which of these shows that you are listening attentively to someone?
hints: Attentive listening means giving full attention.
Look at the speaker.
questions.explanation: Looking at the person speaking shows that you are listening attentively.
misconceptions: Looking out of the window shows distraction.
Talking to a friend is not listening.
Playing with a pencil is a distraction.

questions.stem: What should your body do when you are listening attentively?
options: Turn your back to the speaker
hints: Attentive listening requires a calm body.
Stay quiet and still.
questions.explanation: When listening attentively, your body should stay quiet and still so you can focus on the speaker.

questions.stem: Why should you look at the person speaking?
options: To show you are listening and paying attention
hints: Eye contact shows respect and attention.
It tells the speaker you are listening.
questions.explanation: Looking at the person speaking shows that you are listening and paying attention.
misconceptions: Eye contact should not make someone nervous.
You are not copying their face.
Eye contact is not about finishing quickly.

questions.stem: Ama is looking at the teacher and nodding as the teacher speaks. What is Ama doing?
hints: Ama is looking at the teacher and nodding.
This shows she is paying attention.
questions.explanation: Ama is listening attentively because she is looking at the teacher and nodding.

questions.stem: Which of these is a POOR listening behaviour?
hints: Poor listening means not giving attention.
Interrupting is rude and shows poor listening.
questions.explanation: Interrupting the speaker is a poor listening behaviour because it shows you are not letting them finish.
misconceptions: Looking at the speaker is good listening.

questions.stem: When is it appropriate to maintain eye contact?
options: When someone is speaking to you
When you are watching TV alone
When you are reading a book
hints: Eye contact is for conversations.
Look at the person speaking.
questions.explanation: It is appropriate to maintain eye contact when someone is speaking to you, to show you are listening.
misconceptions: You cannot maintain eye contact while sleeping.
Eye contact is not needed when alone.
Eye contact is for conversations, not reading.

questions.stem: What does it mean if someone looks away while you are speaking to them?
options: They may not be paying attention
hints: Looking away can show distraction.
Eye contact helps show attention.
questions.explanation: If someone looks away while you are speaking, it may mean they are not paying attention.
misconceptions: Looking away usually does not show careful listening.
Anger is not the only reason for looking away.
Happiness is not shown by looking away.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sign of attentive listening?
hints: Attentive listeners engage with the speaker.
Asking questions shows you are following.
questions.explanation: Asking relevant questions shows that you are listening attentively and following what the speaker is saying.

questions.stem: Kojo is talking to his friend while the teacher is explaining a lesson. What should Kojo do instead?
options: Stop talking and listen to the teacher
Ask his friend to talk louder
hints: Good listening means giving attention to the speaker.
The teacher is explaining the lesson.
questions.explanation: Kojo should stop talking and listen to the teacher so he can understand the lesson.
misconceptions: Continuing to talk is poor listening.
Leaving the classroom is not the right response.
Asking his friend to talk louder would make things worse.

questions.stem: What should you do with your eyes when the headteacher is giving an announcement at assembly?
hints: Attentive listening means looking at the speaker.
The headteacher is the speaker.
questions.explanation: You should look at the headteacher to show you are listening attentively to the announcement.
misconceptions: Looking at your shoes shows distraction.
Looking at the sky shows distraction.
Closing your eyes might make you sleepy.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a good listening behaviour?
options: Thinking about what you will say next
hints: Good listening means focusing on the speaker, not yourself.
Thinking about your response distracts you.
questions.explanation: Thinking about what you will say next is not a good listening behaviour because it distracts you from what the speaker is saying.

questions.stem: When you are speaking to someone, why is it good for them to look at you?
options: It shows they are interested and listening
hints: Eye contact shows interest.
When someone looks at you, they are paying attention.
questions.explanation: When someone looks at you while you speak, it shows they are interested and listening.
misconceptions: Eye contact does not make someone look funny.
Eye contact does not help finish faster.
Sleepy people usually close their eyes.

questions.stem: A pupil is looking at the teacher but thinking about football. Is the pupil listening attentively?
options: Yes, because they are looking at the teacher
No, because their mind is on something else
No, because they are sitting down
hints: Attentive listening requires both eyes and mind.
Thinking about football means the mind is distracted.
questions.explanation: The pupil is not listening attentively because their mind is on football, even though their eyes are on the teacher.
misconceptions: Looking at the teacher is not enough if the mind is elsewhere.
Being quiet does not mean listening attentively.
Sitting down does not guarantee listening.

questions.stem: Two pupils are listening to a story. Pupil A nods and smiles at the funny parts. Pupil B looks around and plays with a toy. Who is listening attentively?
options: Pupil A, because they respond to the story
Pupil B, because they are quiet
hints: Pupil A responds to the story.
Pupil B is distracted by a toy.
questions.explanation: Pupil A is listening attentively because they nod and smile at the funny parts, showing they are following the story.
misconceptions: Pupil B is not quiet in the right way; they are distracted.
Pupil B is not listening attentively.

questions.stem: During a conversation, your friend is telling you about her holiday. What should you do to show attentive listening?
options: Look at her, nod and ask questions
hints: Attentive listening means focusing on the speaker.
Ask questions to show interest.
questions.explanation: You should look at her, nod and ask questions to show you are listening attentively to her story.
misconceptions: Looking at your phone shows distraction.

questions.stem: In some cultures, looking an elder directly in the eye may be considered disrespectful. What does this tell us about eye contact?
options: Eye contact is always the same everywhere
Eye contact rules can differ across cultures and contexts
You should never look at anyone
hints: Different cultures have different rules.
What is polite in one culture may differ in another.
questions.explanation: Eye contact rules can differ across cultures and contexts. What is appropriate depends on the situation and the people involved.
misconceptions: Eye contact is not always the same everywhere.
Looking at people is normal in many contexts.
Eye contact is important in many situations.

questions.stem: A pupil is listening to a speaker but keeps checking the time. What does this behaviour likely show?
options: The pupil is distracted or eager to leave
hints: Checking the time usually means waiting for something to end.
It is a sign of distraction.
questions.explanation: Checking the time during a talk likely shows the pupil is distracted or eager for the talk to end, not fully attentive.
misconceptions: Checking the time does not show interest.
It is a sign of distraction, not attention.
Taking notes is different from checking the time.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.6.2: Demonstrate positive listening and viewing attitudes and behaviour by showing attentiveness and understanding
indicator.objective: Listen and view for the entire duration of a text, a speech, a presentation, a video etc.

skills.description: Recognise the importance of listening/watching for the whole duration without distraction
Recall key information from a text, speech, presentation or video heard/viewed
Identify the purpose of listening/viewing (to learn, to enjoy, to follow instructions)

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: You can stop listening once you know the topic
Listening and viewing are separate skills
If you missed something, it wasn't important

questions.stem: Why should you listen to the whole of a speech?
options: So you don't miss important information
So you can talk to your friend
hints: Important information can come at any time.
If you stop listening, you might miss something.
questions.explanation: You should listen to the whole speech so you don't miss important information that may come at any point.
misconceptions: Listening is not about finishing quickly.
Talking to a friend is a distraction.

questions.stem: What should you do while watching an educational video?
options: Watch and listen for the whole duration
hints: Educational videos have information throughout.
Pay attention to the whole video.
questions.explanation: You should watch and listen to the whole educational video to get all the information.
misconceptions: Watching only the beginning means missing information.
Playing with your phone is distracting.
Talking to a friend is distracting.

questions.stem: After listening to a story, what should you be able to do?
options: Tell the main events of the story
hints: Good listening helps you remember.
You should be able to retell the main events.
questions.explanation: After listening to a story, you should be able to tell the main events because you listened attentively.
misconceptions: Good listening helps you remember, not forget.
You should remember more than just the title.
You should remember more than the first word.

questions.stem: Why do we listen to the teacher giving instructions?
hints: Instructions tell you what to do.
Listening helps you follow instructions.
questions.explanation: We listen to the teacher giving instructions so we can learn what to do and follow the instructions correctly.
misconceptions: Enjoying the voice is not the main purpose.
Listening is not to pass the time.
Talking to friends is a distraction.

questions.stem: A teacher reads a short text about malaria. What should you be able to do after listening?
hints: Good listening helps you remember facts.
The text is about malaria.
