questions.explanation: After listening to the text about malaria, you should be able to recall key facts about malaria.
misconceptions: Good listening helps you remember, not forget.
You should remember more than the title.
The teacher's name is not the point of the lesson.

questions.stem: A pupil stops listening after the first minute of a ten-minute presentation. What is likely to happen?
options: They will miss important information from the rest of the presentation
hints: The presentation lasts ten minutes.
Important information can come later.
questions.explanation: If a pupil stops listening after the first minute, they will miss important information from the remaining nine minutes.
misconceptions: They will not remember everything if they stop listening.
They will not understand better if they stop listening.
Missing information does change their understanding.

questions.stem: Why would you listen to a story on the radio?
options: To be entertained and to follow the story
To learn how to repair a car
To find out the weather forecast only
hints: Stories are for enjoyment.
You listen to follow the events.
questions.explanation: You listen to a story on the radio to be entertained and to follow the events of the story.
misconceptions: Stories are not about repairing cars.
The weather forecast is a different type of broadcast.
Advertisements are not the main purpose of a story.

questions.stem: A video shows how to wash your hands properly. What key information should you remember?
hints: The video teaches a process.
Remember the steps.
questions.explanation: You should remember the steps for washing hands properly because that is the key information in the video.
misconceptions: The name of the video is not the key information.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sign that you are NOT listening for the entire duration?
options: Looking at the speaker and nodding
Looking out of the window during the speech
hints: Looking out of the window shows distraction.
Good listening means paying attention to the speaker.
questions.explanation: Looking out of the window during the speech is a sign that you are not listening for the entire duration.
misconceptions: Looking and nodding are signs of good listening.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of listening to a news broadcast?
hints: News is about what is happening.
It informs us about current events.
questions.explanation: The purpose of listening to a news broadcast is to learn about current events.
misconceptions: Jokes are for comedy shows, not news.
Cooking shows teach cooking, not news.

questions.stem: Your teacher plays an audio recording of a story. What should you do to understand it well?
options: Listen to the entire recording carefully
Listen to the first few seconds and stop
Talk to your friend during the recording
hints: The whole story is important.
Listen carefully from start to finish.
questions.explanation: To understand the story well, you should listen to the entire recording carefully.
misconceptions: Stopping early means missing part of the story.
Covering your ears blocks the sound.

questions.stem: A teacher reads a passage about the causes of malaria. Three causes are mentioned: dirty water, mosquito bites and poor sanitation. Which of these was NOT mentioned?
hints: Think about what causes malaria.
Eating too much sugar is not a cause of malaria.
questions.explanation: Eating too much sugar was NOT mentioned as a cause of malaria. Dirty water, mosquito bites and poor sanitation were mentioned.

questions.stem: A pupil listens to a speech by the President. What is the main purpose of listening to this speech?
options: To hear the President's message about the nation
hints: The President speaks about national issues.
The purpose is to hear the message.
questions.explanation: The main purpose of listening to the President's speech is to hear the President's message about the nation.
misconceptions: The President's speech is not music.
It is not a comedy show.

questions.stem: During a video presentation, the teacher pauses and asks a question about what was just shown. Why is it important to have watched attentively?
options: So you can answer the question correctly
So you can ask the teacher to repeat
So you can leave the class
So you can talk to your friend
hints: The teacher will ask about what was shown.
Attentive watching helps you answer.
questions.explanation: It is important to watch attentively so you can answer the teacher's question about what was shown.
misconceptions: Asking the teacher to repeat is not the goal.
Leaving the class is not the goal.
Talking to a friend is not the goal.

questions.stem: A presentation explains three ways to save water at home. Which of these is likely one of the ways?
options: Turning off the tap when not in use
hints: Saving water means not wasting it.
Turning off the tap saves water.
questions.explanation: Turning off the tap when not in use is a way to save water at home.
misconceptions: Leaving the tap running wastes water.
Wasting water is the opposite of saving water.

questions.stem: A video about climate change mentions three effects: rising temperatures, floods and drought. A pupil remembers only rising temperatures and floods. What did the pupil miss?
hints: The pupil remembered two out of three effects.
The third effect is drought.
questions.explanation: The pupil missed drought. They remembered rising temperatures and floods but forgot the third effect.

questions.stem: Two pupils listen to the same speech. Pupil A listens to understand the message. Pupil B listens only to criticise the speaker's accent. Who will benefit more from the speech?
options: Pupil A, because they are focused on understanding the message
Pupil B, because they are paying attention to details
hints: The purpose of a speech is to convey a message.
Pupil A is focused on the message.
questions.explanation: Pupil A will benefit more because they are focused on understanding the message of the speech, not on superficial details.
misconceptions: Criticising accent is not the purpose of listening.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.6.3: Use knowledge of language and communicative skills to participate in conversation
indicator.objective: Engage in collaborative conversation on topics such as myself, family, personalities etc. with peers

skills.description: Describe oneself (name, appearance, likes/dislikes) using descriptive words
Describe a family member using relevant vocabulary (name, age, appearance, character)
Talk about a favourite personality (sports, music, politics) and their characteristics
Participate in a collaborative conversation with peers on a given topic

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Describing yourself means only saying your name
Descriptive words are only for appearance

questions.stem: When you describe yourself, which of these should you include?
options: Your name and what you look like
hints: A good self-description includes more than your name.
Include what you look like and what you like.
questions.explanation: When describing yourself, you should include your name, what you look like, and your likes and dislikes.
misconceptions: Only your name is too short.
Your friend's name is not about you.
Your teacher's name is not about you.

questions.stem: Which of these words describes what someone looks like?
hints: One word describes physical appearance.
Tall is about height.
questions.explanation: 'Tall' describes physical appearance. Honest, happy and kind describe character or feelings.

questions.stem: Which of these is a family member?
hints: Family members are related to you.
A sister is part of your family.
questions.explanation: Your sister is a family member because you are related to her.
misconceptions: Your teacher is not a family member.
Your friend is not a family member.
Your neighbour is not a family member.

questions.stem: Which of these is a personality people might admire?
hints: Personalities are people others look up to.
Asamoah Gyan is a famous footballer.
questions.explanation: Asamoah Gyan is a famous footballer and a personality many people admire.
misconceptions: A stranger on the street is not a known personality.
Someone you don't know is not a personality to you.
A person with no name is not a recognised personality.

questions.stem: Which sentence best describes a pupil named Ama?
options: Ama is a girl in Basic 4. She is tall and has short hair. She likes reading.
hints: A good description includes several details.
The first option includes name, class, appearance and likes.
questions.explanation: The first option is the best description because it includes Ama's name, class, appearance and likes.
misconceptions: Ama is a girl, not a boy.

questions.stem: Which sentence best describes your brother?
options: He is tall, has short hair and likes football
hints: A good description includes appearance and interests.
The first option includes height, hair and likes.
questions.explanation: The first option is the best description because it includes appearance (tall, short hair) and interests (football).
misconceptions: 'He is a person' is too general.
'He is there' does not describe him.
'He is my brother' just states the relationship.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'My favourite personality is a musician. She sings well and is always happy.' What is the personality's profession?
hints: The pupil says the person sings.
A person who sings is a musician.
questions.explanation: The personality's profession is musician because the pupil says she sings well.

questions.stem: Which of these is a good way to start a conversation about yourself?
options: 'Hello, my name is Kofi. I am in Basic 4.'
hints: A good opening is friendly and shares information.
Introduce yourself politely.
questions.explanation: 'Hello, my name is Kofi. I am in Basic 4' is a friendly and appropriate way to start a conversation about yourself.
misconceptions: 'I don't want to talk' is unfriendly.

questions.stem: Which of these best describes your mother?
options: She is kind, works hard and takes care of us
hints: A good description includes character and what she does.
The first option includes kindness, hard work and care.
questions.explanation: The first option is the best description because it includes character (kind), work (hardworking) and role (takes care of us).
misconceptions: 'She is a woman' is too general.
'She is my mother' just states the relationship.
'She is there' does not describe her.

questions.stem: When talking about a favourite personality, what should you include?
options: Their name, what they do, and why you like them
hints: A good description includes several details.
Mention who they are, what they do and why you like them.
questions.explanation: When talking about a favourite personality, you should include their name, what they do and why you like them.
misconceptions: Only their name is too little information.
Only their clothes does not describe the person.
Only their car does not describe the person.

questions.stem: In a group conversation, what should you do when a classmate is speaking?
options: Listen to them and wait for your turn
hints: Good conversation involves listening and taking turns.
Wait for your turn to speak.
questions.explanation: In a group conversation, you should listen to your classmate and wait for your turn to speak.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT part of describing yourself?
hints: Describing yourself is about you, not your friend.
Your friend's house is not about you.
questions.explanation: Your friend's house is NOT part of describing yourself. Describing yourself includes your name, appearance and likes/dislikes.
misconceptions: Your name is part of self-description.
Likes and dislikes are part of self-description.
What you look like is part of self-description.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'My favourite personality is the Minister of Education. I like her because she works hard to improve schools.' What is the pupil's reason for liking this personality?
options: She works hard to improve schools
hints: The pupil gives a reason.
The reason is about improving schools.
questions.explanation: The pupil likes the Minister because she works hard to improve schools.
misconceptions: The pupil does not mention appearance.
The pupil does not mention a car.
The pupil does not mention clothes.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'My sister is short, has a round face and loves to sing.' What is missing from this description?
hints: The description mentions height, face and hobby.
What about her name?
questions.explanation: The description is missing the sister's name. It mentions height (short), face (round) and hobby (singing).

questions.stem: In a group conversation about favourite personalities, a classmate disagrees with you. What should you do?
options: Listen to their opinion and respond politely
hints: Disagreements should be handled politely.
Listen and respond respectfully.
questions.explanation: You should listen to your classmate's opinion and respond politely, even if you disagree.
misconceptions: Leaving the group is not helpful.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'I am tall. I like rice. I have two brothers.' What is one thing missing from this self-description?
hints: The description mentions height, likes and siblings.
What about their name?
questions.explanation: The description is missing the pupil's name. It mentions height (tall), likes (rice) and siblings (two brothers).

questions.stem: Which of these is the best description of your father for a conversation with a classmate?
options: My father is tall and has a beard. He is a farmer. He is hardworking and kind.
hints: A good description includes appearance, work and character.
The first option includes height, beard, work and character.
questions.explanation: The first option is the best because it includes appearance (tall, beard), work (farmer) and character (hardworking, kind).
misconceptions: 'My father is a man' is too general.
'My father is there' does not describe him.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'My favourite personality is my grandmother. She is not famous, but she is kind, wise and always helps people in our community.' Is it appropriate to call her a 'personality'?
options: Yes, because anyone you admire and who has good qualities can be a personality to you
No, because she is not on TV
No, because she is not rich
hints: Personalities can be people you admire.
Fame is not the only thing that makes someone a personality.
questions.explanation: Yes, it is appropriate. Anyone you admire and who has good qualities can be a personality to you, even if they are not famous.
misconceptions: Being on TV is not the only way to be a personality.
Age does not determine if someone is a personality.
Wealth is not required to be a personality.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.6.3: Use knowledge of language and communicative skills to participate in conversation
indicator.objective: Demonstrate turn taking in conversation on different topics and speak audibly, and express thoughts and feelings clearly

skills.description: Recognise and demonstrate taking turns in a conversation (not interrupting, waiting, responding)
Speak clearly and loudly enough to be heard by others
Express thoughts and feelings clearly using appropriate words
Participate in a conversation demonstrating turn-taking, audibility and clarity

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Speaking loudly is the same as speaking clearly
Feelings should not be expressed in conversation

questions.stem: What does 'turn taking' mean in a conversation?
options: Everyone speaks at the same time
Waiting for your turn to speak and listening when others speak
hints: Turn taking is about sharing the conversation.
Wait for your turn and listen to others.
questions.explanation: Turn taking means waiting for your turn to speak and listening when others are speaking.
misconceptions: Speaking at the same time is not turn taking.
Only one person speaking is not a conversation.
Interrupting is the opposite of turn taking.

questions.stem: What should you do when a friend is speaking to you?
options: Listen and wait for your turn
hints: Good conversation means listening.
Wait for your friend to finish.
questions.explanation: You should listen and wait for your turn when a friend is speaking to you.

questions.stem: In a conversation, who should speak first?
options: Anyone who has something to say, taking turns politely
hints: Conversations involve sharing.
Anyone can speak, but take turns politely.
questions.explanation: In a conversation, anyone who has something to say can speak, but people should take turns politely.
misconceptions: Height does not determine who speaks first.
Age does not always determine who speaks first.

questions.stem: What does it mean to speak audibly?
options: Speak loudly enough to be heard
hints: Audibly means you can be heard.
Speak clearly and loudly enough.
questions.explanation: To speak audibly means to speak loudly and clearly enough to be heard by others.
misconceptions: Speaking very quietly is not audible.
Whispering is not audible to a group.
Mumbling is unclear and not audible.

questions.stem: Which of these is a feeling?
hints: A feeling is an emotion.
Happy is an emotion.
questions.explanation: Happy is a feeling. Running, eating and sleeping are actions.

questions.stem: How can you express that you are happy?
hints: Use words to express feelings.
Say how you feel.
questions.explanation: You can express that you are happy by saying 'I am happy'.
misconceptions: Saying nothing does not express feeling.
Looking angry shows anger, not happiness.
Walking away does not express happiness.

questions.stem: Ama is speaking. Kojo wants to speak. What should Kojo do?
options: Wait for Ama to finish, then speak
hints: Good conversation means taking turns.
Wait for Ama to finish.
questions.explanation: Kojo should wait for Ama to finish speaking, then take his turn.
misconceptions: Walking away is not good conversation.

questions.stem: Which of these shows good turn taking?
options: Listening to your friend and responding after they finish
Talking while your friend is talking
hints: Good turn taking means listening and responding.
Wait for your friend to finish.
questions.explanation: Listening to your friend and responding after they finish shows good turn taking.
misconceptions: Talking while others talk is poor turn taking.

questions.stem: In a group conversation, how can you show you want to speak without interrupting?
options: Raise your hand or wait for a pause
hints: There are polite ways to signal you want to speak.
Raise your hand or wait for a pause.
questions.explanation: You can raise your hand or wait for a pause to show you want to speak without interrupting.

questions.stem: A pupil speaks so quietly that no one can hear. What should they do?
hints: If no one can hear, the speaker needs to increase volume.
Speak louder.
questions.explanation: The pupil should speak louder so that others can hear.

questions.stem: Which of these helps you speak clearly?
options: Pronouncing words properly and at a good volume
hints: Clear speech means pronouncing words properly.
Speak at a good volume.
questions.explanation: Pronouncing words properly at a good volume helps you speak clearly.
misconceptions: Turning away makes it harder to hear.

questions.stem: A friend tells you they are sad. How can you express your care?
options: Say 'I am sorry you feel sad. Can I help?'
hints: Expressing care means showing kindness.
Say something supportive.
questions.explanation: Saying 'I am sorry you feel sad. Can I help?' expresses care and kindness.

questions.stem: Which sentence clearly expresses a thought?
options: I think our class should plant more trees.
hints: A clear thought is a complete idea.
The first option expresses a complete thought.
questions.explanation: 'I think our class should plant more trees' clearly expresses a complete thought.
misconceptions: 'I don't know' does not express a thought.

questions.stem: Two pupils are in a conversation. Pupil A asks a question. What should Pupil B do before speaking?
options: Listen to the question and then answer
hints: Good conversation means listening before responding.
Listen to the question, then answer.
questions.explanation: Pupil B should listen to the question and then answer before taking their turn.
misconceptions: Answering before the question is finished is interrupting.
Changing the topic avoids the question.

questions.stem: A pupil is presenting in class but speaks too softly. The teacher asks them to speak audibly. What should the pupil change?
hints: Audibly means loud enough to be heard.
The pupil needs to increase volume.
questions.explanation: The pupil should increase volume — speak louder so the class can hear.
misconceptions: Changing the topic does not make speech louder.
Sitting down does not help volume.
Changing language does not affect volume.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to express that they disagree with a classmate politely. What should they say?
options: 'I see your point, but I think differently because...'
hints: Polite disagreement acknowledges the other person.
Start by recognising their point, then explain yours.
questions.explanation: 'I see your point, but I think differently because...' expresses disagreement politely.
misconceptions: 'You are wrong' is blunt and rude.
'That is a stupid idea' is rude.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'I felt nervous when I had to speak in front of the class.' What feeling is the pupil expressing?
hints: The pupil says 'nervous'.
Nervousness is a feeling of being worried or scared.
questions.explanation: The pupil is expressing nervousness — a feeling of worry or fear about speaking in front of the class.

questions.stem: During a conversation, a pupil says: 'I feel upset when people don't listen to me.' What is the best way for the other pupils to respond?
options: Tell the pupil to stop talking
hints: The pupil is expressing a feeling.
Respond with understanding and kindness.
questions.explanation: The best response is to apologise and listen more carefully, showing respect for the pupil's feelings.
misconceptions: Telling them to stop is disrespectful.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.6.3: Use knowledge of language and communicative skills to participate in conversation
indicator.objective: Ask relevant questions to find out the opinion of others about a given topic

skills.description: Recognise whether a question is relevant to a given topic
Form questions that ask for someone's opinion
Ask follow-up questions based on a previous answer
Ask relevant questions in a real conversation to find out others' opinions

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Yes/No questions are the best way to find opinions
Questions should be about facts, not opinions

questions.stem: The topic is 'My Favourite Food.' Which question is relevant?
hints: The topic is about food.
Choose the question that asks about food.
questions.explanation: 'What is your favourite food?' is relevant because it asks about the topic (food).
misconceptions: Favourite colour is about colour, not food.
Where you live is about location.

questions.stem: Which question asks for someone's opinion?
options: What do you think about our school?
What is the name of our school?
How many pupils are in our school?
hints: Opinion questions ask what someone thinks or feels.
'What do you think' asks for an opinion.
questions.explanation: 'What do you think about our school?' asks for an opinion. The other questions ask for facts.
misconceptions: The school name is a fact.
The number of pupils is a fact.

questions.stem: Which question word is best for asking someone's opinion?
hints: 'What do you think?' is a common opinion question.
What asks about thoughts and ideas.
questions.explanation: 'What' is often used for opinion questions (e.g. 'What do you think about...?').

questions.stem: The topic is 'Our Class Trip.' Which question is NOT relevant?
hints: The topic is about the class trip.
Which question is not about the trip?
questions.explanation: 'What is your favourite colour?' is not relevant because it is not about the class trip.
misconceptions: Where we went is about the trip.
What we enjoyed is about the trip.
What we learned is about the trip.

questions.stem: Your friend says: 'I like football.' What is a good follow-up question?
hints: A follow-up question relates to what was just said.
Ask more about football.
questions.explanation: 'Why do you like football?' is a good follow-up because it asks for more about what your friend said.
misconceptions: Asking their name is not related to football.
Asking where they live is not related.
Asking their age is not related.

questions.stem: Your classmate says: 'I think our school needs a new library.' What is the best follow-up question?
options: Why do you think we need a new library?
What did you eat for breakfast?
hints: The follow-up should be about the library.
Ask why they think that.
questions.explanation: 'Why do you think we need a new library?' is the best follow-up because it asks for more about their opinion on the library.

questions.stem: You want to know how your friend feels about homework. Which question should you ask?
options: How do you feel about homework?
What time do you do homework?
hints: The question should ask for feelings/opinion.
'How do you feel about' asks for opinion.
questions.explanation: 'How do you feel about homework?' asks for your friend's opinion about homework.

questions.stem: The topic is 'Healthy Eating.' Which question is most relevant?
options: What do you think about eating fruits every day?
What is your favourite football team?
How many brothers do you have?
What is the capital of Ghana?
hints: Healthy eating is about food choices.
Which question is about food and health?
questions.explanation: 'What do you think about eating fruits every day?' is most relevant because it is about healthy eating.
misconceptions: Football is not about healthy eating.
Brothers are not about healthy eating.
The capital city is not about healthy eating.

questions.stem: Which of these is an opinion question?
options: Do you think school should start later?
How many subjects do you study?
hints: Opinion questions ask what someone thinks.
'Do you think' asks for an opinion.
questions.explanation: 'Do you think school should start later?' is an opinion question because it asks for someone's view.
misconceptions: School start time is a fact.
Number of subjects is a fact.

questions.stem: The topic is 'Sports Day.' Which question would help you find out someone's opinion?
options: What did you enjoy most about Sports Day?
hints: An opinion question asks what someone thinks or enjoyed.
'What did you enjoy most' asks for opinion.
questions.explanation: 'What did you enjoy most about Sports Day?' asks for an opinion about Sports Day.
misconceptions: When is a fact about time.
Where is a fact about place.
How many is a fact about number.

questions.stem: Your friend says: 'I don't like waking up early.' What is the best follow-up question?
options: Why don't you like waking up early?
What time do you go to bed?
hints: The follow-up should relate to waking up early.
Ask why they don't like it.
questions.explanation: 'Why don't you like waking up early?' is the best follow-up because it asks for more about their opinion.
misconceptions: Asking their name is not related.
Where they sleep is not about the opinion.
Bedtime is related but not as good a follow-up as 'why'.

questions.stem: A classmate says: 'I think reading is fun.' What follow-up question would help you understand their opinion better?
options: What kind of books do you enjoy reading?
hints: The follow-up should be about reading.
Ask what books they enjoy.
questions.explanation: 'What kind of books do you enjoy reading?' is a good follow-up because it asks for more about their opinion on reading.
misconceptions: Colour is not related to reading.

questions.stem: The topic is 'The Weather Today.' Which question is LEAST relevant?
options: Do you think it will rain later?
How does the weather make you feel?
What is your favourite subject in school?
hints: The topic is about the weather.
Which question is not about weather?
questions.explanation: 'What is your favourite subject in school?' is least relevant because it is about school subjects, not the weather.

questions.stem: A classmate says: 'I think we should have more breaks at school.' What is the best follow-up question to understand their opinion?
options: Why do you think we need more breaks?
Where do you go for break?
Who do you play with at break?
hints: Ask why they think that.
The follow-up should explore their opinion.
questions.explanation: 'Why do you think we need more breaks?' is the best follow-up because it asks for the reason behind their opinion.
misconceptions: Where they go for break is a fact, not an opinion follow-up.
Who they play with is a fact.

questions.stem: Your friend says: 'I don't like eating vegetables.' What follow-up question would help you understand why?
hints: The question should ask why they don't like vegetables.
'Why' asks for a reason.
questions.explanation: 'Why don't you like vegetables?' directly asks for the reason behind their opinion.
misconceptions: 'What vegetables have you tried' is related but doesn't ask why.
'Do you like fruits' is about a different food.
Favourite food is related but doesn't ask why.

questions.stem: A pupil is talking to a friend about 'Life in the Village.' Which set of questions is MOST relevant?
options: What do you like about village life? / What is the best thing about living there?
What is your favourite colour? / How old are you?
Where is your school? / How many pupils are in your class?
What do you eat for breakfast? / When do you sleep?
hints: The topic is about life in the village.
Which questions explore opinions about village life?
questions.explanation: The first set is most relevant because both questions ask for opinions about village life.
misconceptions: Colour and age are not about village life.
School location and class size are about school, not village life.
Breakfast and sleep are daily routines but not directly about village life.

questions.stem: A classmate says: 'I think the school rules are too strict.' Which TWO follow-up questions would best help you understand their opinion?
options: Which rules do you think are too strict? / Why do you feel they are too strict?
What is your name? / Where do you live?
Do you like school? / What is your favourite subject?
How old are you? / Who is your teacher?
hints: The follow-ups should be about the school rules.
Ask which rules and why.
questions.explanation: 'Which rules do you think are too strict?' and 'Why do you feel they are too strict?' are the best follow-ups because they explore the opinion in depth.
misconceptions: Name and location are not about rules.
School liking and favourite subject are not about rules.
Age and teacher are not about rules.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Construct meaning from texts based on knowledge of stress, rhythm and intonation

skills.description: Identify how stress on a word changes or emphasises meaning in a sentence
Recognise rhythm patterns in spoken language
Identify how intonation (rising/falling) conveys meaning
Construct meaning from a spoken text using stress, rhythm and intonation cues

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Rhythm is the same as speed

questions.stem: When we put stress on a word, we ___.
hints: Stress is about emphasis.
Stressed words are said with more force.
questions.explanation: When we put stress on a word, we say it with more emphasis or force.
misconceptions: Softness is the opposite of stress.
Speed is not the same as stress.

questions.stem: What is rhythm in spoken language?
options: The pattern of beats or stresses
The colour of the speaker's clothes
hints: Rhythm is about beats.
We can clap the rhythm of a sentence.
questions.explanation: Rhythm in spoken language is the pattern of beats or stresses in speech.
misconceptions: Clothing has nothing to do with rhythm.

questions.stem: What does a rising intonation usually show?
hints: Your voice goes up at the end.
Rising intonation often signals a yes/no question.
questions.explanation: A rising intonation usually shows a question, especially yes/no questions.
misconceptions: Greetings can have varied intonation, not specifically rising.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'I want the RED pen', which word is stressed?
hints: The stressed word is written in capital letters.
It tells us which pen is wanted.
questions.explanation: The word 'RED' is stressed to emphasise which pen is wanted.

questions.stem: What does a falling intonation usually show?
hints: Your voice goes down at the end.
Statements usually end with falling intonation.
questions.explanation: A falling intonation usually shows a statement or a command.
misconceptions: Surprise can be shown through different intonation.
Confusion is not specifically shown by falling intonation.

questions.stem: Say the sentence: 'I did not steal the book.' If you stress the word 'I', what does it mean?
options: Someone else stole the book, not me
hints: Stressing 'I' emphasises the person.
It means 'I' am not the one who stole it.
questions.explanation: Stressing 'I' in 'I did not steal the book' emphasises that the speaker is not the one who stole it — someone else did.
misconceptions: Stressing 'I' is not about stealing something else.
It is not about not stealing anything.
It is not about the book not being stolen.

questions.stem: If you stress the word 'book' in 'I did not steal the book', what does it mean?
options: I stole something else, but not the book
hints: Stressing 'book' emphasises the object.
It means the object stolen was not the book.
questions.explanation: Stressing 'book' means the speaker may have stolen something, but not the book.
misconceptions: Stressing 'book' does not mean nothing was stolen.
It does not mean someone else stole the book.
It implies the book was not stolen, not that it was.

questions.stem: Clap the rhythm of 'The cat sat on the mat.' How many beats (claps) are there?
hints: Clap once for each word.
Count the words in the sentence.
questions.explanation: There are 6 words: The (1) cat (2) sat (3) on (4) the (5) mat (6). So there are 6 beats.

questions.stem: A speaker says 'You are coming?' with a rising voice. What does this show?
hints: Rising intonation often shows a question.
The speaker wants confirmation.
questions.explanation: A rising voice on 'You are coming?' shows the speaker is asking a question to confirm.
misconceptions: Anger is not necessarily shown by rising intonation.

questions.stem: A speaker says 'Sit down.' with a falling voice. What does this show?
hints: Falling intonation often shows a command.
The speaker is telling someone to sit.
questions.explanation: A falling voice on 'Sit down.' shows a command.
misconceptions: Requests are usually more polite and may have different intonation.
Jokes are not shown by falling intonation.

questions.stem: Which sentence has the same rhythm pattern as 'I like to eat rice'?
hints: Count the beats in 'I like to eat rice' — 4 beats.
Find the sentence with 4 beats.
questions.explanation: 'I like to eat rice' has 4 beats. 'We play football' also has 4 beats: We (1) play (2) foot (3) ball (4).
misconceptions: 'She went to the market' has 5 beats.
'The sun is shining' has 4 beats but the rhythm pattern differs.
'He is a teacher' has 4 beats but the stress pattern differs.

questions.stem: A teacher says 'Well done!' with a happy, rising tone. What does the tone tell you?
hints: A happy, rising tone shows positive feeling.
'Well done' is praise.
questions.explanation: The happy, rising tone tells you the teacher is pleased and praising you.
misconceptions: Anger would have a sharp, loud tone.
Sadness would have a low, slow tone.
Tiredness would have a slow, flat tone.

questions.stem: Say the sentence: 'I never said she stole my money.' Which word would you stress to show that someone else said it, not you?
hints: Stressing 'I' contrasts with someone else.
It means 'I' didn't say it — someone else did.
questions.explanation: Stressing 'I' shows that someone else said it, not you.
misconceptions: 'never' shows you didn't say it at all.
'she' shifts emphasis to the person who stole.

questions.stem: A speaker says 'You're going to the party.' with a falling intonation. Another speaker says 'You're going to the party?' with a rising intonation. What is the difference?
options: The first is a statement; the second is a question
The first is a question; the second is a statement
hints: Falling intonation = statement.
Rising intonation = question.
questions.explanation: The falling intonation makes the first a statement. The rising intonation makes the second a question.
misconceptions: Only the second is a question.
Only the first is a statement.
The intonations are different, so the meanings differ.

questions.stem: A storyteller reads a scary part of a story slowly with a low voice. How does this help you understand the story?
options: It makes the story feel suspenseful and scary
hints: Slow pace and low voice can create suspense.
Think about how scary stories are told.
questions.explanation: Reading slowly with a low voice creates suspense and makes the scary part feel more intense.
misconceptions: A slow, low voice is not funny.
It makes the story interesting, not boring.

questions.stem: A radio presenter says: 'The president will visit KUMASI tomorrow.' Why might the presenter stress 'Kumasi'?
options: To emphasise the place the president is visiting
To show the president is angry
hints: Stressing a place name draws attention to it.
It tells listeners where the visit will happen.
questions.explanation: The presenter stresses 'Kumasi' to emphasise the place the president is visiting.
misconceptions: Stress on a place doesn't show anger.

questions.stem: A pupil says 'Sorry' with a rising intonation. Another pupil says 'Sorry' with a flat intonation. Which pupil sounds more sincere?
options: The one with the rising intonation
The one with the flat intonation
hints: A flat tone can sound uninterested.
A rising tone can sound more expressive and sincere.
questions.explanation: The pupil with the rising intonation sounds more sincere because the flat tone can sound careless or uninterested.
misconceptions: A flat tone often sounds less sincere.
Both do not sound equally sincere.
One sounds more sincere than the other.

questions.stem: A teacher reads a story and changes her voice for each character. How does this help the learners?
options: It helps them follow who is speaking and understand the characters
hints: Different voices help distinguish characters.
Voice changes add meaning.
questions.explanation: Changing voice for each character helps learners know who is speaking and understand the characters better.
misconceptions: Voice changes do not make the story longer.
They make the story more interesting, not boring.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Make connections with events in narrative texts

skills.description: Recall the sequence of events in a narrative text heard or read
Connect events to one another (cause and effect, before/after)
Connect events in a narrative to personal experiences or other texts

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: A connection is just saying 'I liked it'
Cause and effect are the same

questions.stem: In the story 'The Hawk and the Hen', what happened first?
hints: Think about how the story began.
Hen had chicks before Hawk came.
questions.explanation: The story begins with Hen having chicks. This is the first event.
misconceptions: Hawk taking a chick happens later.
The deal comes after Hawk sees the chicks.
Hen begging comes after Hawk sees the chicks.

questions.stem: In the story of 'The Tortoise and the Birds', who invited the tortoise to the feast?
hints: The tortoise was invited by birds.
The story is called 'The Tortoise and the Birds'.
questions.explanation: The birds invited the tortoise to the feast in the sky.
misconceptions: The lion did not invite the tortoise.
The elephant is not in the story.
The monkey is not in the story.

questions.stem: In a story, a boy forgot his umbrella and it rained. What happened because he forgot his umbrella?
hints: If you forget an umbrella and it rains, what happens?
You get wet.
questions.explanation: Because the boy forgot his umbrella and it rained, he got wet.
misconceptions: Without an umbrella in the rain, you get wet.
He would not stay dry without an umbrella.
The story does not say he bought one.
The story does not say he went home.

questions.stem: A story is about a girl who lost her pencil. Have you ever lost something? What connection can you make?
options: I also lost something once and felt sad
hints: A personal connection links the story to your own experience.
Think about a time you lost something.
questions.explanation: A personal connection is when you link the story to your own life — like when you also lost something and felt sad.
misconceptions: Liking pencils is not a personal connection to losing something.
Not liking stories is not a connection.
Having a pencil is not a connection to losing one.

questions.stem: In a story, Ama woke up late, missed the bus and walked to school. What was the last thing that happened?
hints: The last thing is at the end.
After missing the bus, what did she do?
questions.explanation: The last event is that Ama walked to school after missing the bus.

questions.stem: In 'The Hawk and the Hen', why did Hen agree to give Hawk one chick every day?
options: Because she wanted to be friends with Hawk
Because she was afraid Hawk would take all her chicks
Because she had too many chicks
hints: Hen was afraid of Hawk.
The deal was a way to protect most of her chicks.
questions.explanation: Hen agreed to give one chick every day because she was afraid Hawk would take all of them.
misconceptions: She did not want to be friends.
She did not have too many chicks.

questions.stem: In a story, Kojo studied hard for his exam. What is likely to happen because he studied hard?
options: He will not write the exam
hints: Studying hard helps you do well.
Hard work usually leads to good results.
questions.explanation: Because Kojo studied hard, he is likely to pass the exam.
misconceptions: Studying hard does not cause failure.
Studying hard helps you remember, not forget.

questions.stem: A story is about a boy who helped his mother in the kitchen. What personal connection can you make?
options: I also help my mother at home
hints: A connection links the story to your life.
Think about a time you helped someone.
questions.explanation: A good connection is 'I also help my mother at home' because it links the story to your own experience.
misconceptions: Liking cooking shows is not a personal experience.
Not liking kitchens is not helpful.
Having a brother is not related.

questions.stem: In a story: 'Esi went to the market. She bought tomatoes. Then she went home and cooked stew.' What did Esi do after buying tomatoes?
options: She went home and cooked stew
hints: What did she do after the market?
She went home to cook.
questions.explanation: After buying tomatoes, Esi went home and cooked stew.
misconceptions: She did not go to school.

questions.stem: In a story, it rained heavily and the river overflowed. What is the effect of the heavy rain?
hints: Heavy rain fills the river.
The river overflowed because of the rain.
questions.explanation: The effect of the heavy rain is that the river overflowed.
misconceptions: Heavy rain does not dry up a river.
The sun coming out is not an effect of rain.
The wind stopping is not mentioned.

questions.stem: A story is about a pupil who was nervous on the first day of school. What connection can you make?
options: I also felt nervous on my first day
hints: A connection links the story to your feelings.
Have you ever felt nervous on the first day?
questions.explanation: A good connection is 'I also felt nervous on my first day' because it links the story to your own feelings.
misconceptions: Liking school is not a connection to nervousness.
Having a uniform is not related.
Walking to school is not related.

questions.stem: Arrange these events from a story in order: (1) The tortoise fell from the sky. (2) The birds invited the tortoise to a feast. (3) The tortoise tricked the birds. (4) The birds learned a lesson.
hints: Start with the invitation.
The trick comes at the feast.
The fall comes after the trick.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: (2) The birds invited the tortoise, (3) the tortoise tricked the birds, (1) the tortoise fell, (4) the birds learned a lesson.
misconceptions: The trick cannot happen before the invitation.
The fall comes after the trick.
The lesson comes at the end.

questions.stem: In a story, a farmer did not weed his farm. What is the likely effect of this?
hints: Weeds compete with crops for nutrients.
Not weeding leads to poor crop growth.
questions.explanation: The likely effect of not weeding is that weeds choked his crops.
misconceptions: Crops do not grow well without weeding.
The story does not mention selling the farm.

questions.stem: A story is about a boy who shared his lunch with a hungry friend. What connection can you make?
options: I also shared something with a friend once
hints: A connection links the story to your own experience.
Think about a time you shared something.
questions.explanation: A good connection is 'I also shared something with a friend once' because it links the story to a personal experience.
misconceptions: Not liking lunch is not a connection.
Having a friend is not specific enough.
Eating lunch is not related to sharing.

questions.stem: In a story, a girl practised the piano every day. Her friend did not practise. At the concert, the girl played beautifully but her friend made many mistakes. What can you conclude?
hints: Compare the girl who practised with the friend who did not.
Practice leads to better performance.
questions.explanation: You can conclude that practising helps improve performance because the girl who practised played beautifully while her friend who did not practise made mistakes.
misconceptions: The friend did not practise more.
The girl's success was due to practice, not luck.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Recognise and discuss moral lessons in a story

skills.description: Identify the moral lesson in a story
Explain how the characters or events teach the moral lesson
Relate the moral lesson to real-life experiences

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Every story has only one moral
The moral is always stated at the end
A story with a bad character has no moral

questions.stem: A story is about a boy who always told lies. In the end, no one believed him even when he told the truth. What is the moral of the story?
options: People should not listen to others
hints: The boy lost trust because he lied.
The story warns against lying.
questions.explanation: The moral is 'Always tell the truth' because the boy who lied was not believed even when he told the truth.
misconceptions: Lying is shown as bad, not good.
The story is about telling the truth, not about not listening.
Telling lies does not help — it causes problems.

questions.stem: A story is about a tortoise that tricked the birds and took all the food. In the end, the tortoise fell from the sky. What is the moral of the story?
hints: The tortoise tricked the birds and was punished.
The story teaches that trickery leads to trouble.
questions.explanation: The moral is 'Trickery does not pay' because the tortoise was punished for tricking the birds.
misconceptions: The story is not about strength.
Flying is not the main lesson.
Food is not the focus of the moral.

questions.stem: A story is about a hardworking farmer who had a good harvest while a lazy farmer had nothing. What is the moral of the story?
hints: The hardworking farmer succeeded.
The lazy farmer had nothing.
questions.explanation: The moral is 'Hard work is rewarded' because the hardworking farmer had a good harvest while the lazy farmer had nothing.
misconceptions: Farming is not shown as easy.
Lazy people are not shown as happy.

questions.stem: A story is about a girl who shared her food with a hungry friend and later the friend helped her when she was in need. What is the moral?
hints: The girl shared and was later helped.
Kindness comes back to you.
questions.explanation: The moral is 'Kindness is rewarded' because the girl's kindness was returned when she needed help.
misconceptions: Sharing is shown as good, not wasteful.
Food is shown as important for sharing.

questions.stem: A story says: 'The ant worked hard all summer while the grasshopper played. When winter came, the ant had food but the grasshopper had none.' How does this story teach the value of hard work?
options: The ant's hard work saved it from hunger
hints: The ant worked and had food.
The grasshopper played and had nothing.
questions.explanation: The story teaches hard work by showing that the ant's hard work saved it from hunger while the grasshopper's laziness left it with nothing.
misconceptions: The grasshopper did not enjoy the winter.
The ant did not play all summer.

questions.stem: A story is about a boy who helped an old woman cross the road. Later, the old woman gave him a gift. How does the story teach kindness?
options: The boy's kind act was rewarded
The boy helped because he wanted a gift
hints: The boy helped and received a gift.
Kindness is shown through helping.
questions.explanation: The story teaches kindness by showing that the boy's kind act was rewarded.
misconceptions: The story does not say the boy helped for a gift.
The old woman was grateful, not unkind.
The boy helped, he did not refuse.

questions.stem: A story teaches the moral 'Honesty is the best policy.' How can you apply this at school?
options: By telling the truth when you make a mistake
hints: Honesty means telling the truth.
Admitting a mistake is honest.
questions.explanation: You can apply honesty at school by telling the truth when you make a mistake.

questions.stem: A story teaches the moral 'Hard work pays.' How can you apply this at home?
options: By doing your chores without being told
By leaving your work for others
hints: Hard work means doing your tasks.
Doing chores without being told is hardworking.
questions.explanation: You can apply hard work at home by doing your chores without being told.
misconceptions: Watching TV all day is lazy.
Leaving work for others is lazy.

questions.stem: A story is about two friends who quarrelled and stopped talking. Later, one friend apologised and they became friends again. What does this story teach about forgiveness?
hints: The apology restored the friendship.
Forgiveness brings friends back together.
questions.explanation: The story teaches that apologising can heal friendships and restore broken relationships.
misconceptions: Quarrelling is shown as something to resolve.
Apologising is shown as strong, not weak.

questions.stem: A story is about a girl who was patient and eventually succeeded, while her impatient friend gave up. What is the moral of the story?
hints: The patient girl succeeded.
The impatient friend gave up.
questions.explanation: The moral is 'Patience brings success' because the patient girl succeeded while the impatient friend gave up.
misconceptions: Impatience is shown as a weakness.

questions.stem: A story teaches the moral 'Kindness is important.' How can you show kindness to a new pupil in your class?
options: By welcoming them and showing them around
hints: Kindness means being friendly and helpful.
A new pupil needs help and welcome.
questions.explanation: You can show kindness to a new pupil by welcoming them and showing them around the school.

questions.stem: A story says: 'The lion thought he was the strongest animal. He laughed at the mouse. Later, the mouse freed the lion from a trap.' What is the moral?
options: Do not look down on others; even the small can help the great
hints: The lion laughed at the mouse but the mouse saved him.
Small creatures can do big things.
questions.explanation: The moral is 'Do not look down on others; even the small can help the great' because the mouse helped the lion despite being small.
misconceptions: Lions are shown as strong but proud.
Mice are not shown as dangerous.
Strength is not shown as everything.

questions.stem: A story is about a boy who disobeyed his parents and went to the river alone. He got into danger and had to be rescued. How does this story teach obedience?
options: Disobedience led to danger, showing why obeying parents is important
The boy was happy he disobeyed
hints: The boy disobeyed and got into danger.
The story warns against disobedience.
questions.explanation: The story teaches obedience by showing that the boy's disobedience led to danger, which shows why obeying parents is important.
misconceptions: The boy was not happy in the end.
The river was dangerous, not safe.

questions.stem: A story is about a rich man who refused to help a poor neighbour. Later, the rich man lost his wealth and the neighbour helped him. What does this story teach?
options: We should help others because we may need help one day
hints: The rich man refused help but later needed it.
The story teaches that circumstances can change.
questions.explanation: The story teaches that we should help others because we may need help one day.
misconceptions: The story is about one rich man, not all rich people.
The neighbour is shown as kind, not lazy.
The story encourages helping, not refusing.

questions.stem: A story teaches the moral 'Unity is strength.' How can you apply this in your class?
options: By working together with classmates on group tasks
hints: Unity means working together.
Group work shows unity.
questions.explanation: You can apply unity by working together with your classmates on group tasks.
misconceptions: Fighting is the opposite of unity.
Refusing to share is not unity.

questions.stem: A story teaches the moral 'Do not judge others by their appearance.' How can you apply this at school?
options: By treating everyone equally regardless of how they look
By making friends only with well-dressed pupils
By laughing at pupils in old clothes
By ignoring pupils who look different
hints: The moral is about not judging by appearance.
Treat everyone equally.
questions.explanation: You can apply this moral by treating everyone equally regardless of how they look.
misconceptions: Choosing friends by appearance is judging.
Laughing at clothes is judging by appearance.
Ignoring pupils who look different is judging.

questions.stem: A story is about a pupil who always helped others and was loved by everyone. Another pupil was selfish and had no friends. What is the moral?
options: Helping is a waste of time
hints: The kind pupil was loved.
The selfish pupil had no friends.
questions.explanation: The moral is 'Kindness wins friends' because the kind pupil was loved while the selfish pupil had no friends.

questions.stem: A story is about a pupil who found a wallet full of money and returned it to the owner. The owner rewarded him. What moral does this teach, and how can you apply it if you find something valuable at school?
options: Honesty is rewarded — return lost items to their owner or a teacher
Hide the item so no one sees
hints: The pupil was rewarded for returning the wallet.
Honesty means returning what is not yours.
questions.explanation: The story teaches that honesty is rewarded. If you find something valuable at school, you should return it to its owner or give it to a teacher.
misconceptions: Giving it to a friend is not returning it to the owner.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Use background knowledge to aid in understanding and building new knowledge while listening to narrative texts

skills.description: Identify what you already know about a topic before listening
Link new information from a text to existing knowledge
Identify new information learned from a text

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: You don't need prior knowledge to understand a story
New knowledge is always better than old knowledge
If you don't know the topic, you can't understand

questions.stem: Before listening to a story about a market, what is something you already know about markets?
options: Markets are places where people buy and sell things
Markets are places where people sleep
Markets are found in the sky
hints: Think about what happens at a market.
People go there to buy and sell.
questions.explanation: You already know that markets are places where people buy and sell things. This background knowledge helps you understand a story about a market.
misconceptions: People do not sleep in markets.
Markets are for people, not just animals.
Markets are on land, not in the sky.

questions.stem: Before listening to a story about a farmer, what is something you already know about farming?
options: Farming involves growing crops and rearing animals
Farming is done in the sky
hints: Think about what farmers do.
Farmers grow crops.
questions.explanation: You already know that farming involves growing crops and rearing animals. This helps you understand a story about a farmer.
misconceptions: Farming is on land, not in the sky.
Farmers work, they do not only sleep.
Farming is done by adults too.

questions.stem: Before listening to a story about a river, what do you already know about rivers?
options: Rivers are bodies of water that flow
Rivers are found in the sky
hints: Rivers contain water.
Water flows in rivers.
questions.explanation: You already know that rivers are bodies of water that flow. This helps you understand a story about a river.
misconceptions: Rivers are not made of fire.
Rivers are on land, not in the sky.
Rivers contain water, they are not dry.

questions.stem: A story says: 'The cocoa tree grows best in the forest.' What new information does this give you?
options: Cocoa trees grow best in the forest
Cocoa trees grow in the desert
Cocoa trees do not need water
hints: The story tells you where cocoa trees grow best.
It says 'in the forest'.
questions.explanation: The new information is that cocoa trees grow best in the forest.
misconceptions: The story says forest, not desert.
Cocoa trees are plants, not animals.

questions.stem: A story says: 'The festival of Homowo is celebrated by the Ga people.' What new information did you learn?
options: Homowo is celebrated by the Ga people
Homowo is a type of food
hints: The story tells you who celebrates Homowo.
It says 'the Ga people'.
questions.explanation: The new information is that Homowo is celebrated by the Ga people.
misconceptions: Homowo is a festival, not a food.
The story does not say December.
Homowo is a festival, not just a dance.

questions.stem: You already know that mosquitoes cause malaria. A story says: 'The mosquito bit the child and later the child fell sick with malaria.' How does your background knowledge help you understand this?
options: I know that mosquito bites can cause malaria
I don't know anything about mosquitoes
hints: Connect what you know about mosquitoes to the story.
Mosquitoes spread malaria.
questions.explanation: Your background knowledge that mosquitoes cause malaria helps you understand why the child fell sick after being bitten.
misconceptions: Most people know mosquitoes cause malaria.
Malaria is not caused by the sun.

questions.stem: You know that plants need water and sunlight to grow. A story says: 'The farmer watered his crops every day and they grew tall and green.' How does your background knowledge help you understand this?
options: I know that water helps plants grow
hints: Connect what you know about plants to the story.
Water helps plants grow.
questions.explanation: Your background knowledge that plants need water helps you understand why the farmer's crops grew tall and green.
misconceptions: Water helps, not stops, plant growth.
Sunlight is also needed, but the question is about water.

questions.stem: You know that fire can burn things. A story says: 'The bush fire destroyed the farmer's crops.' How does your background knowledge help you understand this?
options: I know that fire can destroy things
hints: Connect what you know about fire to the story.
Fire burns and destroys.
questions.explanation: Your background knowledge that fire can destroy things helps you understand how the bush fire destroyed the farmer's crops.
misconceptions: Fire destroys, it doesn't help crops grow.
Bush fires are harmful, not harmless.

questions.stem: A story says: 'Dogs have a very good sense of smell. They can smell things far away.' What new information does this give you?
options: Dogs can smell things far away
hints: The story tells you about dogs' sense of smell.
It says they can smell things far away.
questions.explanation: The new information is that dogs have a good sense of smell and can smell things far away.
misconceptions: The story says dogs can smell well.
The story is about smell, not sight.

questions.stem: A story says: 'The elephant is the largest land animal. It uses its trunk to drink water and pick up food.' What new information did you learn?
options: The elephant uses its trunk to drink water and pick up food
The elephant is the smallest animal
The elephant lives in the sea
hints: The story describes what the elephant does with its trunk.
It uses it for drinking and picking up food.
questions.explanation: The new information is that the elephant uses its trunk to drink water and pick up food.
misconceptions: The elephant is the largest, not smallest, land animal.
The elephant lives on land, not in the sea.

questions.stem: Before listening to a story about a school, what background knowledge can you use?
options: I know that schools are places where pupils learn
hints: Think about what happens at school.
Pupils go to school to learn.
questions.explanation: Your background knowledge that schools are places where pupils learn helps you understand a story about a school.
misconceptions: Everyone in Basic 4 knows about schools.
Schools are for learning, not sleeping.
Schools are for pupils and teachers.

questions.stem: You know that it rains more in the rainy season. A story says: 'The farmers planted their crops at the beginning of the rainy season.' Why does your background knowledge help you understand this?
options: I know that crops need rain to grow, so planting at the start of the rainy season makes sense
I don't know anything about rain
Farmers plant in the dry season
hints: Connect what you know about rain and crops.
Crops need water to grow.
questions.explanation: Your background knowledge that crops need rain helps you understand why farmers plant at the beginning of the rainy season.
misconceptions: Rain helps crops grow, it doesn't destroy them in moderation.
Farmers usually plant when rain is expected.

questions.stem: You know that too much sun can dry up plants. A story says: 'During the dry season, the grass turned brown and the animals had little to eat.' How does your background knowledge help you understand this?
options: I know that without rain and with too much sun, plants dry up and animals lack food
I don't know anything about the dry season
Animals eat grass in the dry season
The dry season is good for plants
hints: Connect what you know about sun and plants to the story.
Too much sun and no rain cause plants to dry up.
questions.explanation: Your background knowledge that too much sun and lack of rain cause plants to dry up helps you understand why the grass turned brown and animals had little food.
misconceptions: Everyone knows about the dry season.
Animals lack food when grass dries up.
The dry season is hard for plants.

questions.stem: You know that eating too much sugar can damage your teeth. A story says: 'The boy ate sweets every day. Soon he had holes in his teeth.' How does your background knowledge help you understand this?
options: I know that sweets contain sugar and too much sugar damages teeth
The boy did not eat sweets
hints: Connect what you know about sugar to the story.
Too much sugar damages teeth.
questions.explanation: Your background knowledge that too much sugar damages teeth helps you understand why the boy had holes in his teeth after eating sweets every day.
misconceptions: Sweets are not good for teeth.
Sugar weakens teeth, it doesn't strengthen them.
The story says he ate sweets.

questions.stem: A story says: 'A caterpillar turns into a butterfly after some time.' What new information does this give you?
options: Caterpillars are the same as butterflies
hints: The story describes a change.
A caterpillar becomes a butterfly.
questions.explanation: The new information is that a caterpillar turns into a butterfly after some time.
misconceptions: Caterpillars are the young stage, not the same as butterflies.
It's the other way round — caterpillars become butterflies.

questions.stem: You are about to listen to a story about 'A Day at the Beach.' Which of these background knowledge would be MOST useful for understanding the story?
options: Knowing that beaches have sand, water and waves
Knowing how to solve a maths problem
Knowing the names of all the planets
Knowing how to ride a bicycle
hints: Think about what a beach is like.
The story is about a beach.
questions.explanation: Knowing that beaches have sand, water and waves is most useful for understanding a story about a day at the beach.
misconceptions: Maths is not related to beaches.
Planets are not related to beaches.
Riding a bicycle is not specifically related to beaches.

questions.stem: You know that trees give us oxygen and help clean the air. A story says: 'The village decided to plant many trees to make the air cleaner.' How does your background knowledge help you understand the village's decision?
options: I know that trees clean the air, so planting trees makes sense for cleaner air
Trees do not affect the air
hints: Connect what you know about trees and air to the story.
Trees help clean the air.
questions.explanation: Your background knowledge that trees clean the air helps you understand why the village planted trees to make the air cleaner.
misconceptions: Trees clean the air, they don't make it dirty.
The village made a good decision.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Identify the main idea/gist and details of texts

skills.description: Identify the main idea or gist of a text
Identify details that support the main idea
Identify themes from texts (e.g. love, greed, honesty, hard work)

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: The main idea is always the first sentence
Theme and main idea are the same
A text can only have one theme

questions.stem: Read this short text: 'Ama goes to school every day. She learns to read and write. She likes her teacher and her friends.' What is this text mostly about?
hints: What is the text mainly describing?
It tells us what Ama does at school.
questions.explanation: The text is mostly about Ama's school life — going to school, learning to read and write, and liking her teacher and friends.

questions.stem: Text: 'Kofi likes fruits. He eats mangoes, oranges and bananas every day.' Which detail supports the idea that Kofi likes fruits?
options: He eats mangoes, oranges and bananas every day
hints: A supporting detail tells us more about the main idea.
The main idea is that Kofi likes fruits. Which detail shows this?
questions.explanation: 'He eats mangoes, oranges and bananas every day' supports the idea that Kofi likes fruits.
misconceptions: Being a boy is not related to liking fruits.
Living in Kumasi is not related.
Having a bicycle is not related.

questions.stem: Text: 'The rain fell heavily. The streets were flooded. People could not go to work.' What is the main idea of this text?
hints: What happened because of the rain?
The streets flooded and people could not go to work.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that heavy rain caused problems — flooding and preventing people from going to work.
misconceptions: The text says the rain caused problems, not that people like it.
The text is about rain, not sun.
The streets were flooded, not dry.

questions.stem: Text: 'Esi is a hardworking pupil. She always does her homework. She listens in class. She asks questions when she does not understand.' Which detail supports the idea that Esi is hardworking?
hints: A supporting detail shows the main idea. The main idea is that Esi is hardworking.
Doing homework shows hard work.
questions.explanation: 'She always does her homework' supports the idea that Esi is hardworking.
misconceptions: Having a school bag is not about being hardworking.
Walking to school is not about hard work.
Having friends is not about hard work.

questions.stem: Text: 'The farmer worked hard every day. He watered his crops and pulled out weeds. At harvest time, he had a big crop.' What theme does this text teach?
hints: The farmer worked hard and got a big crop.
The theme is the lesson the text teaches.
questions.explanation: The theme is 'Hard work is rewarded' because the farmer's hard work led to a big harvest.
misconceptions: Farming is shown as requiring work, not easy.

questions.stem: Text: 'Kwame woke up late. He missed the bus. He had to walk to school. He arrived late and missed the first lesson.' What is the main idea of this text?
options: Kwame had a bad morning because he woke up late
Kwame missed the bus because he was early
hints: What started all the problems?
Waking up late led to missing the bus and being late for school.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that Kwame had a bad morning because he woke up late, which led to a chain of problems.
misconceptions: The text does not say he likes walking.
The text is about one morning, not always.
He missed the bus because he woke up late, not because he was early.

questions.stem: Text: 'The market was busy. Traders were calling out their prices. Women were buying vegetables. Children were running around.' What is the main idea, and which detail supports it?
options: Main idea: The market was busy. Detail: Traders were calling out their prices
Main idea: Children were running. Detail: The market was busy
Main idea: Women were buying. Detail: The market was quiet
Main idea: The market was empty. Detail: Traders were selling
hints: The main idea is the overall picture. What was the market like?
The details describe what people were doing.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that the market was busy. The detail 'Traders were calling out their prices' supports this.
misconceptions: Children running is a detail, not the main idea.
The market was busy, not quiet.
The market was busy, not empty.

questions.stem: Text: 'The ant worked hard all summer, storing food. The grasshopper played and laughed at the ant. When winter came, the ant had food but the grasshopper had nothing.' What theme does this text teach?
options: Hard work pays; laziness leads to suffering
Playing is more important than working
hints: The ant worked and had food. The grasshopper played and had nothing.
The theme is the lesson about work and laziness.
questions.explanation: The theme is that hard work pays and laziness leads to suffering — the ant had food, the grasshopper did not.
misconceptions: The story shows working is better than playing all the time.
Winter is shown as a time of need, not the best season.
The grasshopper is shown as foolish, not smart.

questions.stem: Text: 'Ghana is a beautiful country. It has many tourist sites. People visit the Cape Coast Castle, Kakum National Park and Mole National Park. Tourists enjoy the beaches and the friendly people.' What is the main idea?
options: Ghana has many attractions for tourists
hints: What is the text telling us about Ghana?
It mentions several tourist sites.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that Ghana has many attractions for tourists, including castles, parks and beaches.
misconceptions: The text says Ghana has many sites, not none.
The text says tourists enjoy Ghana.
The text does not say Ghana is small.

questions.stem: Text: 'Malaria is a dangerous disease. It is caused by mosquito bites. People with malaria have fever and headaches. Children under five are most at risk.' What is the main idea, and which detail supports it?
options: Main idea: Malaria is dangerous. Detail: It causes fever and headaches
Main idea: Children are at risk. Detail: Malaria is a disease
Main idea: Mosquitoes are insects. Detail: People have fever
Main idea: Malaria is not serious. Detail: It is caused by mosquito bites
hints: The first sentence often states the main idea.
The details explain why malaria is dangerous.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that malaria is dangerous. The detail 'It causes fever and headaches' supports this.
misconceptions: Children being at risk is a detail, not the main idea.
Mosquitoes being insects is not the main idea.
Malaria is shown as serious, not not serious.

questions.stem: Text: 'A rich man saw a poor beggar on the street. He gave the beggar food and money. The beggar thanked him and prayed for him.' What theme does this text teach?
hints: The rich man gave to the beggar.
Giving to others is generosity.
questions.explanation: The theme is generosity and kindness — the rich man helped the poor beggar.
misconceptions: Greed is the opposite of what is shown.

questions.stem: Text: 'Trees are very important. They give us oxygen to breathe. They provide shade and fruits. They also help to clean the air.' What is the main idea?
hints: The first sentence often states the main idea.
The other sentences explain why trees are important.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that trees are important. The other sentences give reasons.
misconceptions: The text says trees are important.
Trees give more than fruits — oxygen, shade and clean air.
Trees clean the air, they do not cause pollution.

questions.stem: Text: 'Ama woke up early. She swept the compound. She washed the dishes. She helped her mother prepare breakfast. Then she went to school.' What is the main idea of this text?
options: Ama did not go to school
hints: All the events show Ama doing helpful tasks.
What connects sweeping, washing dishes and helping with breakfast?
questions.explanation: The main idea is that Ama was helpful before school — she did many chores before going to school.
misconceptions: The text says she woke up early, not late.
The text says she went to school.
The text shows her working, not playing.

questions.stem: Text: 'The library is a quiet place. Pupils go there to read and study. They must not talk loudly. They must return books on time.' What is the main idea, and which detail supports it?
options: Main idea: The library has rules. Detail: Pupils must not talk loudly
Main idea: Pupils read books. Detail: The library is quiet
Main idea: The library is noisy. Detail: Pupils go there
Main idea: Books are expensive. Detail: Pupils return books
hints: The text gives rules about behaviour.
Not talking loudly is one of the rules.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that the library has rules. 'Pupils must not talk loudly' supports this.
misconceptions: Pupils reading books is a detail, not the main idea.
The library is quiet, not noisy.
The text does not mention book prices.

questions.stem: Text: 'The tortoise tricked the birds and took all the food. The birds were angry. Later, the tortoise fell from the sky and broke his shell. He learned a lesson.' What theme does this text teach?
hints: The tortoise tricked and was punished.
The theme is the lesson about dishonesty.
questions.explanation: The theme is that dishonesty leads to trouble — the tortoise was punished for tricking the birds.
misconceptions: Trickery is shown as bad, not good.
The story is about trickery, not strength.
Flying is not the main theme.

questions.stem: Text: 'Some people think money is the most important thing. But health is more important than money. Without health, you cannot enjoy your money. You cannot work to earn more.' Which sentence best states the main idea?
options: Health is more important than money
Money is the most important thing
Money and health are the same
hints: The text argues that one thing is more important than another.
It says 'health is more important than money'.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that health is more important than money, because without health you cannot enjoy or earn money.
misconceptions: The text argues against money being most important.
It says health is more important, not equal.
The text does not say people should not work.

questions.stem: Text: 'Exercise is good for the body. When you run, your heart becomes stronger. When you play football, your muscles become stronger. Exercise also makes you feel happy.' Which detail does NOT support the idea that exercise is good for the body?
options: Exercise is good for the body
hints: The question asks for a detail that does NOT support the idea.
Feeling happy is about feelings, not directly about the body.
questions.explanation: 'Exercise makes you feel happy' is about emotions, not directly about the body. The other options are about physical benefits.
misconceptions: Running strengthening the heart is a physical benefit.
Football strengthening muscles is a physical benefit.
The main idea itself is not a detail.

questions.stem: Text: 'Kofi studied hard for his exams. He read his books every night. He asked his teacher questions. He practised maths problems. When the results came, he had the best score in his class.' Which statement best expresses the main idea?
options: Kofi is the smartest pupil in the class
Maths is the most important subject
hints: What did Kofi do, and what was the result?
His hard work led to the best score.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that hard work leads to success — Kofi's studying and practice resulted in the best score.
misconceptions: The text does not say Kofi is naturally the smartest, but that he worked hard.
Maths is one subject he practised, not the main idea.
The difficulty of exams is not the main point.
