questions.stem: Text: 'The rich man refused to help his poor neighbour. He said, "I worked for my money. Let him work for his." Later, the rich man lost his job and became poor. The neighbour, who had little, shared his food with him.' Which two themes does this text teach?
hints: The rich man's behaviour shows one theme. The neighbour's behaviour shows another.
The rich man was proud; the neighbour was kind.
questions.explanation: The text teaches two themes: pride (the rich man's refusal to help) and kindness (the neighbour sharing his food).
misconceptions: Greed is shown but laziness is not.
Fear and sadness are not the main themes.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Compare and contrast information (two or more ideas) from texts

skills.description: Identify similarities between two or more ideas or texts
Identify differences between two or more ideas or texts
Compare and contrast information from texts using both similarities and differences

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: If two things are different, they have nothing in common

questions.stem: Ama likes rice. Kofi likes rice. What is one thing Ama and Kofi have in common?
hints: Look for what is the same about both people.
Both Ama and Kofi like rice.
questions.explanation: Ama and Kofi have one thing in common: they both like rice.
misconceptions: The text does not say they like fufu.
They both like rice, not dislike it.
The text does not mention banku.

questions.stem: Ama is tall. Kofi is short. What is one difference between Ama and Kofi?
options: Ama is tall and Kofi is short
hints: Look for what is different about the two people.
One is tall, the other is short.
questions.explanation: The difference is that Ama is tall while Kofi is short.
misconceptions: They are not the same height.

questions.stem: Text 1: 'The dog is a domestic animal.' Text 2: 'The cat is a domestic animal.' What do the two texts have in common?
options: One is domestic and one is wild
hints: Both texts say the same thing about the animal.
Both are domestic animals.
questions.explanation: Both texts say the animal is domestic — that is their similarity.
misconceptions: Neither is said to be wild.
Both are domestic, not one of each.

questions.stem: Text 1: 'The mango is sweet.' Text 2: 'The lemon is sour.' What is one difference between the mango and the lemon?
options: The mango is sweet and the lemon is sour
hints: Look at how each fruit tastes.
One is sweet, the other is sour.
questions.explanation: The difference is that the mango is sweet while the lemon is sour.
misconceptions: They do not both taste sweet.
They do not both taste sour.
They do not taste the same.

questions.stem: Ama is a girl. She likes reading. Kofi is a boy. He likes reading. What is one similarity and one difference between Ama and Kofi?
options: Similarity: both like reading. Difference: Ama is a girl, Kofi is a boy
Similarity: both are boys. Difference: both like reading
Similarity: both are girls. Difference: both like reading
Similarity: none. Difference: both like reading
hints: Find what is the same (likes) and what is different (gender).
Both like reading, but one is a girl and one is a boy.
questions.explanation: They are similar in that both like reading, but they differ in gender — Ama is a girl and Kofi is a boy.

questions.stem: Text 1: 'The coconut tree grows in sandy areas. It has many uses.' Text 2: 'The palm tree grows in sandy areas. It also has many uses.' What is one similarity between the two texts?
options: Both trees grow in sandy areas
Both trees grow in the desert
Both trees are found in water
hints: Look for what both texts say about the trees.
Both grow in sandy areas.
questions.explanation: Both texts say the trees grow in sandy areas and have many uses.

questions.stem: Text 1: 'Kofi walks to school every day.' Text 2: 'Esi takes a trotro to school every day.' What is one difference between Kofi and Esi?
options: Kofi walks to school, but Esi takes a trotro
hints: Look at how each person gets to school.
One walks, the other takes a trotro.
questions.explanation: Kofi walks to school while Esi takes a trotro — that is their difference.

questions.stem: Text 1: 'The market is a place where people buy and sell goods. It is usually busy.' Text 2: 'The bank is a place where people keep and withdraw money. It is usually quiet.' What is one similarity and one difference between the market and the bank?
options: Similarity: both are places where people go for services. Difference: the market is busy, the bank is quiet
Similarity: both are quiet. Difference: both are busy
Similarity: both sell goods. Difference: both keep money
Similarity: none. Difference: the market is busy, the bank is quiet
hints: Find what both places have in common and how they differ.
Both serve people, but one is busy and the other is quiet.
questions.explanation: Both are places where people go for services, but the market is busy while the bank is quiet.
misconceptions: The market is busy, not quiet.
Only the market sells goods; only the bank keeps money.
They do share a similarity (both serve people).

questions.stem: Text 1: 'Malaria is caused by mosquito bites.' Text 2: 'Cholera is caused by drinking dirty water.' What do these two diseases have in common?
options: Both are diseases that can be prevented
Both are caused by mosquito bites
Both are caused by dirty water
hints: Both texts are about diseases.
Both can be prevented.
questions.explanation: Both malaria and cholera are diseases that can be prevented, though they are caused by different things.
misconceptions: Only malaria is caused by mosquito bites.
Only cholera is caused by dirty water.

questions.stem: Text 1: 'The rainy season in Ghana brings a lot of rain. It is good for farming.' Text 2: 'The dry season in Ghana has very little rain. It can be difficult for farming.' What is one difference between the two seasons?
options: The rainy season has a lot of rain; the dry season has very little rain
Both seasons have a lot of rain
Both seasons have very little rain
The dry season is good for farming
hints: Look at how much rain each season has.
One is wet, the other is dry.
questions.explanation: The rainy season has a lot of rain while the dry season has very little rain — that is the difference.
misconceptions: The dry season does not have a lot of rain.
The rainy season does not have little rain.
The rainy season, not the dry season, is good for farming.

questions.stem: Ama is 10 years old. She likes football. Kofi is 10 years old. He likes football. What is one similarity between Ama and Kofi?
options: They are the same age and like the same sport
They are the same age but like different sports
hints: Look for what is the same about them.
Both are 10 years old and like football.
questions.explanation: They are similar because they are both 10 years old and both like football.
misconceptions: They are the same age, not different.
They like the same sport, not different.

questions.stem: Text 1: 'The baobab tree stores water in its trunk and survives in dry areas.' Text 2: 'The cactus stores water in its stem and survives in dry areas.' What is the most important similarity between the two plants?
options: Both store water to survive in dry areas
hints: The key similarity is how they survive in dry places.
Both store water.
questions.explanation: The most important similarity is that both plants store water to survive in dry areas.
misconceptions: The text does not mention thorns.
The text does not say both are found in Ghana.
A cactus is not a tree.

questions.stem: Text 1: 'Kofi is a hardworking pupil who always does his homework.' Text 2: 'Ama is a hardworking pupil but she sometimes forgets to do her homework.' What is one difference between Kofi and Ama?
options: Kofi always does his homework, but Ama sometimes forgets
hints: Look at how they behave with homework.
One always does it; the other sometimes forgets.
questions.explanation: Kofi always does his homework while Ama sometimes forgets — that is the difference.
misconceptions: Ama sometimes forgets, so not both always do homework.
Ama does not always do her homework.

questions.stem: Text 1: 'The village of Boti is known for its beautiful waterfall. It is a tourist site.' Text 2: 'The city of Accra is known for its busy markets and government buildings. It is the capital of Ghana.' What is one similarity and one difference between Boti and Accra?
options: Similarity: both are known for something. Difference: Boti is a village, Accra is a city
Similarity: both are villages. Difference: both are known for waterfalls
Similarity: both are cities. Difference: Accra is the capital
Similarity: both have waterfalls. Difference: Accra is a village
hints: Find what they share and how they differ.
Both are known for something, but one is a village and one is a city.
questions.explanation: Both are known for something (Boti for its waterfall, Accra for its markets and buildings). They differ in that Boti is a village while Accra is a city.
misconceptions: They are not both known for waterfalls.

questions.stem: Text 1: 'Ama helped her mother in the kitchen.' Text 2: 'Kofi helped his father in the garden.' What is one similarity between Ama and Kofi?
options: Both helped their parents with work
hints: Look at what both children did.
Both helped a parent.
questions.explanation: Both Ama and Kofi helped their parents with work, though in different places.
misconceptions: Only Ama helped in the kitchen.
Only Kofi helped in the garden.

questions.stem: Text 1: 'The lion is a wild animal that hunts for food.' Text 2: 'The dog is a domestic animal that is fed by its owner.' What is one difference between the lion and the dog?
options: The lion is wild and hunts; the dog is domestic and is fed by its owner
hints: Look at how each animal lives and gets food.
One is wild, the other is domestic.
questions.explanation: The lion is wild and hunts for food while the dog is domestic and is fed by its owner.

questions.stem: Text 1: 'Nkrumah was a leader who fought for Ghana's independence.' Text 2: 'Mandela was a leader who fought against apartheid in South Africa.' What is one similarity and one difference between them?
options: Similarity: both were leaders who fought for freedom. Difference: Nkrumah fought for Ghana; Mandela fought in South Africa
Similarity: both fought in South Africa. Difference: both were leaders
Similarity: both were farmers. Difference: both fought for freedom
Similarity: none. Difference: both were leaders
hints: Find what both leaders did and where they did it.
Both fought for freedom in different countries.
questions.explanation: Both were leaders who fought for freedom, but Nkrumah fought for Ghana's independence while Mandela fought against apartheid in South Africa.
misconceptions: Nkrumah did not fight in South Africa.
They share a similarity — both fought for freedom.

questions.stem: Text 1: 'The old woman was poor but always shared her food with others.' Text 2: 'The rich man had plenty but never shared with anyone.' What is one similarity and one difference between the two people?
options: Similarity: both had food. Difference: the old woman shared, the rich man did not
Similarity: both were poor. Difference: both shared
Similarity: both were rich. Difference: neither shared
Similarity: both shared. Difference: both had food
hints: Look at what they both had and how they behaved.
Both had food, but only one shared.
questions.explanation: Both had food, but they differed in generosity — the old woman shared while the rich man did not.
misconceptions: The rich man was not poor.
The old woman was not rich.

questions.stem: Text 1: 'Education helps people get good jobs and improve their lives.' Text 2: 'Education helps people make better decisions and contribute to their communities.' What is the main similarity between the two texts?
options: Both texts say education has benefits for individuals and communities
Both texts say education is not important
Both texts say education is only for children
Both texts say education is expensive
hints: Both texts discuss what education does for people.
Both list benefits of education.
questions.explanation: The main similarity is that both texts describe the benefits of education — for individuals (jobs, decisions) and communities.
misconceptions: Both texts say education is important, not unimportant.
Neither says education is only for children.
Neither mentions the cost of education.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'Living in the city is better than living in the village because cities have more shops and hospitals.' Another pupil says: 'Living in the village is better because it is quiet and peaceful.' What is one similarity and one difference between their views?
options: Similarity: both prefer their own way of living. Difference: one values facilities, the other values peace
Similarity: both prefer the city. Difference: both dislike the village
Similarity: both prefer the village. Difference: both dislike the city
Similarity: neither has a preference. Difference: both like cities
hints: Both pupils have a preference. What do they value differently?
One values facilities (city), the other values peace (village).
questions.explanation: Both pupils prefer their own way of living, but they differ in what they value: one values facilities (city), the other values peace and quiet (village).
misconceptions: They do not both prefer the city.
They do not both prefer the village.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.8.1: Demonstrate understanding in asking and answering questions correctly
indicator.objective: Use appropriate pronunciation and intonation in asking and answering questions

skills.description: Recognise and use rising intonation for questions and falling intonation for answers
Pronounce question words and phrases clearly
Use appropriate falling intonation when answering questions
Ask and answer questions with correct pronunciation and intonation in a role-play or conversation

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Intonation does not matter in communication
Speaking loudly is the same as speaking clearly

questions.stem: Which sentence is a question?
hints: A question asks something.
It ends with a question mark.
questions.explanation: 'Are you going to school?' is a question because it asks something and ends with a question mark.
misconceptions: 'You are going to school' is a statement.
'I am going to school' is a statement.

questions.stem: When we ask a question, our voice usually ___ at the end.
hints: Think about how your voice sounds when you ask 'Are you coming?'
It rises at the end.
questions.explanation: When we ask a question, our voice usually goes up (rising intonation) at the end.
misconceptions: A flat voice does not show a question.

questions.stem: Which question word is pronounced clearly in this question: 'What is your name?'
hints: The question word asks for information.
It is the first word.
questions.explanation: The question word 'What' should be pronounced clearly to make the question understandable.
misconceptions: 'is' is a linking word, not the question word.

questions.stem: Which question is pronounced clearly?
hints: Clear pronunciation means saying all the words properly.
The correct option has all words clearly pronounced.
questions.explanation: 'What do you want?' is pronounced clearly because all the words are said properly.
misconceptions: The other options are slurred or unclear.

questions.stem: When we answer a question, our voice usually ___ at the end.
hints: Think about how you say 'Yes, I am.'
Your voice falls at the end.
questions.explanation: When we answer a question, our voice usually goes down (falling intonation) at the end.
misconceptions: A flat voice does not show a clear answer.

questions.stem: Which sentence should be said with a rising intonation?
options: The book is on the table.
hints: Rising intonation is for questions.
Which sentence asks something?
questions.explanation: 'Where are you going?' is a question, so it should be said with rising intonation.
misconceptions: 'I am going home' is a statement.
'The book is on the table' is a statement.

questions.stem: A pupil says 'You are coming to school?' with a rising voice. What is the pupil doing?
hints: Rising intonation signals a question.
The pupil wants to know if you are coming.
questions.explanation: The pupil is asking a question because the voice rises at the end.
misconceptions: Requests are usually more polite and may not use this pattern.

questions.stem: Which question is pronounced most clearly?
hints: Clear pronunciation means saying every word.
The correct option says all three words clearly.
questions.explanation: 'How are you?' is pronounced clearly because all words are said properly.
misconceptions: The other options slur the words together.

questions.stem: Which word should be pronounced clearly in the question 'Where do you live?'
hints: The question word asks about place.
It is the first word.
questions.explanation: The question word 'Where' should be pronounced clearly to make the question understandable.
misconceptions: 'live' is the main verb but 'Where' is the question word.

questions.stem: Someone asks: 'What is your name?' You answer: 'My name is Ama.' How should your voice sound at the end?
hints: Answers usually have falling intonation.
Your voice goes down at the end.
questions.explanation: Your voice should fall at the end of the answer because it is a statement, not a question.
misconceptions: A flat voice is not natural.

questions.stem: Someone asks: 'Are you coming?' You answer: 'Yes, I am.' How should your voice sound at the end?
hints: Answers usually have falling intonation.
Your voice goes down at the end.
questions.explanation: Your voice should fall at the end because 'Yes, I am' is an answer (statement), not a question.
misconceptions: A flat voice is not natural.
Whispering is about volume, not intonation.

questions.stem: Which answer is spoken with correct falling intonation?
hints: An answer should have falling intonation.
The first option is a clear statement with falling intonation.
questions.explanation: 'No, thank you.' is spoken with falling intonation because it is a polite answer.
misconceptions: Rising intonation would make it sound like a question.
Exclamation marks show strong feeling, not standard answer intonation.

questions.stem: A pupil reads: 'What is your name.' with a falling intonation. What is wrong?
options: Questions should have rising intonation, but the pupil used falling
hints: 'What is your name' is a question.
Questions should have rising intonation.
questions.explanation: The pupil used falling intonation for a question, but questions should have rising intonation.
misconceptions: Using falling intonation for a question is incorrect.

questions.stem: A pupil says 'Wher-you-go-in?' instead of 'Where are you going?' What is the problem?
options: The pupil is not pronouncing the words clearly
The pupil is speaking too loudly
The pupil is using falling intonation
The pupil is speaking too slowly
hints: Look at how the words are said.
The words are slurred together.
questions.explanation: The pupil is not pronouncing the words clearly — the words are slurred together instead of being said properly.
misconceptions: Intonation is not the issue here.
Speed is not the main problem.

questions.stem: A pupil answers 'I am fine?' with a rising intonation. What does this sound like?
options: It sounds like the pupil is asking a question instead of answering
It sounds like a normal answer
hints: Rising intonation signals a question.
The pupil is answering but sounds like they are asking.
questions.explanation: The rising intonation makes the answer sound like a question, which is not correct for an answer.
misconceptions: Rising intonation on an answer is incorrect.

questions.stem: Two pupils read the same sentence: 'You are coming.' Pupil A reads it with a rising voice. Pupil B reads it with a falling voice. What is the difference in meaning?
options: Pupil A is asking a question; Pupil B is making a statement
Pupil A is making a statement; Pupil B is asking a question
hints: Rising voice = question.
Falling voice = statement.
questions.explanation: Pupil A's rising voice makes it a question. Pupil B's falling voice makes it a statement.
misconceptions: Only Pupil A is asking a question.
Only Pupil B is making a statement.

questions.stem: A pupil is asked to say 'Where is the Headteacher's office?' clearly. Which version is clearest?
hints: Clear pronunciation means all words are said properly.
The first option has every word clearly pronounced.
questions.explanation: 'Where is the Headteacher's office?' is clearest because every word is pronounced properly.
misconceptions: The other options slur or drop words.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.8.2: Identify and use question tags correctly in speech
indicator.objective: Use positive tags, negative tags and auxiliaries in speech

skills.description: Recognise positive and negative question tags
Form correct question tags using the right auxiliary verb and polarity
Use question tags appropriately in spoken sentences to ask for confirmation
Use question tags correctly in a role-play or conversation

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Any auxiliary can be used in a tag
Question tags are only for questions
Tags are not used in spoken English

questions.stem: What is the question tag in this sentence: 'You are coming to school, aren't you?'
hints: The question tag comes at the end.
It is a short question added to the statement.
questions.explanation: 'Aren't you' is the question tag because it is the short question added to the end of the statement.
misconceptions: 'are coming' is part of the statement.
'you are' is the beginning of the statement.

questions.stem: Which of these is a NEGATIVE question tag?
hints: A negative tag contains 'not' (or n't).
Look for the word with 'n't'.
questions.explanation: 'Isn't it' is negative because it contains 'n't' (not). The others are positive tags.

questions.stem: Which of these is a POSITIVE question tag?
hints: A positive tag does not contain 'not' or 'n't'.
Look for the tag without 'n't'.
questions.explanation: 'Are you' is positive because it does not contain 'n't'. The others are negative tags.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'She is a teacher, isn't she?', what is the auxiliary verb used in the tag?
hints: The auxiliary verb is the helping verb.
It is the same as the verb in the statement.
questions.explanation: The auxiliary verb in the tag is 'is' because it matches the verb 'is' in the statement.

questions.stem: Which statement has a POSITIVE tag?
options: They don't like it, do they?
hints: A positive tag does not have 'n't'.
Look for the tag without 'not'.
questions.explanation: 'You aren't tired, are you?' has a positive tag ('are you') because the statement is negative.
misconceptions: 'do they' is positive but the statement is negative.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'You like mangoes, ___?'
hints: The statement is positive ('You like'), so the tag should be negative.
The verb is 'like' (present simple), so use 'do'.
questions.explanation: The statement is positive, so the tag should be negative: 'don't you'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'Kofi is not coming, ___?'
hints: The statement is negative, so the tag should be positive.
Use the same auxiliary verb 'is'.
questions.explanation: The statement is negative, so the tag should be positive: 'is he'.
misconceptions: 'isn't he' is negative, but the statement is already negative.
'doesn't he' uses the wrong auxiliary and is negative.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'They can swim, ___?'
hints: The statement is positive, so the tag should be negative.
Use the same auxiliary verb 'can'.
questions.explanation: The statement is positive, so the tag should be negative: 'can't they'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'Ama has finished her work, ___?'
hints: The statement is positive, so the tag should be negative.
Use the same auxiliary verb 'has'.
questions.explanation: The statement is positive, so the tag should be negative: 'hasn't she'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'The children didn't go to the farm, ___?'
hints: The statement is negative, so the tag should be positive.
Use the same auxiliary verb 'did'.
questions.explanation: The statement is negative, so the tag should be positive: 'did they'.
misconceptions: 'didn't they' is negative, but the statement is already negative.
'don't they' uses the wrong tense and is negative.

questions.stem: Why do we use question tags?
options: To ask for confirmation or agreement
hints: Question tags turn a statement into a question.
We use them to check if something is true.
questions.explanation: We use question tags to ask for confirmation or agreement about a statement.
misconceptions: Tags are not for making statements stronger.
Tags confirm an existing statement; they don't ask a completely new question.

questions.stem: You think it is going to rain. You say to your friend: 'It is going to rain, ___?' Which tag is most appropriate?
hints: The statement is positive ('It is going to rain').
The tag should be negative and use the same auxiliary 'is'.
questions.explanation: The statement is positive, so the tag is negative: 'isn't it'.
misconceptions: 'don't it' uses the wrong auxiliary and is grammatically incorrect.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'You don't like fufu, do you?' What is the pupil asking?
options: They are asking for confirmation that you don't like fufu
They are saying you like fufu
hints: The statement is negative ('You don't like fufu'), so the tag is positive ('do you').
The pupil wants to confirm their idea.
questions.explanation: The pupil is asking for confirmation that you do not like fufu.
misconceptions: The pupil is not giving fufu.
The pupil is not cooking fufu.

questions.stem: You are in a conversation and want to confirm that your friend is coming to your birthday party. Which sentence is best?
options: You are coming to my party, aren't you?
You are coming to my party, are you?
You come to my party, don't you?
You coming to my party, isn't it?
hints: The statement is positive, so the tag should be negative.
Use the auxiliary 'are' to match 'You are'.
questions.explanation: 'You are coming to my party, aren't you?' is the best because the tag matches the statement correctly.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'The book is on the table, isn't it?' Another pupil says: 'The book is on the table, is it?' Which pupil is using the correct tag for a statement they believe is true?
options: The first pupil, because the statement is positive and the tag is negative
The second pupil, because the statement is positive and the tag is positive
hints: For a positive statement, the tag should be negative.
The first pupil's tag is negative.
questions.explanation: The first pupil is correct: for a positive statement, the tag should be negative ('isn't it').
misconceptions: The second pupil's tag is positive, which is wrong for a positive statement.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a question tag?
hints: The statement uses 'can', so the tag should use 'can'.
The statement is positive, so the tag should be negative.
questions.explanation: 'She can cook, can't she?' is correct because it uses the same auxiliary 'can' and the tag is negative.

questions.stem: Are question tags used in spoken English?
options: Yes, they are common in speech
No, they are only for writing
They are only for old English
They are not used at all
hints: Think about how people talk.
Tags like 'isn't it?' are used in everyday speech.
questions.explanation: Yes, question tags are common in spoken English. People use them to ask for confirmation in conversation.
misconceptions: Tags are not only for writing.

questions.stem: In a conversation, your friend says: 'We are going to the market.' You want to confirm. What should you say?
options: We are going to the market, aren't we?
We are going to the market, are we?
We go to the market, don't we?
We going to the market, isn't it?
hints: The statement is positive, so the tag should be negative.
Use the auxiliary 'are'.
questions.explanation: 'We are going to the market, aren't we?' uses the correct negative tag for a positive statement.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to use a question tag to confirm that their friend has a new pen. Which sentence should they use?
options: You have a new pen, haven't you?
You have a new pen, have you?
You have a new pen, don't you?
You have a new pen, isn't it?
hints: The statement is positive, so the tag should be negative.
The auxiliary verb is 'have'.
questions.explanation: 'You have a new pen, haven't you?' is correct because it uses the negative tag with the matching auxiliary 'have'.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Sub-Strand 9: Giving and Following Commands/Instructions/Directions and Making and Responding to Requests
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.9.1: Use verbs appropriately in commands, requests and directions in speech
indicator.objective: Give and respond to commands, instructions and directions

skills.description: Recognise commands and instructions (imperative verbs)
Respond appropriately to given commands or instructions
Give clear directions using landmarks and sequence words
Give and follow commands, instructions and directions in a role-play or classroom activity

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: A command is the same as a request
Any verb can be used in a command
You can give directions in any order

questions.stem: Which of these is a command?
hints: A command tells someone to do something.
It uses the imperative form of the verb.
questions.explanation: 'Stand up!' is a command because it tells someone to do something.

questions.stem: What is the verb in the command 'Bring your book to me'?
hints: The verb is the action word.
It tells you what to do.
questions.explanation: 'Bring' is the verb in the command because it is the action word.

questions.stem: Your teacher says: 'Close the door.' What should you do?
hints: A command tells you what to do.
Do what the teacher says.
questions.explanation: If the teacher says 'Close the door', you should close the door.
misconceptions: Opening the door is the opposite of the command.
Leaving the door does not follow the command.
Breaking the door is not what the command says.

questions.stem: A pupil is told: 'Walk from the classroom to the Headteacher's office.' What is the pupil asked to do?
hints: The command tells the pupil where to go.
Walk from the classroom to the Headteacher's office.
questions.explanation: The pupil is asked to walk from the classroom to the Headteacher's office.
misconceptions: The command says walk, not run.
The command says go to the office, not stay.
The command says go to the office, not go home.

questions.stem: Which word in 'Sit down and listen carefully' tells you the actions to take?
hints: Action words are verbs.
There are two commands here.
questions.explanation: 'Sit' and 'listen' are the action words (verbs) in the command.

questions.stem: Which word tells you to turn to the right?
hints: It is the opposite of left.
It tells you which side to turn.
questions.explanation: 'Right' tells you to turn to the right side.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving directions to the library. Which direction is clearest?
options: Walk straight, turn left at the water tank, and the library is beside the ICT room
Walk, turn, go, and you will see it
Walk past things and find it
hints: Good directions use landmarks and clear steps.
The first option names landmarks and gives a clear sequence.
questions.explanation: The first option is clearest because it uses landmarks (water tank, ICT room) and a clear sequence.
misconceptions: The other options are vague and do not use landmarks.

questions.stem: Which words help to organise directions in the correct order?
hints: Sequence words show the order of steps.
First, then, finally are sequence words.
questions.explanation: Sequence words like 'first, then, finally' help organise directions in the correct order.
misconceptions: Size words are not sequence words.

questions.stem: Your friend says: 'Please bring me the broom.' What should you do?
options: Bring the broom to your friend
Bring the broom to your teacher
hints: Your friend asked for the broom.
Do what they asked politely.
questions.explanation: You should bring the broom to your friend because they asked for it.
misconceptions: They asked you to bring it to them, not the teacher.
Keeping it does not respond to the request.
Hiding it does not respond to the request.

questions.stem: A teacher says: 'Turn right, walk twenty steps towards the water tank.' What should you do first?
hints: The first action in the command comes first.
Turn right before walking.
questions.explanation: You should first turn right, then walk twenty steps towards the water tank.
misconceptions: Looking for the tank happens while walking.
Stopping is not part of the command.

questions.stem: Which sentence is NOT a command?
hints: A command tells someone to do something.
Which sentence is just describing something?
questions.explanation: 'The boy is running' is a statement, not a command. The others are commands.
misconceptions: 'Run to the field!' is a command.
'Bring your exercise book!' is a command.

questions.stem: Why are landmarks useful when giving directions?
options: They help the person know where to turn or stop
hints: Landmarks are familiar places or objects.
They help people find their way.
questions.explanation: Landmarks are useful because they help the person know where to turn or stop.
misconceptions: Landmarks make directions clearer, not longer.

questions.stem: A pupil is told: 'Go to the classroom, pick up the chalkboard duster, and bring it to the staff room.' What should the pupil do LAST?
options: Bring the duster to the staff room
Go to the staff room first
hints: The last action is the final step in the instruction.
The pupil brings the duster to the staff room last.
questions.explanation: The last step is to bring the duster to the staff room after picking it up from the classroom.
misconceptions: Going to the classroom is the first step.
Picking up the duster is the second step.
Going to the staff room first is out of order.

questions.stem: A stranger asks you how to get to the chief's palace. Which set of directions is clearest?
options: Walk straight along this road, turn left at the big mango tree, and the palace is the large building with red roofs
Go that way and ask someone
Walk and turn and you will find it
hints: Good directions use landmarks and clear sequence.
The first option names landmarks and gives a clear route.
questions.explanation: The first option is clearest because it uses landmarks (mango tree, red roofs) and a logical sequence.
misconceptions: Telling someone to ask another person is not helpful.
Saying 'somewhere around here' is not helpful.

questions.stem: How is a command different from a request?
options: A command is direct; a request is polite and uses words like 'please'
A command is polite; a request is rude
hints: Commands tell someone to do something directly.
Requests are more polite.
questions.explanation: A command is direct ('Close the door'), while a request is polite and often uses 'please' ('Could you please close the door?').

questions.stem: A pupil is given these instructions: 'First, write your name. Then, answer question one. Finally, check your work.' What should the pupil do after answering question one?
options: Give the paper to the teacher
hints: The instruction says 'Finally, check your work'.
Checking comes after answering.
questions.explanation: After answering question one, the pupil should check their work as the final step.
misconceptions: Writing their name is the first step.
Starting question two is not mentioned in the instructions.
Giving the paper to the teacher is not mentioned.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Sub-Strand 9: Giving and Following Commands/Instructions/Directions and Making and Responding to Requests
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.9.1: Use verbs appropriately in commands, requests and directions in speech
indicator.objective: Make and respond to polite requests for help from peers

skills.description: Recognise polite requests (using 'please', 'may I', 'could you', 'can you')
Form polite requests for help from peers using appropriate words
Respond appropriately to requests (accept or decline politely)
Make and respond to polite requests in a role-play or classroom activity

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: You must always say yes to a request
Commands and requests are the same

questions.stem: Which of these is a polite request?
options: Could you please lend me your pen?
hints: A polite request uses words like 'please', 'could you' or 'may I'.
Look for the polite wording.
questions.explanation: 'Could you please lend me your pen?' is polite because it uses 'could you' and 'please'.
misconceptions: 'Give me your pen!' is a command.
'I want your pen' is a demand.

questions.stem: Which word makes a request more polite?
hints: It is a polite word we use when asking for something.
It starts with 'p'.
questions.explanation: 'Please' is the word that makes a request more polite.
misconceptions: 'Hey' is informal and can be rude.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a polite way to ask for help?
options: May I ask for your help?
hints: Polite requests use polite words.
Which option sounds like a command?
questions.explanation: 'Help me now!' is a command, not a polite request.
misconceptions: 'Could you help me, please?' is polite.
'May I ask for your help?' is polite.

questions.stem: Your friend says: 'Please help me carry my bag.' What is a polite way to accept?
options: Yes, of course. I will help you.
hints: A polite acceptance is friendly and willing.
Say yes and offer to help.
questions.explanation: 'Yes, of course. I will help you' is a polite way to accept the request.

questions.stem: Your friend asks: 'Can you help me with my homework?' You are busy. What is a polite way to decline?
options: I'm sorry, I can't right now. Maybe later?
hints: A polite decline apologises and offers a reason.
Look for the kind refusal.
questions.explanation: 'I'm sorry, I can't right now. Maybe later?' is polite because it apologises and suggests another time.

questions.stem: You want to borrow a pencil from your classmate. Which is the most polite way to ask?
options: Could you please lend me a pencil?
hints: Use polite words like 'could you' and 'please'.
The most polite option includes both.
questions.explanation: 'Could you please lend me a pencil?' is the most polite because it uses 'could you' and 'please'.
misconceptions: 'Give me a pencil' is a command.
'I need a pencil' is a statement, not a request.

questions.stem: You want your friend to help you clean the classroom. Which request is polite?
options: Can you please help me clean the classroom?
hints: Use 'can you' and 'please'.
The polite request asks, not commands.
questions.explanation: 'Can you please help me clean the classroom?' is polite because it asks politely with 'please'.
misconceptions: 'Clean the classroom with me' is a command.
'You must help me' is a demand.
'Why won't you help me?' is accusatory.

questions.stem: You want to ask your classmate to pass you the ruler. Which is the most polite way?
options: May I have the ruler, please?
hints: Use 'may I' and 'please'.
The polite request asks permission.
questions.explanation: 'May I have the ruler, please?' is polite because it uses 'may I' and 'please'.
misconceptions: 'Give me the ruler' is a command.
'I want the ruler now' is demanding.

questions.stem: A classmate asks: 'Could you please help me carry these books?' You are free. What should you say?
options: Yes, I'd be happy to help.
hints: If you are free, accept the request politely.
Show willingness to help.
questions.explanation: 'Yes, I'd be happy to help' is a polite and willing response.
misconceptions: Saying no when you are free is not helpful.
Saying you are busy when you are not is dishonest.

questions.stem: A classmate asks: 'Can you help me with my maths homework?' You don't understand the maths yourself. What is the best response?
options: I'm sorry, I don't understand it either. Maybe we can ask the teacher together?
hints: Be honest but kind.
Suggest another solution.
questions.explanation: 'I'm sorry, I don't understand it either. Maybe we can ask the teacher together?' is polite and helpful.
misconceptions: 'No, I won't help you' is unkind.

questions.stem: Which request uses the most polite language?
options: Would you mind helping me with this task?
hints: 'Would you mind' is a very polite way to ask.
The most polite option uses formal polite language.
questions.explanation: 'Would you mind helping me with this task?' is the most polite because it uses 'would you mind'.
misconceptions: 'You need to help me' is a demand.
'I demand your help' is very rude.

questions.stem: You want to ask your friend to wait for you after school. Which is the best polite request?
options: Could you please wait for me after school?
hints: Use 'could you' and 'please'.
The polite request asks, not commands.
questions.explanation: 'Could you please wait for me after school?' is polite and clear.
misconceptions: 'You must wait for me' is a demand.
'Don't go without me!' is a command.

questions.stem: Two pupils want to borrow a book from a classmate. Pupil A says: 'Give me the book.' Pupil B says: 'May I please borrow the book when you are finished?' Which pupil is making a polite request?
options: Pupil B, because they use 'may I' and 'please' and wait for the owner to finish
Pupil A, because they are direct
hints: Polite requests use polite words and consider the other person.
Pupil B uses 'may I', 'please' and considers the owner.
questions.explanation: Pupil B is making a polite request because they use polite language and consider the owner's needs.
misconceptions: Being direct is not always polite.

questions.stem: A classmate asks: 'Could you please help me with my project?' You are very tired and need to rest. What is the most polite way to respond?
options: I'm sorry, I'm really tired right now. Can I help you tomorrow instead?
hints: A polite decline apologises, explains, and offers an alternative.
The best option shows kindness even in refusal.
questions.explanation: 'I'm sorry, I'm really tired right now. Can I help you tomorrow instead?' is polite because it apologises, explains and offers an alternative.
misconceptions: 'Why should I help you?' is rude.

questions.stem: You want to ask your classmate to help you carry a heavy table. Which request is both polite and clear?
options: Could you please help me carry this table? It is too heavy for me alone.
hints: A good request uses polite words and explains why help is needed.
The best option uses 'could you please' and gives a reason.
questions.explanation: 'Could you please help me carry this table? It is too heavy for me alone.' is polite and clear because it uses polite words and explains the need.
misconceptions: 'Help me with this table' is a command.
'You carry the table' is a command.
'This table is too heavy' is a statement, not a request.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to ask a classmate to explain a question they did not understand. Which request is best?
options: Excuse me, could you please explain this question to me? I didn't understand it.
hints: Start with 'excuse me' and use 'could you please'.
Explain why you need help.
questions.explanation: 'Excuse me, could you please explain this question to me? I didn't understand it.' is polite and clear.
misconceptions: 'Explain this to me' is a command.
'You need to explain this' is a demand.

questions.stem: A pupil asks: 'Could you please help me carry my books to the staff room?' Which response is the most polite acceptance?
options: Of course, I'd be glad to help. Let me take some.
hints: A polite acceptance is enthusiastic and helpful.
Look for the response that shows willingness.
questions.explanation: 'Of course, I'd be glad to help. Let me take some.' is the most polite because it shows enthusiasm and willingness.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.10.1: Show knowledge of spoken grammar and register
indicator.objective: Demonstrate awareness of the features of spoken language (contractions, ellipsis e.g. A: How are you? B: Fine)

skills.description: Recognise contractions and their full forms
Form contractions from full forms and vice versa
Recognise ellipsis in conversation
Use contractions and ellipsis appropriately in spoken-style sentences

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Ellipsis means leaving out important information
Spoken language must be exactly like written language
You can't use contractions in speaking

questions.stem: What is the contraction in this sentence: 'I can't come today'?
hints: A contraction is a shortened form of two words.
Look for the word with an apostrophe.
questions.explanation: 'Can't' is the contraction. It is the shortened form of 'cannot'.

questions.stem: Which of these is a contraction?
hints: A contraction uses an apostrophe to replace missing letters.
Look for the word with an apostrophe.
questions.explanation: 'Can't' is a contraction because it uses an apostrophe to replace the missing letters 'no' in 'cannot'.
misconceptions: 'Cannot' is one word but not a contraction.

questions.stem: What is the full form of the contraction 'I'm'?
hints: The apostrophe replaces a missing letter.
'I'm' is short for two words.
questions.explanation: 'I'm' is the contraction of 'I am'. The apostrophe replaces the 'a' in 'am'.

questions.stem: What is the contraction of 'do not'?
hints: The apostrophe replaces the 'o' in 'not'.
The correct contraction has an apostrophe.
questions.explanation: The contraction of 'do not' is 'don't'. The apostrophe replaces the 'o'.
misconceptions: 'do'nt' has the apostrophe in the wrong place.
'do not' is the full form, not the contraction.

questions.stem: What is the contraction of 'she is'?
hints: The apostrophe replaces the 'i' in 'is'.
The correct contraction has an apostrophe.
questions.explanation: The contraction of 'she is' is 'she's'.
misconceptions: 'sh'es' has the apostrophe in the wrong place.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a contraction correctly?
options: I can't go to school today.
I can't to go school today.
hints: The contraction replaces 'cannot'.
Check that the rest of the sentence is grammatically correct.
questions.explanation: 'I can't go to school today' is correct because 'can't' replaces 'cannot' and the sentence is grammatically correct.

questions.stem: Choose the correct contraction: 'They ___ coming to the party.'
hints: The contraction of 'are not' is 'aren't'.
The apostrophe replaces the 'o' in 'not'.
questions.explanation: The correct contraction is 'aren't' (are + not).
misconceptions: 'are'nt' has the apostrophe in the wrong place.

questions.stem: What is the full form of the contraction 'won't'?
hints: 'Won't' is an irregular contraction.
It is the contraction of 'will not'.
questions.explanation: 'Won't' is the contraction of 'will not'. It is irregular because the spelling changes.
misconceptions: 'Want not' is not a standard contraction.

questions.stem: What is the contraction of 'I have'?
hints: The apostrophe replaces the 'ha' in 'have'.
The correct contraction has an apostrophe.
questions.explanation: The contraction of 'I have' is 'I've'.
misconceptions: 'I'ev' has the apostrophe in the wrong place.

questions.stem: A: 'How are you?' B: 'Fine.' What does B mean?
hints: Ellipsis means leaving out words that are understood.
B left out 'I am'.
questions.explanation: B means 'I am fine.' The words 'I am' are left out because they are understood from the question.
misconceptions: B is not saying 'You are fine'.
B is answering the question, not defining a word.
B's answer does not mean 'not fine'.

questions.stem: A: 'Where are you going?' B: 'To the market.' What is the full sentence B means?
options: I am going to the market.
You are going to the market.
To the market is a place.
hints: Ellipsis leaves out words that are understood.
B left out 'I am going'.
questions.explanation: B means 'I am going to the market.' The words 'I am going' are left out.
misconceptions: B is not saying 'You are going'.

questions.stem: A: 'What is your name?' B: 'Esi.' What words are left out in B's answer?
hints: Ellipsis leaves out words that are understood.
The full answer would be 'My name is Esi'.
questions.explanation: The words 'My name is' are left out. The full answer would be 'My name is Esi.'
misconceptions: B is not saying 'Your name is'.
B is not repeating the question.

questions.stem: Which sentence sounds more natural in spoken English?
options: I can't come to the party.
I cannot come to the party.
I can not come to the party.
I am not able to come to the party.
hints: Spoken English often uses contractions.
Which option uses a contraction?
questions.explanation: 'I can't come to the party' sounds more natural in spoken English because it uses the contraction 'can't'.
misconceptions: 'I cannot' is formal and less common in casual speech.
'I am not able to' is very formal.

questions.stem: A: 'Would you like some tea?' B: ___ Which response sounds most natural in a conversation?
options: Yes, I would like some tea.
Yes, I would like to have some tea please.
Yes, tea is what I would like.
hints: Spoken English often uses ellipsis.
Short answers are common in conversation.
questions.explanation: 'Yes, please' is the most natural because it uses ellipsis — the words 'I would like some tea' are understood.
misconceptions: The full sentence is less natural in casual conversation.
The very long sentence is overly formal.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses contractions appropriately for spoken English?
options: She's going to the market, isn't she?
She is going to the market, is not she?
She's going to the market, is not she?
She is going to the market, isn't she?
hints: Spoken English uses contractions in both the statement and the tag.
Which option has contractions in both places?
questions.explanation: 'She's going to the market, isn't she?' uses contractions naturally in both the statement and the tag.
misconceptions: The other options mix full forms and contractions awkwardly.

questions.stem: A: 'Did you finish your homework?' B: 'Not yet.' What does B mean?
options: I have not finished my homework yet.
You have not finished your homework yet.
Not yet is a full sentence.
hints: Ellipsis leaves out words that are understood.
The full answer would be 'I have not finished my homework yet'.
questions.explanation: B means 'I have not finished my homework yet.' The words 'I have finished my homework' are left out.
misconceptions: B is talking about themselves, not 'you'.
'Not yet' is an elliptical answer, not a full sentence.

questions.stem: Which is the correct contraction for 'they would'?
hints: The apostrophe replaces 'woul'.
The correct contraction has an apostrophe.
questions.explanation: The contraction of 'they would' is 'they'd'.
misconceptions: 'the'y'd' has the apostrophe in the wrong place.

questions.stem: A pupil is writing a dialogue for a role-play. Which version sounds most natural for spoken English?
options: I'm sorry, I can't come. I've got too much homework.
I am sorry, I cannot come. I have got too much homework.
I'm sorry, I cannot come. I have got too much homework.
I am sorry, I can't come. I've got too much homework.
hints: Natural spoken English uses contractions throughout.
Which option uses contractions consistently?
questions.explanation: 'I'm sorry, I can't come. I've got too much homework.' uses contractions naturally and consistently.
misconceptions: The other options mix full forms and contractions awkwardly.

questions.stem: Which conversation sounds most natural in spoken English?
options: A: What's your name? B: Esi. A: Where do you live? B: Accra.
A: What is your name? B: My name is Esi. A: Where do you live? B: I live in Accra.
A: What's your name? B: My name is Esi. A: Where do you live? B: I live in Accra.
A: What is your name? B: Esi. A: Where do you live? B: Accra.
hints: Natural spoken English uses contractions and ellipsis.
Which option uses both contractions and short answers?
questions.explanation: Option A uses both contractions ('What's') and ellipsis ('Esi', 'Accra') naturally.
misconceptions: Option B uses no contractions or ellipsis.
Option C mixes contractions and full forms.
Option D uses ellipsis but no contractions.

questions.stem: In a conversation, A says: 'Are you coming to the party?' B replies: 'Maybe.' What does B's reply mean?
options: Maybe I am coming to the party.
Maybe you are coming to the party.
I am definitely coming to the party.
hints: Ellipsis leaves out words that are understood.
B left out 'I am coming to the party'.
questions.explanation: B means 'Maybe I am coming to the party.' The words 'I am coming to the party' are left out.
misconceptions: B is talking about themselves, not 'you'.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.10.1: Show knowledge of spoken grammar and register
indicator.objective: Demonstrate awareness of the differences between spoken and written forms of language e.g. simple and complex sentence structures

skills.description: Identify differences between spoken and written language (simplicity, formality, sentence length)
Recognise formal and informal language and when each is appropriate
Identify simple vs. complex sentence structures in spoken and written contexts

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Formal and written are the same thing
Simple sentences are only for children

questions.stem: Which of these is a spoken sentence?
options: I cannot attend the meeting today.
The undersigned wishes to inform you.
hints: Spoken language often uses contractions and simpler words.
Which sentence sounds like something you would say?
questions.explanation: 'I can't come today' is a spoken sentence because it uses a contraction and simple language.
misconceptions: 'I cannot attend the meeting today' is more formal/written.
The other options use formal written language.

questions.stem: Which sentence is more likely to be found in a written letter than in a conversation?
options: I am writing to inform you that I will be absent.
hints: Written language is often more formal.
Which sentence sounds like a letter?
questions.explanation: 'I am writing to inform you that I will be absent' is more likely in a written letter because it is formal and complete.
misconceptions: 'I can't come' is informal spoken language.
'See you later' is informal spoken language.
'What's up?' is very informal spoken language.

questions.stem: Which of these is an informal way of greeting someone?
hints: Informal language is casual and used with friends.
Which greeting is casual?
questions.explanation: 'Hi!' is an informal greeting used with friends and people you know well.

questions.stem: Which of these is a simple sentence?
options: The boy ran and the girl walked.
The boy who was tall ran quickly.
Although it was raining, the boy ran.
hints: A simple sentence has one subject and one verb.
Which sentence has only one subject and one verb?
questions.explanation: 'The boy ran' is a simple sentence with one subject ('the boy') and one verb ('ran').
misconceptions: 'The boy ran and the girl walked' has two subjects and two verbs.
The third option has a relative clause.
The fourth option has a subordinate clause.

questions.stem: Which of these is formal language?
options: I would like to request your assistance.
hints: Formal language uses complete, polite wording.
Which sentence sounds most official or polite?
questions.explanation: 'I would like to request your assistance' is formal because it uses polite, complete language.

questions.stem: What is one difference between spoken and written language?
options: Spoken language often uses contractions; written language often uses full forms
hints: Think about how you talk versus how you write a letter.
Speech uses contractions like 'can't'; writing often uses 'cannot'.
questions.explanation: Spoken language often uses contractions (can't, don't) while written language often uses full forms (cannot, do not).
misconceptions: Spoken language can be informal or formal.

questions.stem: When would you use formal language?
options: When writing a letter to the headteacher
When talking to your best friend
hints: Formal language is used in official or respectful situations.
Which situation is most official?
questions.explanation: You would use formal language when writing a letter to the headteacher because it is an official situation that requires respect and politeness.
misconceptions: Talking to a best friend is informal.
Chatting with a brother is informal.

questions.stem: Which sentence is more complex?
options: I went to the market and bought some fruit.
hints: A complex sentence has more than one clause.
Which sentence has two actions joined together?
questions.explanation: 'I went to the market and bought some fruit' is more complex because it joins two actions with 'and'.
misconceptions: The other sentences are shorter and simpler.

questions.stem: Which version sounds more like written English?
options: The committee has decided to postpone the meeting until further notice.
hints: Written English is often more formal and uses full sentences.
Which version uses formal, complete language?
questions.explanation: The first option sounds more like written English because it is formal and uses a complete sentence structure.
misconceptions: The other options are informal spoken language.

questions.stem: Which of these is the most informal sentence?
options: I would be grateful if you could attend.
hints: Informal language is casual and may use slang or exclamations.
Which sentence sounds most like a casual chat?
questions.explanation: 'Hey, come over!' is the most informal because it uses casual language and an exclamation.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses simpler structure?
options: The girl who was wearing a red dress sang beautifully at the concert.
Although she was nervous, the girl sang.
The girl sang and the audience clapped.
hints: A simple sentence has one subject and one verb.
Which sentence is the shortest and simplest?
questions.explanation: 'The girl sang' is the simplest because it has one subject and one verb with no extra clauses.
misconceptions: The other sentences contain extra clauses and details.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a compound sentence?
options: I like tea and she likes coffee.
hints: A compound sentence joins two independent clauses.
Look for the sentence with two complete ideas joined by a conjunction.
questions.explanation: 'I like tea and she likes coffee' is a compound sentence because it joins two complete ideas with 'and'.
misconceptions: The other sentences are simple sentences.

questions.stem: A pupil is writing a letter to the headteacher. Which sentence is most appropriate for this formal context?
options: I am writing to request permission to be absent from school.
hints: Formal letters use polite, complete language.
Which sentence sounds most respectful and official?
questions.explanation: 'I am writing to request permission to be absent from school' is appropriate for a formal letter because it is polite and complete.
misconceptions: 'Can I skip school?' is informal and inappropriate.

questions.stem: Why do spoken sentences often have simpler structures than written sentences?
options: Because spoken language is usually more immediate and informal
Because spoken language has no grammar
Because written language is not important
Because spoken language cannot express complex ideas
hints: Think about how quickly we speak compared to how carefully we write.
Spoken language happens in real time.
questions.explanation: Spoken sentences are often simpler because speech is immediate and informal, while writing allows time for more complex structures.
misconceptions: Spoken language can express complex ideas, just differently.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a complex sentence?
options: When the rain stopped, we went outside.
The rain stopped and we went outside.
hints: A complex sentence has a main clause and a subordinate clause.
Look for the sentence with a dependent clause (starting with 'when').
questions.explanation: 'When the rain stopped, we went outside' is complex because it has a subordinate clause ('When the rain stopped') and a main clause ('we went outside').
misconceptions: 'The rain stopped and we went outside' is compound.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an appropriate register for a classroom presentation?
options: Today, I will talk about the importance of reading.
So, like, reading is important and stuff.
hints: A presentation requires a formal but clear register.
Which sentence sounds like a proper presentation opening?
questions.explanation: 'Today, I will talk about the importance of reading' is appropriate for a presentation because it is clear, formal and complete.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches the situation to the register?
options: Talking to a friend — informal register
Writing to the headteacher — informal register
Chatting with a brother — formal register
hints: Informal register is for casual situations; formal register is for official situations.
Talking to a friend is casual.
questions.explanation: Talking to a friend matches informal register because it is a casual situation.
misconceptions: Writing to the headteacher requires formal register.
Chatting with a brother is informal.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains the difference between spoken and written language?
options: Spoken language is usually more interactive and informal, while written language is usually more structured and formal
Spoken language is always better than written language
Written language is always simpler than spoken language
Spoken and written language are exactly the same
hints: Think about the purpose and context of each form.
Speech is interactive; writing is structured.
questions.explanation: Spoken language is usually more interactive and informal, while written language is usually more structured and formal.
misconceptions: One form is not always better.
Written language is often more complex, not simpler.

questions.stem: A pupil writes: 'Although I was tired, I finished my homework because I wanted to do well.' How many clauses are in this sentence?
options: 3 (one main clause and two subordinate clauses)
hints: Count the clauses: 'Although I was tired' (1), 'I finished my homework' (2), 'because I wanted to do well' (3).
There is one main clause and two subordinate clauses.
questions.explanation: The sentence has 3 clauses: 'Although I was tired' (subordinate), 'I finished my homework' (main), 'because I wanted to do well' (subordinate).
misconceptions: It has more than one clause.
It has more than two clauses.
It has three, not four, clauses.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.10.1: Show knowledge of spoken grammar and register
indicator.objective: Demonstrate awareness of how meaning is conveyed through appropriate pace, stress, tone – through stories read aloud

skills.description: Recognise how reading pace affects meaning (slow for suspense, fast for excitement)
Identify how stress on words changes meaning in a story read aloud
Recognise how tone (happy, sad, serious) conveys meaning

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Tone doesn't matter when reading aloud
All parts of a story should be read at the same pace

questions.stem: What does 'pace' mean when reading a story aloud?
options: How fast or slow you read
hints: Pace is about speed.
It tells you how quickly or slowly you read.
questions.explanation: Pace means how fast or slow you read a story aloud.

questions.stem: What does 'tone' mean when reading a story?
options: The feeling or mood in your voice
hints: Tone is about feeling.
It shows whether you are happy, sad, serious, etc.
questions.explanation: Tone is the feeling or mood in your voice when you read — happy, sad, serious, etc.

questions.stem: When we put stress on a word in a story, we ___.
hints: Stress is about emphasis.
Stressed words are said with more force.
questions.explanation: When we put stress on a word, we say it with more emphasis.
misconceptions: Softness is the opposite of stress.
Speed is not the same as stress.

questions.stem: When reading a scary part of a story, you should read ___.
hints: Scary parts need suspense.
Slow and low creates suspense.
questions.explanation: Reading slowly with a low voice creates suspense and makes the scary part feel more intense.
misconceptions: Fast reading is for exciting parts, not scary ones.
Loud and quick does not create suspense.

questions.stem: When reading a happy part of a story, your tone should be ___.
hints: Happy parts need a happy tone.
Cheerful and lively matches happiness.
questions.explanation: When reading a happy part, your tone should be cheerful and lively to match the mood.
misconceptions: Sad and low does not match happiness.
Angry and loud does not match happiness.
Flat and boring does not match happiness.

questions.stem: A story describes a chase. How should you read this part?
hints: A chase is exciting and fast.
Read faster to match the action.
questions.explanation: A chase is exciting and fast, so you should read faster with excitement to match the action.
misconceptions: Slow and quiet does not match a chase.
A sad voice does not match excitement.

questions.stem: A story describes a quiet, peaceful scene. How should you read it?
hints: A peaceful scene is calm.
Slow and soft matches calm.
questions.explanation: A peaceful scene should be read slowly and softly to match the calm mood.
misconceptions: Quick and loud does not match peace.

questions.stem: A story says: 'The old woman wept when she lost her only son.' What tone should you use?
hints: The old woman is weeping.
The tone should match her sadness.
questions.explanation: The tone should be sad and sympathetic because the old woman is grieving.

questions.stem: In a story, the sentence says: 'She found the KEY.' Which word would you stress to show that she found the key, not something else?
hints: The word 'KEY' is in capital letters.
Stressing 'KEY' shows it was the key she found, not something else.
questions.explanation: Stressing 'KEY' shows that she found the key specifically, not something else.

questions.stem: A story says: 'The teacher was very angry with the pupils.' What tone should you use?
hints: The teacher is angry.
The tone should match anger — sharp and stern.
questions.explanation: The tone should be sharp and stern to match the teacher's anger.
misconceptions: Soft and gentle does not match anger.
Happy and playful does not match anger.
Sleepy and slow does not match anger.

questions.stem: Why should you change your pace when reading a story?
options: To match the mood and action of different parts
hints: Pace should match what is happening in the story.
Different parts have different moods.
questions.explanation: You should change your pace to match the mood and action of different parts of the story.
misconceptions: Changing pace is not about finishing quickly.
It does not make the story longer.

questions.stem: In a story, a character says: 'I didn't take your book.' If you stress 'I', what does it mean?
options: I didn't take it — someone else did
hints: Stressing 'I' emphasises the person.
It means 'I' am not the one who took it.
questions.explanation: Stressing 'I' in 'I didn't take your book' emphasises that the speaker is not the one who took it — someone else did.
misconceptions: Stressing 'I' is not about taking something else.
It is not about not taking anything.
It is not about the book not being taken.

questions.stem: A storyteller reads a story. During a sad part, she reads slowly with a low voice. What effect does this have on the audience?
options: It makes the audience feel the sadness of the moment
hints: Slow, low reading matches sadness.
The audience will feel the emotion.
questions.explanation: Reading slowly with a low voice during a sad part helps the audience feel the sadness of the moment.
misconceptions: Slow, low reading does not make people laugh.

questions.stem: A storyteller changes her tone for each character. Why is this important?
options: It helps the audience know who is speaking and understand the characters
It shows off the storyteller's voice
hints: Different characters have different voices.
Tone changes help the audience follow the story.
questions.explanation: Changing tone for each character helps the audience know who is speaking and understand each character's personality.
misconceptions: Tone changes do not make the story longer.
They are for the story's benefit, not showing off.

questions.stem: A story says: 'The small boy carried the HEAVY bag.' Why might the reader stress 'HEAVY'?
options: To emphasise how difficult it was for the small boy
To show the bag is light
hints: The bag is heavy and the boy is small.
Stressing 'HEAVY' emphasises the difficulty.
questions.explanation: Stressing 'HEAVY' emphasises how difficult it was for the small boy to carry the bag.
misconceptions: Stress does not make sentences longer.
HEAVY is the opposite of light.

questions.stem: A pupil reads a story very fast from beginning to end without changing pace. What is the problem?
options: The audience may not understand or feel the story's different moods
The audience will enjoy it more
hints: Different parts of a story have different moods.
Reading at one pace does not match the changing moods.
questions.explanation: Reading too fast without changing pace means the audience may not understand the story or feel its different moods.
misconceptions: Fast reading does not make it more enjoyable.
Speed does not make the story shorter.
It makes it less clear, not more.

questions.stem: Two pupils read the same sentence: 'The monster is coming.' Pupil A reads it slowly with a deep, scary voice. Pupil B reads it quickly with a happy voice. Which reading better conveys the meaning?
options: Pupil A, because the slow, scary voice matches the dangerous meaning
Pupil B, because happy is always better
Both readings convey the same meaning
hints: A monster coming is scary, not happy.
The reading should match the meaning.
questions.explanation: Pupil A's slow, scary reading better conveys the meaning because a monster coming is dangerous and scary.
misconceptions: Happy does not match a monster coming.

questions.stem: In a story, a character says: 'I never said she stole my money.' There are seven words. If the speaker stresses different words, the meaning changes. Which word would you stress to show that someone else said it, not you?
hints: Stressing 'I' contrasts with someone else.
It means 'I' didn't say it — someone else did.
questions.explanation: Stressing 'I' shows that someone else said it, not you.
misconceptions: 'never' shows you didn't say it at all.
'she' shifts emphasis to the person who stole.

questions.stem: A storyteller reads a funny part of a story with a flat, serious tone. How will this affect the audience?
options: The funny part will not seem funny
The audience will understand it better
hints: A flat tone does not match humour.
The tone should match the content.
questions.explanation: A flat, serious tone will make the funny part seem less funny because the tone does not match the humour.
misconceptions: The audience will not laugh more.
A flat tone does not improve understanding.
Tone does not change the length of a story.

questions.stem: A story has three parts: a happy beginning, a sad middle and a happy ending. How should the storyteller adjust her pace and tone?
options: Cheerful and medium pace for the beginning; slow and sad for the middle; cheerful and lively for the ending
No change in pace or tone
hints: Each part has a different mood.
Match the pace and tone to each mood.
questions.explanation: The storyteller should match her pace and tone to each part: cheerful for the happy beginning, slow and sad for the sad middle, and cheerful and lively for the happy ending.
misconceptions: One pace and tone does not match the changing moods.
The middle is sad, so it should not be happy throughout.
Changing pace and tone is important.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.10.2: Demonstrate the ability to communicate with accurate pronunciation and appropriate intonation
indicator.objective: Speak clearly and fluently, using the appropriate voice qualities (pace, tone etc.)

skills.description: Identify appropriate voice qualities for speaking (pace, tone, volume)
Recognise clear speech (good pronunciation, not mumbling)
Demonstrate fluency when speaking on a familiar topic

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Speaking loudly is the same as speaking clearly

questions.stem: What does 'voice quality' refer to when speaking?
options: The pitch, tone and volume of your voice
hints: Voice quality is about how your voice sounds.
It includes how high or low, loud or soft you speak.
questions.explanation: Voice quality refers to the pitch, tone and volume of your voice when speaking.
misconceptions: Clothing colour is not voice quality.
Word choice is vocabulary, not voice quality.
Writing speed is not voice quality.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of clear speech?
options: Pronouncing words properly so people understand
hints: Clear speech means people can understand you.
Pronouncing words properly helps.
questions.explanation: Clear speech means pronouncing words properly so listeners can understand you.
misconceptions: Speaking too fast can make words unclear.
Whispering is not clear to a group.

questions.stem: What does it mean to speak fluently?
hints: Fluency is about smoothness.
It means your speech flows naturally.
questions.explanation: Speaking fluently means speaking smoothly without many long pauses or hesitations.
misconceptions: Fast speech is not necessarily fluent.

questions.stem: When speaking to a friend in class, your voice should be ___.
hints: You want your friend to hear you without disturbing others.
A moderate voice is best.
questions.explanation: When speaking to a friend in class, you should use an audible but not too loud voice.
misconceptions: A whisper may not be heard.

questions.stem: Which of these helps you speak clearly?
hints: Clear speech depends on how you say the words.
Proper pronunciation is key.
questions.explanation: Pronouncing words properly helps you speak clearly.
misconceptions: Looking down can muffle your voice.
Speaking too fast can make words unclear.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a presentation but speaks too softly. What should they adjust?
options: Their topic — choose a new topic
hints: If people can't hear you, you need to increase volume.
Volume is how loud or soft you speak.
questions.explanation: The pupil should increase their volume — speak louder so the audience can hear.

questions.stem: Which sentence is spoken clearly?
hints: Clear speech means pronouncing all words properly.
The correct option has all words clearly pronounced.
questions.explanation: 'I want to go' is spoken clearly because all words are pronounced properly.
misconceptions: 'I wanna go?' slurs and has incorrect intonation.

questions.stem: A pupil reads a sentence with many pauses and says 'um' often. What is lacking?
hints: Pauses and 'um' break the smooth flow.
Fluency is about smooth flow.
questions.explanation: The pupil lacks fluency because the many pauses and 'um's break the smooth flow of speech.

questions.stem: When speaking to a large group, you should use ___.
options: the same voice as talking to one person
hints: A large group needs to hear you.
You need more volume.
questions.explanation: When speaking to a large group, you should use a louder voice than usual so everyone can hear.
misconceptions: A softer voice won't reach the back.
Talking to one person requires less volume.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a good voice quality for speaking?
hints: Mumbling makes words unclear.
Good voice quality helps communication.
questions.explanation: Mumbling is not a good voice quality because it makes words unclear.

questions.stem: How can you improve your fluency when speaking?
hints: Practice makes perfect.
Familiar topics help you speak smoothly.
questions.explanation: You can improve fluency by practising speaking on familiar topics regularly.
misconceptions: Speaking fast does not improve fluency.

questions.stem: Why is it important to use appropriate pace when speaking?
options: So listeners can follow and understand you
hints: Pace is speed.
Good pace helps understanding.
questions.explanation: Appropriate pace is important so listeners can follow and understand what you are saying.
misconceptions: Finishing quickly is not the goal.
Confusing listeners is not the goal.

questions.stem: A pupil speaks with a very high, squeaky voice that is hard to understand. What voice quality should they work on?
hints: High, squeaky voice is about pitch.
Pitch is how high or low your voice is.
questions.explanation: The pupil should work on their pitch/tone to make their voice more natural and understandable.
misconceptions: Pronunciation is about sounds, not pitch.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of clear speech?
options: Pronouncing all sounds in a word correctly
hints: Clear speech means every sound is heard.
Proper pronunciation of all sounds.
questions.explanation: Clear speech involves pronouncing all sounds in a word correctly.

questions.stem: A pupil is asked to speak on 'My School' for one minute. They speak smoothly with only a few short pauses. Is this fluent?
options: Yes, because they spoke smoothly with few pauses
No, because they paused at all
No, because it was only one minute
Yes, because they spoke very fast
hints: Fluency allows a few natural pauses.
Smooth speech with few pauses is fluent.
questions.explanation: Yes, this is fluent because they spoke smoothly with only a few natural pauses.
misconceptions: A few natural pauses are fine.
Length of time does not determine fluency.
Speaking fast is not the same as fluency.

questions.stem: When speaking to a friend, using a very loud voice is ___.
options: the only way to be heard
hints: A very loud voice in a one-to-one conversation is too much.
It can disturb others around you.
questions.explanation: Using a very loud voice when speaking to a friend is inappropriate because it may disturb others.
