misconceptions: It is not appropriate for a one-to-one chat.
There are other ways to be heard.

questions.stem: Two pupils give a short speech. Pupil A speaks clearly and fluently. Pupil B mumbles and pauses often. Who is more effective?
options: Pupil A, because they speak clearly and fluently
Pupil B, because they pause for effect
hints: Clear and fluent speech is easier to understand.
Mumbling and frequent pauses hinder communication.
questions.explanation: Pupil A is more effective because they speak clearly and fluently, making it easy for the audience to understand.
misconceptions: Frequent pauses are not for effect here; they hinder fluency.

questions.stem: Why might speaking too fast affect clarity?
options: Listeners may not catch the words
It makes the speaker sound smarter
hints: Fast speech can blur words together.
Listeners need time to process words.
questions.explanation: Speaking too fast can affect clarity because listeners may not catch all the words.
misconceptions: Shorter speech is not necessarily clearer.
Fast speech can worsen pronunciation clarity.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.10.2: Demonstrate the ability to communicate with accurate pronunciation and appropriate intonation
indicator.objective: Read aloud clearly, at a good pace and with expression

skills.description: Recognise a good reading pace (not too fast, not too slow)
Identify appropriate expression when reading aloud (tone matches meaning)
Read aloud clearly, at a good pace and with expression

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Reading fast shows you are a good reader
You don't need to practise reading aloud

questions.stem: What does a good reading pace mean?
options: Reading at a speed that is clear and easy to follow
hints: A good pace helps listeners understand.
It is not too fast and not too slow.
questions.explanation: A good reading pace is a speed that is clear and easy for listeners to follow.
misconceptions: Reading fast is not always clear.
Reading too slowly can be boring.

questions.stem: What does it mean to read with expression?
options: Reading with feeling and matching your voice to the meaning
hints: Expression is about feeling.
Your voice should match the mood of the text.
questions.explanation: Reading with expression means using feeling and matching your voice to the meaning of the text.
misconceptions: A flat voice has no expression.

questions.stem: When reading a list of items, you should read ___.
options: at a steady pace, pausing slightly between items
hints: Lists need to be clear.
Pausing slightly helps the listener follow.
questions.explanation: When reading a list, a steady pace with slight pauses between items helps clarity.
misconceptions: No pauses makes the list sound like one long word.

questions.stem: When reading a question aloud, your voice should ___ at the end.
hints: Questions usually have rising intonation.
Your voice rises at the end.
questions.explanation: When reading a question aloud, your voice should rise at the end.
misconceptions: A flat voice does not show a question.
Stopping does not convey a question.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sign of a good reading pace?
hints: Good pace is about understanding.
Listeners should be able to follow.
questions.explanation: A good reading pace allows listeners to follow and understand the text.
misconceptions: Finishing quickly is not the goal.

questions.stem: A story says: 'The baby was crying.' What expression should you use?
hints: A crying baby is sad.
Use a tone that matches sadness.
questions.explanation: You should use a sad and gentle expression to match the crying baby.

questions.stem: A text says: 'The team won the match! They were so happy!' What expression should you use?
hints: Winning is exciting and happy.
Match the expression to the happiness.
questions.explanation: You should use an excited and happy expression to match the team's victory.

questions.stem: When reading a sentence with a comma, what should you do?
hints: Commas indicate pauses.
A brief pause helps clarity.
questions.explanation: You should pause briefly at a comma to make the sentence clear.
misconceptions: Reading faster at a comma is wrong.
A long stop is not necessary.

questions.stem: A sentence says: 'Be careful! The floor is wet.' What expression should you use?
hints: The sentence warns of danger.
An urgent tone matches a warning.
questions.explanation: You should use an urgent and warning expression to convey the danger.

questions.stem: Which reading pace is best for reading a recipe aloud?
options: Slowly and clearly, so steps are understood
hints: Recipes need to be followed step by step.
Clarity is important.
questions.explanation: A recipe should be read slowly and clearly so listeners can follow each step.
misconceptions: No pauses makes steps run together.

questions.stem: When reading dialogue in a story, you should change your ___ for each character.
hints: Characters have different voices.
Changing voice helps distinguish speakers.
questions.explanation: Changing your voice for each character helps listeners know who is speaking.

questions.stem: A story says: 'The old man walked slowly down the road, leaning on his stick.' How should you read this?
options: Slowly with a gentle, tired tone
hints: The old man walks slowly.
Match your pace and tone to his slowness.
questions.explanation: You should read slowly with a gentle, tired tone to match the old man's slow walk.
misconceptions: Fast does not match the slow walk.
Angry does not match the gentle description.
Funny does not match the serious tone.

questions.stem: Why is it important to pause at full stops when reading aloud?
options: To take a breath and show the end of a sentence
hints: Full stops mark the end of sentences.
Pausing helps listeners understand where sentences end.
questions.explanation: Pausing at full stops allows you to take a breath and shows listeners where one sentence ends and the next begins.

questions.stem: A story says: 'The lion roared loudly. The other animals ran away in fear.' What expression should you use for the second sentence?
hints: The animals are running away in fear.
Fear needs a scared, urgent tone.
questions.explanation: You should use a scared and urgent expression to match the animals' fear.
misconceptions: Sleepy does not match running away.

questions.stem: A pupil reads a story very fast, without pausing at punctuation. What problem does this cause?
options: The story becomes harder to understand
hints: Punctuation gives structure to reading.
Without pauses, sentences run together.
questions.explanation: Reading too fast without pausing at punctuation makes the story harder to understand.
misconceptions: Fast reading can make it less exciting.
Speed does not change story length.

questions.stem: A text says: 'Congratulations! You have won the first prize!' Which expression is appropriate?
hints: The text is about winning.
Use an excited tone.
questions.explanation: You should use an excited and congratulatory expression to match the good news.

questions.stem: Two pupils read the same sentence: 'Watch out! The car is coming!' Pupil A reads it calmly. Pupil B reads it urgently. Which pupil conveys the meaning better?
options: Pupil B, because the sentence is a warning and needs urgency
Pupil A, because calm is always best
hints: The sentence is a warning of danger.
Urgency matches the warning.
questions.explanation: Pupil B conveys the meaning better because the sentence is a warning and needs an urgent tone.

questions.stem: A pupil is reading a story and changes pace for different parts. Why is this a good strategy?
options: It matches the mood and action, helping listeners understand and enjoy the story
It shows the reader is fast
hints: Different parts of a story have different moods.
Changing pace helps convey the mood.
questions.explanation: Changing pace for different parts matches the mood and action, helping listeners understand and enjoy the story.
misconceptions: Pace changes do not shorten the story.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.10.3: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Identify the purpose and audience of a speech and set goals in the context of assigned topics (e.g. about familiar persons)

skills.description: Identify the purpose of a speech (to inform, persuade, entertain, welcome)
Identify the audience of a speech (peers, teachers, parents, community)
Set goals for a speech based on topic, purpose and audience

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: All speeches have the same purpose
Goals are not needed for a speech
A speech is only for informing

questions.stem: A pupil gives a speech telling the class about the rules of the library. What is the purpose of this speech?
hints: The speech gives information about rules.
Informing means giving facts and information.
questions.explanation: The purpose is to inform because the pupil is giving information about library rules.

questions.stem: A pupil gives a speech asking classmates to keep the school compound clean. What is the purpose?
hints: The pupil is trying to convince others to do something.
Persuading means convincing people.
questions.explanation: The purpose is to persuade because the pupil is trying to convince classmates to keep the compound clean.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a speech at the school assembly. Who is the audience?
options: The whole school — pupils and teachers
hints: Assembly is attended by the whole school.
The audience is everyone at assembly.
questions.explanation: At a school assembly, the audience is the whole school — pupils and teachers.
misconceptions: Only the headteacher is too narrow.
Family is not at school assembly.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a speech to welcome a new pupil to the class. Who is the audience?
options: The new pupil and the class
hints: The speech is to welcome a new pupil.
The audience includes the new pupil and classmates.
questions.explanation: The audience is the new pupil and the class because the speech is to welcome the new pupil.
misconceptions: The headteacher is not the main audience.
Parents are not in the classroom.
The whole community is too broad.

questions.stem: What is a goal for a speech?
options: What you want to achieve with the speech
hints: A goal is what you aim to do.
It is the purpose or target of your speech.
questions.explanation: A goal for a speech is what you want to achieve — for example, to inform, persuade or entertain.
misconceptions: Word count is not a goal.
Clothing colour is not a goal.

questions.stem: A pupil gives a speech about 'My Favourite Person' — their grandmother. What is the purpose?
options: To entertain and share personal feelings
hints: The speech is about a personal topic.
Sharing feelings about a loved one is entertaining and emotional.
questions.explanation: The purpose is to entertain and share personal feelings about the pupil's grandmother.
misconceptions: It is not about school rules.
It is not a welcome speech.

questions.stem: A pupil gives a speech explaining how to plant a tree. What is the purpose?
hints: The speech explains a process.
Explaining how to do something is informing.
questions.explanation: The purpose is to inform because the pupil is explaining how to plant a tree.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a speech to parents at a PTA meeting. Who is the audience?
hints: PTA stands for Parent-Teacher Association.
The audience includes parents and teachers.
questions.explanation: At a PTA meeting, the audience includes parents and teachers.
misconceptions: Only the headteacher is too narrow.
Community elders may not be present.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a speech to classmates about a school trip. Who is the audience?
hints: The speech is in the classroom.
The audience is the class.
questions.explanation: The audience is the classmates and the teacher because the speech is in the classroom.
misconceptions: The whole community is too broad.
Parents are not in the classroom.
The headteacher may not be present.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to give a speech to persuade classmates to stop littering. What is a good goal for this speech?
options: To convince classmates to keep the school clean
To explain how to play football
hints: The purpose is to persuade.
The goal should match the purpose.
questions.explanation: A good goal is to convince classmates to keep the school clean because the purpose is to persuade.
misconceptions: A funny story is for entertainment.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a speech to inform the class about malaria prevention. What is a good goal?
options: To teach classmates how to prevent malaria
hints: The purpose is to inform.
The goal should be to teach or share information.
questions.explanation: A good goal is to teach classmates how to prevent malaria because the purpose is to inform.
misconceptions: Making people laugh is for entertainment.

questions.stem: A pupil gives a speech at a birthday party for a friend. What is the purpose?
hints: A birthday party is a celebration.
The speech is for fun and celebration.
questions.explanation: The purpose is to entertain and celebrate because it is a birthday party.
misconceptions: Welcoming a new pupil is not relevant.

questions.stem: A pupil gives a speech at a community durbar about keeping the town clean. Who is the audience?
hints: A durbar is a community gathering.
The audience includes community members.
questions.explanation: At a community durbar, the audience includes community members and elders.

questions.stem: A pupil gives a speech arguing that pupils should have more break time. What is the purpose?
hints: The speech argues for a change.
Arguing to convince others is persuasion.
questions.explanation: The purpose is to persuade because the pupil is arguing to convince others to agree about break time.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a speech to inform the class about the importance of reading. What goal should the pupil set?
options: To explain why reading is important and encourage classmates to read more
hints: The purpose is to inform about reading.
The goal should be to teach and encourage.
questions.explanation: A good goal is to explain why reading is important and encourage classmates to read more.
misconceptions: Making people laugh is for entertainment.

questions.stem: A pupil gives a speech welcoming a new headteacher to the school. What is the purpose?
hints: The speech is to welcome someone new.
Welcoming is the purpose.
questions.explanation: The purpose is to welcome the new headteacher to the school.

questions.stem: A pupil gives a speech at a school prize-giving day. The audience includes parents, teachers, pupils and the guest of honour. How should the pupil adjust the speech for this audience?
options: Use polite, formal language suitable for all ages
Speak only to the guest of honour
hints: The audience is mixed — different ages and roles.
Polite, formal language is appropriate for all.
questions.explanation: The pupil should use polite, formal language suitable for a mixed audience of parents, teachers, pupils and a guest of honour.
misconceptions: Slang is not suitable for a formal event.
Speaking only to the guest ignores others.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a persuasive speech to classmates about why they should not waste water. What is a clear goal?
options: To convince classmates to save water at school and at home
To explain how water is treated
To tell a story about a river
hints: The purpose is to persuade.
The goal should be to convince others to change behaviour.
questions.explanation: A clear goal is to convince classmates to save water because the purpose is to persuade.
misconceptions: Explaining treatment is informing, not persuading.

questions.stem: A pupil is asked to give a speech about 'The Importance of Education' to three different audiences: (1) classmates, (2) parents, (3) community elders. How should the pupil adapt the speech for each audience?
options: Use different examples and language appropriate for each group
Use the same speech for all three audiences
hints: Different audiences need different approaches.
Adapt examples and language to suit each group.
questions.explanation: The pupil should adapt the speech for each audience by using examples and language appropriate for classmates, parents and community elders.
misconceptions: The same speech may not suit all audiences.
Speaking only to parents ignores others.

questions.stem: A pupil gives a speech that tells a funny story about a cat. The audience laughs. What is the purpose of this speech?
hints: The speech makes the audience laugh.
Making people laugh is entertainment.
questions.explanation: The purpose is to entertain because the speech is a funny story that makes the audience laugh.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to give a speech to inform the class about 'The Dangers of Drug Abuse.' Which goal is most appropriate?
options: To teach classmates about the dangers of drug abuse and how to avoid them
To make classmates laugh about drugs
To persuade classmates to try drugs
hints: The purpose is to inform about dangers.
A good goal is to teach and warn.
questions.explanation: The most appropriate goal is to teach classmates about the dangers of drug abuse and how to avoid them.
misconceptions: Making jokes about drugs is inappropriate.
Persuading to try drugs is harmful.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.10.3: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Draw on prior knowledge to identify the subject matter of a speech

skills.description: Identify what you already know about a speech topic
Identify the subject matter of a speech from its title or opening
Use prior knowledge to contribute ideas to a speech topic

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: You don't need prior knowledge for a speech
Subject matter is always stated in the title

questions.stem: Before listening to a speech about 'Keeping Our School Clean,' what is something you already know about this topic?
options: That we should throw rubbish in bins
That the school is in Accra
That Maths is my favourite subject
hints: Think about what keeping a place clean involves.
It involves not littering.
questions.explanation: You already know that keeping the school clean means throwing rubbish in bins and not littering.
misconceptions: School location is not about cleanliness.
The headteacher's height is not about cleanliness.

questions.stem: Before listening to a speech about 'The Importance of Reading,' what do you already know?
options: That reading helps us learn new things
That we read only at school
hints: Think about what reading does for you.
It helps you learn.
questions.explanation: You already know that reading helps us learn new things, improve vocabulary, and understand the world.
misconceptions: Reading is not always boring; it can be enjoyable.
Book cost is not the main point.
We read in many places, not only school.

questions.stem: A speech is titled 'How to Stay Healthy.' What is the subject matter of this speech?
hints: The title tells you what the speech is about.
It is about staying healthy.
questions.explanation: The subject matter is ways to stay healthy because the title is 'How to Stay Healthy'.
misconceptions: Washing clothes is not the subject.

questions.stem: A speech begins: 'Today, I will talk about the importance of trees.' What is the subject matter?
hints: The opening sentence states the subject.
It says 'importance of trees'.
questions.explanation: The subject matter is the importance of trees because the speaker says 'I will talk about the importance of trees'.
misconceptions: Types of trees is not mentioned.

questions.stem: A speech is about 'Washing Your Hands.' What is one idea from your prior knowledge that you could contribute to this speech?
options: We should wash our hands with soap and water
We should wash our hands only on Sundays
We should never wash our hands
We should wash our hands with sand
hints: Think about how you wash your hands.
Soap and water are used.
questions.explanation: You already know that washing hands with soap and water is important for cleanliness and health.
misconceptions: Washing only on Sundays is not enough.
Sand is not used for washing hands.

questions.stem: A speech is about 'The Importance of Exercise.' What is one idea from your prior knowledge that you could contribute?
options: Exercise makes our bodies strong and healthy
Exercise is a waste of time
hints: Think about what exercise does for the body.
It keeps you healthy.
questions.explanation: You already know that exercise makes our bodies strong and healthy.
misconceptions: Exercise is beneficial, not a waste of time.

questions.stem: A speech is about 'Malaria Prevention.' Which of these is something you already know about malaria?
options: Malaria is caused by mosquito bites
Malaria is caused by eating too much rice
Malaria is caused by sleeping late
Malaria is caused by drinking cold water
hints: Think about how malaria is spread.
It is spread by mosquitoes.
questions.explanation: You already know that malaria is caused by mosquito bites.
misconceptions: Sleeping late does not cause malaria.
Cold water does not cause malaria.

questions.stem: A speech is about 'The Importance of Trees.' Which of these is something you already know about trees?
options: Trees give us oxygen and shade
Trees grow only in the desert
hints: Think about what trees provide.
They give oxygen and shade.
questions.explanation: You already know that trees give us oxygen and shade, and they are important for the environment.
misconceptions: Trees grow in many places, not only deserts.

questions.stem: A speech begins: 'Good morning, everyone. Today, I want to talk about the life of Dr. Kwame Nkrumah.' What is the subject matter?
options: The life of Dr. Kwame Nkrumah
hints: The speaker says the topic directly.
It is about Dr. Kwame Nkrumah.
questions.explanation: The subject matter is the life of Dr. Kwame Nkrumah, as stated in the opening.
misconceptions: Becoming a doctor is not the topic.

questions.stem: A speech is titled 'My Favourite Festival.' What is the subject matter?
options: A festival the speaker likes best
hints: The title says 'My Favourite Festival'.
It is about the speaker's favourite festival.
questions.explanation: The subject matter is the festival the speaker likes best.
misconceptions: It is not about a disliked festival.
It is not about all festivals.

questions.stem: A speech is about 'Road Safety.' Which idea from your prior knowledge could you contribute?
options: We should look both ways before crossing the road
We should play on the road
We should run across the road without looking
hints: Think about how to stay safe on the road.
Look before crossing.
questions.explanation: You already know that looking both ways before crossing the road is important for road safety.
misconceptions: Playing on the road is dangerous.

questions.stem: A speech is about 'Healthy Eating.' Which idea from your prior knowledge could you contribute?
options: We should eat fruits and vegetables every day
We should eat only sweets and cakes
We should skip breakfast every day
We should drink only sugary drinks
hints: Think about what makes a healthy diet.
Fruits and vegetables are healthy.
questions.explanation: You already know that eating fruits and vegetables every day is part of healthy eating.
misconceptions: Sweets and cakes alone are not healthy.

questions.stem: A speech begins: 'Today, I will explain how our school can save water.' What is the subject matter?
options: How the school can save water
How the school can waste water
hints: The speaker says 'how our school can save water'.
That is the topic.
questions.explanation: The subject matter is how the school can save water.
misconceptions: Water sources are not the main topic.

questions.stem: A speech is about 'The Dangers of Bush Burning.' Which of these is something you already know about bush burning?
options: Bush burning can destroy farms and cause soil erosion
Bush burning helps crops grow better
Bush burning is good for the environment
Bush burning only happens in the rainy season
hints: Think about what fire does to land and farms.
It destroys and damages.
questions.explanation: You already know that bush burning can destroy farms and cause soil erosion, among other harms.
misconceptions: Bush burning does not help crops grow better; it harms soil.
Bush burning is harmful, not good.
Bush burning often happens in the dry season.

questions.stem: A speech begins: 'Good afternoon, everyone. I am here to persuade you to stop littering our beautiful school compound.' What is the subject matter?
options: Stopping littering in the school compound
How to make the school more beautiful
The history of the school compound
hints: The speaker says 'stop littering'.
That is the topic.
questions.explanation: The subject matter is stopping littering in the school compound.
misconceptions: Making the school beautiful is related but not the exact subject.
The school's history is not mentioned.
Using a dustbin is a detail, not the subject.

questions.stem: A speech is about 'Saving Energy at Home.' Which idea from your prior knowledge could you contribute?
options: Turning off lights and fans when not in use saves energy
Leaving lights on all day saves energy
Using more electricity is good for the environment
hints: Think about how to reduce energy use.
Turn off appliances when not needed.
questions.explanation: You already know that turning off lights and fans when not in use saves energy.
misconceptions: Using more electricity is not good for the environment.
Energy can be saved through simple actions.

questions.stem: A speech is about 'The Importance of Education.' Which idea from your prior knowledge could you contribute?
options: Education helps people get good jobs and improve their lives
Education is a waste of time
hints: Think about the benefits of education.
It helps people succeed.
questions.explanation: You already know that education helps people get good jobs and improve their lives.
misconceptions: Education is for both boys and girls.
Education is valuable, not a waste of time.

questions.stem: A speech begins: 'Fellow pupils, today I will share three reasons why we should plant more trees in our school.' What is the subject matter, and what can you predict the speech will include?
options: The subject is planting more trees; the speech will include three reasons why
The subject is reasons; the speech will include three trees
The subject is school; the speech will include three pupils
The subject is pupils; the speech will include three schools
hints: The speaker says 'three reasons why we should plant more trees'.
The subject is planting trees, and the speech will list three reasons.
questions.explanation: The subject matter is planting more trees, and the speech will include three reasons to support this.
misconceptions: Reasons are the structure, not the subject.
The school is the setting, not the subject.
Pupils are the audience, not the subject.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.10.3: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Gather and select facts and ideas from one or multiple print and/or non-print sources, appropriate to the purpose, audience, context and culture

skills.description: Identify print and non-print sources (books, newspapers, internet, people)
Select relevant facts and ideas for a given purpose and audience
Choose sources appropriate to purpose, audience, context and culture

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4

questions.stem: Which of these is a print source?
hints: Print sources are written and printed on paper.
A textbook is printed on paper.
questions.explanation: A textbook is a print source because it is written and printed on paper.
misconceptions: A radio programme is a non-print source.
A television show is a non-print source.
A person speaking is a non-print source.

questions.stem: Which of these is a non-print source?
hints: Non-print sources are not on paper.
The internet is digital.
questions.explanation: The internet is a non-print source because it is digital, not printed on paper.
misconceptions: A newspaper is a print source.
A magazine is a print source.
A dictionary is a print source.

questions.stem: Which of these is a person source you could ask for information?
hints: A person source is someone you can talk to.
A teacher can give you information.
questions.explanation: A teacher is a person source — you can ask them for information.
misconceptions: A textbook is a print source.
A newspaper is a print source.
A website is a non-print source.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech about 'The Importance of Trees.' Which fact is most relevant?
options: Trees give us oxygen and shade
hints: A relevant fact supports the importance of trees.
Trees give oxygen and shade — that is important.
questions.explanation: 'Trees give us oxygen and shade' is most relevant to the importance of trees.
misconceptions: Being green is a descriptive fact, not about importance.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech about 'Healthy Eating.' Which fact is most relevant?
options: Eating fruits and vegetables keeps us healthy
hints: A relevant fact should be about health.
Eating fruits and vegetables is about health.
questions.explanation: 'Eating fruits and vegetables keeps us healthy' is most relevant to healthy eating.
misconceptions: Growing on trees is not about health.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech about 'Our School.' Which source is most appropriate?
hints: Choose a source related to the topic.
The headteacher and school records are about the school.
questions.explanation: The headteacher and school records are most appropriate for a speech about our school.
misconceptions: Farming is not about the school.
Football is not about the school.
Cooking is not about the school.

questions.stem: Which of these is a print source?
hints: Print sources are on paper.
A newspaper is printed.
questions.explanation: A newspaper article is a print source because it is printed on paper.

questions.stem: Which of these is a non-print source?
hints: Non-print sources are not printed on paper.
A video is digital.
questions.explanation: A video recording is a non-print source because it is not printed on paper.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech about 'Malaria Prevention.' Which fact is most relevant?
options: Sleeping under a mosquito net prevents malaria
Malaria is a word with seven letters
hints: A relevant fact should help prevent malaria.
Sleeping under a net prevents bites.
questions.explanation: 'Sleeping under a mosquito net prevents malaria' is most relevant because it helps prevent the disease.
misconceptions: The number of letters is not about prevention.
Leg count is not about prevention.
The first letter is not about prevention.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech about 'Road Safety.' Which fact is most relevant?
options: Look both ways before crossing the road
hints: A relevant fact should be about safety.
Looking both ways keeps you safe.
questions.explanation: 'Look both ways before crossing the road' is most relevant to road safety.
misconceptions: Road material is not about safety.
Wheel count is not about safety.
Road length is not about safety.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech about 'The History of Ghana.' Which source is most appropriate?
hints: Choose a source about the topic.
A history book is about history.
questions.explanation: A history book about Ghana is most appropriate for a speech about Ghana's history.
misconceptions: A science textbook is about science.
A football magazine is about football.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech about 'The Importance of Clean Water.' Which source is most appropriate?
options: A health worker and a health pamphlet
hints: Choose a source related to health and water.
A health worker deals with health matters.
questions.explanation: A health worker and a health pamphlet are most appropriate for a speech about clean water and health.
misconceptions: A football coach is about sports.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech about 'Our Community.' Which source is most appropriate?
options: Community elders and a local newspaper
hints: Choose sources related to the community.
Community elders know about the community.
questions.explanation: Community elders and a local newspaper are most appropriate for a speech about our community.
misconceptions: The moon is not about the community.
Science magazines are not about the community.
Weather reports are not about the community.

questions.stem: A pupil is gathering facts about 'The Importance of Trees.' Which combination of sources is best?
options: A science textbook, a website about trees, and a gardener
A cookbook and a football magazine
hints: Choose sources that actually give information about trees.
A science textbook, website and gardener all provide tree information.
questions.explanation: The best combination includes a science textbook (print), a website (non-print) and a gardener (person) — all relevant to trees.
misconceptions: Cooking and football are not about trees.
A phone and TV are devices, not sources about trees.
A computer and radio are devices, not specific sources about trees.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech to persuade classmates to stop littering. Which fact is most useful?
options: Littering makes the school dirty and can cause diseases
hints: A persuasive fact should show the negative effects of littering.
Littering causes dirt and disease.
questions.explanation: 'Littering makes the school dirty and can cause diseases' is most useful for persuading classmates to stop littering.
misconceptions: Liking sweets is not about littering.
Classroom count is not about littering.
Tree colour is not about littering.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a speech about 'The Life of Dr. Kwame Nkrumah.' Which source is most appropriate?
options: A history book about Ghana's first president
hints: Choose a source about Nkrumah or Ghana's history.
A history book about Ghana's first president is relevant.
questions.explanation: A history book about Ghana's first president is most appropriate for a speech about Dr. Kwame Nkrumah.
misconceptions: A novel about animals is fiction.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech to inform classmates about 'The Benefits of Exercise.' Which fact is most relevant?
options: Exercise strengthens the heart and muscles
Exercise is sometimes done in the morning
Some people wear special shoes for exercise
Exercise can be done indoors or outdoors
hints: A relevant fact should explain a benefit.
Strengthening the heart is a benefit.
questions.explanation: 'Exercise strengthens the heart and muscles' is most relevant because it explains a health benefit.
misconceptions: When exercise is done is a detail, not a benefit.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to give a speech about 'The Culture of the Ashanti People.' Which source is most appropriate?
options: An Ashanti elder and a book on Ashanti culture
hints: Choose sources directly about Ashanti culture.
An Ashanti elder and a culture book are relevant.
questions.explanation: An Ashanti elder and a book on Ashanti culture are most appropriate for a speech on Ashanti culture.
misconceptions: European history is not about Ashanti culture.
Chinese food is not about Ashanti culture.
Cars are not about Ashanti culture.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a speech to persuade classmates to exercise every day. They find three facts: (1) Exercise strengthens the heart. (2) Many people exercise at the gym. (3) Exercise can reduce stress. Which facts are most relevant to persuade classmates?
options: Facts 1 and 3 — they show health benefits
Fact 2 only — it is about the gym
All three facts are equally relevant
hints: Persuasive facts should show benefits of exercise.
Heart strength and stress reduction are benefits.
questions.explanation: Facts 1 and 3 are most relevant because they show health benefits that can persuade classmates to exercise.
misconceptions: Gym location is not a persuasive benefit.
Fact 2 is less relevant than 1 and 3.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a speech about 'The Importance of Education' to a rural community. Which source is most appropriate and culturally sensitive?
options: A local teacher, a community elder and a government education pamphlet
A foreign website about elite schools
A novel about a rich city school
hints: Choose sources that connect with the local community.
A local teacher, elder and government pamphlet are culturally appropriate.
questions.explanation: A local teacher, community elder and government education pamphlet are most appropriate and culturally sensitive for a rural community.
misconceptions: A foreign website may not reflect local realities.
A novel about a rich city school may not relate.
A celebrity biography is not about education.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.10.3: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Support ideas and points with visual resources to convey meaning appropriate to purpose and context

skills.description: Identify visual resources (pictures, charts, diagrams, real objects)
Match visual resources to ideas and points
Choose visuals appropriate to purpose and context

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4

questions.stem: Which of these is a visual resource?
hints: Visual resources are things you can see.
A picture is something you can see.
questions.explanation: A picture of a tree is a visual resource because it is something you can see.
misconceptions: A song is heard, not seen.
A poem is read or heard.
A story is read or heard.

questions.stem: Which of these is a chart?
options: A drawing that shows information in rows and columns
hints: A chart presents information visually.
It uses rows and columns.
questions.explanation: A chart is a drawing that shows information in rows and columns.
misconceptions: A song is not a chart.
A story is not a chart.
A poem is not a chart.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech about 'The Parts of a Plant.' Which visual would best support your speech?
options: A diagram of a plant showing roots, stem, leaves and flower
hints: The visual should match the topic.
A diagram of a plant shows the parts.
questions.explanation: A diagram of a plant showing its parts best supports a speech about the parts of a plant.
misconceptions: A car is not a plant.
A market is not a plant.
A house is not a plant.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech about 'Keeping Your Teeth Clean.' Which visual would best support your speech?
options: A picture of a toothbrush and toothpaste
hints: The visual should be about cleaning teeth.
A toothbrush and toothpaste are used for cleaning teeth.
questions.explanation: A picture of a toothbrush and toothpaste best supports a speech about keeping teeth clean.
misconceptions: A football is not about teeth.
A book is not about teeth.
A tree is not about teeth.

questions.stem: Why should you use visuals in a speech?
options: To help the audience understand your ideas better
To show off your drawing skills
hints: Visuals help convey meaning.
They make ideas clearer.
questions.explanation: Visuals help the audience understand your ideas better by showing them what you are talking about.
misconceptions: They are for communication, not showing off.

questions.stem: Which of these is a real object you could use as a visual in a speech about 'Fruits'?
hints: A real object is something you can touch.
An orange is a real fruit.
questions.explanation: An actual orange is a real object you could show during a speech about fruits.
misconceptions: A car is not a fruit.
A song is not a real object.
A poem is not a real object.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech about 'Road Safety.' Which visual would best support your point about crossing the road safely?
options: A picture of pupils using a pedestrian crossing
hints: The visual should show safe road crossing.
A pedestrian crossing shows safe crossing.
questions.explanation: A picture of pupils using a pedestrian crossing best supports the point about crossing the road safely.
misconceptions: A cat is not about road safety.
A house is not about road safety.
A tree is not about road safety.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech about 'The Water Cycle.' Which visual would best support your speech?
options: A diagram showing evaporation, condensation and rainfall
hints: The water cycle involves evaporation, condensation and rain.
A diagram showing these steps is best.
questions.explanation: A diagram showing evaporation, condensation and rainfall best supports a speech about the water cycle.
misconceptions: A fish is not the water cycle.
A boat is not the water cycle.
A beach is not the water cycle.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech to young children about 'Farm Animals.' Which visual is most appropriate?
options: Large, colourful pictures of cows, goats and chickens
A complex chart with many numbers
hints: Young children respond to simple, colourful pictures.
Large pictures of farm animals are appropriate.
questions.explanation: Large, colourful pictures of farm animals are most appropriate for young children.
misconceptions: A complex chart is too hard for young children.
A long text is not visual.
A map is not about farm animals.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech about 'The Human Body.' Which visual is most appropriate?
options: A simple diagram showing the main body parts
A drawing of a car engine
hints: The visual should be about the human body.
A diagram of body parts is relevant.
questions.explanation: A simple diagram showing the main body parts is most appropriate for a speech about the human body.
misconceptions: A landscape is not about the body.
A car engine is not about the body.
A building is not about the body.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech about 'The Importance of Trees.' Which visual would best support your point that trees provide shade?
options: A picture of people resting under a big tree
hints: The visual should show trees providing shade.
People resting under a tree shows shade.
questions.explanation: A picture of people resting under a big tree best supports the point that trees provide shade.
misconceptions: A car is not about shade.
A phone is not about shade.
A book is not about shade.

questions.stem: A pupil is preparing a speech about 'Malaria Prevention.' Which set of visuals would be most useful?
options: A picture of a mosquito net, a poster showing mosquito breeding sites, and a photo of a person with malaria
A picture of a car, a ball and a book
hints: Choose visuals related to malaria prevention.
Mosquito nets and breeding sites are directly related.
questions.explanation: A picture of a mosquito net, a poster showing breeding sites, and a photo of a person with malaria are most useful for a speech on malaria prevention.
misconceptions: Cars, balls and books are unrelated.
A map alone is not specific enough.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a speech to a group of farmers about 'Improving Crop Yields.' Which visual is most appropriate?
options: A diagram showing proper planting techniques and a photo of healthy crops
A cartoon of a smiling sun
A picture of a city skyline
A drawing of a mobile phone
hints: The visual should be about farming and crops.
Planting techniques and healthy crops are relevant.
questions.explanation: A diagram showing proper planting techniques and a photo of healthy crops is most appropriate for farmers.
misconceptions: A cartoon sun is too simple.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a speech about 'The Dangers of Smoking.' Which visual best supports the point that smoking harms the lungs?
options: A picture comparing a healthy lung and a smoker's lung
A picture of a cigarette packet
A picture of a person running
hints: The visual should show harm to lungs.
A comparison of healthy and smoker's lungs shows the harm.
questions.explanation: A picture comparing a healthy lung and a smoker's lung best supports the point about harm to lungs.
misconceptions: A cigarette packet does not show harm to lungs.
Running is about exercise, not smoking harm.
A hospital is general, not specific to lungs.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a speech about 'Our School' to visitors. Which visual is most appropriate?
options: A map of the school showing important buildings
A picture of a different school
A cartoon of a funny character
hints: The visual should show the school.
A school map shows the layout and buildings.
questions.explanation: A map of the school showing important buildings is most appropriate for a speech about our school.
misconceptions: A different school is not our school.
A cartoon is not informative about the school.

questions.stem: Which of these is a diagram?
options: A drawing that explains how something works or is built
hints: A diagram explains something visually.
It shows how something works.
questions.explanation: A diagram is a drawing that explains how something works or is built.
misconceptions: A song is not a diagram.
A story is not a diagram.
A poem is not a diagram.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a speech about 'Climate Change' to a class. They have three possible visuals: (1) a photo of a flooded street, (2) a cartoon of a snowman, (3) a chart showing rising temperatures over the years. Which visual set best supports the speech?
options: Visuals 1 and 3 — they show real effects and data
Visuals 1 and 2 — they are both pictures
hints: Choose visuals that show real effects and data.
A flooded street and a temperature chart are relevant.
questions.explanation: Visuals 1 and 3 are best because a flooded street shows a real effect of climate change and a temperature chart shows data.
misconceptions: A snowman cartoon is not about climate change effects.
Visual 2 is less relevant than 1 and 3.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a speech about 'The Importance of Reading' to a group of parents. Which visual is most appropriate?
options: A chart showing how reading improves children's performance in school
A cartoon of a talking book
A photo of a football match
hints: Parents care about their children's performance.
A chart showing reading improves performance is persuasive.
questions.explanation: A chart showing how reading improves children's performance is most appropriate for parents because it links reading to their children's success.
misconceptions: A cartoon is not persuasive for parents.
A television is not about reading.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a speech about 'The Benefits of Exercise.' They want to use a visual to support the point that exercise makes the heart stronger. Which visual is best?
options: A diagram comparing a resting heart rate and an active heart rate
A picture of a person sleeping
A photo of a healthy meal
A drawing of a heart shape
hints: The visual should show the heart getting stronger with exercise.
Comparing resting and active heart rates shows the effect.
questions.explanation: A diagram comparing a resting heart rate and an active heart rate best supports the point that exercise makes the heart stronger.
misconceptions: A healthy meal is about diet, not exercise.
A heart shape alone does not show strengthening.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.10.3: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Use effective introductions and conclusions

skills.description: Recognise an effective introduction (greeting, topic, purpose)
Recognise an effective conclusion (summary, closing statement, thank you)
Match introductions and conclusions to speeches

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: A conclusion is just saying 'thank you'
Any introduction works for any speech

questions.stem: What is the introduction of a speech?
options: The opening part that greets the audience and states the topic
hints: The introduction comes first.
It greets the audience and introduces the topic.
questions.explanation: The introduction is the opening part of a speech that greets the audience and states the topic.
misconceptions: The title is not the introduction.

questions.stem: Which of these is a good way to start a speech?
options: Good morning, everyone. Today I will talk about...
hints: A good introduction greets and introduces the topic.
The first option does both.
questions.explanation: 'Good morning, everyone. Today I will talk about...' is a good start because it greets the audience and states the topic.
misconceptions: 'Thank you for listening' is a conclusion.

questions.stem: What is the conclusion of a speech?
options: The ending part that summarises and closes the speech
hints: The conclusion comes last.
It summarises and closes the speech.
questions.explanation: The conclusion is the ending part that summarises the main points and closes the speech.
misconceptions: The title is the name of the speech.

questions.stem: Which of these is a good way to end a speech?
hints: A good conclusion thanks the audience or summarises.
'Thank you for listening' is a common closing.
questions.explanation: 'Thank you for listening' is a good way to end a speech because it thanks the audience.
misconceptions: 'Good morning' is a greeting for the beginning.
'Today I will talk about' is an introduction.

questions.stem: Which introduction matches a speech about 'The Importance of Trees'?
options: Good morning. Today I will talk about why trees are important.
Good morning. Today I will talk about football.
Good morning. Today I will talk about cooking.
Good morning. Today I will talk about cars.
hints: The introduction should state the topic.
The topic is 'The Importance of Trees'.
questions.explanation: 'Good morning. Today I will talk about why trees are important' matches the topic of trees.

questions.stem: A pupil starts a speech: 'Good afternoon, teachers and fellow pupils. I am here to talk about the importance of reading.' What does this introduction do?
options: Greets the audience and states the topic
hints: Look at what the introduction includes.
It greets the audience and states the topic.
questions.explanation: The introduction greets the audience ('Good afternoon, teachers and fellow pupils') and states the topic ('the importance of reading').
misconceptions: It does not ask a question.
It does not tell a joke.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT part of an effective introduction?
hints: An introduction opens the speech.
Thanking the audience is usually at the end.
questions.explanation: Thanking the audience for listening is part of the conclusion, not the introduction.
misconceptions: Greeting is part of the introduction.
Stating the topic is part of the introduction.
Stating the purpose is part of the introduction.

questions.stem: A pupil ends a speech: 'In conclusion, trees are very important. Thank you for listening.' What does this conclusion do?
options: Summarises the main idea and thanks the audience
hints: Look at what the conclusion includes.
It summarises and thanks.
questions.explanation: The conclusion summarises the main idea ('trees are very important') and thanks the audience ('Thank you for listening').
misconceptions: It does not introduce a new topic.
It does not tell a story.

questions.stem: Which of these is a good conclusion for a speech about 'The Importance of Reading'?
options: So, reading helps us learn and grow. Thank you.
Today I will talk about reading.
hints: A conclusion summarises and closes.
The first option summarises and thanks.
questions.explanation: 'So, reading helps us learn and grow. Thank you.' is a good conclusion because it summarises and closes the speech.
misconceptions: 'Today I will talk about' is an introduction.

questions.stem: Which conclusion matches a speech about 'Healthy Eating'?
options: So, let us choose healthy foods every day. Thank you.
Today I will talk about cars.
hints: The conclusion should summarise the topic.
The topic is healthy eating.
questions.explanation: 'So, let us choose healthy foods every day. Thank you.' matches a speech about healthy eating.

questions.stem: Why is an introduction important in a speech?
options: It prepares the audience and tells them what the speech is about
hints: The introduction comes first.
It prepares and informs the audience.
questions.explanation: An introduction is important because it prepares the audience and tells them what the speech is about.
misconceptions: Ending the speech is the conclusion.
Thanking is usually in the conclusion.

questions.stem: Why is a conclusion important in a speech?
options: It summarises the main points and gives a sense of closure
hints: The conclusion comes last.
It wraps up the speech.
questions.explanation: A conclusion is important because it summarises the main points and gives a sense of closure.
misconceptions: Introducing the topic is the introduction.

questions.stem: Two pupils start their speeches. Pupil A says: 'Good morning. Today I will talk about the importance of clean water.' Pupil B says: 'Hello.' Which pupil has a more effective introduction?
options: Pupil A, because they greet the audience and state the topic
Pupil B, because it is shorter
hints: An effective introduction greets and states the topic.
Pupil A does both.
questions.explanation: Pupil A has a more effective introduction because they greet the audience and state the topic.

questions.stem: A pupil ends a speech with: 'So, I hope you will all start reading more. Thank you.' Is this an effective conclusion?
options: Yes, because it summarises and calls the audience to action
No, because it does not thank the audience
No, because it is too short
Yes, because it introduces a new topic
hints: The conclusion summarises and encourages action.
It also thanks the audience.
questions.explanation: Yes, this is effective because it summarises the message, calls the audience to action, and thanks them.
misconceptions: It does not introduce a new topic.

questions.stem: Match the introduction to the correct conclusion. Introduction: 'Today I will talk about the dangers of smoking.' Which conclusion matches?
options: So, smoking harms our health. Let us avoid it. Thank you.
So, let us eat more fruits. Thank you.
So, trees are important. Thank you.
So, reading is good. Thank you.
hints: The conclusion should relate to the topic of smoking.
The first option summarises the dangers of smoking.
questions.explanation: 'So, smoking harms our health. Let us avoid it. Thank you.' matches the introduction about the dangers of smoking.

questions.stem: A pupil's introduction is: 'Good morning. My name is Kofi. I am here to talk about the importance of exercise.' What is missing from this introduction?
options: Nothing is missing — it has a greeting, self-introduction and topic
hints: Check if the introduction has all the key parts.
It greets, introduces the speaker, and states the topic.
questions.explanation: The introduction has a greeting ('Good morning'), a self-introduction ('My name is Kofi') and the topic ('the importance of exercise'). Nothing is missing.

questions.stem: A pupil's conclusion is: 'Thank you for listening.' What could be added to make it more effective?
options: A summary of the main points
hints: A good conclusion summarises the main points.
'Thank you' alone does not summarise.
questions.explanation: Adding a summary of the main points would make the conclusion more effective.
misconceptions: A new topic is not appropriate in a conclusion.
A joke may not be appropriate.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a speech at a formal school event. Which introduction is most appropriate?
options: Good morning, respected teachers, parents and fellow pupils. Today I will speak about the importance of discipline.
Hey everyone, what's up? Let me talk about discipline.
Good morning. I will talk about something.
hints: Formal events require formal, respectful language.
The first option greets respectfully and states the topic clearly.
questions.explanation: The first option is most appropriate because it uses respectful, formal language and clearly states the topic.
misconceptions: 'Hey everyone, what's up?' is too informal.
'Hi. Discipline. That's it.' is too brief and informal.

questions.stem: A pupil's conclusion is: 'In conclusion, we should all eat healthy food, exercise regularly and drink plenty of water. Thank you for listening.' Why is this an effective conclusion?
options: It summarises the main points and thanks the audience
hints: The conclusion mentions the main points and thanks.
It summarises and closes.
questions.explanation: It is effective because it summarises the main points (healthy food, exercise, water) and thanks the audience.
misconceptions: It does not introduce a new topic.
Length is not the reason it is effective.

questions.stem: A speech has this introduction: 'Today I will talk about the dangers of drug abuse among young people.' Which conclusion best matches this introduction?
options: So, let us all say no to drugs and protect our future. Thank you.
So, let us plant more trees. Thank you.
So, reading is important. Thank you.
So, let us eat more fruits. Thank you.
hints: The conclusion should relate to drug abuse.
The first option summarises the message about drugs.
questions.explanation: 'So, let us all say no to drugs and protect our future. Thank you.' matches the introduction about drug abuse.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.10.3: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Elaborate on ideas using explanations

skills.description: Recognise elaboration (adding details, examples, explanations)
Add details and examples to elaborate on a given idea
Choose appropriate elaboration for a purpose and audience

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Elaboration makes a speech too long

questions.stem: Which sentence elaborates on the idea 'Trees are important'?
options: Trees give us oxygen, shade and food.
hints: Elaboration adds details or examples that explain why the idea is true.
Which sentence tells us what trees give us?
questions.explanation: 'Trees give us oxygen, shade and food' elaborates on the idea by giving specific reasons why trees are important.
misconceptions: 'Trees are important' just repeats the idea without detail.
'Trees are green' describes colour, not importance.
'Trees are tall' describes height, not importance.

questions.stem: What does it mean to elaborate on an idea?
options: To add details and examples to explain the idea
hints: Elaboration helps the listener understand better.
It involves adding information.
questions.explanation: To elaborate on an idea means to add details and examples that explain it more fully.
misconceptions: Repeating the idea does not elaborate it.
Changing the topic is not elaboration.
Making it shorter is the opposite of elaborating.

questions.stem: You are talking to young children about 'Fruits.' Which elaboration is most appropriate?
options: Fruits like oranges and bananas give us vitamins that keep us healthy.
Fruits are botanical structures containing seeds.
Fruits are sometimes sold in markets.
hints: Young children understand simple, concrete examples.
Which option uses everyday examples?
questions.explanation: 'Fruits like oranges and bananas give us vitamins that keep us healthy' is appropriate because it uses familiar examples and simple language.
misconceptions: 'Fruits are good for you' is too general.
The botanical definition is too advanced.
Mentioning markets does not explain why fruits are good.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of elaboration?
options: I have a dog named Rex. He is brown and loves to play fetch.
hints: Elaboration adds details about the idea.
Which sentence gives more information about the dog?
questions.explanation: 'I have a dog named Rex. He is brown and loves to play fetch' elaborates by giving the dog's name, colour and a habit.
misconceptions: 'I have a dog' is a simple statement without detail.
'Dogs are animals' is a general fact.
'I like animals' is a different idea.

questions.stem: Which is the best elaboration for the idea 'Exercise is good for you'?
options: Exercise makes your heart stronger and helps you feel happy.
Exercise is done in the morning.
Some people wear shoes for exercise.
hints: Elaboration should explain why the idea is true.
Which option gives benefits of exercise?
questions.explanation: 'Exercise makes your heart stronger and helps you feel happy' elaborates by giving specific benefits.
misconceptions: Repeating the idea adds no detail.
When exercise is done is a detail but not a benefit.
Shoe type is not about why exercise is good.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech to parents about 'The Importance of Reading.' Which elaboration is most appropriate?
options: Reading helps children improve their vocabulary and do better in school.
Reading is done in the library.
hints: Parents care about their children's success.
Which elaboration links reading to school performance?
questions.explanation: 'Reading helps children improve their vocabulary and do better in school' is appropriate because it shows parents the benefit for their children.
misconceptions: Mentioning the library does not explain importance.
Book length is not a benefit.

questions.stem: Which sentence does NOT elaborate on the idea 'Malaria is dangerous'?
options: Malaria can cause fever and headaches.
Malaria can lead to death if not treated.
hints: Elaboration gives specific details or examples.
Which sentence just states a general fact without explaining the danger?
questions.explanation: 'Malaria is a disease' does not elaborate on why it is dangerous. The other options give specific effects.
misconceptions: Fever and headaches are specific effects.
Missing school is a specific effect.

questions.stem: Which elaboration uses a concrete example?
options: Fruits like mangoes and oranges are rich in vitamins.
hints: A concrete example names specific things.
Which option names specific fruits?
questions.explanation: 'Fruits like mangoes and oranges are rich in vitamins' uses specific examples (mangoes and oranges) to elaborate.
misconceptions: 'Fruits are sweet' describes taste, not health.
'Fruits grow on trees' is a fact but not an elaboration of health benefits.

questions.stem: You are talking to classmates about 'Preventing Malaria.' Which elaboration is most appropriate?
options: Sleeping under a mosquito net and clearing stagnant water can prevent malaria.
hints: The elaboration should give practical ways to prevent malaria.
Which option suggests actions?
questions.explanation: 'Sleeping under a mosquito net and clearing stagnant water can prevent malaria' is appropriate because it gives specific preventive actions.
misconceptions: Stating the cause does not explain prevention.
Saying some people get malaria does not help prevention.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech to community elders about 'The Importance of Education.' Which elaboration is most appropriate?
options: Education helps children get good jobs and contribute to the development of our community.
Education is free in some places.
hints: Community elders care about the community's future.
Which elaboration links education to community development?
questions.explanation: 'Education helps children get good jobs and contribute to the development of our community' is appropriate because it shows the benefit to the community.
misconceptions: Mentioning free education is not about importance.
Pupil numbers do not explain importance.

questions.stem: Which is the best elaboration for 'We should not litter' using a consequence?
options: Littering makes the environment dirty and can cause diseases.
hints: A consequence explains what happens as a result.
Which option states the result of littering?
questions.explanation: 'Littering makes the environment dirty and can cause diseases' elaborates by giving consequences.
misconceptions: Repeating the idea adds no detail.
'Some people litter' is not a consequence.

questions.stem: In this short speech excerpt, which sentence is the elaboration? 'Our school needs a library. A library would give pupils a quiet place to read and study. It would also provide books that pupils cannot afford to buy.'
options: A library would give pupils a quiet place to read and study.
None of the sentences is an elaboration.
hints: The first sentence states the idea. The other sentences give reasons.
Elaboration adds details or explanations.
questions.explanation: Sentences 2 and 3 elaborate on the idea by giving reasons why a library is needed.
misconceptions: The first sentence is the main idea, not elaboration.
Only one sentence is not the full elaboration.

questions.stem: You are giving a formal speech at a school prize-giving day. Which elaboration style is most appropriate?
options: Using slang and jokes to entertain.
Using polite, clear language and specific examples.
Using very long words to sound clever.
Speaking very quickly to save time.
hints: Formal speeches require clarity and respect.
Which option uses appropriate language?
questions.explanation: Using polite, clear language and specific examples is appropriate for a formal speech.
misconceptions: Slang and jokes are too informal.

questions.stem: You are giving a persuasive speech to farmers about 'Planting Trees.' Which elaboration is most likely to persuade them?
options: Trees are nice to look at.
Planting trees provides shade for your animals and helps keep your soil fertile.
Trees are found in many countries.
hints: Farmers care about their animals and soil.
Which elaboration shows practical benefits for farmers?
questions.explanation: 'Planting trees provides shade for your animals and helps keep your soil fertile' is persuasive because it shows direct benefits to farmers.
misconceptions: Looking nice is not a strong benefit for farmers.
Mentioning other countries is not relevant.
Tree height is not a practical benefit.

questions.stem: Which elaboration best supports the point 'Exercise reduces stress' with a concrete example?
options: After running for twenty minutes, I feel calm and happy.
Exercise is done in many places.
hints: A concrete example describes a specific situation.
Which option gives a personal example of feeling less stressed?
questions.explanation: 'After running for twenty minutes, I feel calm and happy' is a concrete example that supports the point about reducing stress.
misconceptions: Repeating the point adds no example.
Where exercise is done is not about stress.
Frequency is not a concrete example of stress reduction.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.10.3: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Speak with confidence before peers and maintain eye contact

skills.description: Identify confident speaking behaviours (clear voice, steady posture, eye contact)
Understand why eye contact matters when speaking
Speak with confidence before peers and maintain eye contact

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Looking at the floor is fine

questions.stem: Which of these shows that a pupil is speaking with confidence?
options: Looking at the audience and speaking clearly
Looking at the floor and whispering
Covering their face with their hands
hints: Confident speakers look at their audience and speak clearly.
Which option describes someone who is comfortable speaking?
questions.explanation: Looking at the audience and speaking clearly shows confidence.
misconceptions: Looking at the floor shows nervousness.

questions.stem: What should your posture be like when speaking confidently?
hints: Good posture helps you look confident.
Stand straight and steady.
questions.explanation: Standing up straight and steady shows confidence when speaking.
misconceptions: Sitting on the floor is not appropriate for a presentation.

questions.stem: Why should you maintain eye contact when speaking to an audience?
options: It shows you are confident and connects you with the audience
It helps you read your notes
hints: Eye contact shows confidence and connection.
It helps the audience feel involved.
questions.explanation: Maintaining eye contact shows confidence and helps you connect with your audience.
misconceptions: Eye contact does not make the audience uncomfortable if done naturally.
It does not help read notes.
It does not affect the length of the speech.

questions.stem: Where should you look when speaking to your classmates?
hints: Eye contact means looking at the people you are speaking to.
Look at your classmates.
questions.explanation: You should look at your classmates to maintain eye contact and show confidence.
misconceptions: Looking at the ceiling shows distraction.
Looking at the floor shows nervousness.
Looking out of the window shows disinterest.

questions.stem: What does a confident speaker do with their voice?
options: Speaks clearly and loudly enough to be heard
hints: Confident speakers want to be heard.
They speak clearly and at a good volume.
questions.explanation: A confident speaker speaks clearly and loudly enough to be heard by everyone.

questions.stem: A pupil is about to give a speech. They take a deep breath and stand up straight. Why is this helpful?
options: It helps them calm down and look confident
It helps them forget their words
hints: Deep breathing calms nerves.
Good posture shows confidence.
questions.explanation: Taking a deep breath and standing straight helps the pupil calm down and appear confident.
misconceptions: It does not affect the length.
It helps the audience stay engaged.

questions.stem: A pupil looks at the floor while giving a speech. What does this tell the audience?
options: The pupil may be nervous or unsure
hints: Looking down often shows nervousness.
Confident speakers look at the audience.
questions.explanation: Looking at the floor may show the audience that the pupil is nervous or unsure.
misconceptions: Looking at the floor does not show confidence.
Anger is not shown by looking down.
Happiness is not shown by looking down.

questions.stem: How can you maintain eye contact without staring at one person?
options: Move your eyes slowly around the audience, looking at different people
Look at one person the whole time
hints: Staring at one person can make them uncomfortable.
Move your eyes around the room.
questions.explanation: Moving your eyes slowly around the audience helps you maintain eye contact without staring at one person.
misconceptions: Staring at the teacher only ignores the rest of the audience.
Closing your eyes breaks eye contact.
Staring at one person is uncomfortable.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a sign of confidence when speaking?
hints: Confidence is shown by calm, steady behaviour.
Shaking and trembling show nervousness.
questions.explanation: Shaking and trembling are signs of nervousness, not confidence.
misconceptions: Looking at the audience shows confidence.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a speech and forgets a word. What should they do to remain confident?
options: Pause, take a breath, and continue
hints: Everyone forgets words sometimes.
Pausing and continuing shows confidence.
questions.explanation: Pausing, taking a breath, and continuing calmly shows confidence even when you forget a word.
misconceptions: Blaming the audience is unfair and unprofessional.

questions.stem: What does it mean to speak with confidence?
options: Speaking clearly and believing in what you say
hints: Confidence comes from within.
It means speaking clearly and believing in yourself.
questions.explanation: Speaking with confidence means speaking clearly and believing in what you are saying.
misconceptions: Speaking quietly may show lack of confidence.
Not looking at anyone shows nervousness.
Speaking too fast can be unclear.

questions.stem: Two pupils give speeches. Pupil A looks at the audience and speaks clearly. Pupil B looks at the floor and mumbles. Who is more likely to engage the audience?
options: Pupil A, because they look at the audience and speak clearly
Pupil B, because they are quiet
hints: Engagement requires eye contact and clarity.
Pupil A does both.
questions.explanation: Pupil A is more likely to engage the audience because they look at them and speak clearly.
misconceptions: Quietness does not engage an audience.

questions.stem: A pupil is very nervous about speaking in front of the class. What advice would help them?
options: Practise the speech several times before presenting
Speak as fast as possible to finish quickly
hints: Practice builds confidence.
The more you practise, the more comfortable you become.
questions.explanation: Practising the speech several times helps build confidence and reduce nervousness.
misconceptions: Avoiding eye contact does not help confidence.
Speaking fast does not make you less nervous.
Skipping the presentation does not build confidence.

questions.stem: A confident speaker makes a mistake during a speech. How do they handle it?
options: They correct themselves and continue calmly
hints: Confident speakers handle mistakes gracefully.
They correct themselves and keep going.
questions.explanation: A confident speaker corrects the mistake and continues calmly without letting it derail the speech.
misconceptions: Walking away shows lack of confidence.

questions.stem: Why is it important to speak with confidence before your peers?
options: It helps you communicate your ideas effectively and earn respect
It makes you better than everyone else
It helps you avoid making friends
It makes the teacher give you a gift
hints: Confidence helps you communicate.
It also helps others respect you.
questions.explanation: Speaking with confidence helps you communicate your ideas effectively and earn the respect of your peers.
misconceptions: Confidence is not about being better than others.
It helps build relationships, not avoid them.
It is not about getting gifts.

questions.stem: A pupil is giving a speech to a large audience. They feel nervous about eye contact. What is the best strategy?
options: Look at different people briefly, moving around the room
Stare at one person the whole time
hints: Moving your eyes around the room is less intimidating than staring.
Look at different people briefly.
questions.explanation: Looking at different people briefly and moving around the room helps manage nervousness about eye contact.
misconceptions: Staring at one person is uncomfortable for them and unnatural.
Looking only at notes disconnects from the audience.

questions.stem: A pupil is asked to give a speech but is very shy. They decide to practise every day in front of a mirror. How does this help?
options: It helps them get used to speaking and build confidence
It helps them avoid eye contact
hints: Practice builds confidence.
A mirror helps you see how you look and speak.
questions.explanation: Practising in front of a mirror helps the pupil get used to speaking and build confidence.
misconceptions: It does not make the speech longer.
It helps with eye contact, not avoiding it.
It reduces nervousness, not increases it.

questions.stem: Two pupils present their speeches. Pupil A speaks confidently and looks at the audience. Pupil B is nervous and reads from a paper the whole time. Whose presentation is more effective and why?
options: Pupil A's, because they connect with the audience and speak confidently
Pupil B's, because they read every word correctly
hints: Connection with the audience makes a speech effective.
Pupil A looks at the audience; Pupil B does not.
questions.explanation: Pupil A's presentation is more effective because they connect with the audience and speak with confidence, while Pupil B avoids eye contact and just reads.
misconceptions: Reading correctly is not enough if you don't connect with the audience.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.2.2.1: Connect sounds to letters; and blend letters/syllables in order to read and write
indicator.objective: Match sounds to their corresponding letter/letter patterns (e.g. initial/final consonants – m, j, f, s, etc., initial short vowels – a, e, i, o, u, final y as vowel, silent letters etc.)

skills.description: Identify initial and final consonant sounds and match them to their letters
Identify initial short vowel sounds in words
Recognise when final y acts as a vowel
Recognise silent letters in words

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: The letter name is the same as the sound
Every letter in a word is pronounced
Short vowels sound like their letter names

questions.stem: What is the beginning sound in the word 'mat'?
hints: Say the word slowly: mmm-at.
The first sound is the consonant 'm'.
questions.explanation: The word 'mat' begins with the /m/ sound, represented by the letter 'm'.

questions.stem: Which word has the short /a/ sound?
hints: Short /a/ sounds like 'a' in 'cat'.
Say each word and listen for the short vowel.
questions.explanation: 'Cat' has the short /a/ sound (/kæt/). 'Cake' and 'cane' have the long /eɪ/ sound; 'car' has the /ɑː/ sound.

questions.stem: Which letter is silent in the word 'know'?
hints: Say the word slowly: 'n-o'.
The first letter is not pronounced.
questions.explanation: In 'know', the letter 'k' is silent — we say /nəʊ/, not /knəʊ/.
misconceptions: 'w' is part of the vowel sound.

questions.stem: Which letter makes the /f/ sound at the beginning of 'fish'?
hints: Say 'fish' slowly.
The first sound is /f/.
questions.explanation: The word 'fish' begins with the /f/ sound, written with the letter 'f'.

questions.stem: In which word does the final 'y' act as a vowel?
hints: Final 'y' often acts as a vowel at the end of a word.
In 'happy', the 'y' sounds like /i/.
questions.explanation: In 'happy', the final 'y' acts as a vowel, making the /i/ sound. In 'yellow', 'yes' and 'you', 'y' is a consonant.

questions.stem: Which word begins with the same sound as 'sun'?
hints: 'Sun' begins with /s/.
Find the word that also begins with /s/.
questions.explanation: Both 'sun' and 'sit' begin with the /s/ sound.

questions.stem: Which word has the short /e/ sound?
hints: Short /e/ sounds like 'e' in 'bed'.
Say each word and listen.
questions.explanation: 'Bed' has the short /e/ sound (/bed/). The other words have the long /iː/ sound.

questions.stem: What sound does the final 'y' make in the word 'my'?
hints: Say 'my' slowly.
It sounds like 'eye'.
questions.explanation: In 'my', the final 'y' makes the /aɪ/ sound (like 'eye').

questions.stem: Which word has a silent letter?
hints: Say 'comb' slowly.
The last letter is not pronounced.
questions.explanation: In 'comb', the letter 'b' is silent — we say /kəʊm/, not /kɒmb/.

questions.stem: What is the final sound in the word 'cup'?
hints: Say 'cup' slowly.
