questions.stem: Read: 'The village had no clean water. The people walked many kilometres to fetch water from a stream. The water was not safe to drink. Many children became sick.' What problem did the village face?
hints: The text says the village had no clean water.
People walked far to get water that was not safe.
questions.explanation: The village faced a lack of clean water, which caused children to become sick.
misconceptions: Too many schools is not mentioned.
Too much food is not mentioned.
Lack of teachers is not mentioned.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.2.7.1: Process and comprehend level-appropriate texts
indicator.objective: Note and recall main ideas in a sequence

skills.description: Recall the main idea of a text or a paragraph
Arrange events or ideas from a text in the correct order
Recognise and use the SQ3R strategy (Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review) to note main ideas

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: The main idea is always the first sentence
SQ3R means read once and forget it

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi wakes up early. He brushes his teeth and takes his bath. He eats breakfast and goes to school.' What is the main idea of this paragraph?
hints: The paragraph describes what Kofi does in the morning.
All the sentences are about his morning activities.
questions.explanation: The main idea is Kofi's morning routine — the things he does every morning.
misconceptions: Food is only mentioned as breakfast.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama woke up. She took her bath. She ate breakfast. She went to school.' What did Ama do first?
hints: The first event is at the beginning of the text.
What is the very first thing Ama did?
questions.explanation: Ama woke up first, before taking her bath, eating breakfast and going to school.
misconceptions: Taking a bath came after waking up.
Eating breakfast came after the bath.

questions.stem: Read: 'The market was busy. Traders were selling food. Women were buying vegetables. Children were running around.' What is the main idea?
hints: The first sentence tells us the main idea.
All the other sentences describe activity at the market.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that the market was busy.
misconceptions: The text says the market was busy, not empty.

questions.stem: What does the 'S' in SQ3R stand for?
hints: SQ3R is a reading strategy.
The first step is to look over the text.
questions.explanation: The 'S' in SQ3R stands for 'Survey' — looking over the text to get a general idea.
misconceptions: Study is not the first step in SQ3R.
Speak is not part of SQ3R.
Sing is not part of SQ3R.

questions.stem: Read: 'Trees are important. They give us oxygen. They provide shade. They give us fruits. They also help to clean the air.' What is the main idea?
hints: The first sentence states the main idea.
All the other sentences give reasons why trees are important.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that trees are important, and the paragraph gives reasons to support this.
misconceptions: Being green is a detail, not the main idea.

questions.stem: Read: 'The rain started. The pupils ran into the classroom. They shook off the water. They sat down and continued their lesson.' What happened first?
options: The pupils ran into the classroom
hints: The first event is at the beginning of the text.
What caused the pupils to run?
questions.explanation: The rain started first, which caused the pupils to run into the classroom.
misconceptions: Running into the classroom happened after the rain started.
Shaking off water happened after they ran in.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom. They swept the floor. They arranged the desks. They threw the rubbish into the bin.' What is the main idea?
hints: All the sentences describe cleaning activities.
The first sentence tells us the main idea.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that the pupils cleaned the classroom.
misconceptions: They did not go home in the text.

questions.stem: Arrange these events in the correct order: (1) The farmer planted the seeds. (2) The seeds grew into plants. (3) The farmer watered the seeds. (4) The plants produced fruits.
hints: The farmer plants first, then waters.
The seeds grow after watering.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: (1) planted seeds, (3) watered seeds, (2) seeds grew into plants, (4) plants produced fruits.

questions.stem: What does the 'Q' in SQ3R stand for?
hints: The 'Q' step involves asking about the text.
You generate questions about what you are reading.
questions.explanation: The 'Q' in SQ3R stands for 'Question' — generating questions about the content of the text.
misconceptions: Quick is not the correct step.
Quiet is not part of SQ3R.
Quiz is not the correct step.

questions.stem: What are the three 'R's in SQ3R?
hints: The three R's come after Survey and Question.
They are steps in the reading process.
questions.explanation: The three 'R's are Read, Recite and Review.
misconceptions: Run, Rest and Repeat are not correct.
Write is not part of the three R's.
Read, Rest and Return is not correct.

questions.stem: Arrange these events in the correct order: (1) The pot of water was put on the fire. (2) The water started to boil. (3) The pot was removed from the fire. (4) The water became hot.
hints: The pot is put on the fire first.
The water becomes hot before it boils.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: (1) pot put on fire, (4) water became hot, (2) water started to boil, (3) pot removed from fire.
misconceptions: The water cannot be hot before the pot is on the fire.

questions.stem: Read: 'The baobab tree is special. It can store water in its trunk during the dry season. Its leaves can be eaten. Its fruit is rich in vitamins.' What is the main idea?
options: The baobab tree is special and useful
The baobab tree grows in water
hints: The first sentence states the main idea.
The other sentences give reasons why it is special and useful.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that the baobab tree is special and useful.
misconceptions: The text does not say it is dangerous.
The text does not say it is small.
It stores water but does not grow in water.

questions.stem: A pupil uses SQ3R to read a passage. They first skim the headings and look at the pictures. What step of SQ3R are they using?
hints: Looking at headings and pictures is the first step.
This step helps you get a general idea before reading.
questions.explanation: They are using the 'Survey' step — looking over the text before reading.
misconceptions: Question is asking questions, not looking at pictures.
Read is reading the text in detail.
Review is going over the main ideas after reading.

questions.stem: Read: 'The caterpillar hatched from an egg. It ate leaves and grew bigger. It formed a cocoon. It came out as a butterfly.' What is the correct sequence?
hints: The egg comes first.
The butterfly is the final stage.
questions.explanation: The correct sequence is: egg, caterpillar, cocoon, butterfly.
misconceptions: The butterfly is last, not first.
The egg is first, not the caterpillar.
The cocoon comes before the butterfly, not after the egg.

questions.stem: Why is the 'Review' step important in SQ3R?
options: It helps you remember and consolidate what you have read
It helps you skip difficult parts
It replaces the need to read
hints: Review means going over the main ideas again.
This helps you remember.
questions.explanation: The 'Review' step is important because it helps you remember and consolidate the main ideas you have read.
misconceptions: It does not make reading longer.
It does not help you skip parts.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ghana has many beautiful tourist sites. The Cape Coast Castle tells the story of the slave trade. Kakum National Park has a famous canopy walkway. Mole National Park is home to elephants and other wildlife.' What is the main idea?
options: Ghana has many attractive tourist sites
Only Cape Coast Castle is important
hints: The first sentence states the main idea.
The other sentences give examples of tourist sites.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that Ghana has many attractive tourist sites, such as Cape Coast Castle, Kakum and Mole.
misconceptions: The text says Ghana has many sites.
Cape Coast Castle is one example, not the only one.
The text says tourists visit these sites.

questions.stem: Read: 'The sun rose. The farmers went to the farm. They worked until midday. When the sun was hot, they rested under a tree. In the evening, they returned home.' What did the farmers do after working until midday?
hints: Look for what happens after 'They worked until midday'.
They rested because the sun was hot.
questions.explanation: After working until midday, the farmers rested under a tree when the sun was hot.
misconceptions: Returning home happened in the evening.
Going to the farm happened in the morning.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.2.7.1: Process and comprehend level-appropriate texts
indicator.objective: Skim for main ideas in texts

skills.description: Quickly look over a text to get the general idea (reading titles, headings, first sentences)
Identify general information (what the text is about) through skimming

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Skimming means reading every word quickly
Skimming and scanning are the same
You don't need to look at headings
Skimming gives you all the details

questions.stem: What does skimming a text mean?
options: Reading quickly to get the general idea
hints: Skimming is a fast reading strategy.
You look for the main idea, not every detail.
questions.explanation: Skimming means reading quickly to get the general idea of a text.
misconceptions: Reading every word carefully is close reading, not skimming.
Reading only the last sentence is not skimming.
Reading backwards is not a reading strategy.

questions.stem: When you skim a text, what are you looking for?
options: The general idea of what the text is about
hints: Skimming helps you understand the big picture.
You want to know what the text is mostly about.
questions.explanation: When you skim, you are looking for the general idea — what the text is mostly about.
misconceptions: Spelling mistakes are details, not the general idea.
Page numbers are not the focus of skimming.
The author's name is not the general idea.

questions.stem: Which part of a text should you look at FIRST when skimming?
hints: Titles and headings tell you what the text is about.
They are like signposts.
questions.explanation: When skimming, you should look at the title and headings first because they give you a quick idea of the topic.
misconceptions: The last paragraph is not the first place to look.
The middle sentence is not the first place to look.
The page number does not tell you the topic.

questions.stem: A text is titled 'How to Plant a Tree.' What is the general idea of this text?
hints: The title tells you the topic.
It is about planting a tree.
questions.explanation: The general idea is steps for planting a tree, as the title suggests.
misconceptions: Types of trees is not the topic.
Tree height is not the topic.

questions.stem: Skimming is different from scanning because skimming is for ___.
hints: Skimming gives you the big picture.
Scanning is for finding specific facts.
questions.explanation: Skimming is for getting the general idea, while scanning is for finding specific details.
misconceptions: Specific details are found by scanning.
Spelling words is not the purpose.
Counting words is not the purpose.

questions.stem: Read the first sentence: 'The market was full of people buying and selling goods.' What is the text likely about?
hints: The sentence describes people buying and selling.
This is a market scene.
questions.explanation: The first sentence tells us the text is likely about a busy market.

questions.stem: A pupil skims a passage and reads only the title, headings and first sentences of each paragraph. Why is this useful?
options: It helps them understand the main idea quickly
It helps them find spelling errors
It helps them memorise every word
hints: Skimming gives you the main idea fast.
You don't need every word to get the general idea.
questions.explanation: Skimming titles, headings and first sentences helps you understand the main idea quickly.
misconceptions: Spelling errors are not the focus.
Memorising every word is not skimming.
Counting sentences is not the purpose.

questions.stem: Which of these is a good skimming strategy?
options: Read the title, headings and first sentence of each paragraph
hints: Skimming is quick and selective.
Focus on the parts that give the main idea.
questions.explanation: A good skimming strategy is to read the title, headings and first sentence of each paragraph.
misconceptions: Reading every word twice is not skimming.
Reading only the last paragraph is not skimming.
Reading backwards is not a strategy.

questions.stem: A text begins: 'Many pupils in Ghana enjoy playing football during break time.' What is the general idea?
hints: The sentence says pupils enjoy football.
That is the general idea.
questions.explanation: The general idea is that many pupils enjoy playing football.
misconceptions: The text says they enjoy it, not dislike it.

questions.stem: When skimming, why should you look at headings?
options: They tell you what each section is about
hints: Headings act like labels for sections.
They summarise the content.
questions.explanation: Headings tell you what each section is about, helping you get the general idea quickly.
misconceptions: Being bold is a visual feature, not the reason.
Spelling words are not the focus.
Being short is not the main reason.

questions.stem: Read this opening: 'Last Saturday, the pupils of Basic 4 visited the zoo.' What is the text likely about?
hints: The sentence mentions a visit to the zoo.
That is the general idea.
questions.explanation: The text is likely about a visit to the zoo.

questions.stem: A text has these headings: 'What is Malaria?', 'How Malaria Spreads', 'Preventing Malaria'. What is the text about?
options: Malaria and how to prevent it
hints: All headings mention malaria.
The headings cover causes and prevention.
questions.explanation: The text is about malaria and how to prevent it.

questions.stem: A pupil skims a story and says, 'It is about a girl who lost her book.' What did the pupil do?
options: Got the general idea of the story through skimming
hints: The pupil understood the main idea quickly.
This is what skimming helps you do.
questions.explanation: The pupil got the general idea through skimming, which is the purpose of skimming.
misconceptions: Reading every word is not skimming.
Spelling mistakes are not the focus.
Counting pages is not the focus.

questions.stem: Read this first sentence: 'In Ghana, many communities celebrate festivals with drumming and dancing.' What is the general idea?
options: Ghanaian festivals involve drumming and dancing
hints: The sentence mentions drumming and dancing at festivals.
That is the general idea.
questions.explanation: The general idea is that many Ghanaian communities celebrate festivals with drumming and dancing.
misconceptions: The text says they celebrate, not dislike.
The text says many communities, not only Accra.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to know quickly what a passage is about. What should they do?
options: Skim the passage by reading the title, headings and first sentences
hints: Skimming is the fast way to get the main idea.
Focus on key parts, not every word.
questions.explanation: The pupil should skim by reading the title, headings and first sentences to get the main idea quickly.
misconceptions: Starting from the end is not skimming.

questions.stem: Two pupils read a passage. Pupil A skims it and says, 'It is about how to stay healthy.' Pupil B reads every word carefully. Who has used skimming?
options: Pupil A, because they got the general idea quickly
Pupil B, because they read every word
hints: Skimming is quick reading for the main idea.
Pupil A did this.
questions.explanation: Pupil A used skimming because they got the general idea quickly.
misconceptions: Reading every word is not skimming.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.2.7.1: Process and comprehend level-appropriate texts
indicator.objective: Read level-appropriate texts silently and closely for comprehension

skills.description: Recognise the purpose and process of silent reading (reading without vocalising)
Read closely to answer specific questions about a text
Read a text silently and closely for comprehension

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Silent reading means moving your lips
Silent reading is only for enjoyment
Silent reading means reading without understanding

questions.stem: What is silent reading?
hints: Silent means no sound.
You read with your eyes, not your voice.
questions.explanation: Silent reading is reading without making any sound — you read with your eyes and mind.
misconceptions: Reading only the title is not silent reading.
Reading backwards is not silent reading.

questions.stem: Why do we read silently?
options: To concentrate and understand the text better
hints: Silent reading helps you focus.
You can think about the meaning without distractions.
questions.explanation: We read silently to concentrate and understand the text better without distractions.
misconceptions: Silent reading does not make noise.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama has a red bag. She carries her books in it.' What colour is Ama's bag?
hints: Look for the colour word in the text.
The text says 'red bag'.
questions.explanation: Ama's bag is red, as stated in the text.

questions.stem: What should you do with your voice when reading silently?
options: Keep it quiet — do not read aloud
hints: Silent means no sound.
Do not use your voice.
questions.explanation: When reading silently, you should keep your voice quiet and read only with your eyes and mind.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils of Basic 4 went to the library. They borrowed story books and read quietly.' Where did the pupils go?
hints: Look at the first sentence.
The text says they went to the library.
questions.explanation: The pupils went to the library, as stated in the text.

questions.stem: Read: 'The rain started suddenly. The pupils ran into the classroom. They were wet and laughing.' How did the pupils feel?
hints: The text says they were laughing.
Laughing shows they were happy.
questions.explanation: The pupils felt happy and amused because the text says they were laughing.
misconceptions: They were not scared or crying.

questions.stem: A pupil is reading silently but moving their lips. What should they do?
options: Stop moving their lips and read with their eyes only
hints: Silent reading means no lip movement.
Read with your eyes only.
questions.explanation: The pupil should stop moving their lips and read with their eyes only, which is true silent reading.
misconceptions: Continuing to move lips is not silent reading.

questions.stem: Read: 'The old man walked slowly with a stick. He stopped to rest under a tree.' Why did the old man stop?
hints: The text says he stopped to rest.
Look at the second sentence.
questions.explanation: The old man stopped to rest under a tree.

questions.stem: Why is it important to re-read a text when reading closely?
options: To check and confirm your understanding
hints: Re-reading helps you understand better.
You may notice details you missed the first time.
questions.explanation: Re-reading is important because it helps you check and confirm your understanding of the text.
misconceptions: Memorising every word is not the goal.
Spelling errors are not the focus.

questions.stem: Read: 'The farmer worked hard all year. He planted maize and cassava. When harvest time came, he had more food than his family needed.' What can we infer about the farmer?
hints: He worked hard and had more food than needed.
This shows he was successful.
questions.explanation: We can infer that the farmer was hardworking and successful because he worked hard and had more food than his family needed.
misconceptions: He had plenty of food, not none.

questions.stem: Read: 'Malaria is caused by mosquito bites. People with malaria have fever and headaches. To prevent malaria, sleep under a mosquito net.' Which sentence tells us how to prevent malaria?
options: To prevent malaria, sleep under a mosquito net.
Malaria is caused by mosquito bites.
hints: Look for the sentence that gives advice.
It starts with 'To prevent malaria'.
questions.explanation: The sentence 'To prevent malaria, sleep under a mosquito net' tells us how to prevent malaria.
misconceptions: The other sentences describe causes or symptoms, not prevention.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom. They swept the floor, arranged the desks and threw the rubbish into the bin. The teacher was pleased.' Why was the teacher pleased?
options: The pupils cleaned the classroom well
hints: The pupils worked hard to clean.
The teacher was pleased with their work.
questions.explanation: The teacher was pleased because the pupils cleaned the classroom well.
misconceptions: Going home early is not mentioned.

questions.stem: What does 'reading closely' mean?
options: Reading carefully and paying attention to details
hints: Close reading means paying close attention.
You look for details and meaning.
questions.explanation: Reading closely means reading carefully and paying attention to details to understand the text fully.
misconceptions: Reading fast is not close reading.
Reading only the first sentence is not close reading.
Reading without understanding is not close reading.

questions.stem: Read: 'The village had no clean water. The people walked many kilometres to fetch water from a stream. The water was not safe to drink. Many children became sick.' What is the main problem in this passage?
options: The village had too many schools
The children had too much food
The people had too many cars
hints: The first sentence states the problem.
The village had no clean water.
questions.explanation: The main problem is that the village lacked clean water.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.2.7.2: Apply critical reading, implied meaning, higher order thinking, judgment and evaluation
indicator.objective: Respond to a text with reasons

skills.description: Identify points of view or opinions in a text
State reasons for a point of view or answer
Respond to a text with a clear opinion and supporting reasons

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Any opinion is correct without a reason
A reason is just saying 'because I think so'
You can only have one point of view
An opinion and a fact are the same

questions.stem: Read: 'I think every school should have a library because reading helps pupils learn.' What is the writer's opinion?
options: Every school should have a library
hints: An opinion is what someone thinks or believes.
The writer says 'I think every school should have a library'.
questions.explanation: The writer's opinion is that every school should have a library.
misconceptions: The writer wants libraries in schools.

questions.stem: Read: 'In my view, pupils should not play near the road because it is dangerous.' What is the writer's point of view?
options: Pupils should not play near the road
Playing near the road is safe
Pupils should play on the road
hints: The writer says 'In my view'.
The writer says pupils should not play near the road.
questions.explanation: The writer's point of view is that pupils should not play near the road.
misconceptions: The writer says it is dangerous, not safe.
The writer says not to play near the road.
The writer says the road is dangerous.

questions.stem: Read: 'We should plant more trees because they give us shade and clean the air.' What reason does the writer give for planting trees?
options: Trees give shade and clean the air
hints: Look for the word 'because'.
The reason comes after 'because'.
questions.explanation: The reason given is that trees give shade and clean the air.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama is a good pupil because she always does her homework.' Why is Ama described as a good pupil?
hints: Look for the reason after 'because'.
It is about her homework.
questions.explanation: Ama is described as a good pupil because she always does her homework.

questions.stem: Read: 'Some people say children should not watch TV. I disagree because some TV programmes teach children about nature.' What is the writer's response?
options: The writer disagrees because some TV programmes teach children
The writer agrees that children should not watch TV
The writer does not care about TV
The writer thinks TV is always bad
hints: The writer says 'I disagree'.
They give a reason about nature programmes.
questions.explanation: The writer disagrees with the idea that children should not watch TV because some programmes teach children about nature.
misconceptions: The writer says some programmes are educational.

questions.stem: Read: 'In my opinion, every pupil should learn to play a musical instrument. Music helps the brain develop and brings joy to people.' What is the writer's opinion?
options: Every pupil should learn to play a musical instrument
Music is a waste of time
hints: The writer says 'In my opinion'.
The opinion is about learning a musical instrument.
questions.explanation: The writer's opinion is that every pupil should learn to play a musical instrument.
misconceptions: The writer supports music, not dismisses it.
The writer says every pupil, not only adults.
The writer says music helps the brain.

questions.stem: Read: 'We should not waste water because clean water is scarce in many communities.' What reason is given for not wasting water?
options: Clean water is scarce in many communities
hints: Look for the reason after 'because'.
It mentions scarcity of clean water.
questions.explanation: The reason given is that clean water is scarce in many communities.
misconceptions: The text says water is scarce, not easy to find.
The text says water is important.

questions.stem: Read: 'Some people think exams are the best way to test pupils. However, I believe projects and presentations show what pupils really understand.' What is the writer's point of view?
options: Projects and presentations are better than exams for testing understanding
Exams are the best way to test pupils
hints: The writer says 'I believe'.
They prefer projects and presentations over exams.
questions.explanation: The writer's point of view is that projects and presentations show what pupils really understand, unlike exams.
misconceptions: The writer disagrees with exams being the best.
The writer does not say pupils should not be tested.

questions.stem: Read: 'A pupil says: I think we should have a longer break at school. We need more time to eat our lunch and play.' What reason does the pupil give?
options: They need more time to eat and play
They want to go home early
hints: Look for the reason the pupil gives.
It is about eating lunch and playing.
questions.explanation: The pupil gives the reason that they need more time to eat their lunch and play.
misconceptions: They do not say they dislike school.
They do not ask to go home early.
They do not say they are tired of lessons.

questions.stem: Read: 'Some pupils say homework is a waste of time. I do not agree because homework helps us practise what we learn in class.' How does the writer respond?
options: The writer disagrees because homework helps practise what is learnt
The writer agrees that homework is a waste of time
The writer does not care about homework
The writer thinks homework is easy
hints: The writer says 'I do not agree'.
They give a reason about practising.
questions.explanation: The writer disagrees because homework helps pupils practise what they learn in class.

questions.stem: Read: 'I believe that children should help with chores at home. It teaches them responsibility and teamwork.' What is the writer's opinion?
options: Children should help with chores at home
Chores are a waste of time
hints: The writer says 'I believe'.
The opinion is about children helping with chores.
questions.explanation: The writer's opinion is that children should help with chores at home.
misconceptions: The writer says children should help.
The writer says chores teach responsibility.

questions.stem: Read: 'Some people argue that living in the city is better because there are more jobs and hospitals. However, I prefer village life because it is peaceful and the air is fresh.' What is the writer's point of view?
options: The writer prefers village life because it is peaceful and fresh
The writer prefers city life because of jobs
The writer thinks both are equally good
The writer dislikes both city and village
hints: The writer says 'I prefer village life'.
They give reasons about peace and fresh air.
questions.explanation: The writer prefers village life because it is peaceful and the air is fresh.
misconceptions: The writer prefers village life, not city life.
The writer clearly prefers one over the other.

questions.stem: Read: 'The teacher told the pupils to read every day. She explained that reading improves vocabulary and helps pupils do better in all subjects.' What TWO reasons did the teacher give?
options: It improves vocabulary and helps pupils do better in all subjects
It is required by law and parents
It helps pupils sleep better and eat well
hints: Look for the two reasons in the text.
They are about vocabulary and performance in subjects.
questions.explanation: The teacher gave two reasons: reading improves vocabulary and helps pupils do better in all subjects.
misconceptions: Fun and ease are not mentioned.
Law and parents are not mentioned.
Sleep and eating are not mentioned.

questions.stem: Read: 'Some people believe that only boys should play football. I strongly disagree because girls can play football just as well as boys.' What is the writer's response?
options: The writer disagrees because girls can play football as well as boys
The writer agrees that only boys should play football
The writer thinks football is only for adults
The writer does not care about football
hints: The writer says 'I strongly disagree'.
They give a reason about girls playing just as well.
questions.explanation: The writer strongly disagrees because girls can play football just as well as boys.
misconceptions: The writer does not mention adults.
The writer cares about the issue.

questions.stem: Read: 'A pupil says: I think we should have a school garden. We could grow vegetables and learn about plants.' What reason does the pupil give?
options: They could grow vegetables and learn about plants
hints: Look for the reason given by the pupil.
It is about growing vegetables and learning about plants.
questions.explanation: The pupil gives the reason that they could grow vegetables and learn about plants.

questions.stem: Read: 'Some people think that children should not use mobile phones. However, I believe phones can be useful if children use them responsibly. For example, they can use educational apps and call their parents in emergencies.' What is the writer's opinion?
options: Phones can be useful if children use them responsibly
hints: The writer says 'I believe phones can be useful'.
The key condition is 'if children use them responsibly'.
questions.explanation: The writer's opinion is that phones can be useful if children use them responsibly.
misconceptions: The writer does not say never.
The writer says useful, not harmful.
The writer does not limit to adults.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.2.7.2: Apply critical reading, implied meaning, higher order thinking, judgment and evaluation
indicator.objective: Make connections between a text and personal experiences/real life.

skills.description: Connect events or characters in a text to the learner's own experiences
Connect events or characters in a text to real-life situations in the community or world

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: A connection must be exactly the same event
Any connection is a good connection
Only happy experiences can be connections
Connections are not important for understanding

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama was nervous on her first day at a new school.' Have you ever felt nervous about something new? What connection can you make?
options: I also felt nervous on my first day at school
hints: A connection links the text to your own experience.
Think about a time you felt nervous about something new.
questions.explanation: A good connection is 'I also felt nervous on my first day at school' because it links the text to your own experience.
misconceptions: Liking school is not a connection to nervousness.
Having a bag is not related.
Walking to school is not related.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi was happy when he received a gift on his birthday.' What personal connection can you make?
options: I also felt happy when I received a gift on my birthday
I have a friend called Kofi
hints: Connect the feeling in the text to your own experience.
Think about a time you received a gift.
questions.explanation: A good connection is 'I also felt happy when I received a gift on my birthday' because it links to your own experience.
misconceptions: Liking birthdays is not specific enough.
Having a friend called Kofi is not a personal connection to the feeling.
Eating cake is a detail, not a connection.

questions.stem: Read: 'The village had no clean water, so the people walked far to fetch water.' What real-life situation does this remind you of?
options: Some communities in Ghana also struggle to get clean water
hints: Connect the text to a real situation in the world.
Think about communities that lack clean water.
questions.explanation: This reminds us that some communities in Ghana also struggle to get clean water.
misconceptions: City taps are not the same situation.
Water being cheap is not the connection.

questions.stem: Read: 'Malaria is spread by mosquito bites.' What real-life situation does this connect to?
options: People in our community use mosquito nets to prevent malaria
People in our community never get sick
Malaria is not a real disease
hints: Think about how malaria is prevented in real life.
People use mosquito nets.
questions.explanation: This connects to the real-life situation where people in our community use mosquito nets to prevent malaria.

questions.stem: Read: 'Adwoa studied hard for her exam and passed with a good grade.' What connection can you make to your own life?
options: I also studied hard and did well in a test
I have a friend called Adwoa
hints: A good connection links the text to a similar experience.
Think about a time you studied hard and succeeded.
questions.explanation: A good connection is 'I also studied hard and did well in a test' because it links to a similar personal experience.
misconceptions: Not liking exams is not a connection.
Having a friend called Adwoa is not relevant.
Going to school is too general.

questions.stem: Read: 'The children planted trees to help protect the environment.' What real-life situation does this connect to?
options: Communities in Ghana plant trees to fight climate change
hints: Think about how tree planting helps the environment in real life.
It connects to fighting climate change.
questions.explanation: This connects to real-life efforts in Ghana to plant trees to fight climate change.
misconceptions: Trees have many purposes beyond decoration.

questions.stem: Read: 'Esi shared her lunch with a hungry classmate.' What personal connection can you make?
options: I also shared my food with a friend once
hints: Connect the act of sharing to your own experience.
Think about a time you shared something.
questions.explanation: A good connection is 'I also shared my food with a friend once' because it links to your own experience of sharing.
misconceptions: Not liking lunch is not a connection.
Having a classmate is too general.
Eating lunch is not about sharing.

questions.stem: Read: 'The boy was afraid of the dark and could not sleep.' What connection can you make?
options: I also felt afraid of the dark when I was younger
hints: Connect the feeling of fear to your own experience.
Think about a time you were afraid.
questions.explanation: A good connection is 'I also felt afraid of the dark when I was younger' because it links to a personal feeling.
misconceptions: Liking the dark is the opposite.
Sleeping well is not a connection.
Having a torch is a detail, not a connection.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils walked to school in the rain without umbrellas.' What real-life situation does this connect to?
options: Some pupils in our community also walk to school in the rain
Pupils do not walk to school
hints: Think about pupils who walk to school in your community.
Some pupils do not have umbrellas.
questions.explanation: This connects to the real-life situation where some pupils in our community walk to school in the rain.

questions.stem: Read: 'The village chief called a meeting to discuss how to keep the community clean.' What real-life situation does this connect to?
options: Community leaders in Ghana often organise clean-up exercises
Communities do not care about cleanliness
hints: Think about how communities in Ghana organise clean-ups.
Community leaders often lead such efforts.
questions.explanation: This connects to real-life situations where community leaders in Ghana organise clean-up exercises.

questions.stem: Read: 'The girl was nervous about speaking in front of the class but she tried her best and succeeded.' What connection can you make?
options: I also felt nervous about speaking in class but I tried and did well
hints: Connect the feeling of nervousness and success to your own experience.
Think about a time you overcame nervousness.
questions.explanation: A good connection is 'I also felt nervous about speaking in class but I tried and did well' because it links to your own experience.
misconceptions: Saying you never feel nervous is not a connection.
Liking speaking is not the same as overcoming nervousness.
Having a class is too general.

questions.stem: Read: 'The community worked together to build a new school for their children.' What real-life situation does this connect to?
options: Communities in Ghana sometimes come together to build schools or clinics
hints: Think about how communities contribute to development.
Sometimes communities build schools together.
questions.explanation: This connects to real-life situations where communities in Ghana come together to build schools or clinics.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils learned about the importance of washing their hands before eating.' What real-life situation does this connect to?
options: Health workers in Ghana teach people to wash their hands to prevent diseases
hints: Think about health campaigns in Ghana.
Washing hands prevents diseases.
questions.explanation: This connects to real-life health campaigns in Ghana that teach people to wash their hands to prevent diseases.

questions.stem: Read: 'The boy was excited when he scored a goal in the football match.' What connection can you make?
options: I also felt excited when I achieved something in sports
hints: Connect the feeling of excitement and achievement to your own experience.
Think about a time you succeeded in a sport or game.
questions.explanation: A good connection is 'I also felt excited when I achieved something in sports' because it links to a similar personal feeling.
misconceptions: Not liking football is not a connection.
Having a football is not a connection.
Watching football is not a personal achievement.

questions.stem: Read: 'The story is about a girl who had to fetch water from a distant stream every morning before school.' What real-life situation does this connect to?
options: Many children in rural Ghana walk long distances to fetch water before school
All children have water taps at home
Fetching water is easy for everyone
Children do not help at home
hints: Think about rural communities in Ghana.
Many children fetch water before school.
questions.explanation: This connects to the real-life situation of many children in rural Ghana who walk long distances to fetch water before school.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.2.7.2: Apply critical reading, implied meaning, higher order thinking, judgment and evaluation
indicator.objective: Demonstrate awareness of the structure of texts (e.g. introduction, body, conclusion)

skills.description: Identify the introduction, body and conclusion of a text
Summarise each part of a text (introduction, body, conclusion) briefly
Combine part summaries into a full summary of the text

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: The body is the same as the conclusion
The introduction is just the title
You don't need to summarise each part

questions.stem: How many main parts does a well-structured text have?
hints: Think about introduction, body and conclusion.
Count the parts.
questions.explanation: A well-structured text has three main parts: introduction, body and conclusion.

questions.stem: Which part of a text comes first?
hints: The first part introduces the topic.
It comes before the body.
questions.explanation: The introduction comes first in a text.
misconceptions: The body comes after the introduction.
The title is not a main part.

questions.stem: Which part of a text gives the main details and information?
hints: The body contains the main content.
It comes between the introduction and conclusion.
questions.explanation: The body of a text gives the main details and information.

questions.stem: Which part of a text comes last and wraps up the ideas?
hints: It comes at the end.
It summarises the text.
questions.explanation: The conclusion comes last and wraps up the ideas in the text.
misconceptions: The body is in the middle.

questions.stem: Read: 'Trees are very important. (1) They give us oxygen and shade. They provide fruits and medicine. They also help to clean the air. (2) So, we should all plant and protect trees.' Which sentence is the introduction?
options: They give us oxygen and shade.
So, we should all plant and protect trees.
hints: The introduction introduces the topic.
It states the main idea at the beginning.
questions.explanation: 'Trees are very important' is the introduction because it introduces the topic.
misconceptions: The other sentences are details (body) or conclusion.

questions.stem: Read: 'Trees are very important. They give us oxygen and shade. They provide fruits and medicine. They also help to clean the air. So, we should all plant and protect trees.' Which sentence is the conclusion?
options: So, we should all plant and protect trees.
They give us oxygen and shade.
hints: The conclusion wraps up the text.
It often starts with 'So' or 'Therefore'.
questions.explanation: 'So, we should all plant and protect trees' is the conclusion because it wraps up the text.
misconceptions: The other sentences are body details.

questions.stem: Which part of a text contains the supporting details?
hints: Supporting details are in the main part of the text.
They come between the introduction and conclusion.
questions.explanation: The body contains the supporting details.

questions.stem: Read: 'Malaria is a dangerous disease. It is caused by mosquito bites. People with malaria have fever and headaches. Children under five are most at risk. To prevent malaria, sleep under a mosquito net.' What is the main idea of the body?
options: Malaria is caused by mosquito bites and has serious effects
hints: The body gives details about causes and effects.
It says malaria is dangerous and describes symptoms.
questions.explanation: The body's main idea is that malaria is caused by mosquito bites and has serious effects.
misconceptions: The text says malaria is dangerous.
The text says children under five are most at risk.
The text says malaria can be prevented.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi is a hardworking pupil. He always does his homework. He listens carefully in class. He asks questions when he does not understand. So, he always gets good grades.' Which part of the text contains the supporting details?
options: He always does his homework. He listens carefully in class. He asks questions when he does not understand.
So, he always gets good grades.
The whole text is the introduction
hints: Supporting details give evidence for the main idea.
They are in the body, between the introduction and conclusion.
questions.explanation: The sentences about homework, listening and asking questions are supporting details in the body.
misconceptions: The first sentence is the introduction.
The last sentence is the conclusion.
The whole text is not just the introduction.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi is a hardworking pupil. He always does his homework. He listens carefully in class. He asks questions when he does not understand. So, he always gets good grades.' What is the conclusion?
hints: The conclusion wraps up the text.
It often starts with 'So' or 'Therefore'.
questions.explanation: 'So, he always gets good grades' is the conclusion.
misconceptions: The first sentence is the introduction.
The other sentences are body details.

questions.stem: Read: 'Exercise is good for the body. It strengthens the heart and muscles. It helps us maintain a healthy weight. It also makes us feel happy. Therefore, we should exercise every day.' Which part of the text is the introduction?
options: Exercise is good for the body.
It strengthens the heart and muscles.
It helps us maintain a healthy weight.
Therefore, we should exercise every day.
hints: The introduction comes first and states the main idea.
It is the first sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Exercise is good for the body' is the introduction.
misconceptions: The last sentence is the conclusion.

questions.stem: Read: 'Exercise is good for the body. It strengthens the heart and muscles. It helps us maintain a healthy weight. It also makes us feel happy. Therefore, we should exercise every day.' What is the body's main idea?
options: Exercise has many benefits for the body and mind
Exercise is a waste of time
hints: The body gives several benefits of exercise.
It mentions the heart, muscles, weight and happiness.
questions.explanation: The body's main idea is that exercise has many benefits for the body and mind.
misconceptions: The text says exercise is good.
The text says everyone should exercise.
The text says exercise is beneficial.

questions.stem: Which is the best full summary of this text? 'Malaria is a dangerous disease. It is caused by mosquito bites. People with malaria have fever and headaches. Children under five are most at risk. To prevent malaria, sleep under a mosquito net.'
options: Malaria is dangerous, caused by mosquito bites, and can be prevented by sleeping under a net.
hints: A full summary combines the introduction, body and conclusion.
It should include the main idea, key details and conclusion.
questions.explanation: The best summary includes the main idea (malaria is dangerous), key details (caused by mosquito bites, symptoms) and prevention (sleep under a net).
misconceptions: 'Malaria is a disease' is too brief.
'Mosquitoes are insects' is not the topic.

questions.stem: Read: 'Education is the key to success. It helps people get good jobs. It teaches important life skills. It also helps people make better decisions. Therefore, every child should have access to education.' Which part of the text is the conclusion?
options: Therefore, every child should have access to education.
Education is the key to success.
It helps people get good jobs.
hints: The conclusion wraps up the text.
It often starts with 'Therefore'.
questions.explanation: 'Therefore, every child should have access to education' is the conclusion.
misconceptions: The first sentence is the introduction.
The other sentences are body details.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.2.7.3: Demonstrate an understanding of the use of words and phrases as used in a text
indicator.objective: Determine the contextual meaning of words and phrases

skills.description: Determine the meaning of a word based on how it is used in a sentence or passage
Determine the meaning of a phrase (including idiomatic phrases) based on its context

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: A word always has the same meaning
Phrases mean exactly what the individual words say
You can determine meaning without reading the whole sentence
Context clues are always in the same sentence

questions.stem: Read: 'The soup was so hot that it burnt my tongue.' What does 'hot' mean in this sentence?
hints: The soup burnt the tongue.
That tells you it was at a high temperature.
questions.explanation: In this context, 'hot' means high temperature because it burnt the tongue.
misconceptions: Spicy food does not necessarily burn the tongue in this way.
Popular is a different meaning of 'hot'.
Stolen is a different meaning of 'hot'.

questions.stem: Read: 'The baby was crying because she was famished.' What does 'famished' mean?
hints: The baby was crying.
Crying babies often need food.
questions.explanation: 'Famished' means very hungry, which is why the baby was crying.
misconceptions: Sleepy is not indicated by crying for food.
Happy babies usually do not cry.
Angry is possible, but 'famished' means hungry.

questions.stem: Read: 'The old bridge was dilapidated; parts of it had fallen into the river.' What does 'dilapidated' mean?
hints: Parts of the bridge had fallen into the river.
This shows it is old and broken.
questions.explanation: 'Dilapidated' means falling apart or in a state of disrepair.
misconceptions: New and strong is the opposite.
Long is about length, not condition.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils were all ears when the teacher announced the trip.' What does 'all ears' mean?
hints: 'All ears' is an idiom.
It means paying full attention.
questions.explanation: 'All ears' means listening carefully and paying full attention.
misconceptions: It does not mean having many ears.
It is not about being noisy.
It means the opposite of not listening.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils were on cloud nine when they won the competition.' What does 'on cloud nine' mean?
hints: 'On cloud nine' is an idiom.
It describes a strong feeling.
questions.explanation: 'On cloud nine' means very happy or extremely pleased.
misconceptions: Very tired is not the meaning.
Very angry is not the meaning.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupil was scolded for being tardy to class three times in one week.' What does 'tardy' mean?
hints: The pupil was scolded.
Coming late to class is a reason to be scolded.
questions.explanation: 'Tardy' means late, which is why the pupil was scolded.
misconceptions: Absent means not there at all.

questions.stem: Read: 'The lecture was so tedious that many students fell asleep.' What does 'tedious' mean?
hints: Students fell asleep.
What kind of lecture makes people sleep?
questions.explanation: 'Tedious' means boring and tiresome, which is why students fell asleep.

questions.stem: Read: 'The politician's speech was ambiguous, so nobody knew exactly what he meant.' What does 'ambiguous' mean?
hints: Nobody knew exactly what he meant.
The speech was unclear.
questions.explanation: 'Ambiguous' means unclear or having more than one possible meaning.

questions.stem: Read: 'The teacher told the pupils to hit the books before the exam.' What does 'hit the books' mean?
hints: 'Hit the books' is an idiom.
It is about preparing for an exam.
questions.explanation: 'Hit the books' means to study hard.
misconceptions: It does not mean physically hitting books.
It does not mean buying books.
It does not mean closing books.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupil was feeling under the weather, so she stayed home from school.' What does 'under the weather' mean?
hints: She stayed home from school.
This suggests she was not feeling well.
questions.explanation: 'Under the weather' means feeling sick or unwell.
misconceptions: Cold is a possible feeling, but the idiom means sick.

questions.stem: Read: 'The generous woman donated food to the orphanage every month.' What does 'generous' mean?
hints: She donated food every month.
This shows she likes to give.
questions.explanation: 'Generous' means willing to give freely to others.
misconceptions: Being rich is not the meaning.
Being poor is not the meaning.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils were told to keep an eye on the cake while it baked.' What does 'keep an eye on' mean?
hints: 'Keep an eye on' is an idiom.
It means to watch something.
questions.explanation: 'Keep an eye on' means to watch or monitor something carefully.
misconceptions: It does not mean closing your eyes.

questions.stem: Read: 'The news of the victory spread like wildfire.' What does 'spread like wildfire' mean?
hints: Wildfire burns very fast.
The phrase describes how the news moved.
questions.explanation: 'Spread like wildfire' means to spread very quickly.
misconceptions: It is not about actual fire.

questions.stem: Read: 'The teacher's explanation was concise but complete; she covered all the points in just five minutes.' What does 'concise' mean?
hints: She covered all the points in just five minutes.
This shows it was short but complete.
questions.explanation: 'Concise' means short and clear, giving the necessary information without extra words.
misconceptions: Long and detailed is the opposite.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils were told to pull up their socks and work harder.' What does 'pull up their socks' mean?
hints: 'Pull up your socks' is an idiom.
It is about working harder.
questions.explanation: 'Pull up their socks' means to improve their effort and work harder.
misconceptions: It is not about actual socks.
It does not mean wearing new socks.
It does not mean taking off socks.

questions.stem: Read: 'The teacher's words were a bitter pill to swallow for the pupils who had not studied.' What does 'a bitter pill to swallow' mean?
hints: The pupils had not studied.
The teacher's words were hard for them to hear.
questions.explanation: 'A bitter pill to swallow' means something that is hard to accept.
misconceptions: It is not easy to accept.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupil was told that he had bitten off more than he could chew by taking on too many club responsibilities.' What does 'bitten off more than he could chew' mean?
options: Tried to do more than he could manage
hints: He took on too many responsibilities.
The phrase describes trying to do too much.
questions.explanation: 'Bitten off more than he could chew' means trying to do more than you can manage.
misconceptions: It is not about physical mouth size.

questions.stem: Read: 'The teacher told the pupils that the world is their oyster if they study hard and work towards their dreams.' What does 'the world is their oyster' mean?
options: They can achieve anything they want
hints: The phrase is about opportunities.
If they study hard, they can achieve their dreams.
questions.explanation: 'The world is their oyster' means they have many opportunities and can achieve anything they set their minds to.
misconceptions: It is not about finding pearls.
It is not about eating oysters.
It is not about living near the sea.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.2.8.1: Construct meaning from texts read
indicator.objective: Read silently and reasonably for meaning from level-appropriate texts

skills.description: Recognise the purpose of silent reading (to understand, to enjoy, to find information)
Construct meaning from a text read silently (identify what the text is about, recall key points)
Read silently and reasonably for meaning from a level-appropriate text

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Silent reading means reading without understanding
You can't answer questions after silent reading
Silent reading is only for pleasure
Reading silently means moving your lips

questions.stem: What is silent reading?
hints: Silent means no sound.
You read with your eyes, not your voice.
questions.explanation: Silent reading is reading without making any sound — you read with your eyes and mind.
misconceptions: Reading only the title is not silent reading.
Reading backwards is not silent reading.

questions.stem: Why do we read silently?
options: To concentrate and understand the text better
hints: Silent reading helps you focus.
You can think about the meaning without distractions.
questions.explanation: We read silently to concentrate and understand the text better without distractions.
misconceptions: Silent reading does not make noise.

questions.stem: Read silently: 'Ama has a red bag. She carries her books in it.' What colour is Ama's bag?
hints: Look for the colour word in the text.
The text says 'red bag'.
questions.explanation: Ama's bag is red, as stated in the text.

questions.stem: What should you do with your voice when reading silently?
options: Keep it quiet — do not read aloud
hints: Silent means no sound.
Do not use your voice.
questions.explanation: When reading silently, you should keep your voice quiet and read only with your eyes and mind.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils of Basic 4 went to the library. They borrowed story books and read quietly.' Where did the pupils go?
hints: Look at the first sentence.
The text says they went to the library.
questions.explanation: The pupils went to the library, as stated in the text.

questions.stem: Read: 'The rain started suddenly. The pupils ran into the classroom. They were wet and laughing.' How did the pupils feel?
hints: The text says they were laughing.
Laughing shows they were happy.
questions.explanation: The pupils felt happy and amused because the text says they were laughing.
misconceptions: They were not scared or crying.

questions.stem: A pupil is reading silently but moving their lips. What should they do?
options: Stop moving their lips and read with their eyes only
hints: Silent reading means no lip movement.
Read with your eyes only.
questions.explanation: The pupil should stop moving their lips and read with their eyes only, which is true silent reading.
misconceptions: Continuing to move lips is not silent reading.

questions.stem: Read: 'The old man walked slowly with a stick. He stopped to rest under a tree.' Why did the old man stop?
hints: The text says he stopped to rest.
Look at the second sentence.
questions.explanation: The old man stopped to rest under a tree.

questions.stem: When reading silently, where should your eyes be?
hints: You need to look at the words to read them.
Keep your eyes on the text.
questions.explanation: When reading silently, your eyes should be on the text so you can read the words.
misconceptions: Looking at the ceiling means not reading.
Looking at a friend is distracting.
Looking out the window is distracting.

questions.stem: Read: 'The soup was hot and tasty. The children ate it with fufu.' What did the children eat the soup with?
hints: Look for the food mentioned with the soup.
The text says 'with fufu'.
questions.explanation: The children ate the soup with fufu.

questions.stem: Read: 'The farmer worked hard all year. He planted maize and cassava. When harvest time came, he had more food than his family needed.' What can we infer about the farmer?
hints: He worked hard and had more food than needed.
This shows he was successful.
questions.explanation: We can infer that the farmer was hardworking and successful because he worked hard and had more food than his family needed.
misconceptions: He had plenty of food, not none.

questions.stem: Read: 'Malaria is caused by mosquito bites. People with malaria have fever and headaches. To prevent malaria, sleep under a mosquito net.' Which sentence tells us how to prevent malaria?
options: To prevent malaria, sleep under a mosquito net.
Malaria is caused by mosquito bites.
hints: Look for the sentence that gives advice.
It starts with 'To prevent malaria'.
questions.explanation: The sentence 'To prevent malaria, sleep under a mosquito net' tells us how to prevent malaria.
misconceptions: The other sentences describe causes or symptoms, not prevention.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom. They swept the floor, arranged the desks and threw the rubbish into the bin. The teacher was pleased.' Why was the teacher pleased?
options: The pupils cleaned the classroom well
hints: The pupils worked hard to clean.
The teacher was pleased with their work.
questions.explanation: The teacher was pleased because the pupils cleaned the classroom well.
misconceptions: Going home early is not mentioned.

questions.stem: What does 'reading reasonably' mean in the context of silent reading?
options: Reading at a sensible pace and understanding what you read
hints: 'Reasonably' means sensibly.
You read at a good pace and understand.
questions.explanation: Reading reasonably means reading at a sensible pace and understanding what you read.
misconceptions: Reading fast is not always reasonable.
Reading only the first sentence is not reading reasonably.
Reading without thinking is not reasonable.

questions.stem: Read: 'The village had no clean water. The people walked many kilometres to fetch water from a stream. The water was not safe to drink. Many children became sick.' What is the main problem in this passage?
options: The village had too many schools
The children had too much food
The people had too many cars
hints: The first sentence states the problem.
The village had no clean water.
questions.explanation: The main problem is that the village lacked clean water.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.2.8.1: Construct meaning from texts read
indicator.objective: Answer questions based on the passage read

skills.description: Answer factual questions (who, what, when, where) based on a passage read
Answer inferential questions (why, how) based on clues in a passage
Answer applicative questions that connect the passage to real life or other knowledge

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: All answers are directly stated in the text
Only one type of question matters
You don't need to re-read to answer questions

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama woke up at 6 o'clock. She brushed her teeth and took her bath. Then she ate breakfast and went to school.' What time did Ama wake up?
hints: Look for the time mentioned in the first sentence.
The text says '6 o'clock'.
questions.explanation: Ama woke up at 6 o'clock, as stated in the first sentence.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kojo has a small farm. He grows maize and cassava. He also has three goats and some chickens.' What crops does Kojo grow?
hints: Look for the crops mentioned in the text.
The text says maize and cassava.
questions.explanation: Kojo grows maize and cassava.
misconceptions: Rice and beans are not mentioned.
Yam and plantain are not mentioned.
Cocoa and coffee are not mentioned.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils of Basic 4 went to the library. They borrowed story books and read quietly.' Where did the pupils go?
hints: Look at the first sentence.
The text says they went to the library.
questions.explanation: The pupils went to the library.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi has two sisters and one brother.' How many sisters does Kofi have?
hints: Look for the number of sisters.
The text says 'two sisters'.
questions.explanation: Kofi has two sisters.
misconceptions: One is the number of brothers.

questions.stem: Read: 'The sky was dark and the wind was blowing strongly. People hurried home.' Why did people hurry home?
options: They expected rain or a storm
They were going to a party
They were going to the market
hints: The sky was dark and the wind was strong.
This usually means bad weather is coming.
questions.explanation: People hurried home because they expected rain or a storm due to the dark sky and strong wind.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupil was scolded for being tardy to class three times in one week.' Why was the pupil scolded?
options: Because they were late to class
hints: The word 'tardy' means late.
The pupil was late three times.
questions.explanation: The pupil was scolded because they were tardy (late) to class three times.
misconceptions: Absence is not the reason given.

questions.stem: Read: 'The farmer looked at his crops and shook his head sadly. The rains had not come for many months.' How did the farmer feel?
hints: He shook his head sadly.
His crops were dry because there was no rain.
questions.explanation: The farmer felt sad and worried because his crops were dying from lack of rain.
misconceptions: The text says sad, not angry.

questions.stem: Read: 'Malaria is caused by mosquito bites. To prevent malaria, sleep under a mosquito net.' If you want to avoid malaria, what should you do?
hints: The text says to sleep under a mosquito net.
This prevents mosquito bites.
questions.explanation: If you want to avoid malaria, you should sleep under a mosquito net.
misconceptions: Sleeping outside may expose you to mosquitoes.
Avoiding water does not prevent malaria.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom. They swept the floor and arranged the desks.' What can you do in your own classroom to help keep it clean?
options: Sweep the floor and arrange desks
hints: The text shows pupils helping to clean.
You can do the same.
questions.explanation: You can help keep your classroom clean by sweeping the floor and arranging desks.
misconceptions: Writing on walls makes it untidy.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils of Basic 4 went on a trip to Kakum National Park. They saw many trees and animals. They walked on the canopy walkway. Everyone enjoyed the trip.' What did the pupils walk on?
hints: Look for what the pupils walked on.
The text says they walked on the canopy walkway.
questions.explanation: The pupils walked on the canopy walkway.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi was walking home when he saw an old woman struggling with a heavy basket. He stopped to help her carry it.' What kind of person is Kofi?
hints: Kofi stopped to help without being asked.
He carried the basket for the old woman.
questions.explanation: Kofi is kind and helpful because he stopped to help the old woman carry her heavy basket.
misconceptions: Selfish people do not help others.
Unkind people would not stop to help.

questions.stem: Read: 'The village had no clean water. The people walked many kilometres to fetch water from a stream. The water was not safe to drink. Many children became sick.' What can be done to solve this problem?
options: Dig a well or provide a borehole for the village
Ask the children to drink the stream water
hints: The problem is lack of clean water.
Digging a well or borehole would provide clean water.
questions.explanation: Digging a well or providing a borehole would give the village clean water and prevent sickness.
misconceptions: Walking further does not solve the problem.
Ignoring the problem is not a solution.

questions.stem: Read: 'The market was crowded. Women carried baskets on their heads. Traders called out their prices. Children ran between the stalls.' Who carried baskets on their heads?
hints: Look for the sentence about carrying baskets.
The text says women carried baskets.
questions.explanation: Women carried baskets on their heads.
misconceptions: Men are not mentioned in this sentence.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.2.9.1: Read fluently to enhance comprehension
indicator.objective: Read grade-level texts at good pace, with accuracy and expression

skills.description: Recognise a good reading pace (not too fast, not too slow) and how pace affects understanding
Read words correctly without skipping or mispronouncing them
Read with expression (tone, stress, intonation) that matches the meaning and mood of the text
Read a grade-level text aloud at a good pace, with accuracy and expression

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Reading fast means you are a better reader
Accuracy means reading every word perfectly the first time

questions.stem: What does a good reading pace mean?
options: Reading at a speed that is clear and easy to follow
hints: A good pace helps listeners understand.
It is not too fast and not too slow.
questions.explanation: A good reading pace is a speed that is clear and easy for listeners to follow.
misconceptions: Reading fast is not always clear.
Reading too slowly can be boring.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sign of a good reading pace?
hints: Good pace is about understanding.
Listeners should be able to follow.
questions.explanation: A good reading pace allows listeners to follow and understand the text.
misconceptions: Finishing quickly is not the goal.

questions.stem: What does reading with accuracy mean?
hints: Accuracy is about correctness.
You should read the words correctly.
questions.explanation: Reading with accuracy means reading the words correctly without mistakes.
misconceptions: Fast reading is not about accuracy.
Reading without expression is not accurate reading.

questions.stem: What does it mean to read with expression?
options: Reading with feeling and matching your voice to the meaning
hints: Expression is about feeling.
Your voice should match the mood of the text.
questions.explanation: Reading with expression means using feeling and matching your voice to the meaning of the text.
misconceptions: A flat voice has no expression.

questions.stem: When reading a list of items, you should read ___.
options: at a steady pace, pausing slightly between items
hints: Lists need to be clear.
Pausing slightly helps the listener follow.
questions.explanation: When reading a list, a steady pace with slight pauses between items helps clarity.
misconceptions: No pauses makes the list sound like one long word.

questions.stem: A pupil reads a story very fast from beginning to end without changing pace. What is the problem?
options: The audience may not understand or feel the story's different moods
The audience will enjoy it more
hints: Different parts of a story have different moods.
Reading at one pace does not match the changing moods.
questions.explanation: Reading too fast without changing pace means the audience may not understand the story or feel its different moods.
misconceptions: Fast reading does not make it more enjoyable.
Speed does not make the story shorter.
It makes it less clear, not more.

questions.stem: When reading a sentence with a comma, what should you do?
hints: Commas indicate pauses.
A brief pause helps clarity.
questions.explanation: You should pause briefly at a comma to make the sentence clear.
misconceptions: Reading faster at a comma is wrong.
A long stop is not necessary.

questions.stem: A pupil reads 'The cat sat on the mat' as 'The cat sat on the mat.' Did they read accurately?
options: Yes, they read every word correctly
hints: Accuracy means reading words correctly.
The pupil read every word as written.
questions.explanation: The pupil read accurately because they read every word correctly.
misconceptions: They did not skip a word.
Speed is not the focus here.

questions.stem: A pupil reads 'The ship sailed across the sea' as 'The sheep sailed across the sea.' What type of error did they make?
hints: 'Ship' and 'sheep' sound similar but are different words.
The pupil read the wrong word.
questions.explanation: The pupil mispronounced 'ship' as 'sheep', which is an accuracy error.
misconceptions: They did not skip a word.

questions.stem: A story says: 'The baby was crying.' What expression should you use?
hints: A crying baby is sad.
Use a tone that matches sadness.
questions.explanation: You should use a sad and gentle expression to match the crying baby.

questions.stem: A text says: 'The team won the match! They were so happy!' What expression should you use?
hints: Winning is exciting and happy.
Match the expression to the happiness.
questions.explanation: You should use an excited and happy expression to match the team's victory.

questions.stem: A sentence says: 'Be careful! The floor is wet.' What expression should you use?
hints: The sentence warns of danger.
An urgent tone matches a warning.
questions.explanation: You should use an urgent and warning expression to convey the danger.

questions.stem: Why is it important to pause at full stops when reading aloud?
options: To take a breath and show the end of a sentence
hints: Full stops mark the end of sentences.
Pausing helps listeners understand where sentences end.
questions.explanation: Pausing at full stops allows you to take a breath and shows listeners where one sentence ends and the next begins.

questions.stem: A pupil reads a passage and skips the word 'not' in the sentence 'The boy did not go to school.' How does this affect the meaning?
options: It changes the meaning completely — now it says the boy went to school
It does not affect the meaning
hints: 'Not' changes a positive statement to a negative one.
Skipping 'not' changes the meaning.
questions.explanation: Skipping 'not' changes the meaning completely — from 'did not go' to 'went to school'.
misconceptions: Skipping a word does affect meaning.
It does not make the sentence better.
It makes it shorter, not longer.

questions.stem: A story says: 'The old man walked slowly down the road, leaning on his stick.' How should you read this?
options: Slowly with a gentle, tired tone
hints: The old man walks slowly.
Match your pace and tone to his slowness.
questions.explanation: You should read slowly with a gentle, tired tone to match the old man's slow walk.
misconceptions: Fast does not match the slow walk.
Angry does not match the gentle description.
Funny does not match the serious tone.

questions.stem: Two pupils read the same sentence. Pupil A reads every word correctly. Pupil B skips two words and reads one word incorrectly. Who read with accuracy?
options: Pupil A, because they read every word correctly
Pupil B, because they read faster
hints: Accuracy means reading words correctly without skipping.
Pupil A read every word correctly.
questions.explanation: Pupil A read with accuracy because they read every word correctly. Pupil B skipped words and made an error.
misconceptions: Pupil B did not read accurately.

questions.stem: Two pupils read the same sentence: 'Watch out! The car is coming!' Pupil A reads it calmly. Pupil B reads it urgently. Which pupil conveys the meaning better?
options: Pupil B, because the sentence is a warning and needs urgency
Pupil A, because calm is always best
hints: The sentence is a warning of danger.
Urgency matches the warning.
questions.explanation: Pupil B conveys the meaning better because the sentence is a warning and needs an urgent tone.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.2.9.1: Read fluently to enhance comprehension
indicator.objective: Use recognition strategies to confirm understanding of level-appropriate texts

skills.description: Recognise the strategy of re-reading to confirm or correct understanding
Use vocabulary knowledge to figure out unfamiliar words and confirm meaning
Use intonation and punctuation cues to self-correct while reading

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Re-reading is a waste of time
If you don't know a word, you should skip it
Self-correction means you made a mistake

questions.stem: What does re-reading mean?
options: Reading a text again to understand it better
Reading a text once and stopping
hints: 'Re-' means again.
Re-reading means reading again.
questions.explanation: Re-reading means reading a text again to confirm or improve your understanding.
misconceptions: Reading once and stopping is not re-reading.
Reading only the title is not re-reading.

questions.stem: Why is re-reading a useful strategy?
options: It helps you check and confirm your understanding
hints: Re-reading helps you understand better.
You may notice details you missed the first time.
questions.explanation: Re-reading is useful because it helps you check and confirm your understanding of a text.
misconceptions: It does not help skip words.

questions.stem: Read: 'The baby was drowsy and soon fell asleep.' What does 'drowsy' mean?
hints: The baby fell asleep soon after.
What feeling makes you fall asleep?
questions.explanation: 'Drowsy' means sleepy, which is why the baby soon fell asleep.

questions.stem: When you read a sentence that doesn't make sense, what should you do?
options: Stop, re-read the sentence and check the punctuation
hints: If something doesn't make sense, re-read it.
Check punctuation for clues about meaning.
questions.explanation: If a sentence doesn't make sense, you should stop, re-read it and check the punctuation for clues.
misconceptions: Ignoring it means you won't understand.

questions.stem: Read: 'The path was narrow, so only one person could pass.' What does 'narrow' mean?
hints: Only one person could pass.
This means the path is not wide.
questions.explanation: 'Narrow' means not wide — only a small width.

questions.stem: A pupil reads a paragraph and does not understand it. What should they do?
options: Move on to the next chapter
Ask a friend to read it for them
hints: Re-reading helps you understand better.
Try reading it again more slowly.
questions.explanation: The pupil should re-read the paragraph more carefully to improve understanding.
misconceptions: Asking a friend does not build independent reading skills.

questions.stem: How does re-reading help with comprehension?
options: It gives you a second chance to understand details you missed
It helps you memorise every word
It replaces the need to read once
hints: You may notice new details on a second reading.
Re-reading helps confirm meaning.
questions.explanation: Re-reading helps with comprehension by giving you a second chance to understand details you may have missed.
misconceptions: It does not make the text shorter.
It is not about memorising every word.
It does not replace the first reading.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils were very enthusiastic about the trip; they could not stop talking about it.' What does 'enthusiastic' mean?
hints: They could not stop talking about the trip.
This shows they were excited.
questions.explanation: 'Enthusiastic' means very excited and interested.

questions.stem: Read: 'The old bridge was dilapidated; parts of it had fallen into the river.' What does 'dilapidated' mean?
hints: Parts of the bridge had fallen into the river.
This shows it is old and broken.
questions.explanation: 'Dilapidated' means falling apart or in a state of disrepair.
misconceptions: New and strong is the opposite.

questions.stem: A pupil reads 'The boy is happy?' with a rising voice. What should they check?
options: Whether the sentence is a statement or a question
hints: Rising intonation signals a question.
But 'The boy is happy' is a statement.
