questions.explanation: The pupil should check whether the sentence is a statement or a question. The text likely has a full stop, not a question mark.
misconceptions: Word count is not the issue.
Page number is not the issue.

questions.stem: How does punctuation help you self-correct while reading?
options: It tells you where to pause and what tone to use
It tells you the page number
hints: Full stops, commas and question marks guide reading.
They show pauses and tone.
questions.explanation: Punctuation helps you self-correct by showing where to pause and what tone to use.
misconceptions: It does not make the text longer.
It does not help skip words.
It does not tell page numbers.

questions.stem: A pupil reads 'The cat sat on the mat.' but says 'The cat sat on the mat?' with a rising voice. What should they do?
options: Re-read with a falling voice because it is a statement
Continue reading with a rising voice
hints: The sentence ends with a full stop, so it is a statement.
Statements use falling intonation.
questions.explanation: The pupil should re-read with a falling voice because the sentence is a statement, not a question.

questions.stem: Read: 'The teacher's explanation was concise but complete; she covered all the points in just five minutes.' What does 'concise' mean?
hints: She covered all the points in just five minutes.
This shows it was short but complete.
questions.explanation: 'Concise' means short and clear, giving the necessary information without extra words.
misconceptions: Long and detailed is the opposite.

questions.stem: A pupil reads a story and cannot answer a question about it. What should they do?
options: Re-read the relevant part of the story to find the answer
Ask a friend for the answer
hints: The answer is in the text.
Re-reading helps you find it.
questions.explanation: The pupil should re-read the relevant part of the story to find the answer.
misconceptions: Asking a friend does not build skills.
Giving up is not a strategy.

questions.stem: A pupil reads a question but uses a falling voice. How can they self-correct?
options: Re-read the question with a rising voice
hints: Questions use rising intonation.
The pupil should re-read with a rising voice.
questions.explanation: The pupil should re-read the question with a rising voice to match the question mark.
misconceptions: Reading louder does not fix intonation.

questions.stem: Two pupils read a passage. Pupil A reads once and answers questions. Pupil B reads twice and answers questions. Who is likely to understand better?
options: Pupil B, because re-reading improves understanding
Pupil A, because they read faster
hints: Re-reading helps confirm understanding.
Pupil B used the re-reading strategy.
questions.explanation: Pupil B is likely to understand better because re-reading improves comprehension.

questions.stem: Read: 'The politician's speech was ambiguous, so nobody knew exactly what he meant.' What does 'ambiguous' mean?
hints: Nobody knew exactly what he meant.
The speech was unclear.
questions.explanation: 'Ambiguous' means unclear or having more than one possible meaning.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.2.10.1: Read and summarise passages read
indicator.objective: Summarise level-appropriate passages/texts orally

skills.description: Identify the main idea(s) in a paragraph or passage
Restate information read in a few words (orally, in own words)
Summarise a level-appropriate passage/text orally

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: A summary is a copy of the passage
Any short sentence is a summary
Summarising is the same as retelling

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama wakes up early every morning. She brushes her teeth, takes her bath and eats breakfast. Then she walks to school.' What is the main idea of this passage?
hints: What is the passage mostly about?
It describes what Ama does every morning.
questions.explanation: The main idea is Ama's morning routine — the things she does every morning before school.
misconceptions: Food is only mentioned as breakfast.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi has a small farm. He grows maize and cassava. He also has three goats and some chickens.' What is this passage mainly about?
hints: What does Kofi have?
He has a farm, crops and animals.
questions.explanation: The passage is mainly about Kofi's farm and the animals he keeps.

questions.stem: Read: 'The market was crowded. Women carried baskets. Traders called out prices. Children ran between stalls.' What is the main idea?
hints: The first sentence states the main idea.
All sentences describe activity at the market.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that the market was busy.
misconceptions: The text says busy, not empty.

questions.stem: Read: 'Esi went to the market. She bought tomatoes, onions and pepper.' Which sentence best restates this in fewer words?
options: Esi bought vegetables at the market.
Esi went to the market to buy tomatoes, onions and pepper.
Esi likes going to the market.
hints: Restating means saying the same thing in fewer words.
Tomatoes, onions and pepper are vegetables.
questions.explanation: 'Esi bought vegetables at the market' restates the information in fewer words.
misconceptions: The second option repeats all details.
The third option is not about the purchase.
The fourth option leaves out onions and pepper.

questions.stem: Read: 'Malaria is a dangerous disease. It is caused by mosquito bites. People with malaria have fever and headaches. To prevent malaria, sleep under a mosquito net.' What is the main idea?
options: Malaria is dangerous and can be prevented
hints: The first sentence gives the main idea.
The passage also gives prevention.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that malaria is a dangerous disease that can be prevented.
misconceptions: Mosquitoes being insects is a detail.
Fever is a symptom, not the main idea.

questions.stem: Read: 'Trees are important. They give us oxygen and shade. They provide fruits and medicine. They also help clean the air.' What is the main idea?
hints: The first sentence states the main idea.
The rest gives reasons why trees are important.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that trees are important and useful.

questions.stem: Read: 'The farmer worked hard all year. He planted maize and cassava. At harvest, he had more food than his family needed.' Which is the best short restatement?
options: The farmer worked hard and had a good harvest.
hints: Restate the main point in fewer words.
Include the result of his hard work.
questions.explanation: 'The farmer worked hard and had a good harvest' restates the main point in fewer words.
misconceptions: Mentioning only maize leaves out cassava and result.
Working all year is only part of the idea.

questions.stem: Read: 'Clean water is important for good health. It prevents diseases. We use it for drinking, cooking and washing.' What is the main idea?
options: Clean water is important for health
hints: The first sentence gives the main idea.
The rest explains why clean water is important.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that clean water is important for good health.
misconceptions: Cooking is one use, not the main idea.
Diseases are mentioned but not the main idea.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils of Basic 4 went to Kakum National Park. They saw trees and animals. They walked on the canopy walkway.' Which is the best summary sentence?
options: Basic 4 pupils visited Kakum and saw trees, animals and the canopy walkway.
Basic 4 pupils went to the park.
hints: A summary includes the main points.
It should mention the visit and what they saw.
questions.explanation: The best summary includes the visit to Kakum, seeing trees and animals, and the canopy walkway.
misconceptions: The second option is too general.
The third option is a detail.
The fourth option is a detail.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi was walking home when he saw an old woman struggling with a heavy basket. He stopped to help her carry it. The woman thanked him and gave him a piece of bread. Kofi continued home feeling happy.' What is the main idea?
options: Kofi helped an old woman and felt happy
The old woman was selling bread
hints: What did Kofi do?
He helped and felt happy.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that Kofi helped an old woman and felt happy about it.
misconceptions: Hunger is not the main point.
The woman gave bread, she was not selling it.
Walking home is the setting, not the main idea.

questions.stem: Read: 'The village had no clean water. The people walked many kilometres to fetch water from a stream. The water was not safe to drink. Many children became sick.' What is the main idea?
options: The village lacked clean water, causing sickness
hints: What was the problem?
The lack of clean water caused sickness.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that the village lacked clean water, which caused many children to become sick.

questions.stem: Read: 'Exercise strengthens the heart and muscles. It helps maintain a healthy weight. It also makes us feel happy.' Which is the best short restatement?
hints: Restate the overall idea.
It mentions several benefits.
questions.explanation: 'Exercise has many health benefits' restates the main idea in fewer words.
misconceptions: The other options only mention one benefit.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ghana has many tourist sites. Cape Coast Castle tells the story of the slave trade. Kakum National Park has a canopy walkway. Mole National Park is home to elephants.' What is the main idea?
options: Ghana has many attractive tourist sites
Cape Coast Castle is the only site
hints: The first sentence states the main idea.
The other sentences give examples.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that Ghana has many attractive tourist sites.
misconceptions: Cape Coast is one example, not the only one.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.2.10.1: Read and summarise passages read
indicator.objective: Write short summary of a level-appropriate passage/text read

skills.description: Select the most important ideas from a passage for a written summary
Write a short summary of a passage using own words and main ideas

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: A summary should be as long as the passage
You can include examples in a summary
A summary is a list of facts
You can copy sentences from the passage

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama wakes up early. She brushes her teeth, takes her bath and eats breakfast. Then she walks to school.' Which sentence should be included in a summary of this passage?
options: Ama wakes up early and gets ready for school.
hints: A summary includes the main idea, not every detail.
Which sentence covers the whole morning routine?
questions.explanation: 'Ama wakes up early and gets ready for school' covers the main idea. The other options are details.
misconceptions: Walking to school is a detail.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi has a farm. He grows maize and cassava. He also has goats and chickens.' Which sentence should be left out of a summary?
options: Kofi grows crops and keeps animals.
hints: A summary leaves out minor details.
The number of goats is a detail.
questions.explanation: 'Kofi has three goats' is a minor detail and should be left out of a summary.
misconceptions: Having a farm is the main idea.
Growing crops and keeping animals is the main idea.
Being a farmer is the main idea.

questions.stem: Read: 'The market was busy. Women carried baskets. Traders called out prices. Children ran between stalls.' Which sentence best states the main idea for a summary?
options: The market was busy with many activities.
hints: The summary should capture the overall idea.
The first sentence gives the main idea.
questions.explanation: 'The market was busy with many activities' captures the main idea. The other options are supporting details.
misconceptions: Women carrying baskets is a detail.
Traders calling prices is a detail.

questions.stem: Read: 'Esi went to the market. She bought tomatoes, onions and pepper.' Which sentence is the best summary?
options: Esi bought vegetables at the market.
hints: A summary covers the main information.
Tomatoes, onions and pepper are vegetables.
questions.explanation: 'Esi bought vegetables at the market' summarises the main information.
misconceptions: Going to the market leaves out what she bought.
Buying tomatoes leaves out the other vegetables.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom. They swept the floor and arranged the desks.' Which sentence should be included in a summary?
hints: The summary should state the main action.
What did the pupils do overall?
questions.explanation: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom' is the main idea. Sweeping and arranging are details.
misconceptions: Using a broom is not stated.

questions.stem: Read: 'Malaria is a dangerous disease. It is caused by mosquito bites. People with malaria have fever and headaches. To prevent malaria, sleep under a mosquito net.' Which TWO ideas should be included in a summary?
options: Malaria is dangerous and can be prevented.
Mosquitoes are insects and have six legs.
hints: A summary includes the most important ideas.
The passage is about malaria and prevention.
questions.explanation: A summary should include that malaria is dangerous and can be prevented. Symptoms are details; mosquito legs are not mentioned.
misconceptions: Mosquito legs are not in the passage.

questions.stem: Read: 'Trees are important. They give us oxygen and shade. They provide fruits and medicine. They also help clean the air.' Which sentence should NOT be included in a summary?
options: Trees give us oxygen and shade.
hints: A summary includes only the main ideas.
Which sentence is not about why trees are important?
questions.explanation: 'Trees are green and tall' is not about why trees are important and should not be in the summary.
misconceptions: 'Trees are important' is the main idea.
Oxygen and shade are key reasons.
Cleaning the air is a key reason.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi was walking home when he saw an old woman struggling with a heavy basket. He stopped to help her carry it. The woman thanked him and gave him a piece of bread. Kofi continued home feeling happy.' Which sentence best states the main idea?
options: Kofi helped an old woman and felt happy.
The old woman gave Kofi bread.
hints: What is the most important event?
Kofi helped someone and felt good.
questions.explanation: 'Kofi helped an old woman and felt happy' captures the main idea.
misconceptions: Seeing the woman is the beginning, not the main idea.

questions.stem: Read: 'Clean water is important for good health. It prevents diseases. We use it for drinking, cooking and washing.' Which sentence should be left out of a summary?
options: Clean water is important for health.
We use clean water for drinking and cooking.
hints: A summary includes only important information.
Which sentence is obvious and not from the passage?
questions.explanation: 'Water is wet' is not stated in the passage and is not a key idea.
misconceptions: Health importance is the main idea.
Preventing diseases is a key reason.
Uses of water are key details.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils of Basic 4 went to Kakum National Park. They saw trees and animals. They walked on the canopy walkway. Everyone enjoyed the trip.' Which sentence best states the main idea for a summary?
options: Basic 4 pupils enjoyed a trip to Kakum National Park.
They walked on the canopy walkway.
hints: The summary should cover the whole trip.
The first and last sentences give the main idea.
questions.explanation: 'Basic 4 pupils enjoyed a trip to Kakum National Park' captures the main idea.
misconceptions: The canopy walkway is a detail.

questions.stem: Read: 'The farmer worked hard all year. He planted maize and cassava. At harvest, he had more food than his family needed.' Which sentence should be included in a summary?
options: The farmer worked hard and had a good harvest.
hints: A summary covers the main result.
What happened because he worked hard?
questions.explanation: 'The farmer worked hard and had a good harvest' summarises the main idea.
misconceptions: Mentioning only maize leaves out cassava.
Mentioning only cassava leaves out maize.

questions.stem: Read: 'The village had no clean water. The people walked many kilometres to fetch water from a stream. The water was not safe to drink. Many children became sick.' Which sentence should be included in a summary?
options: The village lacked clean water, causing sickness.
The water was not safe to drink.
hints: A summary includes the main problem and its effect.
What was the result of the lack of clean water?
questions.explanation: 'The village lacked clean water, causing sickness' summarises the main problem and effect.
misconceptions: Unsafe water is part of the problem but the summary should include the effect.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.1.1: Apply knowledge of different types of nouns in communication
indicator.objective: Identify and use nouns to identify people, animals, events and objects

skills.description: Identify nouns (names of people, animals, events, objects) in sentences
Use nouns correctly in sentences to name people, animals, events and objects
Classify nouns into people, animals, events or objects

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Any word can be a noun
Nouns are only names of people
Common nouns start with capital letters

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'The boy is running' is a noun?
hints: A noun names a person, animal, place, thing or event.
Which word names a person?
questions.explanation: 'Boy' is a noun because it names a person.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'The dog is barking' is a noun?
hints: A noun can name an animal.
Which word names an animal?
questions.explanation: 'Dog' is a noun because it names an animal.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'The table is broken' is a noun?
hints: A noun can name an object.
Which word names an object?
questions.explanation: 'Table' is a noun because it names an object.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a noun correctly?
hints: A noun should name a person, animal, place, thing or event.
Which sentence has a clear noun?
questions.explanation: 'The cat is sleeping' uses 'cat' as a noun correctly.
misconceptions: The other sentences are grammatically incorrect.

questions.stem: Which of these is a noun that names a place?
hints: A noun can name a place.
Which word names a place?
questions.explanation: 'School' is a noun that names a place.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'Ama went to the market' is a noun?
hints: A noun can name a person.
Which word is a person's name?
questions.explanation: 'Ama' is a noun because it names a person. 'Market' is also a noun, but only 'Ama' is listed as an option.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'The children are playing in the park' is NOT a noun?
hints: Nouns name people, animals, places, things or events.
Which word is a verb?
questions.explanation: 'Are' is a verb, not a noun. 'Children' (people), 'park' (place) and 'The' (article) are not the verb.
misconceptions: 'The' is an article, not a noun, but the question asks for NOT a noun; 'are' is a verb.

questions.stem: Choose the sentence that uses 'market' as a noun correctly.
options: We went to the market to buy food.
Market we went to buy food.
hints: A noun names a place or thing.
'Market' should name the place.
questions.explanation: 'We went to the market to buy food' uses 'market' correctly as a noun.
misconceptions: The other sentences are grammatically incorrect.

questions.stem: Which noun names an event?
hints: An event is something that happens.
Which word is a celebration?
questions.explanation: 'Christmas' is a noun that names an event.

questions.stem: Which noun names an object?
hints: An object is a thing you can touch.
Which word is a thing?
questions.explanation: 'Chair' is a noun that names an object.

questions.stem: Which word is a noun that names a person?
hints: A person is a human being.
Which word names a human being?
questions.explanation: 'Doctor' is a noun that names a person.

questions.stem: How many nouns are in the sentence 'The teacher gave the pupils books'?
hints: Nouns name people, places, things or events.
Teacher (person), pupils (people), books (things).
questions.explanation: There are three nouns: teacher, pupils and books.
misconceptions: 'Gave' is a verb, not a noun.
Only two nouns would miss one.
Only one noun is too few.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'event' as a noun correctly?
hints: 'Event' is a noun naming something that happens.
Which sentence uses it as a naming word?
questions.explanation: 'The school event was enjoyable' uses 'event' correctly as a noun.
misconceptions: The other sentences are grammatically incorrect.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The celebration of Independence Day in Ghana is a joyful event', which word is a noun naming an event?
hints: An event is something that happens.
'Celebration' names an event.
questions.explanation: 'Celebration' is a noun naming an event. 'Independence Day' is also a noun, but not listed as an option.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.1.1: Apply knowledge of different types of nouns in communication
indicator.objective: Identify and use common nouns (printed as 'b. Common Nouns')

skills.description: Recognise common nouns (general names for people, animals, places, objects) in sentences
Use common nouns correctly in sentences, starting with small letters
Distinguish between common nouns and proper nouns

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Common nouns are the same as proper nouns
Common nouns should start with capital letters

questions.stem: Which word is a common noun in the sentence 'The boy is playing'?
hints: A common noun is a general name, not a specific one.
'Boy' is a general name for a young male.
questions.explanation: 'Boy' is a common noun because it is a general name, not a specific person's name.

questions.stem: Which word is a common noun in the sentence 'The dog is barking'?
hints: A common noun is a general name for an animal, person, place or thing.
'Dog' is a general name for an animal.
questions.explanation: 'Dog' is a common noun because it is a general name for an animal.

questions.stem: Which word is a proper noun?
hints: Proper nouns are specific names and start with capital letters.
Ghana is a specific country.
questions.explanation: 'Ghana' is a proper noun because it is a specific country name, starting with a capital letter.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'Ama went to the market' is a common noun?
hints: A common noun is a general name, not a specific one.
Which word is a general place name?
questions.explanation: 'Market' is a common noun because it is a general name for a place. 'Ama' is a proper noun.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly shows a common noun and a proper noun?
hints: A common noun is general; a proper noun is specific.
City is general; Accra is specific.
questions.explanation: 'City' is a common noun (general) and 'Accra' is a proper noun (specific).

questions.stem: How many common nouns are in 'The girl has a book and a pen'?
hints: Common nouns name general people, places or things.
Girl (person), book (thing), pen (thing).
questions.explanation: There are three common nouns: girl, book and pen.

questions.stem: Which word in 'Kofi lives in Kumasi' is a common noun?
hints: Proper nouns are specific names starting with capital letters.
Both 'Kofi' and 'Kumasi' start with capital letters.
questions.explanation: Both 'Kofi' and 'Kumasi' are proper nouns. There is no common noun in the sentence.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'Mrs. Mensah teaches at the school' is a common noun?
hints: A common noun is a general name.
'School' is a general place. 'Mrs. Mensah' is a specific person.
questions.explanation: 'School' is a common noun because it is a general place. 'Mrs. Mensah' is a proper noun.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a common noun?
hints: Common nouns are general names.
Which word is a specific name?
questions.explanation: 'Accra' is a proper noun because it is a specific city name. The others are common nouns.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The festival of Homowo is celebrated by the Ga people', which words are common nouns and which is a proper noun?
options: Common: festival, people; Proper: Homowo, Ga
Common: Homowo, Ga; Proper: festival, people
Common: festival; Proper: Homowo, Ga, people
hints: Proper nouns are specific names starting with capital letters.
'Homowo' and 'Ga' are specific names.
'Festival' and 'people' are general.
questions.explanation: 'Festival' and 'people' are common nouns; 'Homowo' and 'Ga' are proper nouns.
misconceptions: Not all words are common nouns.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.1.1: Apply knowledge of different types of nouns in communication
indicator.objective: Identify and use collective nouns to refer to a group of objects and people

skills.description: Recognise collective nouns (e.g. team, class, swarm, troop, flock, bunch)
Use collective nouns correctly in sentences with singular verbs
Match collective nouns to the groups they describe

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Any group word is a collective noun
Collective nouns are only for animals
Collective nouns are the same as plural nouns

questions.stem: Which word is a collective noun in the sentence 'The team is playing well'?
hints: A collective noun names a group of people or things.
Which word refers to a group of players?
questions.explanation: 'Team' is a collective noun because it refers to a group of players.

questions.stem: Which word is a collective noun in 'A flock of sheep is grazing'?
hints: A collective noun names a group of animals.
Which word means a group of sheep?
questions.explanation: 'Flock' is a collective noun because it refers to a group of sheep.
misconceptions: 'Sheep' is the animal, not the collective noun.

questions.stem: Which collective noun is used for a group of keys?
hints: Think of what we call a group of keys.
We say a 'bunch of keys'.
questions.explanation: A group of keys is called a 'bunch'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The class ___ ready for the lesson.'
hints: Collective nouns take singular verbs.
'Class' is a collective noun, so use 'is'.
questions.explanation: 'The class is ready for the lesson' uses the singular verb 'is' because 'class' is a collective noun.
misconceptions: 'Are' is plural and does not agree with a collective noun.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'A swarm of bees flew over the garden' is a collective noun?
hints: A collective noun names a group of insects.
Which word means a group of bees?
questions.explanation: 'Swarm' is the collective noun for a group of bees.
misconceptions: 'Bees' is the plural noun, not the collective.

questions.stem: Which collective noun matches a group of cattle?
hints: A group of cattle is called a...
It starts with 'h'.
questions.explanation: A group of cattle is called a herd.

questions.stem: Which collective noun matches a group of monkeys?
hints: A group of monkeys is called a...
It starts with 't'.
questions.explanation: A group of monkeys is called a troop.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a collective noun correctly?
options: The team is winning the match.
The team are winning the match.
hints: Collective nouns take singular verbs.
Which sentence has the correct singular verb?
questions.explanation: 'The team is winning the match' uses 'team' as a collective noun with the singular verb 'is'.
misconceptions: 'Are' is plural and does not agree.
The third sentence is missing a verb.

questions.stem: Which word is NOT a collective noun?
hints: A collective noun names a group.
'Dog' names one animal, not a group.
questions.explanation: 'Dog' is not a collective noun; it names a single animal. 'Team', 'class' and 'flock' are collective nouns.

questions.stem: Which collective noun matches a group of sheep?
hints: A group of sheep is called a...
It starts with 'f'.
questions.explanation: A group of sheep is called a flock.

questions.stem: Which collective noun matches a group of students?
hints: A group of students in a school is called a...
It starts with 'c'.
questions.explanation: A group of students is called a class.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a collective noun with the correct verb?
options: A bunch of keys is on the table.
A bunch of keys are on the table.
A bunch of keys were on the table.
A bunch of keys be on the table.
hints: Collective nouns take singular verbs.
'Bunch' is collective, so use 'is'.
questions.explanation: 'A bunch of keys is on the table' uses the singular verb 'is' correctly with the collective noun 'bunch'.

questions.stem: How many collective nouns are in the sentence 'The class and the team are ready'?
hints: A collective noun names a group.
'Class' and 'team' both name groups.
questions.explanation: There are two collective nouns: class and team.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'The flock of birds are flying.' What is wrong with this sentence?
options: The verb should be 'is' because 'flock' is a collective noun.
hints: Collective nouns take singular verbs.
'Flock' is singular, so use 'is'.
questions.explanation: The sentence should be 'The flock of birds is flying' because 'flock' is a collective noun taking the singular verb 'is'.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.1.1: Apply knowledge of different types of nouns in communication
indicator.objective: Identify and use abstract nouns to refer to concepts and ideas.

skills.description: Recognise abstract nouns (names of things that cannot be seen, felt or touched — e.g. air, beauty, peace)
Use abstract nouns correctly in sentences
Distinguish between concrete nouns and abstract nouns

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Abstract nouns can be seen or touched
Abstract nouns are not real nouns

questions.stem: Which of these is an abstract noun?
hints: An abstract noun names something you cannot see or touch.
Love is a feeling — you cannot touch it.
questions.explanation: 'Love' is an abstract noun because it is a feeling that cannot be seen or touched.

questions.stem: Which of these is an abstract noun?
hints: An abstract noun names a concept or idea.
Peace is a concept — you cannot touch it.
questions.explanation: 'Peace' is an abstract noun because it is a concept that cannot be seen or touched.

questions.stem: Which of these is an abstract noun?
hints: An abstract noun names a quality or idea.
Beauty is a quality — you cannot touch it.
questions.explanation: 'Beauty' is an abstract noun because it is a quality that cannot be seen or touched directly.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an abstract noun correctly?
options: She showed great kindness to the old man.
She showed great table to the old man.
She showed great chair to the old man.
She showed great dog to the old man.
hints: Kindness is an abstract noun.
Which sentence uses an abstract noun meaningfully?
questions.explanation: 'She showed great kindness to the old man' uses the abstract noun 'kindness' correctly.
misconceptions: 'Table', 'chair' and 'dog' are concrete nouns and do not fit.

questions.stem: Which word is a concrete noun?
hints: A concrete noun can be seen or touched.
A stone can be seen and touched.
questions.explanation: 'Stone' is a concrete noun because it can be seen and touched.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'She has great wisdom' is an abstract noun?
hints: An abstract noun names a quality or idea.
Wisdom is a quality you cannot touch.
questions.explanation: 'Wisdom' is an abstract noun because it is a quality that cannot be seen or touched.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'His courage helped him win the race' is an abstract noun?
hints: An abstract noun names a quality or feeling.
Courage is a quality you cannot touch.
questions.explanation: 'Courage' is an abstract noun because it is a quality that cannot be seen or touched.

questions.stem: Which word is an abstract noun?
hints: An abstract noun names a feeling or idea.
Happiness is a feeling.
questions.explanation: 'Happiness' is an abstract noun because it is a feeling that cannot be seen or touched.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the abstract noun 'freedom' correctly?
options: The people fought for their freedom.
The people fought for their table.
The people fought for their shoe.
The people fought for their cup.
hints: Freedom is an abstract noun meaning liberty.
Which sentence makes sense with 'freedom'?
questions.explanation: 'The people fought for their freedom' uses 'freedom' correctly.
misconceptions: The other sentences use concrete nouns that do not fit.

questions.stem: Which word is an abstract noun?
hints: An abstract noun names a concept or idea.
Truth is a concept.
questions.explanation: 'Truth' is an abstract noun because it is a concept that cannot be seen or touched.

questions.stem: Which pair contains one concrete noun and one abstract noun?
hints: A concrete noun can be touched; an abstract noun cannot.
'Book' can be touched; 'knowledge' cannot.
questions.explanation: 'Book' is a concrete noun and 'knowledge' is an abstract noun.

questions.stem: How many abstract nouns are in the sentence 'Love and kindness bring happiness'?
hints: Abstract nouns name feelings, qualities or ideas.
Love, kindness and happiness are all abstract.
questions.explanation: There are three abstract nouns: love, kindness and happiness.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an abstract noun correctly?
options: Her beauty is admired by everyone.
Her table is admired by everyone.
Her chair is admired by everyone.
Her bag is admired by everyone.
hints: Beauty is an abstract noun.
Which sentence uses a quality that cannot be touched?
questions.explanation: 'Her beauty is admired by everyone' uses the abstract noun 'beauty' correctly.
misconceptions: The other sentences use concrete nouns.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains BOTH a concrete noun and an abstract noun?
options: The boy showed courage when he saw the lion.
The lion is in the cage.
hints: Concrete nouns can be seen/touched; abstract nouns cannot.
'Boy' and 'lion' are concrete; 'courage' is abstract.
questions.explanation: 'The boy showed courage when he saw the lion' contains concrete nouns ('boy', 'lion') and the abstract noun 'courage'.
misconceptions: The other sentences only contain concrete nouns.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'Happiness is a concrete noun because you can see happy people.' Is this correct?
options: No, happiness is abstract because it is a feeling, not a physical object
Yes, because you can see happy people
Yes, because happiness is a thing
No, happiness is not a noun
hints: Concrete nouns can be touched; abstract nouns cannot.
You can see happy people, but you cannot touch happiness itself.
questions.explanation: No, 'happiness' is an abstract noun because it is a feeling. You can see happy people, but happiness itself cannot be touched.
misconceptions: Seeing happy people does not make happiness concrete.
Happiness is not a physical object.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'The teacher praised the pupil for his honesty and hard work' is an abstract noun?
hints: An abstract noun names a quality or idea.
Honesty is a quality.
questions.explanation: 'Honesty' is an abstract noun. 'Teacher' and 'pupil' are concrete nouns.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.2.1: Apply knowledge of different types of determiners in communication
indicator.objective: Identify and use the definite and indefinite articles 'a' and 'an' to refer to a person, animal, event, time or objects in general

skills.description: Recognise articles (a, an, the) in sentences
Use 'a' before consonant sounds and 'an' before vowel sounds correctly
Recognise nouns that do not need articles (music, soup, soap, water)
Use 'the' to refer to a specific person, animal, event or object

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: 'An' is used before any word starting with a vowel
You can use 'a' before any word

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'I saw a cat' is an article?
hints: Articles are 'a', 'an' and 'the'.
Which word is an article?
questions.explanation: 'A' is an article (indefinite article) in the sentence.

questions.stem: Which word is the definite article?
hints: The definite article refers to something specific.
It is 'the'.
questions.explanation: 'The' is the definite article.

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: 'I ate ___ apple.'
hints: Use 'an' before a vowel sound.
'Apple' starts with a vowel sound.
questions.explanation: We use 'an' before 'apple' because it starts with a vowel sound.

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: 'She has ___ dog.'
hints: Use 'a' before a consonant sound.
'Dog' starts with a consonant sound.
questions.explanation: We use 'a' before 'dog' because it starts with a consonant sound.

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: 'Please close ___ door.' (pointing to a specific door)
hints: Use 'the' for a specific object.
The speaker is pointing to a particular door.
questions.explanation: We use 'the' because the door is specific.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains BOTH a definite and an indefinite article?
options: I saw a dog and the dog was barking.
hints: Definite article = 'the'; indefinite = 'a' or 'an'.
Which sentence has both?
questions.explanation: 'I saw a dog and the dog was barking' contains 'a' (indefinite) and 'the' (definite).
misconceptions: Other sentences have only one type or none.

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: 'He is ___ honest man.'
hints: 'Honest' starts with a vowel sound (the 'h' is silent).
Use 'an' before a vowel sound.
questions.explanation: We use 'an' before 'honest' because it starts with a vowel sound (the 'h' is silent).

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: 'She is ___ university student.'
hints: 'University' starts with a consonant sound (/juː/).
Use 'a' before a consonant sound.
questions.explanation: We use 'a' before 'university' because it starts with a consonant sound (/juː/).

questions.stem: Which sentence does NOT need an article?
hints: Some nouns like music, soup, soap do not take articles in general use.
'Music' is an uncountable noun used generally.
questions.explanation: 'I love music' does not need an article because 'music' is used generally.

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence:
hints: 'Soup' is an uncountable noun used generally.
No article is needed.
questions.explanation: 'I enjoy soup' is correct because 'soup' is used generally and does not need an article.
misconceptions: 'The soup' would refer to a specific soup.

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: '___ sun rises in the east.'
hints: There is only one sun, so it is specific.
Use 'the' for unique things.
questions.explanation: We use 'the' because the sun is unique.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'the' correctly?
options: The book on the table is mine.
A book on the table is mine.
An book on the table is mine.
Book on the table is mine.
hints: 'The' refers to a specific book.
The book is identified by 'on the table'.
questions.explanation: 'The book on the table is mine' uses 'the' because the book is specific (on the table).

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
options: A water is essential for life.
An water is essential for life.
The water is essential for life.
hints: 'Water' is an uncountable noun used generally.
No article is needed.
questions.explanation: 'Water is essential for life' is correct because 'water' is used generally and does not need an article.

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: 'He waited for ___ hour.'
hints: 'Hour' starts with a vowel sound (the 'h' is silent).
Use 'an'.
questions.explanation: We use 'an' before 'hour' because it starts with a vowel sound.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'the' correctly?
options: The pupils in Basic 4 are hardworking.
A pupils in Basic 4 are hardworking.
An pupils in Basic 4 are hardworking.
hints: 'The' refers to a specific group of pupils.
The group is identified as 'in Basic 4'.
questions.explanation: 'The pupils in Basic 4 are hardworking' uses 'the' because the pupils are a specific group.
misconceptions: An article is needed to specify the group.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'I saw a elephant at the zoo.' What is wrong with this sentence?
options: It should be 'an elephant' because 'elephant' starts with a vowel sound.
It should be 'the elephant' because it is specific.
hints: Use 'an' before vowel sounds.
'Elephant' starts with a vowel sound.
questions.explanation: The sentence should be 'I saw an elephant' because 'elephant' starts with a vowel sound.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.2.1: Apply knowledge of different types of determiners in communication
indicator.objective: Identify and use quantifiers to show quantities

skills.description: Recognise quantifiers (some, few, little, many, no, all, every, one, two)
Use quantifiers correctly with countable and uncountable nouns
Distinguish between quantifiers used with countable nouns (few, many) and uncountable nouns (little)

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Few and little mean the same
Any quantifier can go with any noun
Many is used with uncountable nouns

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'I have some books' is a quantifier?
hints: A quantifier shows how much or how many.
'Some' tells us an amount.
questions.explanation: 'Some' is a quantifier because it shows an amount.

questions.stem: Which of these is a quantifier?
hints: A quantifier shows quantity.
'Many' tells us how much or how many.
questions.explanation: 'Many' is a quantifier because it shows quantity.

questions.stem: Choose the correct quantifier: 'I have ___ books.'
hints: Books are countable.
Use 'a few' with countable nouns.
questions.explanation: 'A few' is used with countable nouns like 'books'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct quantifier: 'There is ___ water in the cup.'
hints: Water is uncountable.
Use 'a little' with uncountable nouns.
questions.explanation: 'A little' is used with uncountable nouns like 'water'.

questions.stem: Which quantifier means 'not any'?
hints: 'No' means zero or not any.
Which word shows absence?
questions.explanation: 'No' is a quantifier meaning 'not any'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct quantifier: 'There are ___ apples in the basket.'
hints: Apples are countable.
Use 'many' with countable nouns.
questions.explanation: 'Many' is used with countable nouns like 'apples'.

questions.stem: Which quantifier is used with uncountable nouns?
hints: Uncountable nouns like water, rice, sand use this quantifier.
'Little' is used with uncountable nouns.
questions.explanation: 'Little' is used with uncountable nouns.

questions.stem: Choose the correct quantifier: '___ pupils are playing in the field.'
hints: Pupils are countable.
Use 'some' for an unspecified number of countable nouns.
questions.explanation: 'Some' can be used with countable nouns like 'pupils'.
misconceptions: 'A little' and 'little' are for uncountable nouns.

questions.stem: Choose the correct quantifier: '___ pupils passed the test.' (meaning every pupil)
hints: 'All' means every one.
The sentence says every pupil passed.
questions.explanation: 'All' is used because every pupil passed.
misconceptions: 'Some' means a few, not every one.
'Many' means a large number but not every one.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'few' correctly?
options: There are few books on the table.
There is few water in the cup.
There are few rice in the bowl.
There is few sand on the ground.
hints: 'Few' is used with countable nouns.
Books are countable.
questions.explanation: 'There are few books on the table' is correct because 'few' is used with countable nouns.
misconceptions: 'Few' is not used with uncountable nouns like water, rice or sand.

questions.stem: Choose the correct quantifier: 'There are ___ apples left; we must buy more.'
hints: The sentence says we must buy more.
This means there are zero apples left.
questions.explanation: 'No' is correct because they need to buy more, meaning there are no apples left.
misconceptions: 'Some' would mean there are still apples.
'Many' would mean a lot are left.
'All' would mean every apple is still there.

questions.stem: Choose the best quantifier for this sentence: '___ of the pupils in the class passed the exam.' (meaning 100%)
hints: The sentence says 100% passed.
'All' means every one.
questions.explanation: 'All' is the correct quantifier because 100% of the pupils passed.
misconceptions: 'Many' means a large number but not 100%.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'Every child received a gift' is a quantifier?
hints: A quantifier shows how much or how many.
'Every' tells us each one without exception.
questions.explanation: 'Every' is a quantifier meaning each one without exception.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'much' correctly?
options: There is much water in the bucket.
There are much books on the shelf.
There are much pupils in the class.
There are much apples in the basket.
hints: 'Much' is used with uncountable nouns.
Water is uncountable.
questions.explanation: 'There is much water in the bucket' is correct because 'much' is used with the uncountable noun 'water'.
misconceptions: 'Much' is not used with countable nouns like books, pupils or apples.

questions.stem: A pupil writes: 'There are a little books on the desk.' What is wrong?
options: It should be 'a few books' because books are countable.
hints: 'A little' is for uncountable nouns.
Books are countable, so use 'a few'.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence is 'There are a few books on the desk' because 'books' is countable.
misconceptions: 'Many' is possible but changes the meaning.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the quantifier most appropriately?
options: There is little hope of finding the lost item.
There is few hope of finding the lost item.
There are little hope of finding the lost item.
There are few hope of finding the lost item.
hints: 'Hope' is an uncountable abstract noun.
Use 'little' with uncountable nouns.
questions.explanation: 'There is little hope' is correct because 'hope' is uncountable and takes 'little'.
misconceptions: The verb 'are' does not agree with 'hope'.

questions.stem: Explain why we say 'fewer books' but 'less water'. Which statement is correct?
options: Books are countable so we use 'fewer'; water is uncountable so we use 'less'.
Books are uncountable so we use 'fewer'; water is countable so we use 'less'.
'Fewer' and 'less' mean the same and can be used interchangeably.
'Fewer' is for uncountable nouns and 'less' is for countable nouns.
hints: Countable nouns use 'fewer'.
Uncountable nouns use 'less'.
questions.explanation: We use 'fewer' with countable nouns (books) and 'less' with uncountable nouns (water).
misconceptions: Books are countable, water is uncountable.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.2.1: Apply knowledge of different types of determiners in communication
indicator.objective: Identify and use possessive pronouns to show possession

skills.description: Recognise possessive pronouns (my, your, his, her, our, their) in sentences
Use possessive pronouns correctly in sentences to show ownership
Match possessive pronouns to the person or thing that owns something

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Possessive pronouns are the same as personal pronouns
'His' and 'her' can be used for any person
Possessive pronouns come after the noun

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'This is my book' is a possessive pronoun?
hints: A possessive pronoun shows ownership.
Which word tells us who owns the book?
questions.explanation: 'My' is a possessive pronoun because it shows that the book belongs to the speaker.

questions.stem: Which word is a possessive pronoun?
hints: A possessive pronoun shows ownership.
'His' means belonging to him.
questions.explanation: 'His' is a possessive pronoun showing that something belongs to a male person.

questions.stem: Choose the correct possessive pronoun: 'Ama lost ___ pen.'
hints: Ama is a girl/woman.
Use the possessive pronoun for a female.
questions.explanation: 'Her' is correct because Ama is female and the pen belongs to her.
misconceptions: 'Our' is for the speaker and others.

questions.stem: Choose the correct possessive pronoun: 'Kofi lost ___ bag.'
hints: Kofi is a boy/man.
Use the possessive pronoun for a male.
questions.explanation: 'His' is correct because Kofi is male and the bag belongs to him.
misconceptions: 'Our' is for the speaker and others.

questions.stem: Choose the correct possessive pronoun: 'We love ___ school.'
hints: The subject is 'we'.
Use the possessive pronoun that matches 'we'.
questions.explanation: 'Our' is correct because it matches the subject 'we'.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a possessive pronoun?
hints: A possessive pronoun shows ownership.
Which sentence has a word showing who owns the house?
questions.explanation: 'Their house is big' contains 'their', a possessive pronoun.
misconceptions: The other sentences have no possessive pronoun.

questions.stem: How many possessive pronouns are in the sentence 'My sister lost her bag'?
hints: Look for words that show ownership.
'My' shows the speaker's sister; 'her' shows the sister's bag.
questions.explanation: There are two possessive pronouns: 'my' and 'her'.

questions.stem: Which possessive pronoun matches 'the children'?
hints: 'The children' is a group of people.
Use the possessive pronoun for 'they'.
questions.explanation: 'Their' matches 'the children' because it is the possessive form of 'they'.

questions.stem: Which possessive pronoun matches 'the teacher' (female)?
hints: The teacher is female.
Use the possessive pronoun for 'she'.
questions.explanation: 'Her' matches a female teacher.

questions.stem: Choose the correct possessive pronoun: 'The pupils cleaned ___ classroom.'
hints: The subject is 'the pupils' (plural).
Use the possessive pronoun for 'they'.
questions.explanation: 'Their' is correct because it matches the plural subject 'the pupils'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct possessive pronoun: 'I lost ___ pencil.'
hints: The subject is 'I'.
Use the possessive pronoun for 'I'.
questions.explanation: 'My' is correct because it matches the subject 'I'.

questions.stem: Which word is NOT a possessive pronoun?
hints: A possessive pronoun shows ownership.
'He' is a subject pronoun, not possessive.
questions.explanation: 'He' is not a possessive pronoun; it is a personal pronoun. 'My', 'his' and 'her' are possessive.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the possessive pronoun correctly?
hints: 'Its' is the possessive form (no apostrophe).
'It's' means 'it is'.
questions.explanation: 'The dog wagged its tail' uses 'its' correctly as a possessive pronoun.
misconceptions: 'It' is a personal pronoun, not possessive.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'The girls lost his books.' What is wrong?
options: It should be 'their books' because 'the girls' is plural.
hints: 'The girls' is plural.
Use 'their' for plural subjects.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence is 'The girls lost their books' because 'the girls' is plural.

questions.stem: Choose the correct possessive pronoun: 'The boys and I cleaned ___ classroom.'
hints: The subject includes 'I' (the speaker).
Use the possessive pronoun for 'we'.
questions.explanation: 'Our' is correct because the subject 'the boys and I' is equivalent to 'we'.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.2.1: Apply knowledge of different types of determiners in communication
indicator.objective: Identify and use demonstratives: this/that, these/those

skills.description: Recognise demonstratives (this, that, these, those) in sentences
Use 'this/that' with singular nouns and 'these/those' with plural nouns
Distinguish between near (this/these) and far (that/those) demonstratives

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: This and these mean the same
That and those can be used interchangeably

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'This book is mine' is a demonstrative?
hints: A demonstrative points to something specific.
'This' points to a particular book.
questions.explanation: 'This' is a demonstrative because it points to a specific book.

questions.stem: Which of these is a demonstrative?
hints: Demonstratives are this, that, these, those.
Which word is in that list?
questions.explanation: 'Those' is a demonstrative.

questions.stem: Choose the correct demonstrative: '___ book is interesting.' (near, singular)
hints: Use 'this' for something near and singular.
The noun 'book' is singular.
questions.explanation: 'This' is used for a singular noun that is near.

questions.stem: Choose the correct demonstrative: '___ books are mine.' (near, plural)
hints: Use 'these' for something near and plural.
The noun 'books' is plural.
questions.explanation: 'These' is used for plural nouns that are near.

questions.stem: Which demonstrative is used for something far away and singular?
hints: Far and singular.
'That' is for something far and singular.
questions.explanation: 'That' is used for something far away and singular.

questions.stem: Which demonstrative is used for something far away and plural?
hints: Far and plural.
'Those' is for something far and plural.
questions.explanation: 'Those' is used for something far away and plural.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a demonstrative correctly?
hints: 'Apples' is plural.
Use 'these' or 'those' with plural nouns.
questions.explanation: 'These apples are sweet' is correct because 'apples' is plural and 'these' is a plural demonstrative.
misconceptions: 'Those apple' uses a plural demonstrative with a singular noun.

questions.stem: Choose the correct demonstrative: '___ children over there are playing.' (far, plural)
hints: 'Children' is plural.
Use 'those' for far plural.
questions.explanation: 'Those' is correct because 'children' is plural and they are far away.

questions.stem: Choose the correct demonstrative: '___ boy next to me is my brother.' (near, singular)
hints: 'Boy' is singular.
Use 'this' for near singular.
questions.explanation: 'This' is correct because 'boy' is singular and near.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches near and far for singular nouns?
hints: Singular near and singular far.
'This' is near singular; 'that' is far singular.
questions.explanation: 'This' (near singular) and 'that' (far singular) are the correct pair for singular nouns.
misconceptions: 'This' and 'these' are near but different in number.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches near and far for plural nouns?
hints: Plural near and plural far.
'These' is near plural; 'those' is far plural.
questions.explanation: 'These' (near plural) and 'those' (far plural) are the correct pair for plural nouns.
misconceptions: 'This' and 'these' are near but different in number.

questions.stem: How many demonstratives are in the sentence 'This is mine and that is yours'?
hints: Demonstratives are this, that, these, those.
Both 'this' and 'that' are demonstratives.
questions.explanation: There are two demonstratives: 'this' and 'that'.

questions.stem: Which word is NOT a demonstrative?
hints: Demonstratives are this, that, these, those.
'They' is a personal pronoun.
questions.explanation: 'They' is not a demonstrative; it is a personal pronoun. The others are demonstratives.

questions.stem: A pupil points to a book far away and says, 'These book is mine.' What is wrong?
options: It should be 'That book is mine' because the book is far and singular.
It should be 'This book is mine'.
It should be 'Those book is mine'.
hints: The book is far away and singular.
Use 'that' for far singular.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence is 'That book is mine' because the book is far away and singular.

questions.stem: Choose the correct demonstrative: '___ shoes near the door are mine.' (near, plural)
hints: 'Shoes' is plural.
Use 'these' for near plural.
questions.explanation: 'These' is correct because 'shoes' is plural and near.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses 'those'?
options: Those birds in the sky are flying south.
Those bird in the sky is flying south.
Those birds in the sky is flying south.
Those bird in the sky are flying south.
hints: 'Those' is plural, so the noun and verb must be plural.
Birds (plural) + are (plural verb).
questions.explanation: 'Those birds in the sky are flying south' correctly uses 'those' with the plural noun 'birds' and plural verb 'are'.
misconceptions: 'Bird' is singular and does not match 'those'.
'Is' is singular and does not match 'birds'.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.2.1: Apply knowledge of different types of determiners in communication
indicator.objective: Identify and use interrogative determiners 'which, whose' - to find out about specific persons or objects

skills.description: Recognise interrogative determiners (which, whose) in questions
Use 'which' to ask about a specific person or object from a known set
Use 'whose' to ask about possession (who owns something)

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Which and whose mean the same
Interrogative determiners are the same as interrogative pronouns

questions.stem: Which word in the question 'Which house is bigger?' is an interrogative determiner?
hints: An interrogative determiner comes before a noun in a question.
'Which' comes before 'house'.
questions.explanation: 'Which' is an interrogative determiner because it comes before the noun 'house' to ask a question.

questions.stem: Which word is an interrogative determiner?
hints: An interrogative determiner comes before a noun.
'Whose' comes before a noun to ask about ownership.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' is an interrogative determiner.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: '___ book do you want?' (asking about a choice)
hints: Use 'which' to ask about a choice from a known set.
The speaker is asking the person to choose a book.
questions.explanation: 'Which' is correct because it asks about a choice from a set of books.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: '___ bag is this?' (asking about ownership)
hints: Use 'whose' to ask who owns something.
The speaker wants to know who owns the bag.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' is correct because it asks about ownership of the bag.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'which' correctly?
options: Which dress do you like best?
Whose dress do you like best?
Who dress do you like best?
When dress do you like best?
hints: 'Which' asks about a choice.
The speaker wants the person to choose a dress.
questions.explanation: 'Which dress do you like best?' uses 'which' correctly to ask about a choice.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'whose' correctly?
options: Whose pen is on the table?
Which pen is on the table?
Who pen is on the table?
When pen is on the table?
hints: 'Whose' asks about ownership.
The speaker wants to know who owns the pen.
questions.explanation: 'Whose pen is on the table?' uses 'whose' correctly to ask about ownership.

questions.stem: Which word in the question 'Whose shoes are these?' is an interrogative determiner?
hints: An interrogative determiner comes before a noun.
'Whose' comes before 'shoes'.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' is the interrogative determiner because it comes before the noun 'shoes' to ask a question.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to know which of three books belongs to the teacher. Which question should they ask?
hints: The pupil wants the teacher to choose from a set of books.
Use 'which' for a choice.
questions.explanation: 'Which book is yours, sir?' uses 'which' correctly to ask about a choice from a set.
misconceptions: 'Who' is not used before a noun in this way.

questions.stem: A pupil finds a lost pencil and wants to know who owns it. Which question should they ask?
hints: The pupil wants to know who owns the pencil.
Use 'whose' for ownership.
questions.explanation: 'Whose pencil is this?' uses 'whose' correctly to ask about ownership.
misconceptions: 'Who' is not used before a noun in this way.

questions.stem: How many interrogative determiners are in the question 'Which bag is whose?'
hints: Interrogative determiners are 'which' and 'whose'.
Both words appear in the question.
questions.explanation: There are two interrogative determiners: 'which' and 'whose'.

questions.stem: Which question is correct?
options: Which of the two cars is faster?
Whose of the two cars is faster?
Who of the two cars is faster?
When of the two cars is faster?
hints: The question asks about a choice between two cars.
Use 'which' for a choice.
questions.explanation: 'Which of the two cars is faster?' uses 'which' correctly to ask about a choice.

questions.stem: Which question is correct?
hints: The question asks who owns the shoes.
Use 'whose' for ownership.
questions.explanation: 'Whose shoes are these?' uses 'whose' correctly to ask about ownership.
misconceptions: 'Who' is not used before a noun in this way.

questions.stem: A pupil asks: 'Which pen is red?' What does the pupil want to know?
options: Which one of the pens is red
hints: 'Which' asks about a choice from a set.
The pupil wants to identify the red pen among several pens.
questions.explanation: The pupil wants to know which pen, out of a set, is red.

questions.stem: A pupil asks: 'Whose ruler is on the floor?' What does the pupil want to know?
options: Who owns the ruler on the floor
Which ruler is on the floor
Why the ruler is on the floor
hints: 'Whose' asks about ownership.
The pupil wants to find the owner of the ruler.
questions.explanation: The pupil wants to know who owns the ruler on the floor.

questions.stem: Which sentence does NOT contain an interrogative determiner?
options: The book is on the table.
Which book is on the table?
Whose book is on the table?
Which of the books is yours?
hints: Interrogative determiners are 'which' and 'whose'.
Which sentence has no question word?
questions.explanation: 'The book is on the table' does not contain an interrogative determiner. The others contain 'which' or 'whose'.
misconceptions: 'Which book is on the table?' has 'which'.
'Whose book is on the table?' has 'whose'.
'Which of the books is yours?' has 'which'.

questions.stem: A pupil is looking at three shirts in a shop. Which question should they ask to find out the price of a specific shirt?
hints: The pupil wants to identify a specific shirt from a set.
Use 'which' for a choice.
questions.explanation: 'Which shirt costs the most?' uses 'which' correctly to ask about a specific shirt from a set.
misconceptions: 'Who' is not used before a noun in this way.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.3.1: Apply knowledge of different types of pronouns in communication
indicator.objective: Identify and use different types of pronouns: Personal – to identify people, activities and objects; Interrogative – who, what to find out a person's identity, specific information about a person, time, objects or events

skills.description: Recognise personal pronouns (I, you, he, she, it, we, they) in sentences
Use personal pronouns correctly in sentences to replace nouns
Recognise interrogative pronouns (who, what, where) in questions
Use interrogative pronouns correctly to ask about people, objects, places or events

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Pronouns are the same as nouns
Personal pronouns are only for people
You can use any pronoun to replace any noun

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'She is my sister' is a personal pronoun?
hints: A personal pronoun replaces a person's name.
'She' replaces a female person's name.
questions.explanation: 'She' is a personal pronoun because it replaces a female person's name.

questions.stem: Which word is a personal pronoun?
hints: A personal pronoun replaces a noun.
'They' replaces a plural noun.
questions.explanation: 'They' is a personal pronoun.

questions.stem: Choose the correct pronoun to replace 'Kofi': '___ is my friend.'
hints: Kofi is a male name.
Use the male pronoun 'he'.
questions.explanation: 'He' is correct because Kofi is male.

questions.stem: Choose the correct pronoun to replace 'Ama and Esi': '___ are sisters.'
hints: 'Ama and Esi' is plural.
Use the plural pronoun 'they'.
questions.explanation: 'They' is correct because 'Ama and Esi' is plural.

questions.stem: Which word in the question 'Who is your teacher?' is an interrogative pronoun?
hints: An interrogative pronoun asks a question.
'Who' asks about a person.
questions.explanation: 'Who' is an interrogative pronoun because it asks about a person's identity.

questions.stem: Which word is an interrogative pronoun?
hints: An interrogative pronoun is used in questions.
'What' asks for information.
questions.explanation: 'What' is an interrogative pronoun.

questions.stem: Choose the correct interrogative pronoun: '___ is your name?'
hints: The question asks for a name (information).
Use 'what' to ask for information.
questions.explanation: 'What is your name?' uses 'what' correctly to ask for information.
misconceptions: 'Who' asks about a person's identity, not a name.

questions.stem: Choose the correct interrogative pronoun: '___ is the headteacher?'
hints: The question asks about a person's identity.
Use 'who' for people.
questions.explanation: 'Who is the headteacher?' uses 'who' correctly to ask about a person's identity.

questions.stem: How many personal pronouns are in the sentence 'He gave it to them'?
hints: Personal pronouns replace nouns.
'He', 'it' and 'them' are all personal pronouns.
questions.explanation: There are three personal pronouns: he, it and them.

questions.stem: Choose the correct pronoun to replace 'the book': '___ is on the table.'
hints: A book is an object.
Use 'it' for an object.
questions.explanation: 'It' is correct because a book is an object.

questions.stem: Choose the correct pronoun: 'My mother and I went to the market. ___ bought some fruit.'
hints: 'My mother and I' is equivalent to 'we'.
Use the pronoun for 'we'.
questions.explanation: 'We' is correct because 'my mother and I' is equivalent to 'we'.

questions.stem: Which word in the question 'What is in the box?' is an interrogative pronoun?
hints: An interrogative pronoun asks a question.
'What' asks for information about something.
questions.explanation: 'What' is the interrogative pronoun asking about the contents of the box.

questions.stem: Which question uses 'who' correctly?
hints: 'Who' asks about a person's identity.
The question asks about a person.
questions.explanation: 'Who is your best friend?' uses 'who' correctly to ask about a person.

questions.stem: Which question uses 'what' correctly?
hints: 'What' asks for information about things.
The question asks about a food item.
questions.explanation: 'What is your favourite food?' uses 'what' correctly to ask about a thing.

questions.stem: Which word is NOT a personal pronoun?
hints: A personal pronoun replaces a noun as subject or object.
'Their' is a possessive pronoun, not a personal pronoun.
questions.explanation: 'Their' is a possessive pronoun, not a personal pronoun. 'They', 'them' and 'we' are personal pronouns.

questions.stem: How many interrogative pronouns are in the question 'Who did what?'
hints: Interrogative pronouns ask questions.
Both 'who' and 'what' are interrogative pronouns.
questions.explanation: There are two interrogative pronouns: 'who' and 'what'.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'Me went to the market.' What is wrong?
options: It should be 'I went to the market' because 'me' is an object pronoun.
It should be 'Me goes to the market'.
It should be 'Him went to the market'.
hints: The subject pronoun is 'I', not 'me'.
'Me' is used as an object.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence is 'I went to the market' because 'I' is the subject pronoun.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to know the name of a person. Which interrogative pronoun should they use?
hints: The question is about a person's identity.
Use 'who' for people.
questions.explanation: 'Who' is correct because the pupil wants to know a person's identity.

questions.stem: Choose the correct pronoun: 'The teacher gave the books to ___ students.'
hints: The pronoun is the object of the preposition 'to'.
Use the object pronoun 'us'.
questions.explanation: 'Us' is correct because it is the object of the preposition 'to'.

questions.stem: Which sentence does NOT contain an interrogative pronoun?
options: The book is on the table.
hints: Interrogative pronouns are used in questions.
Which sentence is not a question?
questions.explanation: 'The book is on the table' is a statement and does not contain an interrogative pronoun.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.4.1: Apply the knowledge of adjectives in communication
indicator.objective: Use adjectives to make comparison e.g: fast/slow (Ama is fast but Kofi is slow.), good/bad, fast/faster, slow/slower

skills.description: Recognise adjectives in sentences (words that describe people, animals, objects or places)
Use positive adjectives to contrast two people or things
Form comparative adjectives by adding '-er' to regular adjectives
Use comparative adjectives correctly in sentences to compare two people or things

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: All adjectives form their comparative by adding '-er'
Comparative means the same as positive

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'The tall boy is running' is an adjective?
hints: An adjective describes a noun.
Which word describes the boy?
questions.explanation: 'Tall' is an adjective because it describes the boy.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'The soup is hot' is an adjective?
hints: An adjective describes a noun.
Which word describes the soup?
questions.explanation: 'Hot' is an adjective because it describes the soup.

questions.stem: Which sentence contrasts two people using adjectives?
options: Ama is fast but Kofi is slow.
hints: A contrast shows how two people are different.
'Fast' and 'slow' are contrasting adjectives.
questions.explanation: 'Ama is fast but Kofi is slow' contrasts the two people using adjectives.
misconceptions: The other sentences do not use contrasting adjectives.

questions.stem: What is the comparative form of 'fast'?
hints: Add '-er' to form the comparative of a short adjective.
Fast → faster.
questions.explanation: The comparative form of 'fast' is 'faster'.

questions.stem: What is the comparative form of 'slow'?
hints: Add '-er' to form the comparative.
Slow → slower.
questions.explanation: The comparative form of 'slow' is 'slower'.

questions.stem: How many adjectives are in the sentence 'The big brown dog is friendly'?
hints: Adjectives describe nouns.
'Big' and 'brown' describe the dog; 'friendly' describes the dog too.
questions.explanation: There are three adjectives: big, brown and friendly.

questions.stem: What is the comparative form of 'small'?
hints: Add '-er' to form the comparative.
Small → smaller.
questions.explanation: The comparative form of 'small' is 'smaller'.

questions.stem: What is the comparative form of 'big'?
hints: For adjectives ending in a consonant-vowel-consonant, double the final consonant and add '-er'.
Big → bigger.
questions.explanation: The comparative form of 'big' is 'bigger' (double the 'g' and add '-er').

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly contrasts two objects using adjectives?
options: This bag is heavy but that one is light.
hints: A contrast shows a difference between two things.
'Heavy' and 'light' are contrasting adjectives.
questions.explanation: 'This bag is heavy but that one is light' correctly contrasts two objects.
misconceptions: The other sentences do not contrast the two bags.

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence:
options: Ama is more taller than Kwesi.
hints: Use 'than' after the comparative adjective.
Tall → taller + than.
questions.explanation: 'Ama is taller than Kwesi' uses the comparative 'taller' with 'than' correctly.

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence:
options: This ruler is longer than that one.
This ruler is longer that one.
This ruler is more longer than that one.
This ruler is longest than that one.
hints: Use 'than' after the comparative adjective.
Long → longer + than.
questions.explanation: 'This ruler is longer than that one' uses the comparative 'longer' with 'than' correctly.

questions.stem: What is the comparative form of 'good'?
hints: 'Good' is an irregular adjective.
Its comparative form is 'better'.
questions.explanation: The comparative form of 'good' is 'better' (irregular).

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the comparative form correctly?
options: Kofi is more stronger than Musa.
hints: Use 'than' after the comparative.
Strong → stronger + than.
questions.explanation: 'Kofi is stronger than Musa' uses 'stronger' with 'than' correctly.

questions.stem: What is the comparative form of 'bad'?
hints: 'Bad' is an irregular adjective.
Its comparative form is 'worse'.
questions.explanation: The comparative form of 'bad' is 'worse' (irregular).

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence comparing two places:
options: Accra is more busier than Kumasi.
hints: Use 'than' after the comparative.
Busy → busier + than.
questions.explanation: 'Accra is busier than Kumasi' uses the comparative 'busier' with 'than' correctly.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The hungry children ate the delicious food quickly', which word is an adjective?
hints: An adjective describes a noun.
'Delicious' describes the food.
questions.explanation: 'Delicious' is an adjective because it describes the food.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly compares two people's heights?
options: Ama is more shorter than Esi.
hints: Use 'than' after the comparative.
Short → shorter + than.
questions.explanation: 'Ama is shorter than Esi' uses the comparative 'shorter' with 'than' correctly.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.5.1: Apply the knowledge of verbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use different types of verbs: Main verb, Helping verb (primary auxiliary and modal auxiliary)

skills.description: Recognise main verbs (action or state words) in sentences
Recognise helping verbs (primary auxiliaries and modal auxiliaries)
Distinguish between main verbs, primary auxiliaries and modal auxiliaries in sentences
Use main verbs and helping verbs correctly in sentences

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Helping verbs are the same as main verbs.
A sentence can have only one verb.
Modal auxiliaries change form for tense.

questions.stem: Identify the main verb in the sentence: 'The boy runs fast.'
hints: The main verb is the action word.
What is the boy doing?
questions.explanation: 'Runs' is the main verb because it shows the action.

questions.stem: Identify the helping verb in the sentence: 'She is singing.'
hints: The helping verb comes before the main verb.
'Singing' is the main verb; what helps it?
questions.explanation: 'Is' is the helping verb (primary auxiliary) that helps the main verb 'singing'.

questions.stem: Identify the main verb in the sentence: 'They eat rice.'
hints: The main verb shows the action.
What are they doing with the rice?
questions.explanation: 'Eat' is the main verb because it shows the action.

questions.stem: Which word is a helping verb in the sentence: 'We have finished.'?
hints: The helping verb comes before the main verb.
'Finished' is the main verb; what helps it?
questions.explanation: 'Have' is the helping verb (primary auxiliary) that helps the main verb 'finished'.

questions.stem: Which sentence has BOTH a main verb and a helping verb?
hints: A helping verb helps the main verb.
Look for a sentence with two verbs working together.
questions.explanation: 'He is running' has the helping verb 'is' and the main verb 'running'.
misconceptions: 'He runs' has only a main verb.
'He ran' has only a main verb.

questions.stem: Which word is a modal auxiliary in the sentence: 'You can swim.'?
hints: Modal auxiliaries show ability, permission, obligation, etc.
'Can' shows ability.
questions.explanation: 'Can' is a modal auxiliary showing ability.

questions.stem: What is the helping verb in the sentence: 'The pupils are writing.'?
hints: The helping verb helps the main verb.
'Writing' is the main verb; what helps it?
questions.explanation: 'Are' is the helping verb (primary auxiliary) helping 'writing'.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The teacher gave us homework', what is the main verb?
hints: The main verb shows the action.
What did the teacher do?
questions.explanation: 'Gave' is the main verb because it shows the action.

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence:
hints: After a modal auxiliary, use the base form of the verb.
'Can' is followed by the base verb.
questions.explanation: 'She can sing' is correct because 'can' is followed by the base form 'sing'.

questions.stem: Which word is a primary auxiliary in the sentence: 'He has eaten.'?
hints: Primary auxiliaries include have, has, had, is, am, are, was, were.
'Has' is a primary auxiliary.
questions.explanation: 'Has' is a primary auxiliary helping the main verb 'eaten'.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a modal auxiliary?
hints: Modal auxiliaries include will, can, may, must, should, etc.
'Will' is a modal auxiliary.
questions.explanation: 'I will go' contains the modal auxiliary 'will'.

questions.stem: Identify the modal auxiliary in the sentence: 'We should study hard.'
hints: Modal auxiliaries show obligation, possibility, etc.
'Should' shows obligation.
questions.explanation: 'Should' is the modal auxiliary showing obligation.
