questions.stem: In the sentence 'The children were playing outside', what is the main verb?
hints: The main verb is the action word.
'Were' is a helping verb; what is the action?
questions.explanation: 'Playing' is the main verb; 'were' is the helping verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a helping verb correctly?
hints: After a modal auxiliary, use the base form of the verb.
'Can' is followed by the base verb.
questions.explanation: 'She can dance' is correct because 'can' is followed by the base form 'dance'.

questions.stem: Which sentence has TWO helping verbs?
hints: Look for a sentence with more than one helping verb before the main verb.
'Has' and 'been' are both helping verbs.
questions.explanation: 'She has been working' has two helping verbs: 'has' and 'been'.
misconceptions: 'She is working' has one helping verb.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The work must be done', what are the helping verbs?
hints: There are two helping verbs: one modal and one primary.
'Must' is modal, 'be' is primary.
questions.explanation: Both 'must' (modal auxiliary) and 'be' (primary auxiliary) are helping verbs.

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence:
hints: After a modal auxiliary, use the base form of the verb.
'Might' is followed by the base verb.
questions.explanation: 'He might come later' is correct because 'might' is followed by the base form 'come'.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a main verb, a primary auxiliary AND a modal auxiliary?
hints: Modal auxiliaries include will, can, must. Primary auxiliaries include have, be.
Look for a sentence with three verbs: modal + primary + main.
questions.explanation: 'She will have finished' contains 'will' (modal), 'have' (primary) and 'finished' (main).
misconceptions: 'She will finish' has no primary auxiliary.
'She finishes' has only a main verb.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.5.1: Apply the knowledge of verbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use appropriate subject-verb agreement: Singular/plural

skills.description: Use singular subjects with singular verbs
Use plural subjects with plural verbs
Use collective nouns with singular verbs
Identify and correct subject-verb agreement errors in sentences

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: The verb agrees with the nearest noun
Singular and plural verbs are the same
Subject-verb agreement only matters in writing

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The boy ___ to school every day.'
hints: The subject 'the boy' is singular.
Singular subjects take singular verbs ending in -s.
questions.explanation: The subject 'the boy' is singular, so the correct verb is 'goes'.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'go' because it sounds natural, but 'go' is plural.
Misconception: Using 'going' as a finite verb, but it needs a helping verb.
Misconception: Using 'gone' as present tense, but it is a past participle.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'She ___ a teacher.'
hints: The subject 'she' is singular.
Use 'is' with he, she, it.
questions.explanation: The subject 'she' is singular, so the correct verb is 'is'.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'are' with a singular subject.
Misconception: Using 'be' as a finite verb without a helping verb.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The girls ___ playing in the field.'
hints: The subject 'the girls' is plural.
Plural subjects take plural verbs.
questions.explanation: The subject 'the girls' is plural, so the correct verb is 'are'.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'is' with a plural subject.
Misconception: Using 'be' as a finite verb.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The team ___ playing well today.'
hints: A collective noun like 'team' is treated as singular.
Use a singular verb with collective nouns.
questions.explanation: The collective noun 'team' takes a singular verb, so 'is' is correct.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'are' because the team has many players.
Misconception: Using 'be' as a finite verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
hints: The subject 'the boy' is singular.
Use the singular verb form 'goes'.
questions.explanation: 'The boy goes to school' is correct because the singular subject 'boy' takes the singular verb 'goes'.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'go' with a singular subject.
Misconception: Using 'going' without a helping verb.
Misconception: Using 'gone' as a present tense verb.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The cat ___ on the mat.'
hints: The subject 'the cat' is singular.
Use the singular verb 'sits' for present tense.
questions.explanation: The subject 'the cat' is singular, so the correct verb is 'sits'.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'sit' because it sounds right, but 'sit' is plural.
Misconception: Using 'sitting' without a helping verb.
Misconception: Using 'sat' which is past tense.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'My mother ___ rice every day.'
hints: The subject 'my mother' is singular.
Singular subjects take verbs ending in -s.
questions.explanation: The subject 'my mother' is singular, so the correct verb is 'cooks'.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'cook' because it is the base form.
Misconception: Using 'cooking' without a helping verb.
Misconception: Using 'cooked' which is past tense.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The dogs ___ loudly at night.'
hints: The subject 'the dogs' is plural.
Plural subjects take the base form of the verb.
questions.explanation: The subject 'the dogs' is plural, so the correct verb is 'bark'.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'barking' without a helping verb.
Misconception: Using 'barked' which is past tense.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'We ___ to school every day.'
hints: The subject 'we' is plural.
Plural subjects take the base form of the verb.
questions.explanation: The subject 'we' is plural, so the correct verb is 'walk'.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'walking' without a helping verb.
Misconception: Using 'walked' which is past tense.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The class ___ a new teacher.'
hints: 'Class' is a collective noun and takes a singular verb.
Use 'has' for singular subjects.
questions.explanation: The collective noun 'class' takes the singular verb 'has'.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'have' because the class has many pupils.
Misconception: Using 'having' without a helping verb.
Misconception: Using 'had' which is past tense.

questions.stem: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?
hints: The subject 'the girls' is plural.
Use the plural verb 'are'.
questions.explanation: 'The girls are playing' is correct because the plural subject 'girls' takes the plural verb 'are'.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'is' with a plural subject.
Misconception: Using 'be' as a finite verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
hints: The subject 'she' is singular.
Use 'doesn't' for singular subjects.
questions.explanation: 'She doesn't like fufu' is correct because 'she' is singular and takes 'doesn't'.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'don't' with a singular subject.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'Each of the pupils ___ a book.'
hints: 'Each' is singular, so the verb should be singular.
Use 'has' for singular subjects.
questions.explanation: 'Each' is a singular indefinite pronoun, so the correct verb is 'has'.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'have' because 'pupils' is plural, but the subject is 'each'.
Misconception: Using 'having' without a helping verb.
Misconception: Using 'had' which is past tense.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The children ___ in the park.'
hints: The subject 'the children' is plural.
Plural subjects take the base form of the verb.
questions.explanation: The subject 'the children' is plural, so the correct verb is 'play'.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'playing' without a helping verb.
Misconception: Using 'played' which is past tense.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The flock of birds ___ flying south.'
hints: The subject is 'flock', which is collective and singular.
Use a singular verb with collective nouns.
questions.explanation: The collective noun 'flock' takes the singular verb 'is'.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'are' because 'birds' is plural, but the subject is 'flock'.
Misconception: Using 'were' which is past tense.
Misconception: Using 'be' as a finite verb.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The committee ___ meeting today.'
hints: 'Committee' is a collective noun and takes a singular verb.
Use 'is' for singular subjects.
questions.explanation: The collective noun 'committee' takes the singular verb 'is'.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'are' because the committee has many members.
Misconception: Using 'be' as a finite verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
hints: 'Team' is a collective noun and takes a singular verb.
Use 'is' with singular subjects.
questions.explanation: 'The team is winning' is correct because 'team' is a collective noun taking the singular verb 'is'.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'are' because the team has many players.
Misconception: Using 'be' as a finite verb.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'Either the boys or the girl ___ going to win.'
hints: With 'either...or', the verb agrees with the nearest subject.
The nearest subject is 'the girl' (singular).
questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the nearest subject 'the girl', so the correct verb is 'is'.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'are' because 'boys' is plural, but the verb agrees with the nearest subject.
Misconception: Using 'am' which does not agree with 'girl'.
Misconception: Using 'be' as a finite verb.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The herd of cattle ___ grazing in the field.'
hints: The subject is 'herd', a collective noun, which is singular.
Use a singular verb.
questions.explanation: The collective noun 'herd' takes the singular verb 'is'.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'are' because 'cattle' is plural, but the subject is 'herd'.
Misconception: Using 'were' which is past tense.
Misconception: Using 'be' as a finite verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?
options: Each of the students has a book.
Each of the students have a book.
Each of the students having a book.
Each of the students had a book.
hints: 'Each' is singular, so the verb should be singular.
Use 'has' with singular subjects.
questions.explanation: 'Each of the students has a book' is correct because 'each' is singular and takes 'has'.
misconceptions: Misconception: Using 'have' because 'students' is plural, but the subject is 'each'.
Misconception: Using 'having' without a helping verb.
Misconception: Using 'had' which is past tense (and also singular, but tense is wrong).

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.5.1: Apply the knowledge of verbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use the simple past form of verbs for: Completed actions or events, Regular actions in the past

skills.description: Form the simple past of regular verbs by adding '-d' or '-ed'
Recognise and use the simple past of irregular verbs
Use the simple past to talk about completed actions or events
Use the simple past to talk about regular actions in the past

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: All verbs form their past by adding '-ed'
The simple past is only for regular actions
The simple past and present perfect are the same
You can use the present tense for past events

questions.stem: What is the simple past form of 'walk'?
hints: Regular verbs add '-ed' to form the past.
Walk + ed = walked.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'walk' is 'walked'.

questions.stem: What is the simple past form of 'play'?
hints: Regular verbs add '-ed'.
Play + ed = played.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'play' is 'played'.

questions.stem: What is the simple past form of 'go'?
hints: 'Go' is an irregular verb.
Its past form is 'went'.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'go' is 'went' (irregular).

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the simple past for a completed action?
options: I visit my grandmother every day.
hints: The simple past describes completed actions.
'Visited' shows a completed action.
questions.explanation: 'I visited my grandmother yesterday' uses the simple past 'visited' for a completed action.

questions.stem: What is the simple past form of 'stop'?
hints: Double the final consonant before adding '-ed'.
Stop → stopped.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'stop' is 'stopped' (double the 'p').

questions.stem: What is the simple past form of 'eat'?
hints: 'Eat' is irregular.
Its past form is 'ate'.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'eat' is 'ate'.

questions.stem: What is the simple past form of 'see'?
hints: 'See' is irregular.
Its past form is 'saw'.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'see' is 'saw'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the simple past for a regular action in the past?
options: When I was young, I played football every day.
hints: The simple past can describe repeated actions in the past.
'Played' shows a regular action in the past.
questions.explanation: 'When I was young, I played football every day' uses the simple past 'played' for a regular action in the past.

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence:
hints: 'Yesterday' shows a past time.
Use the simple past with 'yesterday'.
questions.explanation: 'She cooked rice yesterday' correctly uses the simple past with 'yesterday'.

questions.stem: What is the simple past form of 'take'?
hints: 'Take' is irregular.
Its past form is 'took'.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'take' is 'took'.

questions.stem: Which sentence describes a completed action in the past?
hints: The simple past describes completed actions.
'Finished' shows the action is complete.
questions.explanation: 'Kofi finished his homework' describes a completed action in the past.

questions.stem: What is the simple past form of 'cry'?
hints: Change the 'y' to 'i' and add '-ed'.
Cry → cried.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'cry' is 'cried'.

questions.stem: What is the simple past form of 'buy'?
hints: 'Buy' is irregular.
Its past form is 'bought'.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'buy' is 'bought'.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'Every day I went to school and learned new things.' What does this sentence describe?
hints: 'Every day' shows a repeated action.
The simple past 'went' and 'learned' show repeated past actions.
questions.explanation: The sentence describes regular actions in the past because of the repeated action shown by 'every day'.
misconceptions: It is not a single action.

questions.stem: Which sentence is INCORRECT?
options: I goed to the market yesterday.
I went to the market yesterday.
hints: 'Go' is irregular; its past is 'went', not 'goed'.
Which sentence uses a wrong past form?
questions.explanation: 'I goed to the market yesterday' is incorrect because the past of 'go' is 'went'.

questions.stem: What is the simple past form of 'write'?
hints: 'Write' is irregular.
Its past form is 'wrote'.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'write' is 'wrote'.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.5.1: Apply the knowledge of verbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use the simple present form of verbs to relate past events to the present

skills.description: Form the simple present tense correctly (add '-s' or '-es' for third person singular)
Use the simple present to relate past events to the present (e.g. in storytelling)
Use the simple present for habitual actions and general truths

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: The simple present is only for present time
You add '-s' to all verbs in the simple present
The simple present and present continuous are the same
Past events must always use past tense

questions.stem: Choose the correct simple present form: 'She ___ to school every day.'
hints: For third person singular (she), add '-es' to 'go'.
Go → goes.
questions.explanation: The subject 'she' is third person singular, so the correct verb is 'goes'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct simple present form: 'They ___ football every Saturday.'
hints: For plural subjects like 'they', use the base form.
No '-s' is added.
questions.explanation: The subject 'they' is plural, so the correct verb is 'play'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the simple present for a habitual action?
options: I brush my teeth every morning.
I am brushing my teeth now.
I will brush my teeth later.
hints: Habitual actions happen regularly.
'Every morning' signals a habit.
questions.explanation: 'I brush my teeth every morning' uses the simple present for a habitual action.

questions.stem: In storytelling, which sentence correctly uses the simple present to relate a past event?
options: The hero fights the dragon and wins.
The hero fought the dragon and won.
The hero is fighting the dragon.
The hero will fight the dragon.
hints: The simple present can make past events feel immediate in stories.
'Fights' and 'wins' are simple present.
questions.explanation: 'The hero fights the dragon and wins' uses the simple present to relate the past event vividly.

questions.stem: Choose the correct simple present form: 'My mother ___ rice every day.'
hints: The subject 'my mother' is third person singular.
Add '-s' to 'cook' → 'cooks'.
questions.explanation: The subject 'my mother' is singular, so 'cooks' is correct.

questions.stem: Choose the correct simple present form: 'The children ___ in the park every evening.'
hints: The subject 'the children' is plural.
Use the base form 'play'.
questions.explanation: The subject 'the children' is plural, so 'play' is correct.

questions.stem: Which sentence states a general truth using the simple present?
options: The sun rises in the east.
hints: General truths are always true.
'Rises' is simple present for a general truth.
questions.explanation: 'The sun rises in the east' uses the simple present for a general truth.

questions.stem: A storyteller says: 'The tortoise tricks the birds and takes all the food.' What tense is used?
hints: The verbs are 'tricks' and 'takes', which are simple present.
The storyteller uses the present to make the past event vivid.
questions.explanation: The storyteller uses the simple present ('tricks', 'takes') to relate the past event.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the simple present to narrate a past event?
options: The farmer plants seeds and waits for rain.
The farmer planted seeds and waited for rain.
hints: The simple present can narrate past events.
'Plants' and 'waits' are simple present.
questions.explanation: 'The farmer plants seeds and waits for rain' uses the simple present to narrate a past event.

questions.stem: Choose the correct simple present form: 'He ___ his homework every evening.'
hints: 'Do' for third person singular becomes 'does'.
He → does.
questions.explanation: The correct form is 'does' for the subject 'he'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the simple present correctly for a habit?
hints: Habits happen regularly.
'Every morning' shows a habit.
questions.explanation: 'She drinks tea every morning' uses the simple present for a habit.

questions.stem: Why might a writer use the simple present to tell a past event?
options: To make the event feel more immediate and vivid
To show the event happened long ago
hints: The simple present can make past events feel present.
This is common in storytelling.
questions.explanation: A writer uses the simple present to make the past event feel more immediate and vivid.
misconceptions: It does not show long ago; it makes it feel present.
It is not to avoid past tense.

questions.stem: Choose the correct simple present form: 'The class ___ ready for the lesson.'
hints: 'Class' is a collective noun and takes a singular verb.
Use 'is'.
questions.explanation: The collective noun 'class' takes the singular verb 'is'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a correct example of the historical present?
options: The army marches into the city and captures the king.
The army marched into the city and captured the king.
The army is marching into the city.
The army will march into the city.
hints: Historical present uses simple present for past events.
'Marches' and 'captures' are simple present.
questions.explanation: 'The army marches into the city and captures the king' uses the historical present for past events.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.5.1: Apply the knowledge of verbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use the imperative form of the verb to give commands or orders, make suggestions

skills.description: Recognise imperative verbs (base form of the verb used for commands)
Use the imperative to give commands or orders
Use the imperative to make suggestions (e.g. Let's go., Try this.)

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Commands and suggestions are the same

questions.stem: Which sentence is an imperative?
hints: An imperative gives a command or instruction.
It uses the base form of the verb without a subject.
questions.explanation: 'Sit down' is an imperative because it gives a command using the base form of the verb.
misconceptions: Misconception: 'She sits down' is a statement, not a command.
Misconception: 'They sat down' is past tense.
Misconception: 'He is sitting' is present continuous.

questions.stem: Which word is the imperative verb in 'Bring your book'?
hints: The imperative verb is the action word at the start.
It tells you what to do.
questions.explanation: 'Bring' is the imperative verb because it is the command word.
misconceptions: Misconception: There is an imperative verb.

questions.stem: Which imperative gives a command?
hints: A command tells someone to do something.
Which sentence tells someone to do something?
questions.explanation: 'Close the door' is a command using the imperative.
misconceptions: Misconception: 'The door is closed' is a statement.
Misconception: 'She closed the door' is past tense.
Misconception: 'The door will close' is future.

questions.stem: Which sentence makes a suggestion using the imperative?
options: They are going to the park.
hints: A suggestion uses 'let's' or gives gentle advice.
'Let's go' is a suggestion.
questions.explanation: 'Let's go to the park' is a suggestion using the imperative.
misconceptions: Misconception: 'They are going' is present continuous.
Misconception: 'The park is open' is a statement.

questions.stem: Which sentence is NOT an imperative?
hints: An imperative gives a command.
Which sentence is just a statement?
questions.explanation: 'She runs fast' is a statement, not an imperative. The others are commands.

questions.stem: Choose the correct imperative: '___ your hands before eating.'
hints: Imperatives use the base form of the verb.
Wash (base form) is correct.
questions.explanation: The imperative is 'Wash your hands before eating'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the imperative to give a command correctly?
options: He is bringing me the book.
hints: The imperative uses the base form of the verb.
'Bring' is the base form.
questions.explanation: 'Bring me the book' correctly uses the imperative 'bring'.

questions.stem: Which sentence makes a suggestion?
hints: A suggestion uses 'let's' or gives gentle advice.
'Let's try' is a suggestion.
questions.explanation: 'Let's try this exercise' makes a suggestion using the imperative.
misconceptions: Misconception: 'He is trying' is present continuous.

questions.stem: Which of these is a polite imperative?
hints: Adding 'please' makes the imperative polite.
Which sentence includes 'please'?
questions.explanation: 'Please sit down' is a polite imperative because it includes 'please'.
misconceptions: Misconception: 'Sit down!' is a direct command without politeness.
Misconception: 'You must sit down' is not an imperative; it uses 'must'.

questions.stem: How many imperative verbs are in 'Sit down and listen'?
hints: Imperative verbs tell you what to do.
There are two commands joined by 'and'.
questions.explanation: There are two imperative verbs: 'sit' and 'listen'.
misconceptions: Misconception: 'Down' is an adverb, not an imperative verb.
Misconception: Only one imperative verb would miss one.

questions.stem: What makes 'Let's go' different from 'Go!'?
options: 'Let's go' is a suggestion; 'Go!' is a command
'Let's go' is a command; 'Go!' is a suggestion
hints: 'Let's' includes the speaker.
'Go!' is a direct command.
questions.explanation: 'Let's go' is a suggestion including the speaker; 'Go!' is a direct command to someone else.
misconceptions: Misconception: It's the other way round.
Misconception: They are not the same.
Misconception: 'Let's go' is not a question.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses an imperative to give a warning?
options: He watches out for the car.
They watched out for the car.
hints: A warning is a type of command.
Use the imperative 'watch'.
questions.explanation: 'Watch out for the car!' uses the imperative to give a warning.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'Try this exercise again.' Is this a command or a suggestion?
options: A suggestion — it gently advises trying again
hints: A suggestion offers advice gently.
'Try' is used as a gentle suggestion.
questions.explanation: 'Try this exercise again' is a suggestion because it gently advises the listener.
misconceptions: Misconception: It's not a direct command.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the imperative to give a command with a reason?
options: Close the door because it is cold.
hints: The imperative is 'close'.
The reason is 'because it is cold'.
questions.explanation: 'Close the door because it is cold' uses the imperative 'close' with a reason.
misconceptions: Misconception: 'Closing' is not a finite verb.
Misconception: 'The door is closed' is passive.

questions.stem: Which sentence does NOT contain an imperative verb?
options: The teacher speaks to the class.
hints: Imperative verbs give commands.
Which sentence is a statement?
questions.explanation: 'The teacher speaks to the class' is a statement with no imperative verb.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.6.1: Apply the knowledge of different types of adverbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use adverbs of time and place appropriately

skills.description: Recognise adverbs of time and place in sentences
Use adverbs of place correctly to answer 'where?'
Use adverbs of time correctly to answer 'when?'
Place adverbs of time and place correctly in sentences

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Adverbs of time and place are the same
Adverbs can go anywhere in a sentence
Any word ending in '-ly' is an adverb of time/place

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'The cat is here' is an adverb of place?
hints: An adverb of place answers 'where?'.
Where is the cat? It is here.
questions.explanation: 'Here' is an adverb of place because it answers the question 'where?'.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'I will go tomorrow' is an adverb of time?
hints: An adverb of time answers 'when?'.
When will I go? Tomorrow.
questions.explanation: 'Tomorrow' is an adverb of time because it answers the question 'when?'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct adverb of place: 'The children are playing ___.'
hints: Adverbs of place answer 'where?'.
Where are the children playing?
questions.explanation: 'Outside' is an adverb of place because it answers 'where?'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct adverb of time: 'We will eat ___.'
hints: Adverbs of time answer 'when?'.
When will we eat?
questions.explanation: 'Later' is an adverb of time because it answers 'when?'.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'She sang beautifully here yesterday' is an adverb of place?
hints: Adverbs of place answer 'where?'.
Where did she sing? Here.
questions.explanation: 'Here' is the adverb of place. 'Beautifully' is an adverb of manner; 'yesterday' is an adverb of time.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an adverb of place correctly?
options: The book is on the table there.
The book is on the table yesterday.
The book is on the table later.
The book is on the table tomorrow.
hints: Adverbs of place answer 'where?'.
Where is the book? There.
questions.explanation: 'The book is on the table there' uses 'there' correctly as an adverb of place.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an adverb of time correctly?
hints: Adverbs of time answer 'when?'.
When will I see you? Tomorrow.
questions.explanation: 'I will see you tomorrow' uses 'tomorrow' correctly as an adverb of time.

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence:
hints: Adverbs of place usually come after the verb or object.
Adverbs of time can come at the end.
questions.explanation: 'She is here now' uses 'here' (place) and 'now' (time) in natural positions.
misconceptions: The other sentences have awkward adverb placement.

questions.stem: How many adverbs of time and place are in the sentence 'Come here now'?
hints: 'Here' is place; 'now' is time.
Both are adverbs.
questions.explanation: There are two adverbs: 'here' (place) and 'now' (time).

questions.stem: Which sentence places the adverb of time correctly?
options: Yesterday, I went to the market.
I yesterday went to the market.
I went yesterday to the market.
I went to yesterday the market.
hints: Adverbs of time can come at the beginning or end of a sentence.
Yesterday at the beginning is natural.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday, I went to the market' correctly places the adverb of time at the beginning.
misconceptions: The other sentences have awkward or incorrect placement.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an adverb of place to describe a position?
options: The cat is inside the house.
hints: Adverbs of place answer 'where?'.
Where is the cat? Inside.
questions.explanation: 'The cat is inside the house' uses 'inside' as an adverb of place.

questions.stem: Choose the sentence with the correct position of the adverb of place:
hints: Adverbs of place usually come after the verb or object.
Both 'played outside happily' and 'played happily outside' are possible.
questions.explanation: 'The children played outside happily' is a natural placement of the adverb of place.
misconceptions: The other sentences have less natural placement.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'now' as an adverb of time correctly?
hints: 'Now' tells when.
It means at this moment.
questions.explanation: 'I am going now' uses 'now' as an adverb of time.

questions.stem: A pupil writes: 'She here is.' What is wrong with this sentence?
options: The adverb of place 'here' is in the wrong position; it should be 'She is here.'
The sentence needs a question mark.
hints: Adverbs of place usually come after the verb.
'Here' should come after 'is'.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence is 'She is here' because the adverb of place 'here' comes after the verb.
misconceptions: 'She' is correct as a subject pronoun.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'They will arrive soon and wait outside', which words are adverbs?
hints: 'Soon' tells when; 'outside' tells where.
Both are adverbs.
questions.explanation: 'Soon' is an adverb of time and 'outside' is an adverb of place.

indicator.content_standard: B4.3.6.1: Apply the knowledge of different types of adverbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use adverbs of time to modify verbs.

skills.description: Recognise adverbs of time (yesterday, today, tomorrow, now, soon, later, always, never) modifying verbs
Use adverbs of time correctly to modify verbs and show when an action happens
Place adverbs of time correctly in sentences

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Adverbs of time always come at the end of a sentence
Today and tomorrow are the same

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'I will go tomorrow' is an adverb of time?
hints: An adverb of time answers 'when?'.
When will I go? Tomorrow.
questions.explanation: 'Tomorrow' is an adverb of time because it answers 'when?'.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'She came yesterday' is an adverb of time?
hints: An adverb of time tells when.
When did she come? Yesterday.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday' is an adverb of time because it tells when she came.

questions.stem: Choose the correct adverb of time: 'We will eat ___.'
hints: Adverbs of time answer 'when?'.
When will we eat?
questions.explanation: 'Later' is an adverb of time because it answers 'when?'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an adverb of time correctly?
hints: Adverbs of time answer 'when?'.
When will I see you? Tomorrow.
questions.explanation: 'I will see you tomorrow' uses 'tomorrow' correctly as an adverb of time.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'They always play football on Saturdays' is an adverb of time?
hints: An adverb of time tells when or how often.
'Always' tells us how often they play.
questions.explanation: 'Always' is an adverb of time (frequency) modifying the verb 'play'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence:
hints: Adverbs of time can come at the beginning or end of a sentence.
The natural order is subject + verb + object + adverb of time.
questions.explanation: 'I visited my grandmother yesterday' places the adverb of time at the end correctly.
misconceptions: The other sentences have unnatural or incorrect word order.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'now' as an adverb of time correctly?
hints: 'Now' tells when.
It means at this moment.
questions.explanation: 'I am going now' uses 'now' as an adverb of time.

questions.stem: Which sentence places the adverb of time correctly?
options: Tomorrow, we will go to the market.
We tomorrow will go to the market.
We will go tomorrow to the market.
We will go to tomorrow the market.
hints: Adverbs of time can come at the beginning or end of a sentence.
Tomorrow at the beginning is natural.
questions.explanation: 'Tomorrow, we will go to the market' correctly places the adverb of time at the beginning.
misconceptions: The other sentences have awkward or incorrect placement.

questions.stem: How many adverbs of time are in the sentence 'I will see you tomorrow and then we can play later'?
hints: Adverbs of time tell when.
'Tomorrow' and 'later' both tell when.
questions.explanation: There are two adverbs of time: 'tomorrow' and 'later'.
misconceptions: 'Then' is a connector, not an adverb here.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the adverb of time correctly?
hints: Adverbs of frequency like 'always' usually come before the main verb.
'She always arrives' is the natural order.
questions.explanation: 'She always arrives early' correctly places 'always' before the main verb 'arrives'.
misconceptions: The other sentences have awkward placement.

questions.stem: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Yesterday, I went to the market.
I yesterday went to the market.
I went yesterday to the market.
I went to the market yesterday.
hints: Adverbs of time can come at the beginning or end.
Both 'Yesterday, I went to the market' and 'I went to the market yesterday' are correct.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday, I went to the market' is correct. 'I went to the market yesterday' is also correct.
misconceptions: 'I went yesterday to the market' is less natural.

questions.stem: A pupil writes: 'I go to school yesterday.' What is wrong?
options: The verb should be in the past tense: 'I went to school yesterday.'
hints: 'Yesterday' shows past time.
The verb must be in the past tense.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence is 'I went to school yesterday' because 'yesterday' requires a past tense verb.
misconceptions: The sentence needs past tense, not 'will'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the adverb 'never' correctly?
options: I never eat fufu at night.
I eat never fufu at night.
Never I eat fufu at night.
I eat fufu never at night.
hints: Adverbs of frequency like 'never' usually come before the main verb.
'I never eat' is the natural order.
questions.explanation: 'I never eat fufu at night' correctly places 'never' before the main verb 'eat'.
misconceptions: The other sentences have awkward placement.

questions.stem: Which sentence places the adverb of time correctly?
options: We will go to the market tomorrow.
We will go tomorrow to the market.
We tomorrow will go to the market.
Tomorrow we will go to the market.
hints: Adverbs of time usually come at the end or beginning of a sentence.
Both 'We will go to the market tomorrow' and 'Tomorrow we will go to the market' are correct.
questions.explanation: 'We will go to the market tomorrow' is the most natural placement of the adverb of time at the end.
misconceptions: 'We will go tomorrow to the market' is awkward.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses an adverb of time with the present perfect tense?
hints: 'Already' is an adverb of time (frequency).
It usually comes between the helping verb and the main verb.
questions.explanation: 'I have already eaten' correctly places 'already' between the helping verb 'have' and the main verb 'eaten'.
misconceptions: 'I already have eaten' is less natural.
The other sentences have awkward placement.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.7.1: Understand and use idiomatic expressions appropriately in speech and in writing
indicator.objective: Use idiomatic expressions appropriately in communication

skills.description: Recognise idiomatic expressions in sentences
Explain the meaning of common idiomatic expressions
Use idiomatic expressions correctly in sentences to convey meaning
Determine the meaning of an idiom from the context in which it is used

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Idioms mean exactly what the words say
Idioms are only used in spoken English
You can change the words in an idiom

questions.stem: Which of these is an idiom?
hints: An idiom has a meaning different from the literal words.
'Pull someone's leg' means to joke with them, not to actually pull their leg.
questions.explanation: 'To pull someone's leg' is an idiom meaning to joke with someone.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains an idiom?
options: She is feeling under the weather today.
She is standing under the tree.
hints: An idiom has a figurative meaning.
'Under the weather' means feeling sick, not literally under weather.
questions.explanation: 'She is feeling under the weather today' contains the idiom 'under the weather' meaning sick.

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'take after' mean in 'Kofi takes after his father'?
hints: 'Take after' is about similarity.
Kofi looks or behaves like his father.
questions.explanation: 'Take after' means to resemble or look like a family member.
misconceptions: It does not mean to follow.
It does not mean to take away.
It does not mean to run after.

questions.stem: What does 'pull down' mean in 'They tried to pull down the corrupt official'?
hints: 'Pull down' in this context is figurative.
It means to ruin someone's reputation.
questions.explanation: 'Pull down' means to destroy someone's reputation or bring them down.
misconceptions: It does not mean to help.
It does not mean to build.

questions.stem: Read: 'The exam was a piece of cake for Ama because she had studied hard.' What does 'a piece of cake' mean?
hints: Ama had studied hard, so the exam was easy for her.
'A piece of cake' means something easy.
questions.explanation: In this context, 'a piece of cake' means something very easy.
misconceptions: It is not about actual cake.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT an idiom?
options: To let the cat out of the bag
hints: An idiom has a figurative meaning.
'To break a glass' is literal.
questions.explanation: 'To break a glass' is a literal action, not an idiom. The others are idioms.
misconceptions: 'Break the ice' means to start a conversation.
'Let the cat out of the bag' means to reveal a secret.

questions.stem: What does 'hit the books' mean?
hints: It is an idiom about studying.
When exams are near, you hit the books.
questions.explanation: 'Hit the books' means to study hard.
misconceptions: It is not just reading for fun.

questions.stem: Choose the sentence that uses the idiom 'under the weather' correctly.
options: She is feeling under the weather, so she stayed home.
She is standing under the weather.
The weather is under the tree.
She put the weather under the table.
hints: 'Under the weather' means feeling sick.
Which sentence uses it to mean sick?
questions.explanation: 'She is feeling under the weather, so she stayed home' uses the idiom correctly to mean she is sick.
misconceptions: The other sentences use the phrase literally or incorrectly.

questions.stem: Choose the correct idiom to complete the sentence: 'When the teacher asked a difficult question, there was silence. Then Kofi ___ by making a joke.'
hints: The idiom should mean to start a conversation or ease tension.
'Break the ice' means to ease tension.
questions.explanation: 'Broke the ice' is the correct idiom meaning to ease tension or start a conversation.
misconceptions: 'Pulled the leg' means joked with someone, not eased tension.

questions.stem: Read: 'The teacher told the pupils to keep an eye on the cake while it baked.' What does 'keep an eye on' mean?
hints: 'Keep an eye on' is an idiom.
It means to watch something.
questions.explanation: 'Keep an eye on' means to watch or monitor something carefully.
misconceptions: It does not mean to close your eyes.

questions.stem: Which sentence does NOT contain an idiom?
options: He is sitting on the couch.
He let the cat out of the bag.
hints: An idiom has a figurative meaning.
Which sentence is literal?
questions.explanation: 'He is sitting on the couch' is literal. The others are idioms.
misconceptions: 'Let the cat out of the bag' means reveal a secret.

questions.stem: Read: 'The politician's speech was full of empty promises. Many people felt he was just blowing hot air.' What does 'blowing hot air' mean?
options: Talking nonsense or making empty promises
hints: The speech was full of empty promises.
'Blowing hot air' means talking without substance.
questions.explanation: 'Blowing hot air' means talking nonsense or making empty promises.

questions.stem: What does 'see eye to eye' mean?
options: To have the same eye colour
hints: It is about agreement.
When two people see eye to eye, they agree.
questions.explanation: 'See eye to eye' means to agree with someone.
misconceptions: It is not about eye colour.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the idiom 'break a leg' correctly?
options: Before the play, the teacher told the actors to break a leg.
The boy fell and broke a leg.
The table has a broken leg.
hints: 'Break a leg' is an idiom meaning good luck.
It is used before a performance.
questions.explanation: 'Before the play, the teacher told the actors to break a leg' uses the idiom correctly to wish good luck.
misconceptions: The other sentences use 'break a leg' literally.

questions.stem: Read: 'The team was on cloud nine after winning the championship.' What does 'on cloud nine' mean?
hints: Winning the championship is a happy event.
'On cloud nine' means extremely happy.
questions.explanation: 'On cloud nine' means very happy or elated.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.8.1: Apply the knowledge of conjunctions in speech and in writing
indicator.objective: Identify and use simple conjunctions - and, but, or, nor - to link: similar ideas, contrasting ideas, show choices/expressions alternatives

skills.description: Recognise simple conjunctions (and, but, or, nor) in sentences
Use 'and' to link similar ideas or add information
Use 'but' to link contrasting ideas
Use 'or' to show choices/alternatives and 'nor' to link negative alternatives

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: And, but, or, nor are interchangeable
Nor can be used in positive sentences
You can only use one conjunction in a sentence
But means the same as and

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'I bought a pen and a notebook' is a conjunction?
hints: A conjunction joins words or ideas.
Which word connects 'a pen' and 'a notebook'?
questions.explanation: 'And' is a conjunction because it joins 'a pen' and 'a notebook'.

questions.stem: Which word is a conjunction?
hints: Conjunctions join ideas.
Which word can connect two contrasting ideas?
questions.explanation: 'But' is a conjunction.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'I like rice ___ beans.'
hints: Both rice and beans are liked — similar ideas.
Use 'and' to add information.
questions.explanation: 'I like rice and beans' uses 'and' to link similar ideas.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'Esi is tall ___ Ama is short.'
hints: Tall and short are contrasting ideas.
Use 'but' to show contrast.
questions.explanation: 'Esi is tall but Ama is short' uses 'but' to show contrast.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'Would you like tea ___ coffee?'
hints: The question offers a choice.
Use 'or' to show alternatives.
questions.explanation: 'Would you like tea or coffee?' uses 'or' to show a choice.

questions.stem: How many conjunctions are in the sentence 'I want to sing but I cannot, so I will listen or dance'?
hints: Conjunctions join ideas: and, but, or, nor.
'But' and 'or' are conjunctions; 'so' is also a conjunction but not in the target list for this lesson.
questions.explanation: There are two target conjunctions: 'but' and 'or'. ('So' is also a conjunction but not in the list of and, but, or, nor for this indicator.)
misconceptions: There are two of the target conjunctions.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'and' correctly to add information?
hints: 'And' adds similar ideas.
Bread and milk are both items she bought.
questions.explanation: 'She bought bread and milk' uses 'and' correctly to add information.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'but' correctly to show contrast?
options: The food was delicious but expensive.
The food was delicious and expensive.
The food was delicious or expensive.
The food was delicious nor expensive.
hints: Delicious and expensive are contrasting ideas (positive vs. negative).
Use 'but' for contrast.
questions.explanation: 'The food was delicious but expensive' uses 'but' to show contrast.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'or' correctly?
options: You can have mango or orange.
You can have mango and orange.
You can have mango but orange.
You can have mango nor orange.
hints: 'Or' shows a choice between alternatives.
The sentence offers a choice.
questions.explanation: 'You can have mango or orange' uses 'or' correctly to show a choice.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'She neither sings ___ dances.'
hints: 'Neither' is paired with 'nor'.
Use 'nor' in negative alternatives.
questions.explanation: 'She neither sings nor dances' uses 'nor' correctly after 'neither'.

questions.stem: Which sentence does NOT contain a conjunction?
hints: Conjunctions join ideas.
Which sentence has only one idea?
questions.explanation: 'The boy ran fast' has no conjunction. The others contain 'and', 'but' or 'or'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'but' correctly?
options: She is young but very wise.
She is young and very wise.
She is young or very wise.
She is young nor very wise.
hints: Young and wise are contrasting ideas.
Use 'but' for contrast.
questions.explanation: 'She is young but very wise' uses 'but' correctly to contrast age and wisdom.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'I don't like tea nor coffee.' What is wrong?
options: It should be 'or' not 'nor' because 'don't' already makes it negative; 'nor' is used with 'neither'.
hints: In standard English, 'nor' is used with 'neither' or in negative constructions without 'not'.
With 'don't', use 'or'.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence is 'I don't like tea or coffee' because 'don't' already makes it negative; 'nor' is used with 'neither'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'and' to link two independent clauses?
options: I went to the market and I bought some fruit.
I went to the market and bought some fruit.
I went to the market and some fruit.
I went to the market and.
hints: An independent clause has a subject and a verb.
Both parts must be complete ideas.
questions.explanation: 'I went to the market and I bought some fruit' uses 'and' to link two independent clauses.
misconceptions: The third and fourth are incomplete.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'Neither the teacher nor the pupils were happy' is a conjunction?
hints: 'Neither...nor' is a pair of conjunctions.
The second part is 'nor'.
questions.explanation: 'Nor' is the conjunction linking the two negative alternatives.
misconceptions: 'Neither' is also a conjunction but the question asks for the linking word 'nor'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'nor' correctly?
options: She did not eat nor drink.
hints: 'Neither' is paired with 'nor'.
Use 'nor' after 'neither'.
questions.explanation: 'She neither ate nor drank' uses 'nor' correctly with 'neither'.
misconceptions: 'Did not eat nor drink' is nonstandard; use 'or'.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.9.1: Apply the knowledge of modals in speech and in writing
indicator.objective: Use modals to express a variety of meanings

skills.description: Recognise modal verbs (can, may, must, shall, will, could, would, might, should, used to, have to, ought to, need to) in sentences
Use 'can' for ability and 'may' for permission/politeness
Use 'must', 'should', 'have to', 'ought to', 'need to' for obligation and necessity
Use 'might', 'may', 'will', 'shall' for possibility and prediction
Use 'could', 'would' for polite requests

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: All modals mean the same thing
Can and may can be used interchangeably for permission
Must and should mean the same
Would and could are only for past tense

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'She can swim' is a modal verb?
hints: Modal verbs show ability, permission, obligation, etc.
'Can' shows ability.
questions.explanation: 'Can' is a modal verb showing ability.

questions.stem: Which of these is a modal verb?
hints: Modal verbs include can, may, must, will, should, etc.
'Must' is a modal verb.
questions.explanation: 'Must' is a modal verb.

questions.stem: Which modal verb shows ability?
hints: Ability means being able to do something.
'Can' shows ability.
questions.explanation: 'Can' shows ability (e.g. 'I can swim').

questions.stem: Which modal verb shows strong obligation?
hints: Strong obligation means something you have to do.
'Must' shows strong obligation.
questions.explanation: 'Must' shows strong obligation (e.g. 'You must wear a helmet').

questions.stem: Which modal verb is used for a polite request?
hints: Polite requests use 'could' or 'would'.
'Could you help me?' is polite.
questions.explanation: 'Could' is used for polite requests (e.g. 'Could you help me?').

questions.stem: How many modal verbs are in the sentence 'You should study hard and you must pass'?
hints: Modal verbs include should, must, can, may, etc.
Both 'should' and 'must' are modals.
questions.explanation: There are two modal verbs: 'should' and 'must'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct modal: '___ I go out, please?' (asking for permission)
hints: 'May' is used to ask for permission politely.
'May I go out?' is a polite request for permission.
questions.explanation: 'May I go out, please?' uses 'may' correctly to ask for permission.

questions.stem: Choose the correct modal: 'It ___ rain later.' (possibility)
hints: 'Might' shows possibility.
It is not certain, so use 'might'.
questions.explanation: 'It might rain later' uses 'might' to show possibility.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'should' correctly for advice?
options: You should study for your exam.
hints: 'Should' is followed by the base form of the verb.
Use 'study', not 'studying' or 'studied'.
questions.explanation: 'You should study for your exam' uses 'should' + base verb correctly.
misconceptions: The other sentences use incorrect verb forms after 'should'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the most polite request?
options: Could you please pass the salt?
hints: Polite requests use 'could' and 'please'.
Which sentence is the most polite?
questions.explanation: 'Could you please pass the salt?' is the most polite because it uses 'could' and 'please'.

questions.stem: Which modal verb shows a strong prediction?
hints: A strong prediction is more certain.
'Will' shows a strong prediction.
questions.explanation: 'Will' shows a strong prediction (e.g. 'It will rain tomorrow').
misconceptions: 'Might', 'could' and 'may' show possibility, not strong prediction.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'I can to swim.' What is wrong?
options: It should be 'I can swim' because 'can' is followed by the base verb without 'to'.
hints: Modal verbs are followed by the base form of the verb without 'to'.
'Can swim', not 'can to swim'.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence is 'I can swim' because 'can' is followed directly by the base verb.

questions.stem: What is the difference between 'must' and 'should'?
options: 'Must' shows strong obligation; 'should' shows weaker obligation or advice
hints: 'Must' is stronger than 'should'.
'Should' is more like advice.
questions.explanation: 'Must' shows strong obligation, while 'should' shows weaker obligation or advice.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'would' correctly for a polite offer?
hints: 'Would you like...?' is a polite offer.
The question mark is needed.
questions.explanation: 'Would you like some tea?' uses 'would' correctly for a polite offer.
misconceptions: The other sentences are incorrectly punctuated or worded.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'It may rain tomorrow, but I am not sure.' What does 'may' show?
hints: The pupil is not sure.
'May' shows possibility.
questions.explanation: 'May' shows possibility — it might rain, but it is not certain.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a modal verb used for obligation?
hints: Obligation means something you are required to do.
'Must' shows obligation.
questions.explanation: 'You must wear a seatbelt' uses 'must' to show obligation.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.10.1: Apply the knowledge of prepositions in oral and written communication
indicator.objective: Use prepositions to convey a variety of meanings

skills.description: Recognise prepositions in sentences
Use prepositions of position correctly
Use prepositions of direction and time correctly
Use prepositions of purpose and possession correctly
Use prepositions showing support or opposition correctly

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: All prepositions mean the same thing

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'The book is on the table' is a preposition?
hints: A preposition shows position or relationship.
'On' shows where the book is.
questions.explanation: 'On' is a preposition because it shows the position of the book.

questions.stem: Which of these is a preposition?
hints: A preposition shows position or relationship.
'Under' shows position.
questions.explanation: 'Under' is a preposition.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'The clock is ___ the wall.'
hints: Think about where a clock hangs.
A clock is on the wall.
questions.explanation: We say a clock is 'on' the wall because it is attached to the surface.
misconceptions: 'In the wall' would mean inside it.

questions.stem: Which preposition shows direction?
hints: Direction is about movement from one place to another.
'Towards' shows movement in a direction.
questions.explanation: 'Towards' is a preposition of direction.

questions.stem: Which preposition shows purpose in 'I bought a gift for Ama'?
hints: Purpose tells us why something is done.
'For' shows the gift is intended for Ama.
questions.explanation: 'For' shows purpose in this sentence.

questions.stem: How many prepositions are in the sentence 'The cat is under the table near the door'?
hints: Prepositions show position or relationship.
'Under' and 'near' both show position.
questions.explanation: There are two prepositions: 'under' and 'near'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'The bag is ___ the table.' (the table is above the bag)
hints: The table is above the bag, so the bag is below the table.
Use 'under'.
questions.explanation: 'The bag is under the table' shows the bag is below the table.
misconceptions: 'Above' would mean higher than the table.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'He left ___ dawn.'
hints: 'Dawn' is a specific point in time.
Use 'at' with specific times.
questions.explanation: We use 'at' with a specific point in time: 'at dawn'.
misconceptions: 'In' is used with longer periods (in the morning).

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'This gift is ___ Kofi.' (showing possession)
hints: Possession shows who something belongs to.
'For' can show possession or purpose.
questions.explanation: We use 'for' here: 'This gift is for Kofi' (it belongs to/ is meant for him).
misconceptions: 'At', 'in' and 'on' do not show possession here.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'I am ___ you — I will support your idea.'
hints: The sentence says 'I will support your idea'.
Use 'for' to show support.
questions.explanation: 'I am for you' means I support you.
misconceptions: 'With' can mean alongside but 'for' is the preposition of support here.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'They walked ___ the river.' (along the side of the river)
hints: They are walking beside the river.
'Along' means from one end to the other beside something.
questions.explanation: 'Along the river' means walking beside it from one end to another.
misconceptions: 'Across' means from one side to the other.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition for comparison: 'She is taller ___ her brother.'
hints: Comparisons use 'than'.
'Taller than' is the correct phrase.
questions.explanation: We use 'than' in comparisons: 'taller than her brother'.
misconceptions: 'Then' means next or at that time.
'As' is used differently in comparisons (as tall as).

questions.stem: Which sentence uses prepositions of position correctly?
options: The cat is under the table and the dog is beside the chair.
The cat is under table and the dog is beside chair.
The cat under is table and the dog beside is chair.
The cat is table under and the dog is chair beside.
hints: Prepositions come before the noun.
Correct order: preposition + noun.
questions.explanation: 'The cat is under the table and the dog is beside the chair' uses prepositions of position correctly.
misconceptions: The other sentences have incorrect preposition placement or missing articles.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'We waited ___ two hours.'
hints: 'Two hours' is a period of time.
Use 'for' with a period of time.
questions.explanation: 'For two hours' shows a period of time.
misconceptions: 'Since' is used with a starting point.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'The shirt is ___ Kofi.' (the shirt belongs to Kofi)
hints: Possession shows who owns something.
Use 'for' to show belonging.
questions.explanation: 'The shirt is for Kofi' shows possession in this context.
misconceptions: 'At', 'with' and 'by' do not express possession in this way.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'I am against the plan.' What does 'against' show?
hints: 'Against' is the opposite of 'for'.
It shows disagreement.
questions.explanation: 'Against' shows opposition to the plan.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'for' and 'against' correctly to show support and opposition?
options: Many people are for the new rule, but some are against it.
Many people are against the new rule, but some are for it — this is also correct.
Both sentences A and B are correct usages of 'for' and 'against'.
hints: 'For' shows support; 'against' shows opposition.
Both A and B correctly use the prepositions.
questions.explanation: Both sentences correctly use 'for' to show support and 'against' to show opposition. The order does not matter.
misconceptions: Only one is correct — actually both are.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.4.2.1: Copy and rewrite sentences correctly
indicator.objective: Write clearly using joined letters of consistent size

skills.description: Recognise and form joined letters (cursive style) with consistent size and spacing
Identify letters of consistent size and shape in handwriting
Copy sentences and passages clearly using joined letters of consistent size

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Letter size doesn't matter in handwriting
Any handwriting is acceptable as long as it's readable

questions.stem: What does 'joined letters' mean in handwriting?
options: Letters connected smoothly to each other
Letters written in capital letters only
hints: Joined letters are connected.
It is also called cursive writing.
questions.explanation: Joined letters means letters are connected smoothly to each other in handwriting.
misconceptions: Separate letters are print, not joined.
Capital letters can be joined too.
Speed is not the same as joining.

questions.stem: Which of these is a joined letter pair?
hints: Joined letters are connected.
Look for letters written together without lifting the pen.
questions.explanation: 'At' written together is a joined letter pair because the letters are connected.
misconceptions: Capital letters are not the focus here.
A single letter is not a pair.

questions.stem: Why is it important to keep letters the same size in handwriting?
options: It makes the writing clear and easy to read
hints: Consistent size helps readability.
When letters are the same size, it is easier to read.
questions.explanation: Keeping letters the same size makes the writing clear and easy to read.
misconceptions: Speed is not the main reason.
Prettiness is not the main goal.

questions.stem: Which handwriting sample shows consistent letter size?
options: All letters are the same height
Some letters are very big and some are very small
The writing goes up and down
The letters are all different sizes
hints: Consistent means the same.
Look for letters of the same height.
questions.explanation: Consistent letter size means all letters are the same height.
misconceptions: Big and small letters mixed is not consistent.
Writing that goes up and down is not consistent.

questions.stem: Which word is written with joined letters?
hints: Joined letters are connected.
Look for the cursive version.
questions.explanation: 'And' written in cursive is joined.
misconceptions: All capitals are not cursive joined letters in the same way.

questions.stem: A pupil's handwriting has letters of different sizes and heights. What should they work on?
hints: The problem is inconsistent size.
The solution is to keep letters the same size.
questions.explanation: The pupil should work on keeping letters the same size for clearer handwriting.

questions.stem: What does 'consistent size' mean in handwriting?
options: All letters are the same height and width
Some letters are big and some are small
hints: Consistent means the same throughout.
All letters should be the same size.
questions.explanation: Consistent size means all letters are the same height and width.
misconceptions: Very large is not the same as consistent.
Very small is not the same as consistent.

questions.stem: Why is joined handwriting useful?
options: It can be faster and smoother to write
It is the only way to write
It is easier to read than print
hints: Joined handwriting flows smoothly.
It can help you write faster.
questions.explanation: Joined handwriting is useful because it can be faster and smoother to write.
misconceptions: Some find print easier to read.

questions.stem: Which word shows consistent joined writing?
options: k e t t l e (all separate)
hints: Consistent joined writing means all letters are connected and even.
Look for the word written in cursive.
questions.explanation: 'Kettle' written with all letters joined evenly shows consistent joined writing.

questions.stem: A pupil writes: 'The cat sat on the mat.' The 'T' is very big and the 'h' is very small. What should they fix?
options: Make the letters the same size
Make the 'T' smaller and the 'h' bigger to match
hints: The letters are not the same size.
The solution is to make them consistent.
questions.explanation: The pupil should make the letters the same size so the handwriting is consistent.
misconceptions: Writing in capitals is not the solution.

questions.stem: Which stage of joined handwriting involves writing letters with a flick?
hints: The stages go from simple to complex.
The first stage is writing individual letters with a flick.
questions.explanation: Stage 1 involves writing letters with a flick (e.g. a, t, m, n, w, d).

questions.stem: Which sentence is written most clearly with consistent letters?
options: The boy is happy. (all letters even and neat)
The B o y is h a p p y. (mixed sizes)
The boy is happy (no full stop)
hints: Consistent writing is neat and even.
Look for the sentence with even letters.
questions.explanation: 'The boy is happy.' with all letters even and neat is the clearest.
misconceptions: All capitals are not the focus.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of stages for learning joined handwriting?
options: Write letters with a flick → join pairs → join whole words → copy sentences
Copy sentences → join pairs → write letters → join words
Join words → write letters → copy sentences → join pairs
Write letters → copy sentences → join words → join pairs
hints: Start simple and build up.
First letters, then pairs, then words, then sentences.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: write letters with a flick → join pairs → join whole words → copy sentences.
misconceptions: The other orders start with too much complexity.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.4.2.1: Copy and rewrite sentences correctly
indicator.objective: Use simple sentences clearly and correctly

skills.description: Use capital letters correctly for proper nouns and at the beginning of sentences
Use full stops, question marks and commas correctly in simple sentences
Write simple sentences clearly and correctly

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Only the first word of a sentence needs a capital letter
A comma is the same as a full stop
Question marks go at the beginning of questions
Punctuation doesn't matter in simple sentences

questions.stem: Which word should start with a capital letter in the sentence 'esi went to accra'?
hints: Proper nouns (names of people and places) start with capital letters.
Both 'Esi' and 'Accra' are proper nouns.
questions.explanation: Both 'Esi' (a person's name) and 'Accra' (a place name) should start with capital letters: 'Esi went to Accra.'
misconceptions: Only one proper noun would be capitalised.
'Went' is a verb and does not need a capital.

questions.stem: Which punctuation mark should end this sentence: 'What is your name'
hints: The sentence asks a question.
Questions end with a question mark.
questions.explanation: 'What is your name?' is a question, so it ends with a question mark.
misconceptions: A full stop is for statements.
A comma is not used at the end.
An exclamation mark is for strong feelings.

questions.stem: Which punctuation mark should end this sentence: 'I bought a pencil'
hints: The sentence is a statement.
Statements end with a full stop.
questions.explanation: 'I bought a pencil.' is a statement, so it ends with a full stop.
misconceptions: A question mark is for questions.
A comma is not used at the end.
An exclamation mark is for strong feelings.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a comma correctly?
options: I bought a pencil, a ruler and a book.
I bought a pencil a ruler and a book.
I bought, a pencil a ruler and a book.
I bought a pencil a ruler, and a book.
hints: A comma separates items in a list.
The comma should come between the listed items.
questions.explanation: 'I bought a pencil, a ruler and a book' uses a comma correctly to separate items in a list.
misconceptions: The other sentences either lack or misplace the comma.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
hints: The sentence asks a question.
Use a question mark.
questions.explanation: 'Where is my book?' is correctly punctuated with a question mark.
misconceptions: A full stop is for statements.
A comma is not used at the end.
An exclamation mark is for strong feelings.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'We visited cape coast castle' needs a capital letter?
hints: Proper nouns for specific places need capital letters.
Cape Coast Castle is a specific place name.
questions.explanation: 'Cape Coast Castle' is a proper noun, so each word should start with a capital letter.

questions.stem: A pupil writes: 'I like mangoes and I like oranges'. What punctuation is missing?
options: A full stop at the end
A question mark at the end
hints: The sentence is a statement.
Statements end with a full stop.
questions.explanation: The sentence needs a full stop at the end: 'I like mangoes and I like oranges.'
misconceptions: A comma after 'mangoes' is optional and not required.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.4.6.1: Develop, organise and express ideas cohesively in writing for a variety of purposes, audience, and contexts
indicator.objective: Choose appropriate ways and modes of writing for a variety of purposes, audiences, and contexts, and organise facts, ideas and/or points of view in a way appropriate to the mode of delivery, using appropriate text features

skills.description: Recognise different modes of writing (expository, narrative, descriptive, argumentative) from short text samples
Identify the purpose and audience of a given text
Recognise how facts, ideas or points of view are organised in a paragraph
Choose the appropriate mode of writing for a given purpose, audience and context

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: All writing has the same purpose
Mode and purpose are the same thing
Audience doesn't affect how you write
Any organisation of ideas is fine
Descriptive writing and narrative writing are the same

questions.stem: Which of these is a narrative text?
options: A story about a girl who lost her book
hints: Narrative texts tell a story.
Which option tells a story about events?
questions.explanation: A story about a girl who lost her book is a narrative text because it tells a story.
misconceptions: A recipe is expository (how to do something).
A letter is a form of communication, not necessarily narrative.
A poster is persuasive or informative.

questions.stem: Which of these is a descriptive text?
options: A paragraph describing the sights and sounds of a market
An argument for more break time
hints: Descriptive texts paint a picture with words.
Which option describes what something looks, sounds or feels like?
questions.explanation: A paragraph describing the sights and sounds of a market is descriptive because it describes sensory details.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a text that tells a story?
hints: Stories are told to narrate events.
The purpose of a story is to narrate.
questions.explanation: The purpose of a story is to narrate — to tell about events.

questions.stem: Who is the likely audience for a letter to a friend?
hints: A letter to a friend is personal.
The audience is the friend.
questions.explanation: The audience for a letter to a friend is the friend.
misconceptions: A headteacher would receive a formal letter.
The general public receives public notices.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the main idea of this paragraph: 'The market was busy. Traders called out prices. Women bought vegetables. Children ran around.'
hints: The main idea tells what the whole paragraph is about.
The first sentence states the main idea.
questions.explanation: The main idea is 'The market was busy'. The other sentences are supporting details.
misconceptions: Traders calling prices is a detail.
Women buying vegetables is a detail.

questions.stem: You want to explain how to plant a tree. Which mode of writing is most appropriate?
hints: Expository writing explains how to do something.
Planting a tree is a process to explain.
questions.explanation: Expository writing is most appropriate because it explains a process step by step.

questions.stem: Which text is an example of expository writing?
options: A text explaining how rain is formed
A story about a lion and a mouse
A letter to a friend about a holiday
hints: Expository writing explains or informs.
Which text explains a process?
questions.explanation: A text explaining how rain is formed is expository because it explains a process.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of an argumentative text?
options: To persuade the reader to accept a point of view
hints: Argumentative texts argue a point.
The purpose is to persuade.
questions.explanation: The purpose of an argumentative text is to persuade the reader to accept a point of view.

questions.stem: In a well-organised paragraph, what should come first?
options: The main idea or topic sentence
hints: A paragraph usually begins with its main idea.
The topic sentence introduces the paragraph.
questions.explanation: A well-organised paragraph usually begins with the main idea or topic sentence.
misconceptions: Supporting details come after the main idea.
A conclusion comes at the end.

questions.stem: You are writing to the headteacher to ask for a new library. Which mode is best?
hints: You want to convince the headteacher.
Argumentative writing persuades.
questions.explanation: Argumentative writing is best because you are trying to persuade the headteacher to agree with your request.

questions.stem: Which of these is a persuasive text?
options: A speech urging pupils to stop littering
A story about a market day
A description of a beautiful beach
hints: Persuasive texts try to convince you to do something.
The speech urges action.
questions.explanation: A speech urging pupils to stop littering is persuasive because it tries to convince them to change behaviour.

questions.stem: A notice about a school football match is written for whom?
hints: A school notice targets the school community.
Pupils and parents are the main audience.
questions.explanation: A school football match notice is written for pupils and parents.
misconceptions: The President is not the audience for a school notice.
The Ministry is not the audience.
The general public is too broad.

questions.stem: Which arrangement of sentences makes a coherent paragraph? (1) The boy woke up late. (2) He missed the bus. (3) He ran to school. (4) He arrived late.
hints: Events should be in chronological order.
Waking up late causes missing the bus.
questions.explanation: The logical order is: (1) woke up late, (2) missed the bus, (3) ran to school, (4) arrived late.
misconceptions: Starting with missing the bus skips the cause.
The reversed order does not make sense.

questions.stem: You are writing for young children about healthy eating. Which mode and approach is best?
hints: Young children need simple, engaging language.
Descriptive with colourful examples works well.
questions.explanation: Descriptive writing with simple, colourful examples is best for young children because it engages their senses and is easy to understand.
misconceptions: A long story may lose their attention.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between descriptive and narrative writing?
options: Descriptive writing paints a picture; narrative tells a story
hints: Descriptive focuses on describing; narrative focuses on events.
One creates a picture, the other tells a story.
questions.explanation: Descriptive writing paints a picture using sensory details, while narrative writing tells a story with events and characters.
misconceptions: Length is not the key difference.

questions.stem: A text explains the process of making kente cloth. What is its purpose?
hints: Explaining a process is informing.
The text gives information about how kente is made.
questions.explanation: The purpose is to inform because the text explains how kente cloth is made.

questions.stem: Which sentence does NOT belong in a paragraph about the importance of trees?
hints: The paragraph is about importance.
Which sentence is about a fun activity rather than importance?
questions.explanation: 'Trees can be climbed' is about a fun activity, not about why trees are important.
misconceptions: Cleaning the air is a benefit.

questions.stem: You are asked to write a text that convinces the community to stop burning bush. Which mode and audience consideration is most important?
options: Argumentative mode; focus on consequences and solutions
Narrative mode; tell a story about a bush fire
Expository mode; explain how bush fires start
hints: You want to convince people to change behaviour.
Argumentative writing persuades with reasons and evidence.
questions.explanation: Argumentative mode is best because it persuades by presenting consequences and solutions.
misconceptions: Narrative may entertain but not persuade.
Descriptive describes but does not argue.
Expository informs but does not necessarily persuade.

questions.stem: Given a paragraph with mixed-up sentences, which is the best order? (1) Finally, they arrived at the zoo. (2) The children were excited. (3) They saw many animals. (4) They boarded the bus early. (5) They had lunch.
hints: Start with boarding the bus.
Arriving at the zoo comes after the bus ride.
questions.explanation: The logical order is: (4) boarded bus, (2) children excited, (1) arrived at zoo, (3) saw animals, (5) had lunch.
misconceptions: Starting with excitement skips the bus ride.
Arriving first is out of order.

questions.stem: A pupil writes: 'I think we should have more breaks at school.' For this to be persuasive, what should the writer include?
options: Reasons and evidence to support the claim
A story about a break time
A list of break time activities
hints: Persuasive writing needs reasons and evidence.
The writer must support the opinion.
