options: Because libraries provide access to knowledge, every school should have one.
Every school should have a library.
hints: A clause can explain the reason clearly.
The first sentence uses 'Because libraries provide access to knowledge' as a clause.
questions.explanation: The first sentence uses a clause to clarify why every school should have a library.
misconceptions: The other sentences do not use clauses to clarify the relationship.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses 'for example' to support a claim?
options: Reading is important; for example, pupils who read more do better in school.
Reading is important; for example, I like reading.
Reading is important; for example, books are made of paper.
Reading is important; for example, the sky is blue.
hints: 'For example' should introduce a relevant example.
The example should support the claim about reading.
questions.explanation: 'Reading is important; for example, pupils who read more do better in school' uses 'for example' to introduce a relevant supporting example.
misconceptions: The other examples are not relevant to the claim.

questions.stem: A pupil writes: 'We should not waste water. It is important.' How can the pupil strengthen the relationship between claim and reason?
options: Add a linking word: 'We should not waste water because it is important for life.'
hints: A linking word clarifies the relationship.
Use 'because' to link the claim and reason.
questions.explanation: Adding 'because' clarifies that 'it is important for life' is the reason for not wasting water.
misconceptions: Removing the reason weakens the argument.
Changing the topic avoids the argument.

questions.stem: Which sentence best clarifies the relationship between claim and reason using a clause?
options: Since malaria is spread by mosquitoes, we should sleep under mosquito nets.
Malaria is bad. Sleep under nets.
hints: A clause explains the reason clearly.
The first sentence uses 'Since malaria is spread by mosquitoes' as a clause.
questions.explanation: The first sentence uses a clause to clearly link the reason to the claim.
misconceptions: The other sentences do not clarify the relationship.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.4.13.2: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence
indicator.objective: Establish and maintain a formal style

skills.description: Recognise formal style features in an argument (no slang, complete sentences, objective tone)
Distinguish between formal and informal language in argumentative writing
Use formal language to establish and maintain a formal style in an argument

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Slang is acceptable in formal writing

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a formal style?
options: The pupils should complete their homework daily.
The pupils gotta do their homework.
Pupils should do homework and stuff.
hints: Formal style uses complete, standard sentences.
Which sentence avoids slang and slang-like words?
questions.explanation: 'The pupils should complete their homework daily' is formal because it uses standard, complete language.

questions.stem: Which of these is a feature of formal style?
hints: Formal style follows the rules of standard English.
Complete sentences are a feature of formal writing.
questions.explanation: Formal style uses complete sentences and standard grammar.

questions.stem: Which sentence is more formal?
options: I believe that pupils should have more break time.
I reckon pupils should get more break.
Pupils should get more break, yeah?
hints: Formal style uses standard, complete language.
Which sentence sounds most like a written argument?
questions.explanation: 'I believe that pupils should have more break time' is more formal because it uses complete, standard English.

questions.stem: Which word should replace 'gonna' in a formal argument?
hints: Formal style avoids slang and shortened words.
'Gonna' is short for 'going to'.
questions.explanation: In formal writing, 'gonna' should be replaced with 'going to'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is written in a formal style?
options: We must protect our environment for future generations.
We gotta save the earth, man.
hints: Formal style is clear and serious.
Which sentence uses standard, complete language?
questions.explanation: 'We must protect our environment for future generations' is formal because it uses standard language and a serious tone.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses informal language?
options: The experiment produced a clear result.
hints: Informal language is casual and conversational.
'Totally awesome' is informal.
questions.explanation: 'The experiment was totally awesome!' uses informal language ('totally awesome').

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a formal register?
options: The committee has decided to postpone the meeting.
The committee's like, not meeting today.
hints: Formal register uses standard, complete sentences.
Which sentence sounds like an official announcement?
questions.explanation: 'The committee has decided to postpone the meeting' is formal because it uses standard, official language.

questions.stem: Which sentence maintains a formal style?
options: Pupils should not use mobile phones during lessons.
Pupils shouldn't use phones in class and stuff.
Kids shouldn't be on their phones in class.
hints: Formal style avoids contractions and slang.
Which sentence uses complete, standard words?
questions.explanation: 'Pupils should not use mobile phones during lessons' is formal because it avoids contractions and slang.

questions.stem: Which sentence does NOT use a formal style?
hints: Formal style avoids casual words like 'really' and 'cool'.
Which sentence uses informal words?
questions.explanation: 'The results were really cool' uses informal language ('really cool').

questions.stem: Choose the most formal version of this sentence: 'Kids shouldn't eat too much sugar.'
options: Children should not consume excessive sugar.
Kids shouldn't eat too much sugar.
Children shouldn't eat lots of sugar.
Kids should not eat too much sugar.
hints: Formal style uses precise words and avoids contractions.
'Consume excessive sugar' is more formal than 'eat too much sugar'.
questions.explanation: 'Children should not consume excessive sugar' is the most formal version.

questions.stem: Which sentence is more appropriate for a formal letter to the headteacher?
options: I am writing to request permission to be absent from school.
hints: Formal letters use polite, complete language.
Which sentence sounds most respectful?
questions.explanation: 'I am writing to request permission to be absent from school' is appropriate for a formal letter.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses formal language correctly?
options: The pupils were instructed to complete the assignment.
The pupils were told to do the assignment and stuff.
The kids had to do the homework.
The pupils gotta finish their work.
hints: Formal style uses precise, standard language.
'Instructed' and 'assignment' are formal words.
questions.explanation: 'The pupils were instructed to complete the assignment' uses formal language correctly.

questions.stem: Which sentence maintains a formal style throughout?
options: The school should provide more books because pupils need reading materials.
The school should give us more books 'cause we need stuff to read.
The school gotta give more books, right?
We need more books and things, yeah?
hints: Formal style uses complete words and standard grammar.
Which sentence avoids slang and contractions?
questions.explanation: 'The school should provide more books because pupils need reading materials' maintains a formal style throughout.

questions.stem: A pupil is writing an argument about why school should start later. Which sentence is most appropriate for a formal argument?
options: Research indicates that later start times improve pupils' concentration.
I think starting later is way better.
School should start later 'cause everyone's tired.
hints: Formal arguments use evidence and standard language.
Which sentence sounds like a formal argument with evidence?
questions.explanation: 'Research indicates that later start times improve pupils' concentration' is most appropriate for a formal argument.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a formal style and avoids contractions?
options: The pupils cannot complete the task without assistance.
The pupils can't complete the task without help.
The pupils can't do it alone.
The kids can't finish the task.
hints: Formal style avoids contractions like 'can't'.
Which sentence uses 'cannot' instead of 'can't'?
questions.explanation: 'The pupils cannot complete the task without assistance' uses a formal style and avoids contractions.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.4.13.2: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence
indicator.objective: Provide a concluding statement that follows from argument presented

skills.description: Recognise a concluding statement in an argument
Choose a concluding statement that logically follows from the argument presented
Restate the claim or summarise the argument in a conclusion

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: A conclusion introduces a new argument
A conclusion is just a repeat of the introduction
A conclusion can contradict the argument

questions.stem: What is a concluding statement in an argument?
options: A sentence that wraps up the argument and restates the claim
A sentence that introduces a new topic
The first sentence of the argument
A sentence that asks a question
hints: A conclusion comes at the end.
It wraps up the argument.
questions.explanation: A concluding statement wraps up the argument and restates the claim.
misconceptions: It does not introduce a new topic.
It is not the first sentence.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a concluding statement?
options: Therefore, we should all work together to keep our school clean.
First, I will explain why cleanliness matters.
Some pupils throw rubbish on the floor.
hints: A conclusion often starts with 'Therefore' or 'In conclusion'.
Which sentence wraps up the argument?
questions.explanation: 'Therefore, we should all work together to keep our school clean' is a concluding statement.
misconceptions: The other sentences are introductory or supporting.

questions.stem: Argument: 'Reading is important because it improves vocabulary and helps pupils do better in school.' Which conclusion follows from this argument?
options: Therefore, every pupil should read regularly.
hints: A conclusion should follow logically from the reasons given.
If reading is important, what should pupils do?
questions.explanation: 'Therefore, every pupil should read regularly' follows logically from the argument.
misconceptions: The other conclusions contradict the argument.

questions.stem: Argument: 'We should not waste water because many communities lack clean water.' Which conclusion follows?
options: Therefore, we should use water wisely.
Therefore, we should waste more water.
Therefore, we should ignore the problem.
hints: The conclusion should match the argument's message.
If communities lack water, what should we do?
questions.explanation: 'Therefore, we should use water wisely' follows logically from the argument.
misconceptions: The other conclusions contradict the argument.

questions.stem: What should a conclusion restate?
options: The main claim of the argument
hints: A conclusion reminds the reader of the main point.
It restates the claim.
questions.explanation: A conclusion should restate the main claim of the argument.
misconceptions: It does not introduce a new topic.
It does not give a random fact.

questions.stem: Read this argument: 'Trees are important. They give us oxygen and shade. They provide fruits and medicine. Therefore, we should plant and protect trees.' Which sentence is the conclusion?
options: Therefore, we should plant and protect trees.
They give us oxygen and shade.
hints: The conclusion often starts with 'Therefore'.
It is the last sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Therefore, we should plant and protect trees' is the conclusion.
misconceptions: The first sentence is the claim.

questions.stem: Which sentence is NOT a concluding statement?
options: First, let us look at the reasons for planting trees.
In conclusion, trees are essential for life.
Therefore, we must protect our trees.
So, everyone should plant a tree.
hints: A conclusion comes at the end and wraps up.
Which sentence introduces the argument instead?
questions.explanation: 'First, let us look at the reasons for planting trees' is an introduction, not a conclusion.
misconceptions: The other sentences are concluding statements.

questions.stem: Argument: 'Pupils should eat breakfast every day because it gives them energy for school.' Which conclusion follows?
options: Therefore, pupils should not skip breakfast.
hints: The conclusion should follow from the reason given.
If breakfast gives energy, what should pupils do?
questions.explanation: 'Therefore, pupils should not skip breakfast' follows logically from the argument.
misconceptions: The other conclusions contradict the argument.

questions.stem: Which sentence best restates this claim in a conclusion: 'We should keep our school clean.'
options: In conclusion, a clean school is important for everyone.
In conclusion, the school is big.
In conclusion, we have many pupils.
hints: The conclusion should restate the idea of cleanliness.
Which sentence is about keeping the school clean?
questions.explanation: 'In conclusion, a clean school is important for everyone' restates the claim about cleanliness.
misconceptions: The other sentences are unrelated to the claim.

questions.stem: Argument: 'Mobile phones distract pupils in class because they play games instead of listening.' Which conclusion follows?
options: Therefore, pupils should not use phones during lessons.
Therefore, pupils should use phones more often.
Therefore, phones are not a problem.
Therefore, pupils should play more games.
hints: The argument says phones distract pupils.
What is the logical conclusion?
questions.explanation: 'Therefore, pupils should not use phones during lessons' follows logically from the argument.
misconceptions: The other conclusions contradict the argument.

questions.stem: Which conclusion best summarises this argument: 'Exercise is good for the body. It strengthens the heart and muscles. It helps us maintain a healthy weight. It also makes us feel happy.'
options: Therefore, we should exercise regularly to stay healthy and happy.
Therefore, exercise is only for athletes.
Therefore, exercise is a waste of time.
hints: The conclusion should summarise all the benefits mentioned.
Which sentence captures the overall message?
questions.explanation: 'Therefore, we should exercise regularly to stay healthy and happy' summarises the argument.
misconceptions: The other conclusions contradict the argument.

questions.stem: Argument: 'The school library should have more books because pupils have read all the current ones and need new material for their studies.' Which conclusion follows?
options: Therefore, more books should be added to the school library.
Therefore, the library should be closed.
hints: The reason given is that pupils need new books.
What is the logical conclusion?
questions.explanation: 'Therefore, more books should be added to the school library' follows logically.
misconceptions: The other conclusions contradict the argument.

questions.stem: Which sentence best restates this claim: 'Every school should have a library'?
options: In conclusion, all schools should provide a library for their pupils.
In conclusion, some schools have libraries.
In conclusion, the library is a building.
hints: The conclusion should restate the original claim.
Which sentence is closest to 'Every school should have a library'?
questions.explanation: 'In conclusion, all schools should provide a library for their pupils' restates the claim.
misconceptions: The other sentences are facts or opinions, not restatements of the claim.

questions.stem: A pupil writes: 'Trees are important. They give us oxygen, shade, fruits and medicine.' What would be the BEST concluding sentence?
options: Therefore, we should plant and protect trees.
hints: The conclusion should follow from the reasons given.
If trees give us so many things, what should we do?
questions.explanation: 'Therefore, we should plant and protect trees' best concludes the argument.
misconceptions: The other sentences are just facts about trees, not conclusions.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the best conclusion for an argument that says 'We should not waste water'?
options: In conclusion, using water wisely is important for everyone.
In conclusion, the tap is running.
hints: The conclusion should restate the idea of not wasting water.
Which sentence summarises the argument?
questions.explanation: 'In conclusion, using water wisely is important for everyone' restates the argument's message.
misconceptions: The other sentences are unrelated or trivial.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.4.14.1: Write informative essays
indicator.objective: Write words giving information about family

skills.description: Identify and use words related to family members (mother, father, sister, brother, aunt, uncle, grandparents)
Write sentences giving information about family members (name, age, occupation, appearance, character)
Write informative sentences about oneself and one's family

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: You can write about family without details
Informative writing is the same as storytelling

questions.stem: Which word names a family member?
hints: A family member is a person related to you.
Which word names a person in your family?
questions.explanation: 'Sister' names a family member.

questions.stem: Which word names the father of your father?
hints: Your father's father is your...
It starts with 'grand'.
questions.explanation: Your father's father is your grandfather.
misconceptions: An uncle is your parent's brother.
A brother is a male sibling.
A cousin is a child of your aunt or uncle.

questions.stem: Which word names the daughter of your aunt?
hints: Your aunt's daughter is your...
It starts with 'c'.
questions.explanation: Your aunt's daughter is your cousin.
misconceptions: A sister shares the same parents.
A niece is your sibling's daughter.
An aunt is your parent's sister.

questions.stem: Which sentence gives information about a family member?
hints: An informative sentence tells us something specific.
Which sentence tells us what the mother does?
questions.explanation: 'My mother is a teacher' gives information about her occupation.
misconceptions: 'Mother is a word' is a definition.
'I have a mother' is too general.

questions.stem: Which sentence gives information about yourself?
hints: An informative sentence has a subject and a verb and gives a fact.
Which sentence tells us your class?
questions.explanation: 'I am in Basic 4' gives information about your class.

questions.stem: Which sentence gives the most information about a family member?
options: My father is tall and works as a farmer.
hints: The most informative sentence gives details like appearance and occupation.
Which sentence tells us what the father looks like and does?
questions.explanation: 'My father is tall and works as a farmer' gives information about his appearance and occupation.
misconceptions: The other sentences are too general.

questions.stem: Which sentence gives information about a family member's age?
options: My sister is ten years old.
hints: Age tells us how old someone is.
Which sentence mentions a number of years?
questions.explanation: 'My sister is ten years old' gives information about her age.

questions.stem: Which sentence gives information about a family member's character?
options: My brother is very kind and helpful.
hints: Character is about personality.
Which sentence describes how the brother behaves?
questions.explanation: 'My brother is very kind and helpful' gives information about his character.

questions.stem: Which is the best informative sentence about your family?
options: There are five people in my family.
hints: An informative sentence gives a specific fact.
Which sentence gives a number?
questions.explanation: 'There are five people in my family' gives specific information about the size of the family.
misconceptions: The other sentences are general or opinions.

questions.stem: Which sentence tells us where a family member works?
options: My mother works at the hospital.
hints: Workplace tells us where someone works.
Which sentence mentions a workplace?
questions.explanation: 'My mother works at the hospital' gives information about her workplace.

questions.stem: Which word does NOT name a family member?
hints: A teacher is a school worker, not necessarily a relative.
The other words are family relationships.
questions.explanation: 'Teacher' is not a family word (unless the teacher is also a relative). 'Aunt', 'cousin' and 'uncle' are family words.

questions.stem: Read this information: 'My sister's name is Ama. She is twelve years old. She is tall and has long hair. She likes reading.' Which sentence gives information about her appearance?
options: She is tall and has long hair.
hints: Appearance is about how someone looks.
Which sentence describes how she looks?
questions.explanation: 'She is tall and has long hair' gives information about her appearance.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the most informative about a family?
options: My family has six members: my parents, my three siblings and me.
hints: The most informative sentence gives specific details.
Which sentence gives a number and names the members?
questions.explanation: The first sentence gives specific information about the number and composition of the family.
misconceptions: The other sentences are general or opinions.

questions.stem: Which sentence gives information about a family member's occupation?
hints: Occupation is a job.
Which sentence tells us what the uncle does for work?
questions.explanation: 'My uncle is a driver' gives information about his occupation.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.4.14.2: Write an event of the day
indicator.objective: Write picture events about personal experiences and make radio/TV presentations

skills.description: Describe a personal experience or event using words and pictures
Arrange pictures in the correct order to tell an event
Prepare a short radio/TV presentation about a personal experience

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Any picture can represent an event
Pictures do not need to be in order
A presentation is just reading notes
Personal experiences are not suitable for presentations

questions.stem: Which sentence best describes a personal experience?
options: I went to the market with my mother and bought fresh fruit.
hints: A personal experience tells what happened to you.
Which sentence uses 'I' and describes an event?
questions.explanation: The first sentence describes a personal experience of going to the market.
misconceptions: The other sentences are general statements, not personal experiences.

questions.stem: Which sentence tells about an event that happened?
options: Yesterday, I visited my grandmother and we cooked together.
hints: An event is something that happened.
Which sentence tells about a past event?
questions.explanation: The first sentence tells about a past event (visiting grandmother and cooking).
misconceptions: The other sentences are general descriptions.

questions.stem: You have three pictures: (1) a boy waking up, (2) a boy eating breakfast, (3) a boy going to school. What is the correct order?
hints: Think about a morning routine.
The boy wakes up first, then eats, then goes to school.
questions.explanation: The correct order is waking up, eating breakfast, going to school.
misconceptions: The other orders do not follow a logical morning routine.

questions.stem: Pictures show: (1) a seed, (2) a small plant, (3) a big tree. What is the correct order?
hints: A seed grows into a plant, then a tree.
Start with the smallest stage.
questions.explanation: The correct order is seed, small plant, big tree.
misconceptions: The other orders do not follow the growth process.

questions.stem: What is a radio/TV presentation?
options: A short talk prepared to be heard or seen by an audience
hints: A presentation is for an audience.
It can be on radio or TV.
questions.explanation: A radio/TV presentation is a short talk prepared for an audience.
misconceptions: It is not a long essay.

questions.stem: Which sentence best describes a picture of a girl helping her mother cook?
options: A girl is helping her mother cook in the kitchen.
hints: Look at what the girl and mother are doing.
They are in the kitchen cooking.
questions.explanation: The picture shows a girl helping her mother cook.
misconceptions: The other sentences do not match the picture.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to describe a personal experience using pictures. What should the pictures show?
options: The main events in the order they happened
hints: Pictures should tell the story of the experience.
They should be in order.
questions.explanation: Pictures should show the main events in the order they happened.
misconceptions: Random scenes do not tell a clear story.
Only the ending or beginning is incomplete.

questions.stem: A pupil has pictures of a visit to the hospital: (1) the nurse giving medicine, (2) the pupil feeling sick at home, (3) the pupil feeling better. What is the correct order?
hints: First the pupil feels sick, then visits the nurse, then feels better.
Start with feeling sick.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: feeling sick, getting medicine, feeling better.
misconceptions: The other orders do not follow the logical sequence.

questions.stem: Before giving a radio presentation about a personal experience, what should the pupil do first?
options: Plan what to say and practise
hints: Preparation helps a presentation go well.
Plan and practise before presenting.
questions.explanation: The pupil should plan what to say and practise before the presentation.
misconceptions: Speaking immediately may lead to mistakes.
Reading a book is not preparation for this.

questions.stem: Which sentence would be a good opening for a radio presentation about a personal experience?
options: Good morning, listeners. Today I will share my experience of visiting the zoo.
I don't know what to say.
hints: A good opening greets the audience and states the topic.
The first sentence does both.
questions.explanation: The first sentence is a good opening because it greets listeners and introduces the topic.
misconceptions: The other sentences are not proper openings.

questions.stem: A pupil is preparing a TV presentation about their favourite festival. What should they include?
options: The name of the festival, when it is celebrated and what happens
Only the name of the festival
A story about a different topic
hints: A good presentation gives key facts about the topic.
Include the name, time and activities.
questions.explanation: The presentation should include the name, time and activities of the festival.
misconceptions: Only the name is too little.

questions.stem: Which sentence best describes this picture: a boy is helping an old woman cross the road.
options: A kind boy is helping an old woman cross the busy road.
hints: Look at the people and what they are doing.
The boy is helping the woman cross.
questions.explanation: The picture shows a boy helping an old woman cross the road.
misconceptions: The other sentences do not match the picture.

questions.stem: Pictures of a school day: (1) pupils in class, (2) pupils going home, (3) pupils arriving at school. What is the correct order?
hints: Arrive at school first, then class, then go home.
Start with arrival.
questions.explanation: The correct order is arriving at school, being in class, going home.
misconceptions: The other orders do not follow the school day.

questions.stem: A pupil is nervous about giving a radio presentation. What can they do to feel more confident?
options: Practise the presentation several times before the day
Read from a book during the presentation
hints: Practice builds confidence.
Rehearsing helps you feel prepared.
questions.explanation: Practising the presentation several times helps the pupil feel more confident.
misconceptions: Reading from a book is not a presentation.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the best closing for a radio presentation about a personal experience?
options: Thank you for listening. That was my experience.
hints: A closing thanks the audience and wraps up.
The first sentence does that.
questions.explanation: The first sentence is a good closing because it thanks listeners and ends the presentation.
misconceptions: The other sentences are openings or questions.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.4.15.1: Write informal letters on given topics
indicator.objective: Write to friends about personal experiences using appropriate letter formats

skills.description: Recognise the features of an informal (friendly) letter: address, date, greeting, body, closing, signature
Use appropriate greetings and closings in informal letters
Write about a personal experience in the body of an informal letter
Write a complete informal letter to a friend about a personal experience using appropriate letter format

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Informal letters don't need an address
Any greeting works for a friend
The body can be about anything
A letter needs only a greeting and body
Informal letters are the same as formal letters

questions.stem: Which of these is a feature of an informal (friendly) letter?
options: The writer's address and the date
hints: Informal letters still include the writer's address and date.
Friendly letters have a personal address and date.
questions.explanation: An informal letter includes the writer's address and the date at the top.
misconceptions: A stamp is on the envelope, not the letter.

questions.stem: Which part of an informal letter comes first?
hints: The address and date come at the top.
They set the context.
questions.explanation: The writer's address and date come first in an informal letter.
misconceptions: The greeting comes after the address.
The body comes after the greeting.
The closing comes at the end.

questions.stem: Which greeting is most appropriate for an informal letter to a friend?
hints: Informal letters use the friend's first name.
Choose the greeting with a first name.
questions.explanation: 'Dear Ama,' is appropriate for an informal letter to a friend.
misconceptions: 'To Whom It May Concern,' is very formal.

questions.stem: Which closing is most appropriate for an informal letter to a friend?
hints: Informal letters use friendly closings.
'Your friend,' is warm and personal.
questions.explanation: 'Your friend,' is appropriate for an informal letter.

questions.stem: Which sentence would be appropriate in the body of an informal letter about a personal experience?
options: I had a wonderful time at the beach with my family.
The meeting has been postponed until further notice.
Please find enclosed the requested documents.
I am writing to apply for the position.
hints: A personal experience is about something that happened to you.
Which sentence is friendly and personal?
questions.explanation: The first sentence describes a personal experience in a friendly tone.
misconceptions: The other sentences are formal or business-like.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a part of an informal letter?
hints: Reference numbers are used in formal letters.
Informal letters do not need reference numbers.
questions.explanation: A reference number is not part of an informal letter; it is used in formal correspondence.
misconceptions: The address is part of an informal letter.
The date is part of an informal letter.
The greeting is part of an informal letter.

questions.stem: Where does the greeting go in an informal letter?
options: After the address and date, before the body
hints: The greeting comes after the address and date.
It introduces the main message.
questions.explanation: The greeting comes after the address and date and before the body of the letter.
misconceptions: The greeting does not come before the address.
It does not come after the body.
It is not at the end.

questions.stem: Which sentence best describes a personal experience for an informal letter?
options: Last weekend, I helped my mother plant vegetables in our garden.
Vegetables are an important part of a healthy diet.
The garden is located behind the house.
Plants need water and sunlight to grow.
hints: A personal experience uses 'I' and tells what happened.
The first sentence uses 'I' and describes an event.
questions.explanation: The first sentence describes a personal experience.
misconceptions: The other sentences are general facts.

questions.stem: Which pair of greeting and closing is correct for an informal letter?
options: To Whom It May Concern, ... Respectfully, Ama
hints: Informal letters use first names and friendly closings.
'Dear Kofi' and 'Your friend' match.
questions.explanation: 'Dear Kofi,' and 'Your friend,' are appropriate for an informal letter.

questions.stem: Which opening sentence for the body of an informal letter is most appropriate?
options: How are you? I hope you are doing well. I want to tell you about my holiday.
I am writing to inform you that...
I am writing to apply for...
hints: Informal letters often start with a friendly enquiry.
The first sentence asks how the friend is and introduces the topic.
questions.explanation: The first sentence is friendly and introduces the personal experience.

questions.stem: Read this letter opening: 'Ama Mensah, P.O. Box 123, Accra. 12th May 2024. Dear Kofi, How are you?...' What is missing from this opening?
options: Nothing is missing — it has the address, date and greeting
hints: Check if the address, date and greeting are present.
All three are present.
questions.explanation: The opening includes the address, date and greeting. Nothing is missing.
misconceptions: The body comes after the greeting.
The closing is at the end.
The writer's name is in the closing.

questions.stem: Which sentence would NOT be appropriate in the body of an informal letter about a personal experience?
options: The meeting has been rescheduled to 3 p.m.
I had a great time at the party.
Guess what happened at school today!
I can't wait to tell you about my trip.
hints: Informal letters use friendly, conversational language.
Which sentence sounds like a formal notice?
questions.explanation: The first sentence is formal and not personal, so it does not fit an informal letter.
misconceptions: The other sentences are friendly and personal.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of parts in an informal letter?
options: Address, date, greeting, body, closing, signature
hints: The address comes first.
The greeting comes after the date.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: address, date, greeting, body, closing and signature.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.5.2.1: Show understanding of how punctuations are used appropriately in writing
indicator.objective: Use the comma: before and after 'Yes' and 'No' in sentences; after addressing a person, e.g. Kofi, can you help me?

skills.description: Use a comma after 'Yes' and 'No' at the beginning of a sentence
Use a comma after addressing a person by name
Identify correct comma usage in given sentences
Correct sentences where commas are missing or wrongly placed

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: A comma is not needed after 'Yes' or 'No'
The comma goes before the person's name
Any punctuation mark can be used after 'Yes' or 'No'
Commas are optional in short sentences
You only need one comma in a sentence

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a comma correctly?
hints: A comma is needed after 'Yes'.
Look for the comma after 'Yes'.
questions.explanation: 'Yes, please.' uses a comma correctly after 'Yes'.
misconceptions: 'Yes. please.' uses a full stop instead of a comma.
'Yes; please.' uses a semicolon instead of a comma.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a comma correctly when addressing a person?
hints: A comma comes after the person's name.
Look for the comma after 'Kofi'.
questions.explanation: 'Kofi, can you help me?' uses a comma correctly after addressing Kofi.
misconceptions: The comma should not be after 'you'.
The third sentence is missing the comma.

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence:
hints: A comma is needed after 'No'.
Look for the comma after 'No'.
questions.explanation: 'No, thank you.' uses a comma correctly after 'No'.
misconceptions: The second sentence is missing the comma.
The third uses a full stop.

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence when addressing Ama:
hints: A comma comes after the name.
Look for the comma after 'Ama'.
questions.explanation: 'Ama, please sit down.' uses a comma correctly after addressing Ama.
misconceptions: The comma should not be after 'please'.
The third sentence is missing the comma.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
hints: A comma is needed after 'Yes' and after 'Kofi'.
Look for commas after both 'Yes' and 'Kofi'.
questions.explanation: 'Yes, Kofi, you may go.' correctly uses commas after 'Yes' and after addressing Kofi.
misconceptions: The other sentences miss one or both commas.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
hints: A comma is needed after 'No'.
Look for the comma after 'No'.
questions.explanation: 'No, I don't want any.' uses a comma correctly after 'No'.
misconceptions: The other sentences use wrong punctuation after 'No'.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly addresses the teacher?
hints: A comma comes after 'Madam'.
Look for the comma after 'Madam'.
questions.explanation: 'Madam, may I go out?' uses a comma correctly after addressing the teacher.
misconceptions: The comma should not be after 'go'.
The third sentence is missing the comma.

questions.stem: Which sentence does NOT use a comma correctly?
hints: Check each sentence for the correct comma placement.
Which sentence is missing a comma after 'Yes'?
questions.explanation: 'Yes I will come.' is missing the comma after 'Yes'.
misconceptions: The other sentences use commas correctly.

questions.stem: Correct the sentence: 'Kofi can you help me'
hints: Add a comma after 'Kofi'.
Add a question mark at the end.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence is 'Kofi, can you help me?'
misconceptions: The other options place the comma incorrectly or miss it.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a comma after 'Yes'?
options: Yes, I have finished my homework.
Yes I have finished, my homework.
Yes I have finished my homework.
Yes; I have finished my homework.
hints: A comma is needed after 'Yes'.
Look for the comma after 'Yes'.
questions.explanation: 'Yes, I have finished my homework.' uses a comma correctly after 'Yes'.
misconceptions: The comma should not be after 'finished'.
The third sentence is missing the comma.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly addresses Esi?
hints: A comma comes after 'Esi'.
Look for the comma after 'Esi'.
questions.explanation: 'Esi, please close the door.' uses a comma correctly after addressing Esi.
misconceptions: The comma should not be after 'please'.
The third sentence is missing the comma.

questions.stem: A pupil writes: 'Yes Kofi you can go.' What is the correct punctuation?
hints: Add commas after 'Yes' and after 'Kofi'.
Both commas are needed.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence is 'Yes, Kofi, you can go.'
misconceptions: The other options miss one or both commas.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
options: No, Ama, you cannot go out.
No Ama, you cannot go out.
No, Ama you cannot go out.
No Ama you cannot go out.
hints: A comma is needed after 'No' and after 'Ama'.
Look for commas after both 'No' and 'Ama'.
questions.explanation: 'No, Ama, you cannot go out.' correctly uses commas after 'No' and after addressing Ama.
misconceptions: The other sentences miss one or both commas.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
hints: Commas are needed after 'Yes' and after 'Madam'.
Both commas should be present.
questions.explanation: 'Yes, Madam, I have finished.' correctly uses commas after 'Yes' and after addressing 'Madam'.
misconceptions: The other sentences miss one or both commas.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.5.3.1: Apply knowledge of different types of nouns in communication
indicator.objective: Identify and use nouns in sentences to identify people, animals, events and objects

skills.description: Identify nouns (people, animals, events, objects) in sentences
Use nouns correctly in written sentences to name people, animals, events and objects
Classify nouns into people, animals, events or objects

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Any word can be a noun
Nouns are only names of people
Common nouns start with capital letters

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'The girl is reading' is a noun?
hints: A noun names a person, animal, event or object.
Which word names a person?
questions.explanation: 'Girl' is a noun because it names a person.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'The dog is barking' is a noun?
hints: A noun names an animal, person, event or object.
Which word names an animal?
questions.explanation: 'Dog' is a noun because it names an animal.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a noun correctly?
hints: A noun should name a person, animal, event or object.
Which sentence has a clear noun?
questions.explanation: 'The table is broken' uses 'table' correctly as a noun.
misconceptions: The other sentences are grammatically incorrect.

questions.stem: Which of these is a noun that names a place?
hints: A noun can name a place.
Which word names a place?
questions.explanation: 'School' is a noun that names a place.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'Ama went to the market' is a noun?
hints: A noun can name a person.
Which word is a person's name?
questions.explanation: 'Ama' is a noun because it names a person. 'Market' is also a noun, but 'Ama' is the option given.

questions.stem: Choose the sentence that uses 'market' as a noun correctly.
options: We went to the market to buy food.
Market we went to buy food.
hints: A noun names a place or thing.
'Market' should name the place.
questions.explanation: 'We went to the market to buy food' uses 'market' correctly as a noun.
misconceptions: The other sentences are grammatically incorrect.

questions.stem: Which noun names an event?
hints: An event is something that happens.
Which word is a celebration?
questions.explanation: 'Christmas' is a noun that names an event.

questions.stem: Which noun names an object?
hints: An object is a thing you can touch.
Which word is a thing?
questions.explanation: 'Chair' is a noun that names an object.

questions.stem: How many nouns are in the sentence 'The teacher gave the pupils books'?
hints: Nouns name people, places, things or events.
Teacher (person), pupils (people), books (things).
questions.explanation: There are three nouns: teacher, pupils and books.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'event' as a noun correctly?
hints: 'Event' is a noun naming something that happens.
Which sentence uses it as a naming word?
questions.explanation: 'The school event was enjoyable' uses 'event' correctly as a noun.
misconceptions: The other sentences are grammatically incorrect.

questions.stem: Which word is a noun that names a person?
hints: A person is a human being.
Which word names a human being?
questions.explanation: 'Doctor' is a noun that names a person.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'The celebration of Independence Day in Ghana is a joyful event' is a noun naming an event?
hints: An event is something that happens.
'Celebration' names an event.
questions.explanation: 'Celebration' is a noun naming an event.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a noun correctly to name an object?
options: The pencil is on the desk.
The pencil is on the run.
The pencil is on the quickly.
The pencil is on the happy.
hints: A noun names an object.
Which sentence uses a real object as the location?
questions.explanation: 'The pencil is on the desk' uses 'desk' correctly as a noun naming an object.
misconceptions: The other sentences use verbs or adjectives where nouns should be.

questions.stem: Which set contains only nouns?
hints: Nouns name people, animals, places, events or objects.
Which set has no verbs or adjectives?
questions.explanation: The first set contains only nouns: teacher (person), dog (animal), market (place), Christmas (event).

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.5.3.1: Apply knowledge of different types of nouns in communication
indicator.objective: Identify and use common nouns (printed as 'Common nouns')

skills.description: Recognise common nouns (general names) in sentences
Use common nouns correctly in written sentences, starting with small letters
Distinguish between common nouns and proper nouns

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Common nouns are the same as proper nouns
Common nouns should start with capital letters

questions.stem: Which word is a common noun in the sentence 'The boy is playing'?
hints: A common noun is a general name, not a specific one.
'Boy' is a general name for a young male.
questions.explanation: 'Boy' is a common noun because it is a general name, not a specific person's name.

questions.stem: Which word is a common noun in the sentence 'The dog is barking'?
hints: A common noun is a general name for an animal, person, place or thing.
'Dog' is a general name for an animal.
questions.explanation: 'Dog' is a common noun because it is a general name for an animal.

questions.stem: Which word is a proper noun?
hints: Proper nouns are specific names and start with capital letters.
Ghana is a specific country.
questions.explanation: 'Ghana' is a proper noun because it is a specific country name, starting with a capital letter.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'Ama went to the market' is a common noun?
hints: A common noun is a general name, not a specific one.
Which word is a general place name?
questions.explanation: 'Market' is a common noun because it is a general name for a place. 'Ama' is a proper noun.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly shows a common noun and a proper noun?
hints: A common noun is general; a proper noun is specific.
City is general; Accra is specific.
questions.explanation: 'City' is a common noun (general) and 'Accra' is a proper noun (specific).

questions.stem: How many common nouns are in 'The girl has a book and a pen'?
hints: Common nouns name general people, places or things.
Girl (person), book (thing), pen (thing).
questions.explanation: There are three common nouns: girl, book and pen.

questions.stem: Which word in 'Kofi lives in Kumasi' is a common noun?
hints: Proper nouns are specific names starting with capital letters.
Both 'Kofi' and 'Kumasi' start with capital letters.
questions.explanation: Both 'Kofi' and 'Kumasi' are proper nouns. There is no common noun in the sentence.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'Mrs. Mensah teaches at the school' is a common noun?
hints: A common noun is a general name.
'School' is a general place. 'Mrs. Mensah' is a specific person.
questions.explanation: 'School' is a common noun because it is a general place. 'Mrs. Mensah' is a proper noun.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a common noun?
hints: Common nouns are general names.
Which word is a specific name?
questions.explanation: 'Accra' is a proper noun because it is a specific city name. The others are common nouns.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The festival of Homowo is celebrated by the Ga people', which words are common nouns and which is a proper noun?
options: Common: festival, people; Proper: Homowo, Ga
Common: Homowo, Ga; Proper: festival, people
Common: festival; Proper: Homowo, Ga, people
hints: Proper nouns are specific names starting with capital letters.
'Homowo' and 'Ga' are specific names.
'Festival' and 'people' are general.
questions.explanation: 'Festival' and 'people' are common nouns; 'Homowo' and 'Ga' are proper nouns.
misconceptions: Not all words are common nouns.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.5.3.1: Apply knowledge of different types of nouns in communication
indicator.objective: Identify and use collective nouns to refer to a group of objects and people

skills.description: Recognise collective nouns in written sentences
Use collective nouns correctly in written sentences with singular verbs
Match collective nouns to the groups they describe

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Any group word is a collective noun
Collective nouns are only for animals
Collective nouns are the same as plural nouns

questions.stem: Which word is a collective noun in the sentence 'The team is playing well'?
hints: A collective noun names a group of people or things.
Which word refers to a group of players?
questions.explanation: 'Team' is a collective noun because it refers to a group of players.

questions.stem: Which word is a collective noun in 'A flock of sheep is grazing'?
hints: A collective noun names a group of animals.
Which word means a group of sheep?
questions.explanation: 'Flock' is a collective noun because it refers to a group of sheep.
misconceptions: 'Sheep' is the animal, not the collective noun.

questions.stem: Which collective noun is used for a group of keys?
hints: Think of what we call a group of keys.
We say a 'bunch of keys'.
questions.explanation: A group of keys is called a 'bunch'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The class ___ ready for the lesson.'
hints: Collective nouns take singular verbs.
'Class' is a collective noun, so use 'is'.
questions.explanation: 'The class is ready for the lesson' uses the singular verb 'is' because 'class' is a collective noun.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'A swarm of bees flew over the garden' is a collective noun?
hints: A collective noun names a group of insects.
Which word means a group of bees?
questions.explanation: 'Swarm' is the collective noun for a group of bees.

questions.stem: Which collective noun matches a group of cattle?
hints: A group of cattle is called a...
It starts with 'h'.
questions.explanation: A group of cattle is called a herd.

questions.stem: Which collective noun matches a group of monkeys?
hints: A group of monkeys is called a...
It starts with 't'.
questions.explanation: A group of monkeys is called a troop.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a collective noun correctly?
options: The team is winning the match.
The team are winning the match.
hints: Collective nouns take singular verbs.
Which sentence has the correct singular verb?
questions.explanation: 'The team is winning the match' uses 'team' as a collective noun with the singular verb 'is'.
misconceptions: The third is missing a verb.

questions.stem: Which word is NOT a collective noun?
hints: A collective noun names a group.
'Dog' names one animal, not a group.
questions.explanation: 'Dog' is not a collective noun; it names a single animal. 'Team', 'class' and 'flock' are collective nouns.

questions.stem: Which collective noun matches a group of sheep?
hints: A group of sheep is called a...
It starts with 'f'.
questions.explanation: A group of sheep is called a flock.

questions.stem: Which collective noun matches a group of students?
hints: A group of students in a school is called a...
It starts with 'c'.
questions.explanation: A group of students is called a class.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a collective noun with the correct verb?
options: A bunch of keys is on the table.
A bunch of keys are on the table.
A bunch of keys were on the table.
A bunch of keys be on the table.
hints: Collective nouns take singular verbs.
'Bunch' is collective, so use 'is'.
questions.explanation: 'A bunch of keys is on the table' uses the singular verb 'is' correctly with the collective noun 'bunch'.

questions.stem: How many collective nouns are in the sentence 'The class and the team are ready'?
hints: A collective noun names a group.
'Class' and 'team' both name groups.
questions.explanation: There are two collective nouns: class and team.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'The flock of birds are flying.' What is wrong with this sentence?
options: The verb should be 'is' because 'flock' is a collective noun.
hints: Collective nouns take singular verbs.
'Flock' is singular, so use 'is'.
questions.explanation: The sentence should be 'The flock of birds is flying' because 'flock' is a collective noun taking the singular verb 'is'.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.5.3.1: Apply knowledge of different types of nouns in communication
indicator.objective: Identify and use abstract nouns to refer to concepts and ideas

skills.description: Recognise abstract nouns in written sentences
Use abstract nouns correctly in written sentences
Distinguish between concrete nouns and abstract nouns

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Abstract nouns can be seen or touched
Abstract nouns are not real nouns

questions.stem: Which word is an abstract noun in the sentence 'She showed great kindness to the old man'?
hints: An abstract noun names a quality or idea that cannot be seen or touched.
'Kindness' is a quality.
questions.explanation: 'Kindness' is an abstract noun because it is a quality that cannot be seen or touched.

questions.stem: Which word is an abstract noun in the sentence 'His courage helped him win the race'?
hints: An abstract noun names a quality or feeling.
'Courage' is a quality.
questions.explanation: 'Courage' is an abstract noun because it is a quality that cannot be seen or touched.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the abstract noun 'freedom' correctly?
options: The people fought for their freedom.
The people fought for their table.
The people fought for their shoe.
The people fought for their cup.
hints: 'Freedom' is an abstract noun meaning liberty.
Which sentence makes sense with 'freedom'?
questions.explanation: 'The people fought for their freedom' uses 'freedom' correctly.
misconceptions: The other sentences use concrete nouns that do not fit.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the abstract noun 'patience' correctly?
options: She showed patience while waiting for the bus.
hints: 'Patience' is the ability to wait calmly.
Which sentence makes sense with 'patience'?
questions.explanation: 'She showed patience while waiting for the bus' uses 'patience' correctly.
misconceptions: The other sentences use concrete nouns that do not fit.

questions.stem: Which word is a concrete noun?
hints: A concrete noun can be seen or touched.
A stone can be seen and touched.
questions.explanation: 'Stone' is a concrete noun because it can be seen and touched.

questions.stem: Which word is an abstract noun in the sentence 'The teacher praised the pupil for his honesty'?
hints: An abstract noun names a quality or idea.
'Honesty' is a quality.
questions.explanation: 'Honesty' is an abstract noun because it is a quality.

questions.stem: Which word is an abstract noun in the sentence 'The beauty of the flowers amazed everyone'?
hints: An abstract noun names a quality.
'Beauty' is a quality.
questions.explanation: 'Beauty' is an abstract noun because it is a quality that cannot be touched.

questions.stem: Which pair contains one concrete noun and one abstract noun?
hints: A concrete noun can be touched; an abstract noun cannot.
'Book' can be touched; 'knowledge' cannot.
questions.explanation: 'Book' is concrete and 'knowledge' is abstract.

questions.stem: Which word is an abstract noun?
hints: An abstract noun names a feeling or idea.
Happiness is a feeling.
questions.explanation: 'Happiness' is an abstract noun because it is a feeling.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the abstract noun 'wisdom' correctly?
options: The old man shared his wisdom with the children.
The old man shared his table with the children.
The old man shared his chair with the children.
The old man shared his bag with the children.
hints: 'Wisdom' is the quality of being wise.
Which sentence makes sense with 'wisdom'?
questions.explanation: 'The old man shared his wisdom with the children' uses 'wisdom' correctly.
misconceptions: The other sentences use concrete nouns that do not fit.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the abstract noun 'truth' correctly?
hints: 'Truth' is the quality of being true.
Which sentence makes sense with 'truth'?
questions.explanation: 'She always tells the truth' uses 'truth' correctly.
misconceptions: The other sentences use concrete nouns that do not fit.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains BOTH a concrete noun and an abstract noun?
options: The boy showed courage when he saw the lion.
The lion is in the cage.
hints: Concrete nouns can be seen/touched; abstract nouns cannot.
'Boy' and 'lion' are concrete; 'courage' is abstract.
questions.explanation: 'The boy showed courage when he saw the lion' contains concrete nouns ('boy', 'lion') and the abstract noun 'courage'.
misconceptions: The other sentences only contain concrete nouns.

questions.stem: How many abstract nouns are in the sentence 'Love and kindness bring happiness'?
hints: Abstract nouns name feelings, qualities or ideas.
Love, kindness and happiness are all abstract.
questions.explanation: There are three abstract nouns: love, kindness and happiness.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the abstract noun 'beauty' correctly?
options: Her beauty is admired by everyone.
Her table is admired by everyone.
Her chair is admired by everyone.
Her bag is admired by everyone.
hints: 'Beauty' is an abstract noun.
Which sentence uses a quality that cannot be touched?
questions.explanation: 'Her beauty is admired by everyone' uses 'beauty' correctly.
misconceptions: The other sentences use concrete nouns.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'Happiness is a concrete noun because you can see happy people.' Is this correct?
options: No, happiness is abstract because it is a feeling, not a physical object
Yes, because you can see happy people
Yes, because happiness is a thing
No, happiness is not a noun
hints: Concrete nouns can be touched; abstract nouns cannot.
You can see happy people, but you cannot touch happiness itself.
questions.explanation: No, 'happiness' is an abstract noun because it is a feeling. You can see happy people, but happiness itself cannot be touched.
misconceptions: Seeing happy people does not make happiness concrete.
Happiness is not a physical object.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'The teacher praised the pupil for his honesty and hard work' is an abstract noun?
hints: An abstract noun names a quality or idea.
Honesty is a quality.
questions.explanation: 'Honesty' is an abstract noun. 'Teacher' and 'pupil' are concrete nouns.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.5.4.1: Demonstrate understanding of verbs in everyday language
indicator.objective: Use the singular and plural subjects and the verb forms that go with them

skills.description: Match singular subjects with singular verbs and plural subjects with plural verbs in written sentences
Identify and correct subject-verb agreement errors in written work
Use correct subject-verb agreement in a short piece of writing

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: The verb agrees with the nearest noun
Singular and plural verbs are the same
Indefinite pronouns like 'everyone' take plural verbs

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The girl ___ to school every day.'
hints: The subject 'the girl' is singular.
Singular subjects take singular verbs ending in -s.
questions.explanation: The singular subject 'girl' takes the singular verb 'walks'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The boys ___ football every Saturday.'
hints: The subject 'the boys' is plural.
Plural subjects take the base form of the verb.
questions.explanation: The plural subject 'boys' takes the plural verb 'play'.

questions.stem: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?
hints: The subject 'the dog' is singular.
Use the singular verb 'barks'.
questions.explanation: 'The dog barks loudly' is correct because the singular subject 'dog' takes the singular verb 'barks'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'My mother ___ rice every day.'
hints: The subject 'my mother' is singular.
Add '-s' to 'cook'.
questions.explanation: The singular subject 'my mother' takes the singular verb 'cooks'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
options: The children play in the park.
The children plays in the park.
The children playing in the park.
The children played in the park.
hints: The subject 'the children' is plural.
Use the base form 'play'.
questions.explanation: 'The children play in the park' is correct because the plural subject 'children' takes the plural verb 'play'.

questions.stem: Which sentence has incorrect subject-verb agreement?
hints: Check if the subject and verb match in number.
'The girls' is plural but 'is' is singular.
questions.explanation: 'The girls is playing' is incorrect because 'the girls' is plural and needs the plural verb 'are'.
misconceptions: The other sentences have correct agreement.

questions.stem: Correct the sentence: 'The teacher give the pupils homework.'
options: The teacher gives the pupils homework.
The teacher give the pupils homework.
The teacher giving the pupils homework.
The teacher gave the pupils homework.
hints: The subject 'the teacher' is singular.
Add '-s' to 'give'.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence is 'The teacher gives the pupils homework' because 'teacher' is singular.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The pupils ___ their homework every evening.'
hints: The subject 'the pupils' is plural.
Use the base form 'do'.
questions.explanation: The plural subject 'pupils' takes the plural verb 'do'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The baby ___ loudly at night.'
hints: The subject 'the baby' is singular.
Change the 'y' to 'i' and add '-es'.
questions.explanation: The singular subject 'baby' takes the singular verb 'cries'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The committee ___ meeting every month.'
hints: 'Committee' is a collective noun and takes a singular verb.
Use 'has'.
questions.explanation: The collective noun 'committee' takes the singular verb 'has'.

questions.stem: Which sentence has correct agreement?
options: The team is winning the match.
The team are winning the match.
The team be winning the match.
hints: 'Team' is a collective noun and takes a singular verb.
Use 'is'.
questions.explanation: 'The team is winning the match' is correct because 'team' is a collective noun taking the singular verb 'is'.
misconceptions: The third is missing a verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a subject-verb agreement error?
options: Each of the pupils have a book.
Each of the pupils has a book.
hints: 'Each' is singular.
Use 'has' with 'each'.
questions.explanation: 'Each of the pupils have a book' is incorrect because 'each' is singular and takes 'has'.
misconceptions: The other sentences have correct agreement.

questions.stem: Correct the sentence: 'Everybody in the class know the answer.'
options: Everybody in the class knows the answer.
Everybody in the class know the answer.
Everybody in the class knowing the answer.
Everybody in the class knew the answer.
hints: 'Everybody' is an indefinite pronoun and is singular.
Use 'knows'.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence is 'Everybody in the class knows the answer' because 'everybody' is singular.

questions.stem: Read this paragraph: 'The pupils in Basic 4 are hardworking. They studies every day and always does their homework.' What is the error?
options: 'Studies' and 'does' should be 'study' and 'do' because the subject is plural.
hints: The subject 'they' is plural.
Plural subjects take plural verbs.
questions.explanation: The error is 'studies' and 'does'; they should be 'study' and 'do' because the subject 'they' is plural.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.5.4.1: Demonstrate understanding of verbs in everyday language
indicator.objective: Demonstrate the use of the simple past form in speech and in writing to express past conditions

skills.description: Recognise the simple past form of regular and irregular verbs in written sentences
Use the simple past form correctly in writing to express past conditions
Rewrite a present-tense sentence or short paragraph in the simple past tense

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: All verbs form their past by adding '-ed'
The simple past is only for actions
The simple past and present perfect are the same
You can use the present tense for past conditions

questions.stem: What is the simple past form of 'walk'?
hints: Regular verbs add '-ed' to form the past.
Walk + ed = walked.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'walk' is 'walked'.

questions.stem: What is the simple past form of 'go'?
hints: 'Go' is an irregular verb.
Its past form is 'went'.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'go' is 'went' (irregular).

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'She ___ to school yesterday.'
hints: 'Yesterday' shows past time.
Use the past form 'walked'.
questions.explanation: 'She walked to school yesterday' uses the simple past correctly.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the simple past?
hints: Simple past shows completed actions in the past.
'Ate' is the past form of 'eat'.
questions.explanation: 'I ate rice yesterday' uses the simple past 'ate'.

questions.stem: What is the simple past form of 'eat'?
hints: 'Eat' is irregular.
Its past form is 'ate'.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'eat' is 'ate'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'They ___ football last Saturday.'
hints: 'Last Saturday' shows past time.
Use the past form 'played'.
questions.explanation: 'They played football last Saturday' uses the simple past correctly.

questions.stem: Which sentence expresses a past condition?
hints: A past condition tells how someone felt in the past.
'Was' is the past form of 'be'.
questions.explanation: 'I was tired yesterday' expresses a past condition using 'was'.
misconceptions: The other sentences are present or future.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The baby ___ all night.'
hints: The action happened in the past.
Use the past form 'cried'.
questions.explanation: 'The baby cried all night' uses the simple past correctly.

questions.stem: What is the simple past form of 'buy'?
hints: 'Buy' is irregular.
Its past form is 'bought'.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'buy' is 'bought'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is INCORRECT?
options: I goed to the market yesterday.
I went to the market yesterday.
hints: 'Go' is irregular; its past is 'went', not 'goed'.
Which sentence uses a wrong past form?
questions.explanation: 'I goed to the market yesterday' is incorrect because the past of 'go' is 'went'.
misconceptions: The other sentences use correct past forms.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the simple past to express a past condition?
options: She was very happy when she received the gift.
She is very happy when she receives the gift.
She will be very happy when she receives the gift.
hints: A past condition describes how someone felt in the past.
'Was' is the past form of 'be'.
questions.explanation: 'She was very happy when she received the gift' correctly uses the simple past to express a past condition.
misconceptions: The other sentences are present or present perfect.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the simple past form correctly?
options: The pupils cleaned the classroom yesterday.
The pupils clean the classroom yesterday.
The pupils cleaning the classroom yesterday.
The pupils will clean the classroom yesterday.
hints: 'Yesterday' shows past time.
Use the past form 'cleaned'.
questions.explanation: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom yesterday' uses the simple past correctly.

questions.stem: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: She didn't go to school yesterday.
She didn't went to school yesterday.
She not went to school yesterday.
She no go to school yesterday.
hints: After 'didn't', use the base form of the verb.
'Didn't go' is correct.
questions.explanation: 'She didn't go to school yesterday' is correct because after 'didn't' we use the base form 'go'.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.5.4.1: Demonstrate understanding of verbs in everyday language
indicator.objective: Use the present perfect form of verbs to relate past events to the present

skills.description: Form the present perfect correctly (has/have + past participle)
Use the present perfect to relate past events to the present
Distinguish between the simple past and the present perfect in context

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: The present perfect is the same as the simple past
You can use any past participle after 'has/have'
The present perfect is only for recent events

questions.stem: What is the present perfect form of 'eat'?
hints: Present perfect is has/have + past participle.
The past participle of 'eat' is 'eaten'.
questions.explanation: The present perfect of 'eat' is 'has eaten' (or 'have eaten').

questions.stem: Choose the correct present perfect: 'She ___ finished her homework.'
hints: Use 'has' with she, he, it.
Finished is the past participle.
questions.explanation: She is singular, so we use 'has finished'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the present perfect to relate a past event to the present?
options: I have lost my pen, so I need a new one.
I lose my pen every week.
I will lose my pen tomorrow.
hints: Present perfect connects a past action to a present result.
'I have lost my pen' means I don't have it now.
questions.explanation: The first sentence shows a past event (losing the pen) with a present result (needing a new one).
questions.misconception: Using simple past when the present result is important.

questions.stem: Which sentence is in the present perfect?
hints: Present perfect uses has/have + past participle.
'Have visited' is present perfect.
questions.explanation: 'They have visited' is present perfect.
questions.misconception: Mistaking simple past 'visited' for present perfect.

questions.stem: Choose the correct present perfect: 'The pupils ___ their work.'
hints: The subject 'pupils' is plural, so use 'have'.
The past participle of 'complete' is 'completed'.
questions.explanation: The plural subject 'pupils' takes 'have completed'.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of 'write'?
hints: The past participle is used after has/have.
Write → wrote → written.
questions.explanation: The past participle of 'write' is 'written'.
questions.misconception: Using 'wrote' (simple past) as the past participle.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the present perfect to show a past event with a present result?
options: She has broken her leg, so she cannot walk.
She broke her leg last year.
hints: Present perfect connects past to present.
The broken leg affects her now.
questions.explanation: The first sentence shows a past event (breaking her leg) with a present result (cannot walk).
questions.misconception: Using simple past when the present effect is the focus.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
options: I have lived here for five years.
I have lived here since five years.
I lived here for five years.
I live here for five years.
hints: Use 'for' with a length of time.
Present perfect with 'for' shows an action continuing to now.
questions.explanation: 'I have lived here for five years' is correct because 'for' is used with a period of time.
questions.misconception: Using 'since' with a period of time instead of a starting point.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the simple past, not the present perfect?
hints: Simple past shows a completed action at a specific past time.
'Yesterday' signals simple past.
questions.explanation: 'We ate rice yesterday' uses simple past because of the specific past time 'yesterday'.
questions.misconception: Using present perfect with a specific past time like 'yesterday'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the present perfect correctly?
options: He has gone to the market.
He has went to the market.
He have gone to the market.
He has go to the market.
hints: Use 'has' + past participle.
The past participle of 'go' is 'gone'.
questions.explanation: 'He has gone' is correct because 'has' is followed by the past participle 'gone'.

questions.stem: Why is the present perfect used in 'I have lost my keys'?
options: To show a past action with a present result
To show a past action at a specific time
hints: Present perfect links past to present.
The keys are still lost now.
questions.explanation: The present perfect shows that the action happened in the past and has a result now (the keys are still missing).
questions.misconception: Thinking present perfect is only for recent events.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the present perfect?
options: She has been to Accra three times.
She has went to Accra three times.
She have been to Accra three times.
She been to Accra three times.
hints: Use 'has' with 'she'.
The past participle of 'be' is 'been'.
questions.explanation: 'She has been' is correct because 'has' + 'been' forms the present perfect.

questions.stem: Which sentence is incorrect?
options: I have never seen that movie.
hints: The past participle of 'see' is 'seen'.
Use 'seen' after 'have'.
questions.explanation: 'I have saw' is incorrect; it should be 'I have seen'.
questions.misconception: Using the simple past form after 'have'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct present perfect sentence.
hints: Use 'have' with 'they'.
The past participle of 'eat' is 'eaten'.
questions.explanation: 'They have already eaten' is correct: 'have' + past participle 'eaten'.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.5.5.1: Demonstrate understanding of adjectives in speech and in writing
indicator.objective: Use adjectives to make comparisons e.g. fast/slow, good/bad, fast/faster, slow/slower

skills.description: Recognise adjectives in written sentences
Form comparative adjectives by adding '-er' to regular adjectives
Use comparative adjectives correctly in written sentences to compare two people or things
Recognise and use irregular comparative forms (good → better, bad → worse)

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: All adjectives form their comparative by adding '-er'
Comparative means the same as positive

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'The tall boy is running' is an adjective?
hints: An adjective describes a noun.
Which word describes the boy?
questions.explanation: 'Tall' is an adjective because it describes the boy.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'The soup is hot' is an adjective?
hints: An adjective describes a noun.
Which word describes the soup?
questions.explanation: 'Hot' is an adjective because it describes the soup.

questions.stem: What is the comparative form of 'fast'?
hints: Add '-er' to form the comparative of a short adjective.
Fast → faster.
questions.explanation: The comparative form of 'fast' is 'faster'.

questions.stem: What is the comparative form of 'slow'?
hints: Add '-er' to form the comparative.
Slow → slower.
questions.explanation: The comparative form of 'slow' is 'slower'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence:
options: Ama is more taller than Kwesi.
hints: Use 'than' after the comparative adjective.
Tall → taller + than.
questions.explanation: 'Ama is taller than Kwesi' uses the comparative 'taller' with 'than' correctly.

questions.stem: What is the comparative form of 'good'?
hints: 'Good' is an irregular adjective.
Its comparative form is 'better'.
questions.explanation: The comparative form of 'good' is 'better' (irregular).

questions.stem: How many adjectives are in the sentence 'The big brown dog is friendly'?
hints: Adjectives describe nouns.
'Big' and 'brown' describe the dog; 'friendly' describes the dog too.
questions.explanation: There are three adjectives: big, brown and friendly.

questions.stem: What is the comparative form of 'big'?
hints: Double the final consonant and add '-er'.
Big → bigger.
questions.explanation: The comparative form of 'big' is 'bigger' (double the 'g').

questions.stem: What is the comparative form of 'happy'?
hints: Change the 'y' to 'i' and add '-er'.
Happy → happier.
questions.explanation: The comparative form of 'happy' is 'happier'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence:
options: This ruler is longer than that one.
This ruler is longer that one.
This ruler is more longer than that one.
This ruler is longest than that one.
hints: Use 'than' after the comparative.
Long → longer + than.
questions.explanation: 'This ruler is longer than that one' uses 'longer' with 'than' correctly.

questions.stem: What is the comparative form of 'bad'?
hints: 'Bad' is irregular.
Its comparative form is 'worse'.
questions.explanation: The comparative form of 'bad' is 'worse'.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly compares two places?
options: Accra is more busier than Kumasi.
hints: Use 'than' after the comparative.
Busy → busier + than.
questions.explanation: 'Accra is busier than Kumasi' correctly uses the comparative 'busier'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the comparative correctly?
options: Kofi is more stronger than Musa.
hints: Strong → stronger + than.
Use 'than' after the comparative.
questions.explanation: 'Kofi is stronger than Musa' uses 'stronger' correctly.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'better' correctly?
options: This mango is better than that one.
This mango is gooder than that one.
This mango is more better than that one.
This mango is best than that one.
hints: 'Better' is the comparative of 'good'.
Use 'than' after 'better'.
questions.explanation: 'This mango is better than that one' uses 'better' correctly.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.5.5.1: Demonstrate understanding of adjectives in speech and in writing
indicator.objective: Differentiate between how the comparative and superlative adjective forms are used in sentences

skills.description: Distinguish between comparative (comparing two) and superlative (comparing three or more) forms
