Form superlative adjectives correctly (add '-est' to regular adjectives; use 'most' for longer adjectives; irregular forms like best, worst)
Use superlative adjectives correctly in sentences (e.g. 'Ama is the tallest girl in the class.')
Choose the correct adjective form (positive, comparative or superlative) for a given context

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Comparative and superlative are the same
You can use the superlative to compare two things
Irregular adjectives follow the same rules

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a comparative adjective?
options: Kofi is the tallest in the class.
hints: Comparative compares two people or things.
Which sentence compares Kofi and Ama?
questions.explanation: 'Taller than' compares two people, so it is comparative.
misconceptions: The superlative compares three or more.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a superlative adjective?
options: Ama is the tallest girl in the class.
hints: Superlative compares three or more and often uses 'the' and '-est'.
Which sentence compares Ama to the whole class?
questions.explanation: 'The tallest girl in the class' is superlative because it compares Ama to all the girls.

questions.stem: What is the superlative form of 'fast'?
hints: Add '-est' to short adjectives.
Fast → fastest.
questions.explanation: The superlative of 'fast' is 'fastest'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence:
options: Musah is the tallest boy in the class.
Musah is taller than in the class.
Musah is tallest than the class.
Musah is more tallest in the class.
hints: Superlative uses 'the' and '-est'.
Which sentence compares Musah to all the boys?
questions.explanation: 'Musah is the tallest boy in the class' correctly uses the superlative 'tallest'.
misconceptions: The other sentences mix comparative and superlative incorrectly.

questions.stem: Choose the correct adjective form: 'This is the ___ book I have ever read.'
hints: Compare one book to all others you have read.
Use the superlative form.
questions.explanation: 'Best' is the superlative form of 'good'.

questions.stem: Which sentence compares exactly two things?
options: The mango is sweeter than the orange.
The mango is the sweetest fruit.
hints: Comparative compares two things.
Which sentence has 'than'?
questions.explanation: 'Sweeter than' compares two fruits, so it is comparative.
misconceptions: The superlative compares three or more.

questions.stem: Which sentence compares three or more things?
options: This is the biggest house on our street.
This house is bigger than that one.
hints: Superlative compares three or more.
Which sentence uses 'the biggest'?
questions.explanation: 'The biggest house on our street' compares this house to all houses on the street.

questions.stem: What is the superlative form of 'big'?
hints: Double the final consonant and add '-est'.
Big → biggest.
questions.explanation: The superlative of 'big' is 'biggest'.

questions.stem: What is the superlative form of 'happy'?
hints: Change 'y' to 'i' and add '-est'.
Happy → happiest.
questions.explanation: The superlative of 'happy' is 'happiest'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence:
options: She is the most intelligent pupil in Basic 4.
She is more intelligent than Basic 4.
She is the intelligentest pupil in Basic 4.
hints: Long adjectives use 'most' for superlative.
Intelligent → most intelligent.
questions.explanation: 'The most intelligent pupil' correctly uses 'most' for the superlative.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'Between Kofi and Ama, Kofi is ___.'
hints: We are comparing two people.
Use the comparative form.
questions.explanation: 'Taller' is correct because we are comparing two people.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly shows comparative and superlative forms of 'slow'?
hints: Comparative: add '-er'; superlative: add '-est'.
Slow → slower → slowest.
questions.explanation: 'Slower' is comparative and 'slowest' is superlative.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
options: This is the most beautiful dress in the shop.
This is the more beautiful dress in the shop.
This is the beautifulest dress in the shop.
This is the most beautifulest dress in the shop.
hints: Long adjectives take 'most' for superlative.
Beautiful → most beautiful.
questions.explanation: 'The most beautiful dress' is correct for the superlative.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'Of all the pupils, Ama is ___.'
hints: Compare Ama to all pupils (more than two).
Use the superlative.
questions.explanation: 'The tallest' is correct because Ama is compared to all pupils.

questions.stem: What is the superlative form of 'bad'?
hints: 'Bad' is irregular.
Bad → worse → worst.
questions.explanation: The superlative of 'bad' is 'worst'.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.5.6.1: Understand and use adverbs correctly in speech and in writing
indicator.objective: Use adverbs to talk about when and where the action of a verb took place

skills.description: Recognise adverbs of time (when) and place (where) in written sentences
Use adverbs of time correctly in writing to show when an action happened
Use adverbs of place correctly in writing to show where an action happened
Place adverbs of time and place correctly in written sentences
Write a short narrative using adverbs of time and place to describe when and where events happened

spec.difficultyPlan: 4 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 6 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: Adverbs of time and place are the same
Adverbs can go anywhere in a sentence
Any word ending in '-ly' is an adverb of time or place
You only need one adverb per sentence

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'The pupils played outside yesterday' is an adverb of place?
hints: An adverb of place answers 'where?'.
Where did the pupils play? Outside.
questions.explanation: 'Outside' is an adverb of place because it answers 'where?'. 'Yesterday' is an adverb of time.
questions.misconception: Choosing 'yesterday' as place instead of time.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'We will visit Grandma tomorrow' is an adverb of time?
hints: An adverb of time answers 'when?'.
When will we visit Grandma? Tomorrow.
questions.explanation: 'Tomorrow' is an adverb of time because it answers 'when?'.

questions.stem: How many adverbs are in the sentence 'The children are playing happily outside now'?
hints: Adverbs describe verbs, adjectives or other adverbs.
Happily (manner), outside (place), now (time).
questions.explanation: There are three adverbs: happily (manner), outside (place) and now (time).

questions.stem: Which sentence contains BOTH an adverb of time and an adverb of place?
hints: Look for a word telling when and a word telling where.
'Here' is place; 'yesterday' is time.
questions.explanation: The first sentence contains 'here' (place) and 'yesterday' (time).
questions.misconception: Missing one of the two adverb types.

questions.stem: Choose the correct adverb of time: 'We will eat ___ after the lesson.'
hints: The sentence asks 'when?'.
Which word tells when?
questions.explanation: 'Soon' is an adverb of time because it answers 'when?'.
questions.misconception: Choosing a place adverb instead of a time adverb.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an adverb of time correctly?
options: I will do my homework later.
I will do my homework outside.
I will do my homework here.
I will do my homework there.
hints: 'Later' tells when.
The other options tell where.
questions.explanation: 'Later' correctly tells when the homework will be done.
questions.misconception: Confusing place adverbs with time adverbs.

questions.stem: Choose the correct adverb of time: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom ___.'
hints: The sentence needs a word telling when.
'Yesterday' tells when.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday' is the adverb of time.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses TWO adverbs of time correctly?
options: She will come tomorrow and then we will play later.
She will come here and then we will play outside.
She will come tomorrow and then we will play outside.
She will come here and then we will play later.
hints: Look for two words that tell when.
'Tomorrow' and 'later' both tell when.
questions.explanation: The first sentence uses 'tomorrow' and 'later', both adverbs of time.

questions.stem: Choose the correct adverb of place: 'The children are playing ___.'
hints: The sentence asks 'where?'.
Which word tells where?
questions.explanation: 'Outside' tells where the children are playing.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an adverb of place correctly?
options: The book is on the table there.
The book is on the table tomorrow.
The book is on the table later.
The book is on the table soon.
hints: 'There' tells where.
The other options tell when.
questions.explanation: 'There' correctly tells where the book is.
questions.misconception: Confusing time adverbs with place adverbs.

questions.stem: Choose the correct adverb of place: 'She looked for her pen ___.'
hints: The sentence asks 'where?'.
'Everywhere' tells where she looked.
questions.explanation: 'Everywhere' is an adverb of place.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an adverb of place to describe a position?
options: The cat is inside the house.
hints: 'Inside' tells where.
The other sentences tell when.
questions.explanation: 'Inside' is an adverb of place describing where the cat is.
questions.misconception: Choosing a time adverb as place.

questions.stem: Choose the sentence with the correct position of the adverb of place:
hints: Adverbs of place usually come after the verb or object.
'Played outside' is natural.
questions.explanation: 'The children played outside happily' places the adverb of place correctly.

questions.stem: Which sentence places the adverb of time correctly?
options: Yesterday, I went to the market.
I yesterday went to the market.
I went yesterday to the market.
I went to yesterday the market.
hints: Adverbs of time can come at the beginning or end.
'Yesterday,' at the beginning is natural.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday, I went to the market' correctly places the adverb of time.
questions.misconception: Placing 'yesterday' between subject and verb awkwardly.

questions.stem: A pupil writes: 'She here is now.' What is wrong with this sentence?
options: The adverb of place 'here' is in the wrong position; it should be 'She is here now.'
The sentence needs a question mark.
hints: Adverbs of place usually come after the verb.
'Here' should come after 'is'.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence is 'She is here now' because 'here' comes after the verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence has the most natural placement of both adverbs?
options: The pupils worked quietly outside yesterday.
The pupils outside quietly yesterday worked.
Outside yesterday the pupils quietly worked.
The pupils quietly outside worked yesterday.
hints: Natural order: manner, place, time.
'Quietly' (manner), 'outside' (place), 'yesterday' (time).
questions.explanation: The first sentence follows the natural order: manner, place, time.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.5.7.1: Apply the knowledge of prepositions in oral and written communication
indicator.objective: Use prepositions to convey a variety of meanings: Direction, e.g. up; Period of Time, e.g. for; Purpose, e.g. to; Possession, of; Comparison e.g. taller than

skills.description: Recognise prepositions in written sentences
Use prepositions of direction correctly (up, down, towards, along, to)
Use prepositions of time correctly (for, at, in, on, during)
Use prepositions of purpose (to, for) and possession (of, for) correctly
Use prepositions of comparison correctly (than)
Use prepositions correctly in a short piece of writing to convey a variety of meanings

spec.difficultyPlan: 4 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 6 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: All prepositions mean the same thing

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'The cat is under the table' is a preposition?
hints: A preposition shows position or relationship.
'Under' shows where the cat is.
questions.explanation: 'Under' is a preposition because it shows the position of the cat.

questions.stem: Which word is a preposition?
hints: A preposition shows direction, time, purpose, possession or comparison.
'Towards' shows direction.
questions.explanation: 'Towards' is a preposition showing direction.
questions.misconception: Confusing verbs or adjectives with prepositions.

questions.stem: How many prepositions are in the sentence 'The bird flew over the tree and into the nest'?
hints: Prepositions show position or direction.
'Over' and 'into' both show direction.
questions.explanation: There are two prepositions: 'over' and 'into'.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a preposition of comparison?
options: She is taller than her brother.
The book is on the table.
hints: Comparison uses words like 'than'.
Which sentence compares two people?
questions.explanation: 'Than' is a preposition of comparison in 'taller than her brother'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition of direction: 'The pupils walked ___ the classroom.'
hints: The sentence shows movement to a place.
'Into' shows direction.
questions.explanation: 'Into' correctly shows direction (moving into the classroom).
questions.misconception: Choosing a preposition of purpose or comparison.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'She climbed ___ the ladder.'
hints: The sentence shows upward movement.
'Up' shows direction.
questions.explanation: 'Up' correctly shows the direction of climbing.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a preposition of direction correctly?
options: They are taller than the market.
They bought things of the market.
hints: Direction shows movement toward a place.
'Towards' shows direction.
questions.explanation: 'Towards' correctly shows direction.
questions.misconception: Confusing direction with other preposition types.

questions.stem: A pupil writes: 'The ball rolled down the hill.' What does 'down' show?
hints: 'Down' shows movement downward.
It tells the direction of the roll.
questions.explanation: 'Down' shows the direction of movement.
questions.misconception: Thinking 'down' shows position only, not direction.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition of time: 'We waited ___ two hours.'
hints: 'Two hours' is a period of time.
Use 'for' with periods of time.
questions.explanation: 'For' correctly shows a period of time.
questions.misconception: Using 'since' with a period instead of a starting point.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition of time: 'The lesson starts ___ 8 o'clock.'
hints: '8 o'clock' is a specific time.
Use 'at' with specific clock times.
questions.explanation: 'At' is used with a specific time like 8 o'clock.
questions.misconception: Using 'in' or 'on' with a clock time.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a preposition of time correctly?
hints: Days of the week use 'on'.
'On Monday' is correct.
questions.explanation: 'On Monday' correctly uses 'on' with a day of the week.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'during' correctly?
options: The pupils played during break time.
The pupils played for break time.
The pupils played than break time.
The pupils played of break time.
hints: 'During' means throughout a period.
'During break time' is correct.
questions.explanation: 'During' correctly shows that the action happened within the break time period.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition of purpose: 'I bought a book ___ my sister.'
hints: The book is intended for the sister.
'For' shows purpose.
questions.explanation: 'For' correctly shows purpose (the book is meant for the sister).

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition of possession: 'This gift is ___ Kofi.'
hints: The gift belongs to Kofi.
'For' can show possession.
questions.explanation: 'For' correctly shows possession (the gift belongs to Kofi).

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'for' to show purpose?
options: I saved money for a new bike.
hints: Purpose shows why something is done.
Saving money for a bike shows purpose.
questions.explanation: 'For a new bike' shows purpose.
questions.misconception: Confusing purpose with time or possession.

questions.stem: A pupil writes: 'The key is for the door.' What does 'for' show?
hints: The key is used to open the door.
It shows the purpose of the key.
questions.explanation: 'For' shows the purpose of the key.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition of comparison: 'She is taller ___ her brother.'
hints: Comparisons use 'than'.
'Taller than' is correct.
questions.explanation: 'Than' correctly shows comparison.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a preposition of comparison correctly?
options: This book is more interesting than that one.
This book is more interesting for that one.
This book is more interesting of that one.
This book is more interesting at that one.
hints: Comparison uses 'than'.
'More interesting than' is correct.
questions.explanation: 'Than' correctly shows comparison between two books.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Sub-Strand 9: Using Simple, Compound and Complex Sentences
indicator.content_standard: B4.5.9.1: Apply knowledge of grammatical rules to form words, phrases and sentences
indicator.objective: Identify subjects and verbs in simple sentences

skills.description: Recognise the subject in a simple sentence
Recognise the verb in a simple sentence
Divide a simple sentence into subject and predicate

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: The subject is always the first word
The subject is always a person
The object of the sentence is the subject

questions.stem: What is the subject in the sentence 'The dog barks loudly'?
hints: The subject is the person, animal or thing doing the action.
Who or what barks? The dog.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'The dog' because it is the one doing the barking.
misconceptions: Choosing the verb 'barks' as the subject.

questions.stem: What is the verb in the sentence 'The children play football'?
hints: The verb is the action word.
What are the children doing? Playing.
questions.explanation: The verb is 'play' because it shows the action.

questions.stem: What is the subject in the sentence 'Ama sings a song'?
hints: The subject is the person doing the action.
Who sings? Ama.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'Ama' because she is the one singing.

questions.stem: What is the verb in the sentence 'The sun shines brightly'?
hints: The verb is the action or state word.
What does the sun do? It shines.
questions.explanation: The verb is 'shines' because it tells us what the sun does.

questions.stem: What is the subject in the sentence 'The tall boy runs quickly'?
hints: The subject includes all the words that tell us who is doing the action.
Who runs quickly? The tall boy.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'The tall boy' because it is the complete noun phrase doing the action.

questions.stem: What is the verb in the sentence 'The girls are singing a song'?
hints: The verb can be a single word or a verb phrase.
What are the girls doing? They are singing.
questions.explanation: The verb phrase is 'are singing'.

questions.stem: What is the verb in the sentence 'My mother cooks delicious food'?
hints: The verb tells what the subject does.
What does the mother do? She cooks.
questions.explanation: The verb is 'cooks'.

questions.stem: What is the subject in the sentence 'The pupils in Basic 4 study hard'?
hints: The subject is the group of people doing the action.
Who studies hard? The pupils in Basic 4.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'The pupils in Basic 4'.

questions.stem: What is the verb in the sentence 'She always helps her friends'?
hints: The verb is the action word.
What does she do? She helps.
questions.explanation: The verb is 'helps'.

questions.stem: Identify the subject and verb in the sentence 'The teacher gave us homework.'
hints: The subject does the action; the verb is the action.
Who gave? The teacher. What did she do? Gave.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'The teacher' and the verb is 'gave'.
misconceptions: Confusing the object 'homework' with the subject.
Confusing the indirect object 'us' with the subject.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The cat sleeps on the mat', which part is the subject?
hints: The subject is the doer of the action.
What sleeps? The cat.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'The cat'. The predicate is 'sleeps on the mat'.
misconceptions: Choosing the verb 'sleeps' or the prepositional phrase.

questions.stem: Which sentence has the subject 'The children'?
options: The children are playing in the park.
The park is full of children.
hints: The subject is the noun phrase that performs the action.
In which sentence do the children perform the action?
questions.explanation: In 'The children are playing in the park', 'The children' is the subject.
misconceptions: Choosing sentences where 'children' is not the subject.

questions.stem: What is the subject in the sentence 'My friends and I went to the market'?
hints: The subject includes all the people doing the action.
Who went? My friends and I.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'My friends and I' (a compound subject).

questions.stem: In the sentence 'Sit down', what is the subject?
hints: Imperative sentences have an implied subject.
Who is being told to sit? You.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'You' (understood), even though it is not written.
misconceptions: Thinking imperative sentences have no subject.
Choosing the verb 'sit' as the subject.

questions.stem: What is the subject in the sentence 'Here comes the bus'?
hints: The subject is the thing that performs the action.
What comes? The bus.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'the bus', even though it comes after the verb.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'Under the tree sat an old man', what is the subject?
hints: The subject is the person or thing doing the action.
Who sat under the tree? An old man.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'an old man', even though the sentence begins with a prepositional phrase.
misconceptions: Choosing 'the tree' or 'Under' as the subject.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Sub-Strand 9: Using Simple, Compound and Complex Sentences
indicator.content_standard: B4.5.9.1: Apply knowledge of grammatical rules to form words, phrases and sentences
indicator.objective: Construct simple sentences correctly

skills.description: Recognise that a simple sentence must have a subject and a verb and express a complete thought
Complete a simple sentence by adding a missing subject or verb
Construct grammatically correct simple sentences from given words or pictures
Identify sentence fragments (incomplete sentences) and correct them into simple sentences

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: A sentence is just any group of words
You can put the subject and verb in any order
A sentence fragment is a complete sentence
Adding an object makes it a compound sentence

questions.stem: Which of these is a complete sentence?
hints: A complete sentence needs a subject and a verb.
Which option has both a subject and a verb?
questions.explanation: 'The boy runs' has a subject ('the boy') and a verb ('runs'), so it is a complete sentence.
misconceptions: 'In the garden' has no subject or verb.

questions.stem: What two things must a simple sentence have?
options: A capital letter and a full stop
hints: A sentence needs someone or something doing an action.
It also needs the action word.
questions.explanation: A simple sentence must have a subject and a verb.
misconceptions: Capital letters and full stops are punctuation, not the core parts.
An object is not always required.

questions.stem: Which group of words is a complete sentence?
hints: Look for a subject and a verb together.
'The dog barks at night' has both.
questions.explanation: 'The dog barks at night' has a subject ('the dog') and a verb ('barks'), so it is complete.
misconceptions: The other groups are missing either a subject or a verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence is complete and expresses a full thought?
options: In the classroom with the teacher.
hints: A complete thought has a subject and a verb.
'The pupils are learning English' has both.
questions.explanation: 'The pupils are learning English' is complete because it has a subject ('the pupils') and a verb ('are learning').
misconceptions: The other options lack a subject or verb.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with the correct verb: 'The girls ___ football.'
hints: The subject 'the girls' is plural.
Use the plural verb 'play'.
questions.explanation: The plural subject 'girls' takes the verb 'play'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with the correct subject: '___ is reading a book.'
hints: The verb 'is' is singular.
Choose the singular subject.
questions.explanation: 'She' is singular and matches the singular verb 'is'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with the correct verb: 'The sun ___ in the east.'
hints: The subject 'the sun' is singular.
Use the singular verb 'rises'.
questions.explanation: The singular subject 'the sun' takes the verb 'rises'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'The pupils ___ in the library.'
hints: The subject 'the pupils' is plural.
Use the base form 'read'.
questions.explanation: The plural subject 'pupils' takes the verb 'read'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'Although it was raining, ___.'
options: the pupils still went to school
hints: The sentence needs a complete main clause.
Which option has a subject and verb?
questions.explanation: 'The pupils still went to school' is a complete clause with a subject and verb.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sentence fragment (not a complete sentence)?
options: The children run in the park.
hints: A fragment is missing a subject or a verb.
'Running in the park' has no subject.
questions.explanation: 'Running in the park' is a fragment because it has no subject.
misconceptions: The other options are complete sentences.

questions.stem: Read: 'The boy ran to the shop.' Is this a complete sentence?
options: Yes, it has a subject and a verb and expresses a complete thought.
No, it is missing a verb.
No, it is missing a subject.
hints: The sentence has 'the boy' (subject) and 'ran' (verb).
It expresses a complete thought.
questions.explanation: It is a complete sentence because it has a subject, a verb and expresses a complete thought.

questions.stem: A pupil writes: 'In the morning before school.' What is wrong with this?
options: It is a fragment — it has no subject or verb.
hints: Look for a subject and a verb.
There is no subject or verb.
questions.explanation: It is a fragment because it has no subject or verb; it is just a prepositional phrase.
misconceptions: Punctuation does not fix a fragment.

questions.stem: Read this group of words: 'The tall boy with the red cap in the corner.' What is missing to make it a complete sentence?
hints: The group has a subject ('the tall boy'), but what is the boy doing?
Add an action word.
questions.explanation: It is missing a verb, e.g. 'The tall boy with the red cap in the corner is reading.'

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B4.5.10.1: Spell words accurately
indicator.objective: Use invented spelling to increase fluency and free writing

skills.description: Understand that invented spelling is a step towards correct spelling and helps fluency in writing
Use knowledge of letter-sound correspondences to attempt the spelling of unfamiliar words
Identify and correct misspelt words using knowledge of spelling patterns and context
Spell subject-specific vocabulary correctly in context (shopping, transportation, agriculture)
Use accurate spelling in a short piece of free writing, applying spelling strategies

spec.difficultyPlan: 4 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 6 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: If a word sounds right, it is spelt right
Spelling doesn't matter if the reader understands
You can only spell words you have memorised
Spelling is only tested in spelling tests

questions.stem: What is invented spelling?
options: Attempting to spell a word using known sounds and patterns
hints: Invented spelling is an attempt.
You use the sounds you know to spell a word.
questions.explanation: Invented spelling is attempting to spell a word using the sounds and patterns you know.
questions.misconception: Thinking invented spelling means spelling is not important.

questions.stem: Why is invented spelling useful for young writers?
options: It helps them keep writing without stopping to ask for every word
It teaches them to spell incorrectly forever
It replaces the need to learn correct spelling
hints: Invented spelling keeps the flow of writing.
It helps fluency.
questions.explanation: Invented spelling helps young writers keep writing and build fluency while they learn correct spelling.
questions.misconception: Thinking invented spelling is the final goal.

questions.stem: A pupil writes 'becos' for 'because'. What is this an example of?
hints: The pupil used the sounds they know.
The spelling is not correct yet.
questions.explanation: 'Becos' is an example of invented spelling — the pupil wrote the sounds they heard.
questions.misconception: Thinking invented spelling is always acceptable in final drafts.

questions.stem: Why should a teacher encourage invented spelling in a first draft?
options: It helps pupils focus on getting ideas down without being blocked by spelling
It teaches pupils to spell wrong forever
hints: First drafts are about ideas, not perfection.
Invented spelling keeps the flow.
questions.explanation: Invented spelling is encouraged in first drafts so pupils can focus on ideas without being blocked by spelling.
questions.misconception: Thinking invented spelling is never corrected.

questions.stem: If you hear the sound /k/ at the beginning of a word, which letter could you use?
hints: Both 'c' and 'k' can make the /k/ sound.
Examples: cat, kite.
questions.explanation: The /k/ sound can be written with 'c' or 'k'.
questions.misconception: Thinking only one letter can make the /k/ sound.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to spell 'fone' for 'phone'. What strategy are they using?
hints: The pupil wrote the sounds they heard.
'Fone' sounds like 'phone'.
questions.explanation: The pupil is using sound-spelling mapping by writing the sounds they hear.
questions.misconception: Thinking sound spelling is always correct.

questions.stem: Which spelling best matches the sounds /s/ /t/ /r/ /i/ /ŋ/?
hints: Blend the sounds: s-t-r-i-ng.
The word has the blend 'str'.
questions.explanation: The sounds /s/ /t/ /r/ /i/ /ŋ/ make the word 'string'.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
hints: Think about the 'ie' or 'ei' rule.
'Friend' is spelled f-r-i-e-n-d.
questions.explanation: 'Friend' is the correct spelling.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
hints: It starts with 'sch'.
The correct spelling has 'oo' in the middle.
questions.explanation: 'School' is the correct spelling.

questions.stem: Find the misspelled word in this sentence: 'The children are happy becuase they won the game.'
hints: Look for the word that is not spelled correctly.
The word should be 'because'.
questions.explanation: 'Becuase' is misspelled; it should be 'because'.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling error?
options: The dog is runing in the park.
The dog is running in the park.
The dog is playing in the park.
The dog is sleeping in the park.
hints: Look for a word with a doubled consonant.
'Running' has a double 'n'.
questions.explanation: 'Runing' is misspelled; it should be 'running'.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
hints: Think about the letters in 'beautiful'.
It has 'beau' at the beginning.
questions.explanation: 'Beautiful' is the correct spelling.
questions.misconception: Missing the 'a' or adding an extra 'l'.

questions.stem: Find the spelling error: 'The teacher gave us a quiz on Wensday.'
hints: The day of the week is misspelled.
It should be 'Wednesday'.
questions.explanation: 'Wensday' should be 'Wednesday'.

questions.stem: Which word is a correct spelling for a shopping context?
hints: Think about the word for a place where goods are sold.
It is spelled 'market'.
questions.explanation: 'Market' is the correct spelling.
questions.misconception: Using invented spelling in a final draft.

questions.stem: Choose the correctly spelled word for a transportation context: 'The ___ is late.'
hints: The common spelling of the local minibus is 'trotro'.
It is one word.
questions.explanation: The accepted spelling is 'trotro'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses correct spelling in an agriculture context?
options: The farmer planted maize and cassava on his farm.
The farmer planted maze and cassava on his farm.
The farmer planted maise and cassava on his farm.
The farmer planted mazie and cassava on his farm.
hints: The grain is called 'maize'.
Check the spelling of 'maize'.
questions.explanation: 'Maize' is the correct spelling for the crop.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Sub-Strand 1: Building the Love and Culture of Reading
indicator.content_standard: B4.6.1.1: Read widely for pleasure, personal development, and demonstrate independent reading and learning in the literary content areas
indicator.objective: Read a variety of age- and level appropriate books and present a two-paragraph summary of each book read

skills.description: Choose age- and level-appropriate books for independent reading
Understand the importance of reading widely for pleasure and personal development
Identify the main ideas and key details from a book to include in a summary
Understand the structure of a two-paragraph summary
Write a two-paragraph summary of a book read
Present a two-paragraph summary orally to the class

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4
misconceptions: A summary is a retelling of the whole story
A two-paragraph summary should have one paragraph for the beginning and one for the ending
Any book is appropriate for independent reading
You don't need to read the whole book to summarise it
Presenting a summary means reading the book aloud

questions.stem: Which book is most appropriate for a Basic 4 pupil to read independently?
options: A simple storybook with pictures and short sentences
A newspaper article about international politics
A novel with very long chapters and no pictures
hints: Basic 4 pupils need books with simple words and pictures.
Choose the book that matches their reading level.
questions.explanation: A simple storybook with pictures and short sentences is age- and level-appropriate for Basic 4.
misconceptions: Newspaper articles on politics are too complex.
Long novels without pictures may be too difficult.

questions.stem: A pupil wants a book about animals. Which book is best for a Basic 4 pupil?
options: A picture book about farm animals with simple text
An encyclopedia with dense scientific text
A PhD thesis on animal genetics
A medical journal article on animal diseases
hints: The book should be about animals and easy to read.
Picture books are suitable for Basic 4.
questions.explanation: A picture book about farm animals with simple text is appropriate for a Basic 4 pupil.
misconceptions: A PhD thesis is far too advanced.
A medical journal is not for children.

questions.stem: Which book would be too difficult for a Basic 4 pupil to read independently?
options: A book with long paragraphs and no pictures about advanced science
A simple picture book about animals
A collection of short poems for children
hints: Basic 4 pupils need simple language and pictures.
The book with long paragraphs and advanced science is too hard.
questions.explanation: A book with long paragraphs and advanced science is too difficult for independent reading at Basic 4.

questions.stem: A pupil says they want to read a book that is 'age- and level-appropriate'. What does this mean?
options: A book that matches their age and reading ability
A book that is very long and difficult
hints: 'Age-appropriate' means suitable for their age.
'Level-appropriate' means suitable for their reading level.
questions.explanation: Age- and level-appropriate means the book matches the pupil's age and reading ability.
misconceptions: Long and difficult books are not age-appropriate.
Adult books are not for children.
Books with no pictures can be too hard.

questions.stem: Why is it good to read books for pleasure?
options: It helps you learn new words and enjoy stories
hints: Reading for pleasure is enjoyable and helps learning.
It improves vocabulary and imagination.
questions.explanation: Reading for pleasure helps you learn new words and enjoy stories.
misconceptions: Reading is not tiring if you enjoy it.
It is not a waste of time.
Reading is for life, not just school.

questions.stem: How often should a Basic 4 pupil read independently?
options: Every day or as often as possible
Only when the teacher forces them
hints: Reading regularly builds fluency.
Daily reading is best.
questions.explanation: Pupils should read independently every day or as often as possible to build fluency and a love of reading.
misconceptions: Once a year is not enough.

questions.stem: What should a pupil do if they start reading a book and find it boring?
options: Choose a different book that they enjoy
hints: Reading should be enjoyable.
It's okay to choose another book.
questions.explanation: A pupil should choose a different book they enjoy if they find one boring.
misconceptions: Giving up reading is not necessary.
Reading only the cover is not reading.

questions.stem: Why is it important for a pupil to read a variety of books?
options: It exposes them to different ideas and vocabulary
It is a waste of time
hints: Different books have different topics and words.
Variety helps learning.
questions.explanation: Reading a variety of books exposes pupils to different ideas and vocabulary.
misconceptions: Variety makes reading interesting, not boring.
It is not a waste of time.
It is not only for adults.

questions.stem: What should a summary include?
options: The main ideas and key details of the story
Every single word from the book
Only the names of the characters
hints: A summary is short and focuses on the main points.
It includes important details, not everything.
questions.explanation: A summary includes the main ideas and key details of the story.
misconceptions: Including every word is not a summary.
Only the title is too brief.

questions.stem: Read: 'The story is about a girl named Ama who finds a lost puppy and returns it to its owner.' What is the main idea?
options: Ama finds and returns a lost puppy
hints: The main idea tells what happens in the story.
What is the most important event?
questions.explanation: The main idea is that Ama finds and returns a lost puppy.
misconceptions: The other options are details, not the main idea.

questions.stem: Which detail should be included in a summary of 'The Tortoise and the Birds'?
options: The tortoise tricks the birds and takes their food
The tortoise has a hard shell
hints: A summary includes key events that drive the story.
The trick is the main event.
questions.explanation: The key event is that the tortoise tricks the birds and takes their food.
misconceptions: Shell, feathers and slow walking are details, not key events.

questions.stem: How many paragraphs should a summary have for this task?
hints: The indicator says 'two-paragraph summary'.
It is two paragraphs.
questions.explanation: The task requires a two-paragraph summary.
misconceptions: Three or five are more than required.

questions.stem: What should the first paragraph of a summary contain?
options: The main idea and key events of the story
hints: The first paragraph introduces the story and its main events.
It covers the main idea.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph should contain the main idea and key events.
misconceptions: It should not introduce a new story.
A list is not a paragraph.

questions.stem: What should the second paragraph of a summary contain?
options: The conclusion or resolution of the story
hints: The second paragraph wraps up the summary.
It includes how the story ends.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph should contain the conclusion or resolution of the story.
misconceptions: A new beginning is not a summary.
The title and author are not paragraph content.

questions.stem: Which is the best structure for a two-paragraph summary?
options: Paragraph 1: main idea and key events; Paragraph 2: conclusion and personal reflection
Paragraph 1: all characters; Paragraph 2: all events
hints: A summary should cover the whole story logically.
Paragraph 1 covers the main story; Paragraph 2 wraps it up.
questions.explanation: The best structure is: Paragraph 1 — main idea and key events; Paragraph 2 — conclusion and personal reflection.
misconceptions: Title and author alone are not a summary.
Listing all characters and events is not concise.
